text:
Nora wanted to play outside in the snow. But first she needed her coat. She found it on the hook. It was red and soft like a sheep.

"One arm," said Nora. She pushed her arm in. "Two arms." She pushed the other arm in. Now the coat was on. But the zipper was stuck. Nora pulled it. It would not move. She pulled again, and the zipper made a loud zzzzzip sound. It went up a little! She pulled some more. Zzzzip. The coat closed all the way to her chin. Warm air stayed inside the coat.

Nora ran to the window. Mommy was putting on her boots. "I did it myself!" said Nora. She opened the door and stomped into the snow.

Miles went to the library with his mom. They rode the bus. The bus was not heavy to ride, but his bag felt heavy. Miles wanted to draw a cat on the big tablet.

Miss Amy, the librarian, showed him the little round button. Miles pushed it. The screen lit up. He tapped the drawing app. A white page appeared. Miles drew a cat with orange ears. Then he drew a dog too.

"My picture is gone," he said. He had tapped a red X. Miss Amy showed him the back arrow. He tapped it. His cat came back. "It was hiding," said Miles. He laughed. When he was done, he pushed the button again. The screen went dark. He helped hang the tablet on its charging hook. "All done," he said. "Bye bye, cat."

Thomas wanted to wash his hands. He ran to the bathroom. Daddy came too.

Thomas saw two taps on the sink. He touched the cold tap. Cold water came out. Brrr! His hands felt icy.

Then he reached for the red tap. Daddy put his hand on top. "Let me," said Daddy. Daddy turned the red tap a little. Warm steam floated up. Thomas held his hand near it. Warm, but too hot for a little boy.

"I want to do it," said Thomas. Daddy turned the red tap off. Thomas turned the cold tap himself. He got lots of soap bubbles.

Afterward, Daddy dried Thomas's hands with the rough blue towel. "Don't forget your cookie," said Daddy. Thomas smiled. He ran to the kitchen with clean, warm hands.

Cooper wanted to play with the big red truck. His sister Mia had it first. She pushed it across the floor. Cooper grabbed the truck. Mia began to cry.

Mom came in from the rain. Her umbrella was wet. "Let's try again," she said. She held up the truck. "First Mia. Then Cooper." Mia pushed the truck once. Then she gave it to Cooper. Cooper pushed it far under the table. He gave it back to Mia. The truck went back and forth. Both of them laughed.

Later they drew at the table. There was one blue crayon. Cooper wanted it. Mia held it out to him. "Your turn," she said. Cooper drew a big wet street with puddles. Then he gave the crayon back. Mia drew the rain.

Amelia went to the library with her mother. She found a book about a red fire truck. The cover had words on it. "Those words say fire truck," said her mother. Amelia touched the letters. They were little and black.

She sat on a small green chair. She opened the book. "Start at the front," said her mother. Amelia turned one page. Then another. The fire truck went beep, beep! Amelia made the sound too. A boy nearby laughed.

At the desk, a lady scanned the book. "You can take it home," she said. Amelia hugged it tight.

At home, Amelia read the book four times. Then she put it under her pillow. "It sleeps with me," she said.

But the book had to go back. Other kids wanted to read it too. So on the last day, Amelia waved to the fire truck. "Bye, bye, truck," she said. At the library, she set it on the desk. Then she found a book about a big yellow bus.

Scarlett wanted to help Mom make soup. Mom said, "You can watch from here." Scarlett stood on her special stool, far from the stove. The pot went on the hot stove. Steam rose up. Steam looked soft, like a cloud. Scarlett reached out one finger. Mom caught her hand. "Steam is hot like the pot," Mom said. Scarlett pulled her hand back.

Then Mom gave her a job. "Put this cold spoon in the bowl." The spoon came from the fridge. It felt cool on Scarlett's fingers. She dropped it in the bowl. Clang! Mom poured the soup. The soup was too hot for Scarlett. Mom put the bowl on the windowsill. "We wait," said Mom. "Waiting keeps us safe."

Scarlett waited. She watched the steam go away, little by little. She touched the outside of the bowl. It was warm now, like her bed in the morning. Mom said, "All cool." Scarlett sat by Mom at the table. She took a small sip. It was just right. Mom smiled. Scarlett felt tired and happy. She rolled her spoon in the bowl, round and round.

Livia went to the art gallery with her mama. Big pictures hung on the walls. "I want to paint too," said Livia. "You can," said a kind lady named Rosa. Rosa had a paint table just for kids.

Rosa gave Livia three pots. "This one is red," said Livia. "This one is blue. This one is yellow!" Rosa smiled and nodded.

Livia dipped her brush in red. She made a big red circle. Then she dipped the same brush in blue. She painted next to the circle. "Oh no," said Livia. "The red followed the blue. Now it looks purple!"

Some paint dripped on the floor. A little boy almost stepped in it. "Watch out," said Livia. Rosa wiped the drip with a cloth. The wet cloth came away purple too. Livia laughed at the noise the brush made, swish, swish. She held up her painting for mama to see. "Look! Red and blue made purple!"

Aubrey sat at the dinner table. Her tummy wanted the soup. But the soup was too hot. "Wait a bit," said Mom. Aubrey was lucky. She had five ways to check.

First, her eyes looked. She saw steam rise up. "I see steam," she said. Steam meant hot.

Next, her nose sniffed. She smelled carrots and warm bread. Then her ears listened. She heard the soup go pop, pop. Little bubbles jumped.

Aubrey put one finger near the bowl. Her skin felt the warm air. "Still hot," she said. Mom passed her the bread. "Try this first," said Mom.

Aubrey touched the bread. Warm, not hot. She took a little bite. Her tongue tasted salt and butter. "Yum," she said.

Aubrey counted on her fingers. "Eyes, nose, ears, hands, tongue. Five helpers!"

The steam went away. No more steam. Aubrey touched the bowl. Just right now. She tasted the soup. "Warm and good," she said. Mom smiled and gave her more.

Declan ran to the little window at daycare. Yesterday, he had planted a seed in a cup. Today, the cup sat on the sunny sill. But the dirt looked the same. "Where is my plant?" Declan asked. Miss Rosa smiled. "It is not time yet. The seed sleeps now. It wakes up later." Declan touched the dirt. It was soft and damp. He gave the seed more water from a small cup. The water went down, down, down. Then he stuck a paper sun on the window. "Now the seed has two suns," he said. Miss Rosa laughed. "Come back tomorrow, Declan. Tomorrow will be different." Declan clapped his hands. He would wait. After nap time, he looked again. Still just dirt. But tomorrow was coming, and tomorrow, his plant might peek out.

Charlie wanted to make her own breakfast like a big girl. Daddy put warm toast on her plate. He put the butter dish next to it. Charlie held the butter knife in her hand.

"What does the butter do?" she asked. Daddy said, "Try it and look." Charlie pushed the cold butter. It stayed in a lump. Then she pushed the soft butter on the warm toast. It went smooth and shiny. The warm toast made the butter soft! "One, two, three," said Charlie, counting her strokes. The butter spread out thin, like a blanket on the toast.

Next came the milk. Charlie lifted the jug. It was heavy. The milk splashed over the edge of the cup. "Oh no," said Charlie. She looked at the puddle on the table. She wiped it up with a towel.

Then she tried again, slowly. "One, two, three," she said, counting the cup filling up. The milk stayed inside. Charlie took a bite of her toast. "Look, Daddy! A flower!" she said, pointing at the picture on his mug. Daddy smiled and poured one more cup, just for her.

Emilia went to the store with Dad. She wanted a red balloon for Ben's present. But a boy was at the balloon stand first. He pointed at the red balloon too.

Emilia waited. She held Dad's hand and counted the balloons. There were ten. The man gave the boy the red balloon. Then the man pulled a new red balloon from the deep, deep box. It grew big and round.

The boy looked back at Emilia. He saw her sad face. He walked over with his balloon. "You can have this one," he said. "I will take a blue one." Emilia smiled. "Thank you," she said. "Blue is my next favorite." The man gave the boy a blue balloon. Emilia held her red balloon all the way to the party.

Lydia went to the big game with Dad. They sat with Gran and her friend Tom. Lydia wanted to clap like everyone else.

The crowd began to cheer. Lydia clapped her hands. The claps made a big sound. But then everyone stopped, and her claps were small. "Too little," said Lydia.

Then Tom stood up. He waved his hands high. Lydia stood up too. She waved her hands high. Now the waves were big! Dad waved. Gran waved. One wave, two waves, three waves, all together.

The players looked up. They saw the waving crowd. They smiled and waved back. Lydia skipped in a little circle. Her tummy felt jumpy and happy. "We did that!" she said. Tom laughed and clapped for her. "Lydia wins the waving game," said Gran. Lydia waved one last big wave. The players waved back again.

Maria put on her new hat. She ran to the backyard. "I will find something!" she said.

Her grandma sat on the step. "Stay where I can see you," said Grandma. Maria stayed close. She saw the grill. It was hot. The air above it wiggled. Grandma held a long fork. She did not let Maria touch.

Maria saw a shiny tool on the grass. She reached for it. "Not that one," said Grandma. "It is sharp." Grandma picked it up and put it far away.

Maria touched the cold birdbath instead. The water felt cool on her fingers. She touched her hat. The hat was warm from the sun. "This is warm," said Maria. "The water is cold."

Grandma smiled. "Come sit with me," she said. Maria wiped her wet hands on her dress. She sat by Grandma on the step. They watched a bird hop and drink.

"Stay close," said Grandma. Maria stayed close. The sun went down slow. The bird flew away. "Good night, bird," said Maria, waving her new hat.

Sara went to the library with her dad. She was excited. "Books!" she said.

Sara saw a boy crying by the shelves. His face was sad. He had lost his teddy bear. Sara looked under a table. No bear. She looked by the big chair. There it was! She ran and got it. The boy stopped crying. He smiled a big, happy smile. "Thank you," he told Sara.

Then a big book fell with a loud bang. Sara jumped. She felt scared. She held her dad's hand. Dad gave her a hug. Soon she felt better.

At the desk, a girl was angry. She wanted the last dinosaur book, but it was gone. Sara found a tiger book on the returns cart. The book had a wild tiger with big teeth. "Here," Sara said. The girl's face went soft. She smiled. "A wild tiger!" she said.

Sara picked three books for herself. Dad read them to her on the soft rug. Sara turned the last page and said, "Can we come back tomorrow?"

Alice went to the store with her brother. He was hungry for apples. Mom said, "We need ten apples."

Alice held the bag. Mom put in one apple. Then two apples. Then three. The bag felt a little heavy.

"Can I try?" Alice asked. Mom smiled and gave her an apple. Alice counted, "Four, five, six." The bag got heavier and heavier. Each apple she added made the bag sag down.

"Seven, eight, nine," said her brother. He dropped in an apple too. Alice laughed. "Ten!" she said. The bag was too heavy to lift with one hand.

Mom held the big bag. Alice held her brother's hand. They walked to the apples one more time, because Alice wanted to count again. "One, two, three," she said.

Today was Madeline's birthday. Grandma's house smelled like cake. Big cousins ran by with balloons. Madeline wanted to blow out the candles. But the candles were not on the cake yet.

Grandpa carried the cake out slow. He set it on the table. The candles were not lit. "Wait," said Grandma. She struck one match. One candle lit. Then she touched it to each wick. The little flame made each candle light up, one by one. Madeline watched. One small fire made many candles burn.

"Now sit in your chair," said Daddy. Madeline sat. Everyone began to sing. Her voice felt warm inside. She took a big breath and blew. All the candles went out. Smoke curled up like thin gray ribbons. The candles felt cool when Daddy cut the cake near them.

Madeline got the first slice. It was chocolate, her favorite. Her friend Ben clapped for her. Madeline licked the frosting off her fork and grinned. "Happy birthday, Madeline!" everyone called. She waved her fork like a little flag.

Chloe wanted to help Grandma bake cookies. "First, you must pass the sense test," said Grandma. "Five senses, five body parts. Can you name them?"

Chloe looked around the kitchen. She heard a buzzing sound. It came from the mixer! "Ears hear," said Chloe. "My ears heard the mixer!"

Grandma held up a lemon. "Close your eyes," she said. Chloe sniffed the lemon. Her nose wrinkled. "Yuck! My nose smells it!"

Grandma gave Chloe a crunchy apple slice. Crunch, crunch, crunch. "My mouth tastes," said Chloe, chewing. "And my mouth feels crunchy things too!"

"Now stop," said Grandma. She put the cookies in the oven. "Stay back, it is hot. What do your eyes do?"

"My eyes see the cookies!" said Chloe. She pressed her hands on the warm counter edge. "And my hands feel warm!"

"That is five," said Grandma. "Ears, nose, mouth, eyes, hands. You passed!"

Chloe clapped. "Can I taste the test again tomorrow?"

Henry went to the library today. Yesterday the library had been closed. Henry had felt sad about that. But today the big doors were open.

"Story time is now," said the librarian, Miss Rose. Henry sat down on a soft red mat. He heard a story about a bear who baked a cake. The bear let a rabbit lick the spoon. Henry laughed at that part.

Then Henry found a book with a fire truck. "Can I take it home?" he asked. "Yes," said Miss Rose. "Bring it back tomorrow." Henry hugged the book tight.

"Is tomorrow soon?" Henry asked his mama. "Later," she said. "First we go home. Then we eat lunch. Tomorrow we come back." Henry looked out the window. The sun was up now. Tomorrow the sun would come up again.

At home, Henry put the book by his bed. "Read it now?" he asked. Mama read it two times. Henry patted the last page. "Again tomorrow," he said. Mama smiled and turned off the light.

Emilia held her bear tight. Today she would get a shot! She stood in the line with Mom. A girl ahead cried a little. Emilia's tummy felt weak.

"Will it hurt?" she asked.

"Just a tiny pinch," said Mom. "Then it is done."

The nurse smiled. "Squeeze your bear really hard," she said. Emilia counted, "One, two, three!" She squeezed with all her might. Then the nurse said, "All done!" Emilia looked down. The shot was over! She had not even felt it. Squeezing hard had made the pinch seem tiny.

The nurse put a bandage on Emilia's arm. It had little stars on it. Emilia held up her arm for everyone in the line to see.

"Look at my stars!" she said.

Henry ran to the park. He wanted to find something new. His eyes saw a big red truck. The truck was digging a hole!

Henry listened with his ears. The truck went rumble, rumble. It was very loud. Henry put his hands over his ears. Then the truck stopped digging. The loud sound stopped too. Henry took his hands down. "It talks when it digs!" said Henry.

Henry smelled something with his nose. It was popcorn! Dad said, "We can buy some." Henry touched the warm bag with his fingers. It felt bumpy and warm. Henry took one piece and put it in his mouth. It tasted salty and yummy. A dog ran by. It was a smelly dog, but it was friendly. Henry patted its soft fur.

"Dad, my nose found the popcorn!" said Henry. Dad laughed and gave him one more piece.

Andrew was a shy boy at the lake pool. He held the wall with both hands. "Come kick with me," said Dad. Andrew did not let go.

Dad held Andrew's tummy. "Kick your legs," said Dad. Andrew kicked one foot. Then he kicked the other. Little bubbles popped by his toes. Andrew kicked more. The bubbles popped faster. And then Andrew moved! He moved forward in the water. He kicked and kicked, all the way to Dad's arms.

"I did it!" said Andrew. "You did," said Dad. They tried again. And again. Andrew kicked and moved, slow and steady. Soon his eyes were sleepy. They sat in the sun on a big towel. "Nap time," said Dad. Andrew yawned. He watched the water sparkle, and he closed his eyes.

Hayden went to the library with Mom. He wanted a book about elephants. The library was big and quiet.

He found a shelf with toy books. One book had a red fire truck. One book had a bouncy ball. Then he found a shelf with animal books. A big blue elephant smiled on the cover. "There he is!" Hayden whispered.

He pulled the elephant book out. A whole row of books leaned. They wobbled. "Oh no," said Hayden. He pushed the book back in. The row stood straight again. Books have their own home, just like animals and toys and foods.

He put the book under his arm. It felt a little loose, so he hugged it close. At the desk, the librarian stamped it. "Roar," said Hayden, very softly. The librarian winked and stamped her own hand too.

Chloe wanted toast like a big girl. Daddy made the toast, because the toaster was hot and not for little hands. Then he gave Chloe a dull little knife and soft butter. Chloe pressed the butter on the toast. It made a hole. "Oops," said Chloe. Daddy laughed. "Try little bits." Chloe took little bits. She slid the knife slowly. The butter spread like a soft, warm blanket. "Look at my blanket!" said Chloe. "Very cozy toast," said Daddy. Now Chloe wanted milk in her cup. She held the cup with one hand and the little jug with the other. She poured too fast. Milk ran down the side like a small, stormy river. Daddy wiped it up. "Slow hands," he said. Chloe poured again, very slowly. This time the milk went into the cup, not past it. Not one drop slipped away. Chloe clapped. Then she took a big bite of toast and a big sip of milk. "All by myself," she said, with a milk smile on her face.

Lincoln pulled off his coat at the corner store. On the shelf sat two baskets of apples. One basket had a red sign. One basket had a green sign.

Linlin wanted to buy the basket with more apples. But which one had more? He counted the red basket. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six apples! Then he counted the green basket. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven apples. Seven was more than six.

But wait. What if he counted wrong? He touched the red apples again. This time he started from the other end. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Still six! He smiled a big smile. The last number was six both times. So the green basket really had more.

Lincoln carried the green basket to the counter. "Seven apples, please," he said. The apples smelled sweet, like the inside of a pie.

William was at the festival with Grandma. There was a big long table. Lots of people sat at it. William was hungry. He wanted to eat the warm bread right away.

"Wait," said Grandma. "We say our word first." She put her hands together. So William put his hands together too. He said his word, small and quiet. Nobody heard him. His face felt warm and he looked down at the playground far away.

"Try again, one more time," said Grandma. William took a big breath. He said his word again, loud and clear. The people at the table heard him. They smiled and said it back to him. Then everyone ate the warm bread together. William took a big bite. Grandma gave him a thumbs up. "Again tomorrow?" she asked. William nodded, with bread still in his cheeks.

Blake walked on the nature trail with Gran. She wanted to play a game called Five Senses. But she did not know them all yet.

"Let's find them one by one," said Gran. Blake heard a bird. "That is hearing," she said. "My ears hear it!" Then she smelled a flower. "My nose smells it!" She touched a smooth rock. "My hands feel it!" She looked at a green leaf. "My eyes see it!"

One sense was left. Blake did not know it. Gran poured water from a bottle onto a berry bush. Little drops fell like rain. "Look how neat," said Gran. Blake stuck out her tongue. A drop landed on it. "My tongue tastes water!" she said. "That is the fifth one!" She counted her senses on her fingers, all the way to five.

Anna went to the playground with her red lion toy. The lion wanted to go on the big slide. Anna held him up high. "Slide with me, lion," she said.

A boy was standing at the slide. Anna wanted a turn too. "Can I have a turn, please?" she asked. The boy smiled and moved over. "Yes! You can go first." Anna sat down. Whoosh! Down she went, with the lion in her lap. "Thank you!" she called. "You're welcome," said the boy.

Next Anna wanted to climb the wall. It was too tall for her. "Can you help me, Mama?" she asked. Mama held her hand. Anna climbed up, up, up. From the top, Anna could see the whole playground. It was getting dark in the shade under the big tree.

Anna ran to the sandbox. Oops! She bumped into a girl. The girl dropped her bucket. "Sorry," said Anna. She picked up the bucket and gave it back. "It's okay," said the girl. "Want to make a castle?" Anna put her lion in the sand. "Yes, please!" she said. The lion sat on top of the castle like a king.

The hall was big and noisy. Joshua sat at a long table with Grandma. Outside the window, the sky was cloudy. A dog outside began to bark. "Woof, woof!" said Joshua. Grandma laughed. "That dog is hungry too."

Big bowls of warm rice came to the table. Joshua grabbed his spoon right away. "Wait," said Grandma. "We say our words first." Grandma put her hands together. Joshua put his hands together too. "Thank you for our food," Grandma said slowly. "Thank you for our food," said Joshua.

Then Grandma picked up her spoon. Everyone at the table picked up a spoon. Joshua picked up his spoon too. "You said the words, so we eat!" said Uncle Ben. He took a big bite of rice. Joshua took a big bite too. "Again tomorrow?" asked Joshua. "Again tomorrow," said Grandma, and she winked.

Axel ran into his classroom. Snow was falling outside the window. It made a thick white blanket on the fence.

"Today we sing the counting song," said Miss Kim. "I need ten friends in a line."

Axel jumped up. He loved the counting song. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!

Miss Kim tapped each head. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine." Then she stopped. "We are one short."

Axel looked around. Mia was at the art table. "Mia, come quick!" he called. "We need you!"

Mia ran over and stood next to Axel. Miss Kim tapped her head. "Ten! Now we can sing."

The line sang loud. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Axel clapped at the end.

"Why did we need ten?" Mia asked.

Axel grinned. "Because Miss Kim taps one head for each number. Nine friends, then you!"

Miss Kim laughed. "Let's sing it again," she said. "Ten times fast!"

Bennett buckled into his car seat. "Are we almost there?" he called. "Almost!" said Dad. They were going to get ice cream. Big news! The best news!

Bennett looked out the window. A big truck went by. It was slow. A little red car zoomed past. It was fast. "Go, little car, go!" said Bennett. The sun came in through the glass. The sun made his arm warm. "My arm is hot!" he said. Dad turned the air on. Cool air blew on his face. "Cold air!" said Bennett. He laughed and laughed.

At the ice cream shop, Dad ordered two cones. One cone was big. It was for Dad. One cone was small. It was for Bennett. The ice cream was cold on his tongue. It was yummy, yummy, yummy. Bennett saw the sun shine on Dad's cone. Drip, drip, drip. It melted fast. His little cone stayed cold in the shade. Bennett held his cone up high. "My small one wins!" he called. Dad licked and licked his melting cone. "Yummy anyway," said Dad. Bennett took one big, happy bite.

Michael ran into Grandma's house. Tonight was Hanukkah! He wanted to see the candles.

Grandpa set the menorah on the table. Michael gave it a good spot near the window. Then Grandpa struck the match. Michael stayed back, just like Grandma said.

The flame touched the first wick. It lit up! The flame touched the second wick. That one lit too. But the last candle did not light. It was crooked. Its wick was too far away.

"The candle is crooked," said Michael. "The flame can't reach it!"

Grandpa pushed the candle straight. Then the flame touched the wick. Bright!

Michael clapped. All the candles shone now. The family sang songs. Michael sang loud. He spun the dreidel and won.

After, the dog, Grandma's pet, flopped by his feet. Michael was sleepy. He watched the candles glow and glow.

"Good night, candles," he whispered.

Grandma was coming to stay for a week. Violet wanted her room to feel like home. But Grandma looked sad at the table. "I miss my tea at my own house," Grandma said. Dad said, "I will make tea now." Violet watched Dad fill the kettle. Dad held the hot cup and set it down. "Careful, it is hot," Dad said. Violet stayed back.

Then the window turned white with fog. The hot tea made the glass fog up. Violet touched it with one finger. She drew a big round sheep. The fog held the shape. "That is funny," said Grandma. Grandma drew a little lamb next to it. Violet drew grass under the sheep. Grandma laughed and laughed. "My kitchen at home has a foggy window too," Grandma said. All week, they drew a new sheep every morning. On the last day, the whole window was full of sheep. Grandma hugged Violet tight. "Same time tomorrow," Grandma said, and tapped the glass.

Andrew went to the park with his dad. He wanted to slide down the big slide. He held his dad's hand all the way there.

Near the slide, Andrew saw a metal grill. It was hot. Dad said, "Stand back, buddy." Andrew saw steam rise from it. He felt warm air on his face, even from far away. He put his hands behind his back and watched.

A small dog ran by with a shiny can in its mouth. Andrew wanted to grab it. The can had sharp edges. Dad knelt down and said, "That could cut you. Let it be." Andrew nodded. He kept walking.

Then he reached the slide. He climbed up, up, up. He sat down and let go. Whee! He slid down fast and landed on the snowy cold ground. "Brrr!" said Andrew. Dad laughed and held out his mittens.

"One more time?" asked Andrew. "You got it," said Dad.

Blake went to the library with her dad. She saw a new puzzle on the low table. It had a picture of a blue lake with ducks on it. A boy named Sam was already playing with it.

Blake wanted the puzzle too. She grabbed a duck piece. Sam held on tight. The piece would not move at all.

"Can we both play?" Blake asked.

"Yes," said Sam. "You do the sky. I do the lake."

Blake put in the sky pieces. Sam put in the ducks. Then they traded, and Blake got the ducks. The puzzle got bigger and bigger. When it was done, the whole lake shone blue.

"We win!" said Sam. Blake clapped her hands.

Then Blake picked up a book about ducks. She sat down next to Sam on the little carpet. "Do you want to look too?" she asked.

"Yes, please," said Sam. They turned the pages together, one at a time.

Iris wanted to wear her red shoe. But it was not on her feet. It was not by the door. "Where did it go?" she asked. "Yesterday you wore it in the jam," said Mom. "It got sticky." So Mom washed the shoe. Then she set it on the shelf to dry.

"Now we wait," said Mom. Iris touched the shoe. It was still wet. "Not now," said Mom. "Later it will be dry." Iris looked at her toes. They wiggled in the dark. She wiggled them again. "My toes tickle me," she said. Mom laughed.

Iris put on her slippers. She brushed her teeth. She picked two books, not three. Mom read them slow. Then Iris looked at the shelf one more time. The shoe sat there, quiet and wet.

"In the morning it will be dry," said Mom. "Tomorrow you can wear it." Iris got in bed. She pulled the blanket up high. Tomorrow felt like a long way off. But tomorrow would come after sleep. Iris closed her eyes. She thought about her red shoe, waiting on the shelf. "Goodnight, shoe," she whispered. "See you tomorrow."

Aiden ran to the park with his red balloon. The sun did shine on the big slide. Aiden felt excited. He held the balloon string tight.

A little girl was on the swing. She looked sad. Her ice cream had dropped on the ground. Aiden watched the ice cream drip down. The girl began to cry. Aiden felt sad too.

Then a big dog ran by. The dog jumped up. Its nose hit the balloon. Pop! The balloon was gone. Aiden felt angry. He stamped his foot. Then he felt a little scared, because the dog was big.

But the dog licked his hand. It was a friendly dog. Aiden laughed and patted its soft ears. The sad girl came over. She laughed too. The dog's tail wagged far and wide. Aiden felt happy again.

The girl's mom gave them each a new ice cream. The three friends sat on the warm bench. The dog rested at their feet. "Good dog," said Aiden, and the dog wagged some more.

Brielle stood in the reading corner. It had a soft red rug and a shelf full of books. She wiggled her toe in her sock and smiled.

"Today you get your own library card," said Mom. "Then you can pick a book."

Brielle picked a book about a big yellow truck. The librarian put the book in a bag. "You can take it home," she said. "Bring it back in one week."

"One week is very long," said Brielle. "I want to keep the truck book forever."

Mom shook her head. "The book belongs here. Other kids want to read it too."

Brielle held the bag tight. She did not want to let it go. Then she saw a boy by the shelf. He was looking for a truck book. There were no more truck books on the shelf.

Brielle looked at her bag. Then she looked at the boy. She gave the book to the librarian. "He can have it first," she said.

The boy smiled big. "Thank you," he said.

The librarian stamped a paper. "You can have it after him," she told Brielle. Brielle put the paper in her pocket.

"Can we come back next week?" she asked Mom.

"Yes," said Mom. "And we will read it two times."

Beatrice went to Grandma's house in the morning. Grandma had a big piano in the front room. Beatrice wanted to play a song all by herself.

She pressed one key. It made a low sound, boom. She pressed another key. It made a high sound, ding. One key, one sound. Two keys, two sounds.

"Grandma, can I make three sounds?" asked Beatrice. Grandma smiled. "Press three keys, one by one." Beatrice pressed one, two, three. Ding, ding, boom! The sleepy cat sat up and opened her eyes.

Beatrice played the keys fast. The cat's tail began to swish. Beatrice played the keys slow. The cat's tail went still and soft. Fast keys made the tail fly up. Slow keys made the tail rest down.

Beatrice laughed. She played a slow song for the sleepy cat. The cat walked over and curled up on the piano bench. "Good morning, cat," said Beatrice. She played one more soft key, ding.

Oliver sat at the picnic table at camp. He was making a lion mask from a paper plate. Miss Ana had cut two holes for eyes. Oliver painted the plate yellow with a big brush.

Then he wanted to add an orange mane. He squeezed lots of glue around the edge. He stuck on orange paper strips one by one. But the glue was wet and shiny. A strip slid off the plate and onto the table.

"Why does my mane keep falling off?" Oliver asked. Miss Ana smiled. "The glue is still wet. Wet glue is slippery. It cannot hold the paper yet."

So Oliver put the strips back. He pressed each one with his palm. Then Miss Ana carried the mask to a sunny bench. "The sun will help," she said. Oliver watched. The glue went from shiny to dull. Soon it was dry. Dry glue held the strips tight.

Oliver picked up the mask. He pulled one strip gently. It did not move. "My mane is stuck on!" he said. He put the mask on his face. He gave a big roar. Then his friend Mia came over, holding a plain white plate. She looked sad. Her paint had spilled.

Oliver ran to the craft box. He came back with his yellow paint pot. "You can share mine," he said. Mia dipped her brush. She painted a sun on her plate. Then she pointed at Oliver. "Roar again," she said. Oliver lifted his lion head and roared.

Lily sat at Grandma's big table. She wanted to write her name all by herself. Grandma put a pencil in her hand. But Lily held it way up high. The pencil slipped. Her lines came out wiggly and light. "That is not my name," said Lily.

Grandma showed her how to pinch the pencil down low, near the point. Lily tried it. She pressed down. The pencil did not slip. A dark line stuck to the paper and stayed there. "It stays!" said Lily. She made a big L. Then an i with a dot. Then l and y. There it was. L-I-L-Y.

Lily held up the paper. "Look, Grandma! My name!" Grandma clapped. "Can I write it again?" Lily asked, pulling a fresh sheet from the empty tray. Outside, a car went by on the street, but Lily did not look up. She was busy making letters.

Matteo wanted to help bake bread at daycare. Miss Ana said, "You can help mix." Matteo touched the dough with his fingers. It was soft and squishy. He poked it. It made a little dent. Then the dent went away. How did that happen? The dough was stretchy, so it came back.

Miss Ana let Matteo smell the flour. It smelled like nothing much. But soon the bread went into the big oven. Miss Ana put it in, because the oven could burn little hands. Matteo stayed back and watched. Then a warm smell filled the room. Matteo sniffed with his nose. "What is that smell?" he asked. "It is our bread," said Miss Ana. Could a smell tell him something? Yes, it could.

The bell went ding. Matteo heard it with his ears. The bread was ready. Miss Ana cut one short piece for each child. Matteo tasted his piece. It was warm and good on his tongue. Outside, they ate snack on a small hill of grass. The bread was gone, but the smell still sat in Matteo's nose. "Again tomorrow?" he asked. "Again tomorrow," said Miss Ana, and she held up the empty bowl.

Henri woke up early. The sun made a bright triangle on his wall. Today was his first day of school. He did not want to go. He hid his shoe under the bed.

"Where is your shoe?" Mama asked. Henri pointed at the cat. "The cat chased it," he said. Mama looked under the bed. She found the shoe. "Let's put it on," she said.

Henri stamped his feet. His shoes made a happy sound. Stomp, stomp, stomp. Then the cat ran to him. The cat liked the sound too. The cat chased Henri's feet all the way to the door. Henri laughed.

Mama held his hand. They walked to school. The cat sat on the step and waved its tail.

At school, Henri saw a big rug. It had red triangles on it. He sat down on a red triangle. A boy next to him smiled. "I like your shoes," the boy said.

Henri looked at his shoes. They still made a happy sound. He stomped one foot, soft and small. The boy stomped too.

"Henri, time for juice," the teacher said. Henri ran to the table. He was wide awake now. "Mama will come back," the teacher said. "After juice and songs."

Henri drank his juice. He sang the songs. Then the door opened. It was Mama. Henri ran fast. "I stomped and made a friend," he said.

Josephine went to the park with her grandma. She wanted to find a duck to feed. She held grandma's hand the whole way. Stay close, stay close, that was their game.

Near the pond, Josephine saw a grill. It was smoking. A kind man was cooking corn on it. "Is it fire?" Josephine asked. "Yes, a little fire," said grandma. "Fire is hot. We look with our eyes only." Josephine looked and looked. The man turned the corn with a long stick. He did not touch the fire with his hands.

Then Josephine saw a shiny thing in the grass. It was a broken bottle. She reached out her hand. Grandma caught her fingers right away. "Not that one," grandma said. "Sharp things can hurt you." The man in a green vest came and picked it up with a glove. He put it in a bag.

"Why is the corn so puffy?" Josephine wondered. The man smiled. He gave one warm ear to grandma, and grandma held it with her sleeve. Grandma blew on it, once and twice. Then Josephine took a little bite. It was hot, then just right. "More corn, please!" Josephine begged. Grandma laughed and said, "One more, and then we find the ducks."

Sara stood by the farm gate with a little bag of seeds. She wanted her own vegetable garden. Grandpa gave her a small patch of dirt near the fence.

Sara dug a little hole. She dropped a seed in. She poured water on top. The water began to sink into the dirt. "Where did it go?" Sara asked. "Down into the ground," said Grandpa. "The seed drinks it."

Sara came back each day. She watered her seeds again and again. The water would sink, sink, sink. Then one morning, Sara saw a green sprout. "Grandpa, look!" she called. "My seed woke up!" Grandpa smiled. "Water it some more," he said. Sara poured the water slowly. A pretty butterfly landed on the fence to watch. "Grow, little plant, grow," said Sara. The sprout stood up tall in the sun.

Harrison stood on the balcony with Daddy. He held a small pot of dirt. "I want a big garden," he said.

"We can plant three seeds," said Daddy. "One, two, three." Harrison pushed the seeds into the dirt. He patted the soil until it was smooth. Then he watered the pot. Every morning he ran to look. Nothing came up. "Where are my seeds?" he asked.

"Rain makes plants grow," said Daddy. "We can give them rain from the tap." So they watered the pot every day. Soon a tiny green tip peeked out. Harrison pointed at it. "It came up!" he said. More tips came, one, two, three. Daddy helped him write the letter H on the pot. Harrison smiled and gave the little plants one more drink of water.

Claire went to Grandma's house. She wanted a house of her own. But Grandma had no little play house. Claire felt sad. Grandma smiled and said, "Look what a blanket can do." Grandma hung a big blanket over two chairs. It made a roof. Claire crawled under it. Now she had a house. Claire put her bear inside too. She wrapped Bear in a small towel. Bear closed his eyes and went to sleep, just like that. Claire patted Bear softly. She sang him a little song. Then she heard a sound outside her blanket house. It went tweet, tweet. Claire peeked out. A bird was on the window. It began to fly in big circles. "Grandma, come see!" said Claire. Grandma came and sat down next to her. They watched the bird together until the last circle, and then the bird flew away.

Victor wanted to paint a fire truck at school. But the red paint pot was empty. He needed help.

He walked to his teacher. "Can you help me, please?" he asked. Miss Amy smiled. "Yes, I can help you." She opened a big bottle. She began to pour red paint into the pot. Drip, drip, drip. The paint looked like a shiny red river.

Victor sat down to paint. He made a big red fire truck. Then his elbow bumped the water cup. Splash! Water ran across the table and onto Ben's paper. Victor felt his tummy go tight. "I am sorry, Ben," he said. Ben looked at his wet paper. Then he said, "That is okay. Can you help me dry it?" Victor ran to get paper towels. They patted the paper together. Pat, pat, pat. Soon it was dry.

Ben shared his crayons with Victor. "Thank you," said Victor. "Thank you," said Ben. By lunch time Victor was very sleepy. He yawned a big yawn. Miss Amy put his painting on the wall to dry. "Look at your fire truck," she said. Victor looked up and smiled.

Brooklyn went to the bookshop with her dad. She wanted to find a book about cats. "Where do we look?" she asked. Dad said, "Let's look at the letters."

They found a big sign with letters on it. Brooklyn pointed at the first one. "That is B," she said. Dad made the sound. "Buh, buh, B," he said. Brooklyn laughed. "B is for Brooklyn!"

Then something funny happened. Dad said, "Buh, buh." And Brooklyn heard a word. "Book!" she said. "Book starts with B!" Dad clapped. "Yes! The letter B makes the buh sound. So book begins with B."

Brooklyn looked around the shop. What else started with B? She saw a shelf of books. She saw a bear on a cover. "Bear!" she said. "Buh, buh, bear!" A friendly shop lady walked over. "Would you like a cat book?" she asked. Brooklyn thought hard. "Cuh, cuh," she said slowly. "Cat starts with C!"

The lady took Brooklyn to the C shelf. There it was. A little book with a cat on the front. Brooklyn hugged it tight. "Can we spell my name at home?" she asked Dad. Dad smiled. "We can spell it after dinner."

At home, Brooklyn turned to the last page. There was a mirror on it. In the mirror, she saw a girl holding a cat book. Under the mirror were five letters. Brooklyn pointed at each one. "B," she said. "R. O. O. K." She stopped at the last letter. "That one is N!" she shouted. "N is for Nyah!" The cat on the cover seemed to wink at her, and Brooklyn winked right back.

Joshua's dog Ruff was barking at the door. Ruff's tail wagged and wagged. Joshua felt happy inside. "Grandpa is here!" Dad opened the door. Grandpa held a big red box. Joshua jumped up and down. He felt so excited. "Is that for me?" he asked. "It is," said Grandpa.

Joshua pulled at the ribbon. It would not open. He pulled harder. Then he felt angry. His face got hot. He threw the ribbon on the floor. "It won't open!" he shouted.

Grandpa sat down next to him. "Let's try together," he said. Grandpa held the box. Joshua tugged the ribbon with his teeth. It slipped loose! The box opened. Inside was a cool blue fire truck with a long ladder.

Just then Ruff barked very loud. A clap of thunder boomed outside. Joshua grabbed Grandpa's hand. His tummy felt tight and scared.

The rain came. Joshua could not play outside. A little tear rolled down his cheek. He felt sad.

Grandpa patted the rug. "Trucks can drive in here," he said. Joshua pushed the fire truck across the floor. It went fast. Ruff chased the wheels and barked. Joshua laughed and laughed. The rain tapped on the window, and the ladder clicked up, up, up.

Margot sat at the little red table. The tablet lay there, dark and still. She wanted to draw a snowman, but the screen showed nothing. She pressed the edge. Nothing happened. She pressed the back. Still nothing.

"Where is the picture?" Margot asked. Her teacher sat beside her. "Try the round button," she said. Margot found the round button. She pushed it. The screen woke up. It was bright and full of colors. Margot clapped her hands.

She tapped the blue crayon icon. The drawing app opened. She drew a big snowman with a winter hat. Then the teacher said it was time for snack. Margot pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She slid the tablet into its soft gray bag. "I can do it all by myself," she said, and smiled at the bag on the shelf.

Isaac was in the family car. His toy bunny was gone. "Where did Bunny go?" he asked. He wanted Bunny right now.

Isaac looked under the seat. He looked by his feet. He looked out the window. No Bunny. He turned and turned in his seat. Now his head felt dizzy. "Too much turning," said Dad. Dad pulled the car over. "Let's look together."

The sun was bright. Dad opened the back door. The sun shone inside. And there was a flash of white on the floor. The sunlight had touched something soft. It was Bunny! The sun showed Isaac right where to look.

"Bunny!" Isaac grabbed him fast. He hugged Bunny tight. Dad shut the door and got in. "Home we go," said Dad. "We can have a snack in the kitchen." Isaac held Bunny up to the window. "Look, Bunny, the sun!" he said. The sun made Bunny's ear glow.

Gabriella sat on the small red rug. Miss Ada, her music teacher, sat by the piano. "Today we will clap and sing," said Miss Ada. "Watch me first."

Miss Ada played a song. She clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. The claps sat right on the beat, like feet walking. Gabriella tried. Her claps went too fast. Then they went too slow. "I can't do it," she said. Her lip wobbled.

"Watch my hands," said Miss Ada. "Clap when my hands come together." Gabriella looked and looked. She clapped when the hands met. Clap, clap, clap. Her claps matched the piano. Then she sang, "Baa, baa, black sheep, have you any wool?" All by herself, with no words on the wall.

At home, Mama let her see a small toy sheep on the shelf. Gabriella clapped and sang the whole rhyme again. "More," she said, and clapped her hands.

Wesley was a small boy in a big forest. He found a soft, round pinecone on the ground. He picked it up. "You are my baby," he said. The pinecone had a scratch on one side. "You need a bandage," Wesley said. He wrapped it in a green leaf. The pinecone looked cozy now. Wesley wanted to make a house for it. He put two sticks in the moss. He laid more sticks across the top. The sticks made a little roof. The pinecone fit under it just right. "Now you have a bed," Wesley said. A chipmunk ran by and stopped. Wesley had an idea. He held the leaf up like a blanket. "Time for night-night," he whispered. He patted the pinecone gently. Then he carried his baby home to show Daddy. "Look, I am the daddy now," Wesley said.

Hazel wants a book about a chicken. She walks to the big shelf. The shelf is too tall. The chicken book sits up high.

Hazel tries to reach it. She stands on her toes. Her fingers touch nothing. A boy is sitting on the floor. She bumps his tower of books. Crash! The books fall down.

"Sorry," Hazel says. The boy nods. He stacks them again. Hazel helps. She hands him each fresh book from the pile.

Then Hazel sees a lady at the desk. She tugs her mom's hand. Mom walks with her. "Please, can you help?" Hazel asks the lady. The lady smiles. She reaches up. She gets the chicken book down.

"Thank you," says Hazel. The book feels smooth. It smells like paper. The boy waves at her from his swing of a chair. Hazel sits by her mom. She opens the book. "Cluck, cluck," says the chicken on page one.

Logan stood at the big library desk. He wanted a book about trucks. But first he needed a card. The librarian typed his name. Then she handed him a small blue card. "Now you can borrow books," she said. Logan held the card with both hands.

He found a truck book on a low shelf. He sat on the floor to look at it. His sock was loose, so he pulled it up over his knee. The pages showed a big red dump truck. Logan wanted to keep it forever.

The librarian stamped a paper inside the book. "Bring it back next week," she said. "Then other kids can read it too." Logan hugged the book tight. "I can bring it back," he said. At home, his mom read it three times. Logan turned the last page himself and said, "Thank you, truck book. See you next week."

Stella loved the little play kitchen at school. But today it was empty. No pots. No cups. Where did they go? Ben had taken them to the sand table.

"I need a pot for my soup," Stella said.

Then she saw a big wooden block on the shelf. It was round and fat. "Hello, pot!" she said. She put the block on the toy stove.

Next she needed a baby to feed. She found a sock with a button eye. "Hello, baby!" she said. She wrapped the sock in a small towel.

The baby needed a bed. Stella turned a basket upside down. The basket was soft inside. She laid the sock baby down.

"I am so lucky," said Stella. "This is the best house ever."

Then Stella scratched her chin, like a mama thinking. "Is the soup ready?" she asked. She looked at the block. "Yes it is!" she said. "Time to eat."

Stella picked up the block pot and fed her sock baby first.

Dylan wanted warm milk before bed. He ran to the kitchen. Mama was at the stove. The pot went hiss, hiss, hiss. Steam rose up like a little cloud.

Dylan reached out his hand. "Stop," Mama said. She caught his fingers. "That pot is hot." She turned on the cold tap. Cold water ran over her own hand. Then she touched the pot holder. "See? The cloth keeps my hands safe."

Dylan touched the pot holder too. It was soft and cool. He put a safe step back from the stove. "Can I help?" he asked. "Yes," said Mama. She poured the warm milk into his cup. Dylan held the cup with both hands. It was warm, not hot. He drank it all up.

Then he wanted his crunchy crackers. But the crackers were high up. He looked at the tall shelf. He did not climb. "Mama, please," he said. She smiled and got them down. Dylan stayed close to her feet. He munched his crackers. "Bed soon," said Mama. Dylan gave her a big hug. She held him all the way to his room.

Emily was at Grandma's house. On the table was a big red book. "Whose book?" asked Emily. "It is a library book," said Grandma. "We can take it home. But we must bring it back by Saturday. Then other people can read it too."

Emily sat on the soft rug. She held the book. She opened the front cover first. Grandma turned the pages from front to back. On each page were little marks. "Those marks are words," said Grandma. "Words tell the story." Emily touched the marks with one finger. The words said bear, and there was the bear! Emily turned more pages. Front to back, front to back.

Then Emily hugged the book to her neck. "I want to keep it forever," she said. "It is mine." Grandma sat down beside her. "Saturday is coming," she said softly. "The book must go back. Then we can borrow a new one."

Emily felt her eyes go hot. A tear did not fall, but her throat hurt a little. Then Grandma said, "You can pick the next book. Any one you like." Emily looked at the red book. It was slimy where the dog had licked it, so Grandma wiped it clean.

On Saturday, Emily held the book all the way to the library. She gave it to the lady at the desk. Then Emily ran to the shelves. She found a blue book with a duck on it. She opened the front cover first. "Words," said Emily, and turned the pages, front to back. "This one comes home with us. Then it goes back too."

Zoey stood in the garage. Dad had a big drum there. It sat on a box made of wood. "Can I play it?" she asked. "You need soft taps first," said Dad.

Zoey tapped the drum. It went boom. She tapped harder. It went BOOM BOOM. Her dog Max ran under the workbench. "Too loud for Max," said Dad. "He needs quiet ears."

Zoey looked at Max. She tapped very soft. Pum. Pum. Max came out. He sat down near her feet. Zoey tapped soft again. Max wagged his tail. "You like this song," she said. She tapped slow and soft. Pum. Pum. Pum.

Max put his head on her shoe. Dad picked up a little drum too. "May I join?" he asked. Zoey smiled. They played together, soft and slow. Max closed his eyes.

Georgia sat with Grandpa in the big chair. The game was on TV. Everyone wore striped shirts, blue and white. Mama wore one too.

Georgia wanted to cheer like the big people. They clapped and yelled when the team ran. But Georgia clapped too early. The room went quiet. Her hands clapped all alone.

"Watch the ball," Grandpa said. So Georgia watched the ball. The ball went this way. Then that way. Then it went through the net. The people on TV jumped up. Then everyone in the room jumped up too.

Georgia waited. She watched the ball again. It ran and ran. Then it went through the net. The people on TV jumped up. Georgia clapped her hands. Everyone clapped too. Mama picked her up. "You cheered at the right time!" said Mama.

Georgia watched some more. The night got dark outside the window. The ball went through the net one more time. Georgia clapped and clapped.

"Again!" said Georgia.

Sienna stood at the school gate. The playground was big and loud. She held her new red cup of bubble soap. "Can I try?" she asked her teacher.

"First dip the wand in," said Miss Ana. "Then blow slow air through the hole." Sienna dipped the wand. It came out wet and shiny. She blew too hard. The soap flew off. No bubble came. She tried again. This time she blew slow, thin air, like a tiny sigh. A round bubble grew. It got bigger and bigger.

"Look! I made it!" said Sienna. The bubble floated up. A boy named Theo ran to see it. It popped on the slide with a little sound. Theo laughed. "Do it again!" he said. Sienna dipped the wand. She blew slow air once more. Two bubbles went up this time, side by side, one small and one big. Theo clapped his hands.

"My turn next," said Theo. Sienna gave him the wand. "Blow slow," she said. "Like this."

Adam wants to help at snack time. "Can I put out the cups?" he asks. Ms. Rosa smiles. "Yes. But how many cups do we need?" Adam looks at the rug. He counts his friends. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." He runs to the shelf. He takes cups, one by one. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven cups for seven friends. Each friend gets a cup. Nobody is left out. A small green leaf fell off the plant. Adam picks it up. He puts it back in the pot. Then Ms. Rosa brings apple slices. They smell fresh. Adam takes a big bite. Crunch! Then they sing the counting song together, all the way to ten. "Ten!" shouts Adam, clapping his hands.

Rehmat wanted to find her cat, Milo. He was hiding in the backyard. She called him. "Milo! Milo!" No cat came.

Rehmat looked with her eyes. She saw the big mountain of leaves by the fence. She touched the leaves with her hands. They were soft and a little wet. No Milo there.

Then her ears heard a sound. It was a tiny "meow." It came from the shiny red wagon! Rehmat ran to the wagon. She peeked in with her eyes. There was Milo, curled up and sleeping.

Rehmat smelled something good. Dad was cooking fish on the grill, far away. He waved. "Almost done," he said. Milo woke up. He smelled the fish too. He jumped out of the wagon and ran to Dad.

Milo sat by Dad's feet. He licked his lips with his tongue. Rehmat gave him a tiny taste of fish in his bowl, after Dad said it was cool. Milo ate it all up. Then he rubbed his soft head on Rehmat's hand.

Colton went to the grocery store with Mama. He held his soft bunny in his arms. Then Colton saw the big apples. He let go of bunny to touch one apple. Round apples rolled down the pile. When the apples rolled, Colton saw something gray underneath. It was soft. It was bunny!

"Bunny, there you are!" said Colton.

A teacher from Colton's school was there too. She helped pick up the apples. "The apples rolled away when you pulled one," she said with a smile. Colton put the apples back on the pile, one by one.

"Thank you," said the apple man. He gave Colton a thick paper bag. Colton drew on the bag with his crayon while Mama paid. He drew a picture of bunny sitting on the apples.

Mama picked Colton up for a hug. "You found bunny all by yourself," she said.

Colton hugged bunny tight. "No more rolling, apples," he said.

Brielle stood in the nursery room. There was a new little bed. There was a new little blanket. A baby was in the little bed. It was her new baby brother.

Brielle wanted the baby to look at her. She waved her hand. The baby did not look. She made a soft sound. "Ooo," said Brielle. The baby still did not look. She waited. Then she tried again.

Mommy held the baby up. "Say hello," said Mommy. Brielle clapped her hands, very soft. Clap, clap. The baby turned his head. His eyes found Brielle. He made a small smile. "He looked at me!" said Brielle. "He is so cute." The sun came in the window. It made a warm spot on the blanket. The baby blinked at the light. "Hello, baby brother," said Brielle. She clapped again, one more time, very soft. Clap.

Bennett wanted to help Dad cook outside. Dad had the grill in the backyard. "Can I do a job?" Bennett asked. "Yes," said Dad. "You can carry the cold buns."

Bennett picked up the bun bag. It felt cool and soft in his hands. The grill was hot. Dad said, "Stay back from the grill." Bennett saw the grill puff out smoke. The smoke made the air wiggle. He took one big step away.

Then Bennett saw a tall stick on the ground near the grill. He reached for it. "Stop," said Dad. "Sticks stay out of the fire." Dad picked up the stick himself. He put it in a bucket of water. The water made a hiss. Bennett held his buns tight. "Buns going on now," said Dad. He opened the grill and laid them in. Bennett stayed close and watched the smoke curl up. "Now we wait," said Dad. "I can wait," said Bennett.

Peyton sat at the math club table. There were two plates of cookies. She wanted the plate with more cookies. But which one had more?

Miss Joy said, "Count them, Peyton."

Peyton picked a cookie from the red plate. She counted, "One, two, three, four, five." Five cookies!

Her friend Ben said, "Count again, but start from the other end!"

Peyton giggled. She turned the plate around. She counted, "One, two, three, four, five."

"Five again!" she said. "The last number is the same!"

Now she counted the blue plate. "One, two, three, four." Four cookies.

"Five is more than four," said Peyton. She picked up the sweet red plate. "I pick this one!"

Ben laughed. "You counted it two ways, Peyton."

Peyton bit her cookie. "Mmm," she said. "Cookies taste the same from both ends too."

Leo went to the park with his dad. Leo held his dad's hand. "Stay close," said Dad. Leo wanted to see the ducks.

Leo ran ahead. Dad was far away. Leo looked back. He could not see his dad. He stopped and stood still.

Then he heard his dad call, "Leo!" Dad came close and took his hand. Leo held on tight. Now they could see the ducks together.

Near the ducks was a big grill. A man was cooking corn. Leo saw smoke rise up. The grill looked red and hot. Leo reached out his hand.

Dad caught it right away. "That is hot," said Dad. Dad put his own hand near the air above the grill. Dad pulled it back fast. "Ooh, hot!" said Dad.

Leo put his hand near the air too, far away. He felt warm air on his fingers. Leo pulled his hand back fast, just like Dad. "Hot!" said Leo.

They sat on a rough log. Leo kicked a little stone. It rolled into the grass. Dad gave Leo a cold juice box from the bag. It felt cool in Leo's hands. Leo drank it all up. His tummy felt happy.

"Want more corn?" asked Dad. The man at the grill handed Dad a hot corn stick with a glove. Dad blew on it. Then Leo touched the corn. It was warm, not hot. Leo took a big bite.

"Yum," said Leo. He held his dad's hand all the way home.

Amira stands at the little table. Today she will make bread for her family. The teacher pours flour into the bowl. Amira stirs it with a big spoon. The flour is dry and crumbly. It will not stick. It falls apart in her hands. Amira wants a ball of dough, but she only has a messy pile.

The teacher gives her a cup of milk. Amira pours it in, little by little. She stirs and stirs. Now the flour sticks together. The milk makes the crumbs turn into one soft ball. Amira knows just what to do. She pushes the dough flat with her hands. "Look," she says. "I made it stick!"

She cuts out little sheep shapes with a round cutter. The sheep look so nice with their curly edges. The teacher puts the tray in the hot oven. Amira waits at the safe table. Soon the smell fills the room. Mommy comes in and smiles. "Is one of these sheep for me?" she asks. Amira holds up the biggest one and says, "This sheep is for you, Mommy."

Sebastian went to the library with his mom. Craft day was at the big table. The librarian, Miss Jo, put out paper, glue, and paint.

"One brush, two brushes, three brushes," said Miss Jo. "Pick one to paint with."

Sebastian picked the biggest brush. He wanted to paint a blue dog. He dipped the brush in water. Then he dug the brush into the blue paint. He pulled it across the paper. The line came out thin and pale. The blue was light, like the sky.

He looked at his friend Maya's paper. Her red was dark and bright. Sebastian watched her brush. It was dry. His brush was dripping wet.

So he tried it his way. He dug his brush into the paint with no water at all. The paint was smooth and thick. He pulled it across the paper. Now his blue was dark, like the night sky. The wet brush had made the blue pale. The dry brush made it dark.

Sebastian painted the dog blue, blue, blue. Then he added one ear, two ears, and one waggy tail.

Miss Jo held it up. "A blue dog!" she said.

"He looks like a kitchen mop," said Sebastian.

Everyone laughed softly. Sebastian smiled and painted one more dog, dark blue all over.

Jules sat at the dinner table. His tummy made a hungry sound. "When is the spaghetti coming?" he asked. "Soon," said Dad. Jules was so excited. He kicked his feet under the table.

Then the big pot went clank on the stove. Dad stirred it. Steam went up, up, up. Jules felt happy. But then his tooth hurt a little. He touched it with his tongue. His loose tooth was wiggly. "Ow," he said. His face went sad.

Mom sat near him. "Is your tooth bothering you?" she asked. "A little," said Jules. Then the dog barked loud. Jules jumped. He felt scared for a second. "It is just the doorbell," said Mom. It was Grandma! Jules felt so happy again. But his brother grabbed his cup, and Jules felt angry. He made a big frown.

"Here," said Grandma. She gave him a soft bread roll. The bread was soft, so his tooth did not hurt. Dad set down the spaghetti. It smelled warm and good. Jules took one bite and smiled. "Can we eat like this every night?" he asked. Grandma laughed. "Yes, every night, my love."

Levi wanted to paint a dragon egg. He looked at the paint pots. "Red, yellow, blue," he said, tapping each one. "Red, yellow, blue." But there was no green pot. His dragon egg needed green, because dragons sleep in green nests.

Miss Ana got him a brush. Levi dipped it in blue. He painted a thin stripe on his egg. Then he dipped the brush in yellow. He swirled it on the blue stripe. The colours squished together. The stripe turned green! Levi blinked. He looked at his brush.

"It made a new colour," he whispered. He mixed red and yellow too. That made orange, like a little sunset. He finished the egg with green and orange stripes.

Miss Ana held it up. "A real dragon egg," she said.

Levi smiled. "Now it will hatch."

Noah waited at the train station. His grandpa was coming to stay for a week. The train was late. Noah held up his sign. It said "Grandpa" in big red letters.

Then the train came in. It made a big wind. The wind blew the sign right out of Noah's hands. "Oh no!" said Noah. The paper flew down the platform. It went too far to reach.

Grandpa stepped off the train. "Where is your sign?" he asked. "The train blew it away," said Noah. He felt sad. Grandpa smiled. "Let's make a new one," he said. "We can make it at home."

At home, Mom helped them paint. Noah painted the word "Grandpa" again. Then he put beans in a bowl. He set the new sign in the bowl. "Now it can't blow away," he said. Grandpa tested it. He blew as hard as he could. The sign wobbled. But it did not fall.

The next week, they went back to the station. Grandpa held the bowl and the sign. "Read it to me," said Grandpa. Noah pointed at each letter. "G-R-A-N-D-P-A!" he said. Grandpa hugged him tight.

Everett ran to the swing at the playground. The sky was cloudy and soft. But three kids were already in line.

"My turn next," said a girl named Mia. She held the swing rope tight.

Everett wanted to be a dragon. Dragons do not wait in lines. He jumped in front of Mia and grabbed the rope too.

Then Mia let go of the rope. The boy behind her stepped back too. The line went quiet and still. Nobody swung. Everybody just stood.

Everett pulled the swing, but it felt wrong. A dragon swing is only fun if you fly high. He could not fly with everyone standing still and sad.

He let go of the rope. "You can go first," he said.

Mia smiled. She hopped on and pumped her legs. The swing went up, up, up, past the tall tree. "Look at me! I fly!" she called.

When Mia jumped off, she pointed at Everett. "Now it is the dragon's turn."

Everett climbed on. The line behind him clapped and cheered. His swing went up, up, up. He roared a big dragon roar.

"Rawr!" he shouted. "Next friend, come fly!"

Wyatt wanted to help Dad cook lunch. But first Dad said, "Stay close to me." Wyatt stayed close to Dad in the backyard.

Dad lit the grill. The grill got hot. Wyatt could feel the heat on his face. He stepped back two big steps. Dad nodded. Wyatt put his milk cup on the table, far from the hot grill. A drop of milk ran down the cup. The table was wet where the milk dripped.

Then Wyatt saw a shiny knife on the grass. He reached for it. Dad said, "Stop. I pick up knives." Dad picked up the knife and put it high on a shelf. Wyatt waved his hand near the grill again. Hot. He waved it near his milk cup. Cold. He touched the wet table. Cool too.

Wyatt stayed close. Dad stayed close. They watched the burgers sizzle together. "Lunch soon," said Dad. Wyatt sat down on his little chair and waited. "I can taste the burgers already," he said. Dad smiled and flipped one over.

Margot sat down at the dinner table. Her plate had ten little meatballs on it. Ten! That was a lot.

"Can I count them?" she asked.

"Of course," said Mama.

Margot touched each one with her fork. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Then she ate one. It was warm and yummy. She counted again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine."

Only nine now! When she ate one, the number got smaller.

"I pretend I am an owl," said Margot, opening her eyes wide. "Owls count at night. Is the dark scary for owls?"

"Owls love the dark," said Mama. "They watch it all night."

Margot ate another meatball. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight."

Eight. The plate was getting empty. Her tummy was getting full.

She ate and counted all the way down. "One." She popped it in her mouth.

"Zero meatballs left," she said, and held up her empty plate.

Sadie stood in the school hallway. She held her new backpack tight. It had a little red boat on it. Sadie wanted to go in, but the door was shut. It was big and gray and heavy.

Sadie could not reach the handle up high. She looked and looked. Then she saw a round button by the door. It was flat and shiny. She pushed the button with one finger.

The big door swung open all by itself. Sadie walked through. Behind her, a boy saw what she did. He pushed the button too. The door opened for him as well. He smiled at Sadie.

A teacher came to the hallway. "Hello, Sadie," she said. "Come see our room." Sadie hung her new backpack on a little hook. On the table there was a tub of water and some toy boats. Sadie picked up a boat and stirred the water round and round. The little waves went splash, splash.

"My boat can float," said Sadie.

James was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to play outside in the snow. Grandpa handed him his red coat. "Can you put it on yourself?" Grandpa asked.

James pushed his arms in. But the coat looked wrong. The tag was on his chin. The zipper was on his back. "Hmm," said James. He could not reach it. Grandpa turned him around, so the tag sat at his neck. Now the zipper hung in front, right by his tummy.

James pulled the zipper down. He pushed the little slide into the slot at the bottom. Then he pulled it up, up, up. Zip! The coat closed all the way to his chin. He was warm now, and not thirsty for cold air.

"Grandpa, look! I did it!" said James. "Thank you for waiting," said Grandpa.

Grandpa gave him a sandwich in his pocket. James ran out the door into the snow.

Chloe woke up early. She looked out the window. The backyard was all white! "Snow!" she shouted. Mama came to see. "No school today," said Mama. "It is a snow day."

Chloe wanted to play outside fast. She put on her boots. She put on her big red coat. Then she ran out the back door. The snow went crunch, crunch under her boots. It was cold on her nose. She made a snowball with her mittens.

Chloe threw the snowball at the fence. Thump! The snow stuck to the wood. It did not fall down. Chloe laughed. She threw another one. Thump! That one stuck too. The fence was turning white and bumpy.

Mama called, "Come see!" There was a card in the mailbox, a letter from Grandma. Chloe ran inside. Her mittens were wet and snowy. She set them on the warm radiator. Then she watched. Soon the snow on her mittens turned to little wet drops. The mittens got dry and soft. "My mittens are warm," said Chloe. "Can we go back out after snack?"

Matthew went to the farmers' market with his dad. They saw red apples and orange carrots. They saw a shiny fish on the ice. "I want to cook dinner," said Matthew. "Okay," said Dad. "Let's pick things."

Matthew picked three big potatoes. He carried them in a little bag. At home, Dad put water in a pot. Dad put the pot on the stove. "You can wash the potatoes," said Dad. Matthew washed them in the sink. The water turned brown. "Look, Dad! The dirt came off!"

Dad peeled the potatoes with a knife. Matthew stood far away and watched. Dad dropped the potatoes into the pot. The pot began to bubble. "The bubbles mean the potatoes are cooking," said Dad. Matthew clapped his hands.

The potatoes got soft. Dad used a fork to mash them. "Now you can add the milk," said Dad. Matthew poured the milk in. The potatoes turned white and fluffy. He mixed and mixed and mixed.

Mom and the baby came to the table. Matthew wore his big apron to serve dinner. Everyone took a big bite. "Mmm," said Mom. "Matthew made this!" Matthew smiled. He passed the shiny spoon to Dad. "More potatoes, please," said Dad. Matthew gave him more.

Avery sat in her car seat. She was going to Grandma's house today. "Is it now?" she asked. "Yes, we are driving now," said Mama.

Yesterday, Avery had dropped her bunny at Grandma's house. She missed bunny. Tomorrow was bunny's tea party. But today was the day to get bunny back.

Avery looked out the window. The sun was in her eye. It made a warm spot on her sleeve. Then the car turned. A big truck went by. The warm spot went away. Where did it go? "The truck made shade," said Mama. The truck was gone now, and the sun came back. The warm spot was back too.

Avery wiggled her ear. She heard the turn signal. Click, click. The car turned left. That meant Grandma's street. Later they would have cookies. But first, the car stopped. Grandma stood at the door. She held something soft and thin, with long ears. "Bunny missed you," said Grandma. Avery held out both arms. "Now we can go home together," she said.

Anthony sat with Mom and Dad at a big table. A big screen glowed on the wall. It showed a football game. Everyone was excited. Uncle Ben waved his hands. Aunt Mia clapped.

Anthony wanted to see the game too. But the tall man in front of him sat right in the way. Anthony stood on his toes. He still could not see. "I can't see!" he said.

Then Anthony had a smart idea. He pulled his chair to the side, near Aunt Mia. Now the tall man was not in the way. Anthony could see the whole screen. The players ran. The crowd on the screen made a big noise.

The whole restaurant made a big noise too. Everyone jumped up. "They did it!" Dad shouted. Anthony clapped and clapped. Uncle Ben sent a fry flying across the table. Anthony laughed and caught it in his cup. Aunt Mia hugged him tight.

Nova went to the park today. Yesterday it rained, so the slide was wet. Nova touched the slide. Her hand got drippy. "I want to slide now," she said.

Dad opened his bag. He pulled out a small towel. He wiped the slide, top to bottom. The wet went away. The slide was dry now. Nova climbed up. She slid down fast. "Again," she said. She slid down three more times.

Later, Nova saw a big puddle by the swings. The sun was warm on her back. They waited and waited. Nova watched the puddle get smaller and smaller. Then the puddle was gone. Dad kissed her head. "We will come back tomorrow," he said. "Maybe the ducks will be in the pond." Nova laughed. "Ducks are funny," she said. She ran to the gate.

Raphael was at Grandma's house. He wanted to make a card for his dad. Grandma gave him red paper and glue.

Raphael spread the glue on the paper. He stuck on a cotton ball. It looked like a fluffy cloud. He stuck on more and more. Soon the card was full.

Then Raphael pushed a cotton ball with his finger. Squishy! The glue came up through the cotton. It felt cold and sticky on his skin. He pushed another one. Squish! More glue came out.

"Look, Grandma!" he said. "The glue comes up when I push!"

"That happens with wet glue," said Grandma. "Let's add one more cloud."

They pushed one more cotton ball together. Then they set the card by the window. Raphael watched it all afternoon. The glue dried and the cotton balls stopped being sticky.

"Is it ready now?" he asked.

"It is ready," said Grandma.

Raphael held the card up high. "Dad will love his fluffy clouds!"

It was sharing day at school. Willow had a big red bag. She wanted to show her toy bunny to the class. But when she opened the bag, the bunny was not there. Only an apple was inside.

"Oh no," said Willow. "My bunny is gone."

Her teacher, Miss Pam, came to help. "Let's look together," she said. They looked in the cubby. They looked under the rug. Then Willow had an idea. The apple was a food, not a toy. Somebody might have her bag by mistake.

Tommy sat at the next table. His bag was red too, the same color. He opened it and pulled out a soft gray bunny.

"That's my bunny!" said Willow.

"And this apple is mine," said Tommy. "My mom packed it today."

They traded bags and laughed. Willow learned that looking closely was a good tool for finding lost things. She hugged her bunny tight.

"Now we both have the right things," said Willow. Tommy took a big bite of his apple.

Anthony looked out the window. Snow was falling on the grass. Snow was falling on the car. School was closed today!

"Snow day!" Anthony shouted. He jumped up and down. "Can we play outside, Mom?"

"Yes," said Mom. "But your boots are wet from yesterday."

Anthony frowned. He wanted his boots now. He looked at his boots by the door. They were dark with water. Mom put them near the warm heater. "We will wait a little," she said.

Anthony waited. He counted the snowflakes on the window. One, two, three. He drew a rainbow with his crayons. One, two, three colors. Then he touched his boot. It was still wet. He touched it again later. It was warm and dry!

"The heater made my boots dry!" said Anthony. "Now can we go outside?"

Mom laughed. "Yes, little snow bunny. Boots on!"

Anthony pulled on his warm, dry boots. He ran out the door. The snow went crunch, crunch under his feet. He made one big snowball. He made one small snowball. He put the small one on top. "Hello, Mr. Snowman," said Anthony. "You need a carrot nose."

Elias sits in a big chair at the doctor's office. Dad holds his hand. The nurse has a small bandage and a tiny white stick.

"Will it hurt?" asks Elias.

"Just a quick pinch," says Dad.

The nurse taps Elias's arm. "Look at your hand," she says. Elias opens his fingers, one by one. While he looks down, the nurse gives the shot. Elias feels the pinch. Then the pinch goes away.

"It is done!" says Elias. He got a shiny red bandage. The nurse gives him a sticker of a happy dog. Elias smiles.

"What made the pinch stop hurting?" Elias asks Dad.

"Playing helps it stop," says Dad.

So Elias squeezes his teddy bear tight. The pinch feels smaller. Then Dad lets him jump to the door. The pinch feels smaller still.

Afterward they go to the ice cream shop. Elias picks pink ice cream. He licks it. "Dad! The pinch is all gone!" he says.

Elias lifts his arm up high. He waves the red bandage at the ice cream man.

"Vanilla or strawberry?" the man asks.

"Strawberry, please," says Elias.

Sofia stood by the kitchen table. Mom had made warm toast, but Mom was busy with the baby. Sofia wanted to butter her own toast today.

She picked up the butter knife. Mom had put soft butter in a little dish. Sofia dipped the knife in. She pressed hard on the toast. The bread tore, and a big lump of butter sat in one spot. "Hmm," said Sofia. She looked at the lump. Would the toast rip again?

She tried again, easy this time. She touched the butter lightly. Then she slid the knife across, slow and gentle. The butter went on thin. It spread from edge to edge. The whole slice turned shiny and yellow. "It pays to go slow," Mom said with a smile, peeking over.

Next came the milk. Sofia held the small cup with one hand. She held the little pitcher with the other. She poured fast, and milk splashed onto the table. She stopped. She wiped it up with a towel. She tried once more, tipping the pitcher just a little. The milk ran in a thin white line. It went all the way to the top. Not one drop spilled.

Sofia took a bite of her toast. The butter tasted real and sweet. "I did it myself," she said, and she raised her cup like a tiny queen.

Myles went to Dad's office. He saw a tablet on the desk. "Can I draw?" he asked. "You can," said Dad. "First you push the little button."

Myles pushed the button. The screen lit up. He pushed it again and the screen went dark. He laughed. He pushed once more and the light came back. "Like magic," he said. Dad showed him the drawing app. Myles tapped it. A white page opened. He drew a big sun and a red car on a busy street. He drew his dad smiling next to him.

Soon the tablet looked tired, just like Myles. "Time to put it away," said Dad. Myles pushed the button and the screen went dark. He folded the cover over it, slow and careful. He set it on the desk. Then he took Dad's hand and said, "Now can we draw on paper too?"

Max got on the big yellow bus. He sat by the window. He held his little red backpack tight.

The bus door closed with a whoosh. Then the bus began to roll. Max looked out. The trees went by. The houses went by. When the bus stopped, the door opened. When the bus went, the door shut again. Max tapped the window with his finger. "Stop means open," he said. "Go means shut."

A girl sat down next to him. Her name was Lily. "Want to see?" Max asked. The bus stopped, and the door opened. Lily clapped her hands. "You teach me the bus!" she said.

At school, the driver smiled. "Have a sweet first day," she said. Max waved. Then he took Lily's hand and walked to his classroom door.

Liam turned three today. His party was at the big park. Grandma brought a cake with candles on top.

Dad lit the candles with a match. "Watch the little flames," said Dad. Liam puffed air from his mouth at them. One flame went out. He puffed again. Another flame went out. Liam laughed. He puffed and puffed until every flame was gone.

"Make a wish!" said Mom. Liam closed his eyes. Then he clapped his hands. The candles stayed dark. "No more flames," he said. "That is true," said Grandma. "You blew them all out, big boy."

After cake, Liam and his cousin Ben walked to the pond. They held paper cups of duck food. Liam threw some food in the water. A duck swam over fast. He threw more food. More ducks came. "The ducks think it is their birthday too," said Ben. Liam threw the last bit. The biggest duck gobbled it up.

"Happy birthday, ducks," said Liam.

Matteo had a library book about trucks. He loved it so much. He wanted to keep it forever.

Mama sat with him on the big sofa. She opened the front cover first. "We start here," she said. She pointed at the little black marks on the page. Her finger slid under them. "Truck," she read. The picture popped up. A big red truck! The marks told Mama what to say. Matteo put his own finger under the marks. "Truck!" he said. Every page had more marks. More words. He turned the pages, one by one, all the way to the back.

Then Mama said, "We have a problem. The book belongs to the library. Other kids want to read it too. We take it back soon." Matteo held the book tight to his chest. "My book," he said. His eyes got hot and watery.
