Mama hugged him close. "We can borrow it again," she said. "And we can pick fresh books too." So they went back to the library. Matteo gave the truck book to the librarian. She smiled and put a stamp on a card. Then Matteo found a new book about diggers. He opened the front cover. He put his finger under the marks.

"Digger!" said Matteo.

Gabriel ran to the playground. The sun was hot. His slide was hot too. He touched it. "Ouch!" He pulled his hand back fast.

He wanted to slide, but the slide was too hot. What could he do? He looked around. The big kids were slow and careful on the hot slide. The small kids sat in the shade. Gabriel sat in the shade too. He drank cold water from his bottle. It was quiet under the tree.

Then the clouds came. The sun went away. Gabriel touched the slide again. Now it was cold! He climbed up fast. He slid down. "Whee!" He splashed in a little puddle at the bottom. His mom gave him a towel for his wet shoes. "Again!" said Gabriel.

Sienna went to the store with Dad. She wanted apples for snack time. Dad said, "Let's pick ten apples."

Sienna held the bag. She put one apple in. Then she put two more. Dad said, "One, two, three."

Sienna counted too. "Four, five, six." The apples rolled in the bag. She dropped one. It rolled under the shelf. Dad got down low. He reached slowly. He waited. Then his hand came out with the apple.

"Seven," said Sienna. She put in one more. "Eight." Dad handed her one. "Nine."

"One more," said Dad. Sienna looked in the bin. She picked a big red apple. She held it with both hands. She set it in softly. "Ten!"

At home, Dad washed the apples. Sienna watched the water dance down the sides. Dad gave her one apple, cut in slices. The messy juice ran down her chin. She counted her slices. "One, two, three, four." Then she ate every one.

Rose sat in a big seat at the stadium. The game was down on the green field. But a tall man sat right in front of her. She could not see the players at all.

"Daddy, I can't see," said Rose. Dad planted his feet, held her hands, and lifted her up. Now Rose could see everything. She saw the players run. She saw the red and yellow hats all around.

Then Rose spotted a man with a camera. The camera was looking at the crowd. Rose began to wave her arms, big and slow. The camera man pointed at her. Rose looked up at the giant screen. There she was, waving, right next to Dad's head. She waved even faster. The whole crowd made a noise like a storm, loud and happy. Mom laughed and waved too.

"Look at us!" said Rose. She waved until her arm was tired.

Brooklyn stood at the bus stop with Grandma. The wind blew. Her coat was in her arms, not on her.

"I want to do it myself," said Brooklyn. She pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. The coat hung crooked. One sleeve was empty.

"Try again," said Grandma. "We can wait for the bus."

Brooklyn counted her arms. "One arm. Two arms." She pulled the coat on. Now it was straight. She felt the furry collar on her chin. It was soft.

Next came the zipper. She held the bottom. She pushed the little part in. Click. She pulled it up. Up, up, up. The zipper made a loud zzzip sound.

"Now I am warm," said Brooklyn. The wind blew again. This time the wind did not get in.

Grandma smiled. "The bus is coming," she said.

Brooklyn zipped her coat all the way to the top. "Zzzip!" she said.

Logan ran to the big window. He wanted to play outside. "Look, Mommy, it is sunny!" he said. The sun made a warm spot on the floor. Logan put his hand in the sun spot. It felt warm, like toast.

He put on his sun hat. He found his little shoes. Then the sky turned gray. Tap, tap, tap. Rain hit the window. "Oh no," said Logan. "Now it is rainy!" Mommy gave him his red rain boots. She gave him his rain coat with the hood. Logan jumped in a puddle. Splash! His boots kept his socks dry.

A big wind came. It was windy! The wind blew his hood off his head. The wind blew the leaves round and round. Logan held his hat with both hands. "My hat almost flew away!" he laughed.

Then white flakes fell down. "Snowy!" Logan shouted. He caught one on his glove. The snowflake melted into a tiny wet dot. Soon Logan was cold and sleepy, like a tired puppy with a tired bone. Mommy brought him in. She wrapped him in a soft blanket. "Warm cocoa?" she asked. Logan nodded and held his cup with both hands.

Audrey had a cough. She wanted it to go away. Mom said, "We will call the pharmacy." Mom picked up the phone. The man there said he had medicine for coughs.

Mom took Audrey to the pharmacy. It was bright inside. Audrey saw boxes and bottles on the shelves. The man gave Mom a small bottle. "Take this at home," he said. Audrey held Mom's hand tight. The floor was slippery, so she walked slowly.

At home, Mom poured a spoon of medicine. It tasted like cherry. Audrey swallowed it. She rested on the couch. She coughed less. Then she coughed even less. "My cough is going away," Audrey said. Mom pulled the blanket up. "Look at that," said Mom. Audrey smiled and hugged her teddy bear.

Juliette was on the swim team. The team met at the big pool every week. Coach Ana gave each kid a kickboard.

Juliette held the board tight. She kicked her legs fast. Kick, kick, kick. The water made splashes. And Juliette moved! She moved all the way to the rope.

But then her legs got tired. She stopped kicking. The splashes stopped too. And Juliette stopped moving. She stayed right there, floating like a little boat.

"Look at you," said Coach Ana. "You went so far." Juliette frowned. "I stopped," she said. "I want to go to the rope again."

Coach Ana smiled. "Try small kicks. Little ones." Juliette kicked small and slow. Kick, kick, kick. The splashes came back. Juliette moved again, slow and steady, all the way to the rope. The tall girl on the team clapped for her.

After swim time, Juliette sat with her dad by the pool. They shared a snack. "Swim team makes me hungry," she said. Dad laughed. "Then it's a good thing it's dinner time soon."

Juliette looked at the water. "Kick, kick, kick," she said softly, and her feet wiggled under the towel.

Dylan sat in the waiting room. He wanted to eat his crackers. But his hands felt sticky.

The nurse came by with a big smile. "Time to wash hands first," she said. Dylan ran to the little sink. He put his hands under the water. He pumped the soap. Bubbles came out!

"Look at that!" said Dylan. He rubbed his palms together. The bubbles grew and grew. He rubbed the backs of his hands. More bubbles! He rubbed between his fingers. The sticky spots went away.

"How long do I rub?" Dylan asked. "We sing the happy song," said the nurse. They sang it together. "Happy birthday to you!" When the song was done, the bubbles rinsed off. The water carried them down the drain.

Dylan held up his hands. They were clean and shiny. He smelled them. "Mmm, like flowers!" he said. He looked at his hands all over. The sticky was gone. The world looked ready for crackers now.

Dylan ran back to his chair. He picked up a cracker with his clean fingers. Crunch! It tasted so good. "My hands are clean, so my cracker stays clean," said Dylan. The nurse gave him a thumbs up. Dylan grinned and took another big bite.

Mia was four years old today. The sky was cloudy, but the party was still on. Her friends came to the big park. There were balloons and hats for everyone.

Dad put the cake on the table. He lit the four little candles. Mia wanted to blow them out. But her friend Sam was sad. His balloon had flown away. Mia gave him one of her own. Sam smiled big.

Then everyone sang the birthday song. Mia took a big breath. She blew and blew. All four candles went out. Up went little curls of smoke. Mia laughed. "Look! The smoke goes up when the candles go out!" she said. Mom cut the cake with the big knife. Mia helped pass out plates. After cake, Grandpa was sleepy. He took his nap under a tree. Dad clicked the cooler closed to lock in the ice. Mia waved her smoke curl goodbye.

Asher went to the store with Mama. It was a rainy day. The floor was wet near the door.

Asher wanted a red apple. He looked in the big bin. He saw green apples too. He reached for a red one.

"Can I hold it?" he asked.

"Yes," said Mama. "Hold it gently."

The red apple felt smooth and cold. Asher put it in the cart. Then he saw bananas. They were yellow. "I want one," he said. Mama put three yellow bananas in the cart.

Next they passed the milk. The carton was blue like the sky. Asher tapped it. "Blue!" he said. A man nearby smiled.

At the wall, Asher saw green balloons. He touched one. It slid down the string and bounced back up. Asher laughed and did it again.

"Time to pay," said Mama. Asher helped put the red apple on the counter. He heard the beep, beep of the register.

They walked out into the rain. Asher held Mama's hand tight. He carried the bag with the yellow bananas.

"My apple is in here," he said.

"Yes," said Mama. "We will wash it and eat it at home."

Paisley sat in her car seat. Today was the day for Grandma's house. "Are we there now?" she asked. "Not now," said Mom. "Later, after the sun goes past that big tree."

Paisley looked out the window. Yesterday she had seen a wild goose by the pond. The goose was gone today. "Where did it go?" she asked. "Maybe it will come back tomorrow," said Mom. Paisley watched and watched, but no goose came.

"I want to see Grandma now," said Paisley. "We get there later," said Mom. "First we drive. Then we stop. Then we are there." Paisley tapped her shoes. One, two, three. She saw the sun move past the tree. She saw the road bend. Then the car stopped, and Grandma opened the door.

Paisley ran to her. Grandma held out her hand. In it was one small white egg. "The hen laid this today," said Grandma. "Yesterday there was no egg. Tomorrow there may be one more." Paisley held the egg very carefully. "Can we look for another one tomorrow?" she asked. Grandma smiled and took her hand.

Romy wanted to make tea for her teddy bear. But the tea set had a big pot and one small cup. The big pot was too big for one small bear.

First she needed real tea. Dad filled the kettle. The kettle got hot, so Dad poured the tea. "Careful, it's hot," said Dad. Romy watched from her step stool. She blew on the cup. She blew slow puffs. Then she touched the side. "Cold now," she said. The tea had gone from hot to cold.

Romy poured the small cup for teddy. Then she ran fast around the playroom with him. The tea spilled. "Too fast," said Romy. So she walked slow, holding the cup with two hands. Not one drop spilled.

Just then teddy slipped. His tea went all over the floor. Romy felt mad for a second. Then she saw something. The spill made a big wet spot on the rug. She dropped one small drop of tea next to it. The small drop made a small spot.

"Dad! Big spills make big spots," said Romy. "Small drops make small ones." Dad smiled and brought a towel. Romy wiped up the big spot first. Then she wiped the small one. "Teach me the slow walk again," said teddy's voice, and Dad laughed. Romy held her bear close and gave him one more small drop.

Naomi stood in the reading corner. She was four years old today. Her mama knelt down beside her. "You can try for your very own library card," Mama said.

The librarian smiled. She gave Naomi a small card. It was red and white. It said Naomi on it. Naomi held it with both hands.

Then Naomi found a book. It had a bear on the cover. The bear was making a big circle in the snow. "I want this one," said Naomi. "Forever and ever."

The librarian shook her head softly. "You can take it home. But you must bring it back. Then other kids can read it too. I will mark the day it is due."

Naomi frowned. She did not want to let the bear book go. But then a boy came in. He was looking for a bear book. He looked sad.

Naomi thought and thought. She could read it lots of times at home. Then she could bring it back. The boy could have a turn.

"Okay," she said. "I will bring it back." The librarian stamped the card. Naomi put the book in her bag. She hugged the bag all the way home.

At bedtime, they read about the bear and his circle in the snow. "Again," said Naomi. "Read it again."

Layla wants to help make a cake for Grandma. It is a gift for Grandma's visit.

Mama says, "First we wash our hands." Layla washes her hands. Her wet hands feel cold. She touches the soft flour. It is white and light. Then she touches the sugar bowl. The sugar feels like little sand.

Mama cracks the eggs. Layla listens. Tap, tap. The bowl sounds like that. Then Mama turns on the mixer. It is loud. Layla covers her ears. She waits until it is quiet again.

The cake goes in the oven. Mama puts it in, not Layla. The oven is hot. Soon Layla smells something sweet. "I can smell it with my nose!" she says. They wait and wait. Layla watches the oven door.

At last the cake is out. It is cool now. Mama cuts a little piece. Layla puts it in her mouth. It tastes sweet and yummy. "Grandma will love it," says Layla. She jumps up and down. The heavy cake sits safe on the table, waiting for Grandma.

Audrey was in the playroom with her friend Ben. There was one big red truck. They both wanted it.

Audrey grabbed the truck. Ben grabbed it too. The truck tipped over. Blocks went everywhere. Some water from a small cup did spill on the rug.

Mama came in. She sat down on the soft rug. "Let's try the timer," she said. Mama turned the timer. It went tick, tick, tick.

Audrey pushed the truck. "Vroom," she said. She made a slow ramp with one block. Then the timer rang. Now it was Ben's turn. Audrey gave him the truck. Ben pushed it fast. Then the timer rang again. Back to Audrey.

Ben said, "I like the ramp. What is its name?" Audrey said, "His name is Truckey." Ben laughed. They counted the blocks together. One, two, three, four.

Audrey found one more cookie in her pocket. She broke it in half. She gave the big half to Ben. "You take this one," she said. Ben said, "Thank you, Audrey." The timer ticked on the shelf. They played until snack time. "Your turn, Ben," said Audrey.

Iris sat at the dinner table. Her tummy made a little scratchy sound, like a tiny cat at the door. She wanted bread, and she wanted it now.

"Mama, is the bread done?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Mama. "It is baking now. We will eat it later."

Iris sighed. Waiting made her feel a little mad. She watched the oven door. Then she smelled it. Warm bread, bread, bread.

"Yesterday we had soup," said Mama. "Today we have bread. Tomorrow we will have berries."

Iris counted on her plate. "Yesterday, today, tomorrow." One, two, three.

Then the oven beeped. Mama opened the door. The bread came out, big and warm.

"Is it now?" asked Iris.

"It is now," said Mama.

Iris took a big, soft bite.

Milo wanted his red truck. It rolled under the big bed. He got down on his knees. He could see the truck way in the back. His arm was too short.

Milo went to find Dad. "Dad, can you help me, please?" he asked. Dad smiled. He got down on the floor too. Dad reached far under the bed. Out came the shiny red truck.

"Thank you!" said Milo. He gave Dad a hug.

Then Milo ran fast with his truck. He bumped into the cat's water bowl. Water went all over the floor. "Sorry, cat," said Milo. The cat licked one wet paw.

Dad brought a towel. Milo helped wipe the floor. It took a long time. They wiped and wiped. At last the floor was dry and shiny.

Milo set the bowl back in its spot. He put his truck beside it, nice and safe. "Good spot," said Dad. The cat curled up on the bed for a nap.

Charlie was at soccer practice. The coach had one big red ball. Charlie wanted it first.

Milo held the ball. Charlie ran up and grabbed it. The ball popped out of both hands. It rolled under the bench. Milo sat down and did not smile.

The coach got the ball out. She gave it back to Milo. "Your turn first, Milo," she said. Charlie put his hands behind his back. He waited. He counted his shoes. One, two. Still he waited.

Then Milo kicked the ball. It rolled right to Charlie. "Now you," said Milo. Charlie laughed. The ball came to him when he waited! He kicked it back. Milo kicked it again. The ball went back and forth, back and forth.

"Nice waiting, Charlie," said the coach. She put a gold star sticker on his shirt. Milo gave him a friendly pat on the back. At juice time, Charlie let Milo go first in the line. Milo sent him a big grin.

James sat at the big art table. He had a pot of red paint and a pot of blue paint. His teacher had asked everyone to paint a frog. James wanted to paint a green frog. But he looked and looked. There was no green paint.

He looked at his friend Mia. She had yellow paint. She made a big yellow sun. James wanted green, not yellow. He sighed and tapped his brush.

Then he dipped his brush in the red pot. He made a red frog on his paper. Then he dipped the same brush in the blue pot. He painted blue over the red frog. He waited for it to dry. The frog turned green!

"Look, look!" said James. "My frog is green now!" Mia came to see. She dipped her brush in yellow. Then she dipped it in blue. She made a blue-yellow pond for the frog. The pond turned green too.

"Green pond for a green frog," said Mia.

James smiled. Green was his new favorite color. He added one more dot of red. It turned into a little green bug.

Sienna sat at the dinner table. Her cup was empty. "More milk, please," she said. Dad poured the milk. "Thank you," said Sienna. Dad smiled big.

Then Sienna reached for the bread. It was far away. She stretched. She stretched more. The basket began to tip. CRASH. The bread rolled under the table. "Sorry," Sienna said quietly. "That's okay," said Mom. "Ask for help next time."

Sienna slid down from her chair. She counted the bread rolls under the table. One, two, three. She reached for them. One, two, three back in the basket. Mom held the basket while Sienna put them in.

Now Sienna wanted the butter. She remembered the bread basket. She did not stretch. "Mom, can you help me, please?" she asked. Mom passed the butter. "Thank you," said Sienna. She buttered her bread all by herself. "Yummy," she said, and took a big bite. Dad raised his milk cup. "To Sienna," he said. "To Sienna," said Mom. Sienna raised her cup too. "To me," she said.

Lily stood on a little stool in the big restaurant kitchen. She wanted to make breakfast all by herself.

"Can I butter the toast?" she asked.

"Yes," said Cook. He cut warm bread for her. Lily held the butter knife. She pressed too hard. The toast tore into holes.

"That is not good," said Lily.

"Try little strokes," said Cook. "Go slow and be gentle." Lily made soft little strokes. The butter sat on top, shiny and smooth.

"Now the milk," said Cook. He set the jug high on the counter and tipped it for her. Milk splashed over the cup edge. Lily gasped. She watched the cup. She poured slowly. The milk went up, up. It stopped right at the rim.

"No spill," said Lily.

Cook hung a star next to her name on the kitchen map. Lily spread butter on one more slice, just for Dad.

Ella went to the pet store with Dad. A bell went ring as the door opened. Ella looked at the cages. She looked at the tanks. Then she saw a little orange fish. "That one," said Ella. Dad said, "Okay. That fish comes home with us."

The shop lady put the fish in a bag. The bag was full of water. Ella held one side, and Dad held the other. "The bag is heavy," said Ella. "Hold it strong," said Dad. They walked home slow. The fish swam in small circles.

At home, Dad poured the fish into its bowl. Ella wanted to feed it. She shook the food jar, and lots of flakes fell in. The flakes covered the top of the water. Dad took them out with a little net. "Just two flakes," said Dad. Ella put in two flakes. The fish came up and ate one. Ella put in two more, and the fish ate those too. "You like your food," said Ella. The fish blew a tiny bubble.

Ayla went to the band room with her class. She wanted to play the big drum. The teacher, Mr. Bell, said, "You can try, Ayla." Ayla tapped the drum with her little hand. It made a tiny sound. "Why is it so quiet?" she asked. "Try the drumstick," said Mr. Bell. Ayla picked up the drumstick. She tapped once, soft. Tum. She tapped again, hard. BOOM! The big sound filled the room. "I did that!" said Ayla. She tapped soft, then hard. Tum, BOOM. Tum, BOOM. The band children looked up and smiled.

At home, Ayla told Mama all about it. "We can shop for a little drum for you," said Mama. Mama pulled the zipper on Ayla's coat, straight up to her chin. "Can I play it every day?" asked Ayla. "Yes," said Mama. Ayla smiled and patted her knees. Tum, BOOM. Tum, BOOM.

Jaxson wanted warm cocoa. His tummy was hungry for it. He stood next to Grandma in the kitchen. "Stay right here," said Grandma. "I will stay close," said Jaxson.

Grandma turned on the stove. The pot began to hum. Then steam rose up from the pot. The steam went high, like a little cloud. "The steam is hot," said Grandma. "Watch, do not touch." Jaxson watched the steam dance. He took one step back.

Then the pot was taken off the stove. Grandma poured the cocoa into a cup. Jaxson touched the cup with just one finger. The cup was warm, not too hot. "You waited so well," said Grandma. Jaxson sat by her feet and drank slowly. The lazy cat came over and sniffed his cup. "Not for you," said Jaxson. He smiled and took another little sip.

Camille sat down at the dinner table. There was one big bowl of peas. Daddy put some peas on her plate. Then he put some on Ben's plate. Camille looked at the two plates. They had the same amount. "How does he know?" she wondered.

Camille wanted the yellow cup. But Ben had the yellow cup. Ben saw her face. He drank a little sip. Then he slid the cup across the table. "Your turn," he said. Camille smiled. She took a sip. Then she slid it back. Back and forth the cup went, like a little boat.

A tiny bug walked on the window. Camille watched it. The bug went up. Then the bug went down. "Even the bug takes turns going up and down," she thought. Daddy used a knife to cut the bread. He cut one piece for Camille. He cut one piece for Ben. Same size again.

Then Daddy brought out the smelly cheese. Camille held her nose. "Pee-yew!" she said. Daddy laughed and cut the cheese into small bits. He put one bit on her plate. Camille touched it with one finger. She sniffed it close. "Still smelly," she said, "but I will try a tiny bite."

Bennett stood by his bedroom window. Yesterday it rained. He could not go on the swing. "Where is the sun now?" he asked. Mama smiled. "The sun is here now," she said. "Look. Now the sky is blue." Bennett saw the round yellow sun. It made a warm spot on his bed.

Today the sun was out. "Can we swing today?" Bennett asked. "Yes," said Mama. "We will swing after lunch. First we eat, then later we swing." Bennett clapped his hands. "Later we swing," he said. "Later we swing!" He put his bear on the bed. The sun spot moved. It moved from the pillow to the floor. Bennett watched it go. The sun was making the spot move, little by little.

After lunch, Mama called him. "It is later now," she said. Bennett ran outside. He sat on the swing. Mama pushed him, up and up. Bennett laughed. "The sun is up too," he said. "Tomorrow can we swing again?" "Yes," said Mama. "Tomorrow is a new day, just like today." Bennett swung high and touched his toes.

Benjamin had a red shirt with a big number three. It was his team shirt for soccer. He wanted to kick the ball into the net. But the ball was still. It sat on the grass like a rock.

A butterfly landed on the grass near him. Benjamin watched it open and close its wings. Then he ran to see it better. The butterfly flew up. It flew away over the fence. Benjamin kept watching it.

Then he saw something. The wind was blowing. The wind pushed the butterfly up and away. The wind also pushed a leaf across the grass. Benjamin looked at the ball. The wind pushed the ball too. It rolled a little bit toward the net. Benjamin ran and kicked it. The ball went in. "Goal!" said Daddy from the side. Benjamin jumped up and down and hugged his juicy orange slice after the game.

Rosalie sat down at the dinner table. She was very hungry. Mom had made a surprise.

"What is it?" Rosalie asked.

"Look in the pot," said Mom.

Rosalie peeked in. She saw carrots and peas and noodles. "Foods!" she shouted. "So many foods!"

Then she saw something small in her cup. It was her toy duck. It had fallen in the water.

"Oh no," said Rosalie. "My duck is thirsty too!"

She pulled the duck out. It was all wet. She gave it a little pat with her napkin.

The duck sat on the table by her plate. Rosalie held it up. "Do you like carrots?" she made the duck speak in a small voice. "Quack, quack, yes!"

Mom laughed. "Your duck is a funny gift at dinner."

Rosalie took a big bite of noodles. She drank her water. The duck watched.

"You can't eat," Rosalie told the duck. "You're a toy, not an animal." She fed the duck a pretend bite anyway.

The duck got a tiny carrot kiss on its beak. "Quack," said Rosalie. Mom smiled and gave Rosalie one more spoonful of peas.

Rosalie held the duck up high. "Dinner for everyone!"

Jaxon went to Mia's house. Mia had a drum. It went boom, boom, boom.

"Listen," said Mia's mom. She sang a song. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." She clapped her hands on every boom. Jaxon watched her hands. Up, down. Up, down.

Could he do that too? Jaxon clapped. His claps were too fast. The song ran ahead of him. He tried again. He waited for the boom. Then he clapped. Boom, clap! Boom, clap! Now his hands matched the drum.

Mia's baby brother was so young. He could not talk yet. But he heard the claps. He clapped his little hands too. He did not stop when the song did. His claps went on and on. Then he laughed so big he fell over.

Mia sang the star song. Jaxon knew the words now. He sang "like a diamond in the sky." Mia's mom pointed at the window. The sun shone through a rainbow sticker. "A diamond!" said Jaxon. He clapped one more boom. The baby clapped back.

Wyatt sat at the little table in art class. He wanted to paint his cat, Max. But his cat looked like a big blob on the paper. Wyatt felt upset. "My cat looks like a puddle," he said.

Miss Amy sat down next to him. "Let's look at Max in the picture," she said. Wyatt looked. Max had a round head. A circle! His ears were pointy triangles. His body was long like a rectangle. His food bowl was a square.

Wyatt painted a circle first. Then he painted two triangles on top. Then a long rectangle for the body. A square for the bowl.

"It's Max!" said Wyatt. "I made a cat from shapes!" He painted a tiny green plant in the corner too. Then he held his picture up high for everyone to see.

Hazel loved the little kitchen at school. She wanted to play house with her friend Mia. But Mia was already holding the baby doll.

"You be the big sister," said Mia. "I am the mama."

Hazel did not want to be the big sister. She wanted to be the mama too. Her lip went wobbly. She almost wanted to yell.

Then Hazel saw the tiny teddy bear on the shelf. It sat all alone in the middle of the rug. Nobody was holding it.

"Your baby is crying," Hazel said. She picked up the teddy. She patted its back, nice and slow. She gave it a soft hug.

Mia watched. "The teddy needs a mama," said Mia.

"Yes," said Hazel. "I will be its mama."

Hazel wrapped the teddy in a small blanket. She fed it a pretend bottle. The teddy stopped crying.

Mia brought a little cup. "Tea for two mamas?" she asked.

"Yes, please," said Hazel.

They sat together by the toy kitchen. Two mamas, two babies, one happy tea party.

Luka went to the library with his mom. He wanted a book about big trucks. The library was quiet. Too quiet. Luka felt a little scared of the tall shelves.

A girl sat at a small table. She cried soft tears. Her book had a torn page. She looked sad. Luka found a sticky dot on the table. He pressed it over the tear. The page lay flat again. The girl smiled a big smile. Now she looked happy.

Luka asked the librarian, "Where are truck books?" The librarian pointed. Luka ran. Then he stopped. Running made the librarian frown. Luka said sorry. He walked like a cat instead. He found a truck book with a shiny red cover. His eyes went wide. He felt so excited. At home, he read it three times with mom. "A sweet end to a good day," mom said. Luka hugged the book.

Grandpa came on the big bus. He carried one red bag. Ali wanted Grandpa to stay in his room, but the crib was too small.

"I am too big for that bed," said Grandpa. Ali felt sad. Then he saw the big bed in the guest room. Mom let Grandpa put his bag there. Grandpa would sleep in the big bed for a whole week.

Ali wanted to make Grandpa's bed cozy. He put his teddy bear on the pillow. Then he put a banana next to the bear. Mom laughed. "That will not be comfy," she said.

Ali took the banana away. He put a soft blanket on instead. Grandpa patted the bed. "Soft as a cloud," he said. He lay down and hugged the teddy bear. The bear's hat fell over Grandpa's nose.

"That hat tickles," said Grandpa. Ali giggled and giggled. Grandpa put the hat on Ali's head instead. It was much too big. "A tidy bed and a silly hat," said Grandpa. "Best room in the house."

Ali carried a pillow to the floor. He lay down next to the bed. "I sleep here too," he said. Grandpa snored a small pretend snore. Ali snored back.

Clara rode in the car to the big field. Her team wore red shirts. The grass smelled green and fresh. The dirt was soft under her shoes.

Clara wanted to hit the ball far. She held the bat with both hands. Coach tossed the ball. Clara swung. Miss. She waited and tried again. Swing. Miss again. The bat felt heavy, so she held it tighter.

Coach tossed a slow one. Clara swung hard. Tink! The ball hit the bat and flew over the dirt. It rolled and rolled into the quiet green grass. Clara dropped the bat and ran. Her feet went fast, fast, fast. The crowd made a big happy sound.

Her friend Ben picked up the ball and threw it back. "Good hit, Clara!" said Coach. Clara patted the bat gently. "You did that," she whispered to it. Then she ran to her place in the field, and the sun felt warm on her red shirt.

Parker stood by the little pool in the backyard. His dad was in the water, holding out his arms. "Come in, Parker," said Dad. Parker wanted to swim to Dad, but his feet would not move.

Then Parker saw a green ball float by the edge. He reached out and pushed it. The ball went splash, and it slid across the water. Parker looked at his hands. He pushed the water the same way. His body moved forward, right into Dad's arms.

"I swam!" said Parker. "You did," said Dad. Parker pushed the water again and again. He chased the green ball all the way to the other side. "Lunch soon," said Dad. Parker laughed and splashed one more time. "Again," he said, reaching for the ball.

It was a stormy summer day, so Sienna went to the community centre. Miss Ana put crackers on two plates.

"Which plate has more?" asked Miss Ana.

Sienna pointed at the big plate. "That one!" But Ben said, "No, my plate has more!"

Sienna counted the big plate. "One, two, three, four, five." Then she counted Ben's plate. "One, two, three, four." Ben had fewer crackers. "Five is more than four," said Sienna.

Ben looked sad, like he might cry. "Count again," he said. "Start with the round cracker."

Sienna counted from the round one. "One, two, three, four, five. Still five!"

Then Ben counted his own plate backwards. "Four, three, two, one. Still four!"

Miss Ana gave Ben one more cracker. Ben grinned and counted fast. "One, two, three, four, five. Five!"

"Now we both have five," said Sienna. "Hooray!"

They munched their crackers together.

Milo went to the farmers' market with Dad. He saw big red tomatoes on a table. He wanted to grow his own tomatoes at home.

Dad bought a small tomato plant in a pot. Milo held the pot near his tummy all the way home. In the yard, Dad dug a hole. Milo set the plant in the hole. Dad pushed the dirt back. Then Milo watered the dirt with his little can.

Days went by. The plant stood tall. Small yellow flowers came out. Then Milo saw a tiny green ball near a flower. "Dad, look!" said Milo. Dad smiled. The flower had made a little tomato. Milo watered the plant every day. The green ball grew big and red. Dad picked it with two hands. "My tomato," said Milo. He held it up to the warm sun.

Hunter ran out to the school playground. His little blue truck was gone. "Where did you go?" he asked. He looked under the slide. He looked by the swing. No truck.

Then Hunter saw the wind blow a red leaf. The leaf rolled across the ground. It stopped by the fence. Hunter stopped too. "Did the wind move my truck?" he said out loud. "Maybe it did. I will look where the wind goes."

He walked to the fence. The wind had pushed papers there too. One paper was his friend Mia's. "Is this yours?" he asked. "Yes! Thank you, that was polite," said Mia. They looked together by the fence.

Mia pointed. "Look, Hunter. Something blue." It was the truck, tucked in the grass. Hunter held it to his heart. "Now we can play," he said. "You can pretend it is a race car," said Mia. Hunter pushed the truck, and the wheels went round and round, all the way to the sandbox.

Emily wanted warm soup for lunch. Mom put a big pot on the stove. Emily stood far away and watched. The pot was big. Her little cup was small. "Mom, will the soup get hot?" she asked. "Yes, very hot," said Mom.

Emily put a small jug of milk on the table. The milk was cold. She touched the jug with one finger. Brrr. Then Mom poured the soup into a bowl. The bowl sat and sat. Emily waited. Was it still too hot? Mom helped her blow on it. The steam went away. Now Emily touched the bowl. It was warm, not hot. "It changed!" said Emily.

Emily ate fast, and the soup went down to the bottom. She ate slow, and the bowl stayed full. Then she saw something in her cup. A noodle had fallen in the milk. It floated and wiggled. It looked like it could swim. Emily laughed. "Mom, look! My noodle is swimming in the cold milk." Mom came to look, and the noodle bobbed up and down, small and white in the big blue cup.

Daniel sat in his car seat. He looked for his doll. Where was it? "I had it yesterday," he said. Yesterday was the day at Grandma's house. The doll was lost.

Dad said, "We are going to Grandma's house now." Daniel looked out the window. He saw one tree. Then two trees. Then three trees. "Are we there now?" he asked. "Not now," said Dad. "Later." So Daniel watched. One cow. Two cows. Three cows. Then Dad pulled the car over. They were there! Grandma held the doll in her hand. She had found it under her big chair. "You left it here yesterday," she said. Daniel hugged his doll tight. "Today we drive home," he said. "Tomorrow I will show Bear the doll." He climbed back in his seat. "Now we can go," said Daniel. Dad smiled and buckled him in.

Chloe was cold. She wanted to go outside and play. She pulled her coat off the hook. The coat had a big zipper. Chloe pushed her arm in one sleeve. Then the other arm. The coat hung crooked. One sleeve was inside out, like a hiding place for her hand.

Mama waited by the door. She did not hurry. Chloe pulled the sleeve out. She shook her arm. The sleeve popped out, all warm. Chloe laid the coat on the wood floor. She pushed her arms in again. This time the coat sat just right.

The zipper was stuck at the bottom. Chloe pulled it up, down, up. The zipper slid, and the coat closed all the way to her chin. Chloe patted the zipper. "I did it," she said. Mama smiled and opened the door. Cold air rushed in. Chloe ran out to the wild, windy yard.

Felix sat at the kitchen table. His apple waited on his plate. But his hands were messy from playing in the sand. He looked at his fingers. They were dusty and a little stinky.

"I want my apple now," said Felix.

Mom said, "First we wash. Then we eat."

Felix went to the sink. Mom turned on the water. It was warm and gentle. She put soap on his hands. "Now we make bubbles," she said. "We sing the happy song two times."

Felix rubbed his hands together. Bubbles grew big and white. He sang the song once. He kept rubbing. He sang it again. "Are twenty seconds done yet?" he asked.

"Yes, all done," said Mom.

She helped him rinse. The bubbles slid down the drain. The water carried the dust away too. Felix held up his hands. They were clean and shiny. "Where did the dirt go?" he asked.

"Down the drain," said Mom. "The water took it."

"I made bubbles, and the bubbles took the dirt!" said Felix.

"Sing it again," said Mom with a smile.

"Bubbles took the dirt! Bubbles took the dirt!"

Then Felix dried his hands on the little towel. He sat down and picked up his apple. He took one big, happy bite. His clean hands held it tight.

Ellie went to the pet store with Dad. She wanted a fish of her own. "Can I pick one?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. Ellie looked at all the fish. One little fish was orange. It swam right up to her hand on the glass. "That one," said Ellie.

At home, Dad helped her set up the bowl. Ellie put in the water and the little stones. The fish swam around and around. Then it bumped the glass, and bumped it again. "Is it sorry?" Ellie asked. "I think it wants food," said Dad. He showed Ellie the tiny food jar. Ellie turned the lid and dropped one small bit in. The fish saw the food. It swam fast and gobbled it up. Ellie clapped her hands. "You were hungry!" she said. The fish blew a little bubble. Ellie dropped in one more bit, and the fish chased it all around the bowl.

Abigail could not find her bunny. She looked under her pillow. No bunny there. She looked in her toy box. No bunny there either.

"Bunny is lost," said Abigail. "I want my real bunny back."

Dad came to help. "Let's look in your room," he said. First they picked up the blocks. Then Dad helped Abigail clean the floor. They put the blocks in the box.

Abigail pulled the blanket off the bed. She pulled it all the way down. Then something happened. Bunny slid off the bed with the blanket. Bunny slid right onto the clean floor.

"Bunny!" said Abigail. She gave Bunny a big hug. Bunny was dusty from under the blanket.

Abigail brushed Bunny off with her hand. "You slid down," she told Bunny. "I found you."

Dad smiled. "Blankets make things slide," he said. "Now let's tuck Bunny in tight."

Abigail laid Bunny on the pillow. She pulled the blanket up, just a little bit. Bunny stayed safe and warm.

"Good night, Bunny," said Abigail.

Alexis lived with Grandma for a whole rainy week. On Monday he lost his favorite red sock. "It went somewhere," said Grandma. "Let's look."

They looked under the bed. Alexis found one dusty shoe. They looked behind the chair. He found two paper balls. "Not socks," said Alexis.

They counted what they found, out loud. One, two, three hair pins in a jar. Four, five, six shiny buttons in a cup. "My sock is not here," said Alexis. His lip went down.

Grandma hummed a counting song. "Seven, eight, nine," she sang, peeking into the warm laundry basket. It smelled like soap and clean towels.

Alexis lifted a folded towel. There it was, sock number ten. "You were hiding!" he said. He hugged the soft, warm sock to his cheek.

Grandma laughed. "Ten things found, one happy boy," she said, and she poured warm milk for them both.

Leon was in the backyard. He had two cups of paint. One cup was red. One cup was yellow.

"I want green," said Leon. He looked and looked. There was no green paint.

Mama sat with him on the grass. "Let's mix," she said. Leon put his brush in the red cup. Drip, drip. Then he put it in the yellow cup. Swish, swish.

Red and yellow made orange! The paint was orange like a pumpkin. Leon touched it with one finger. It was cool and smooth.

"Now I need blue," said Leon. Mama brought a cup of blue paint. Blue like the ocean, deep and dark. Leon mixed blue and yellow. Swish, swish, swish.

Green! Green like the grass! Leon laughed. He painted a big green leaf.

Then his cup tipped over. The red paint sank into the grass. "Sorry, grass," said Leon softly. Mama wiped his hands with a warm cloth.

"I can make orange, and green, and..." Leon held up his brush. "What can red and blue make?"

Mama smiled. "Let's see."

Connor and his mom walked into the hotel room. Connor carried his little brown bear. "This is our room for tonight," said Mom. Connor looked around. There was a big bed and a big window.

Soon it was nap time. Connor lay down with his bear. But the sun came in through the window. It was too bright. Connor put his hands over his eyes. "I can't sleep," he said. Mom said, "Maybe you can fix that."

Connor looked at the window. There were big curtains. He pulled them across, all by himself. The curtains covered the window. The room went dark and cozy. The sun could not come in anymore.

"Mom, look!" Connor yelled. "I made it dark!" Mom smiled. "Good job, kid," she said. She tucked him in. Connor hugged his bear tight. Then Mom gave him a kiss on his head. The dark room felt soft and warm. Soon all Mom could hear was a small snore from the bed.

Hayden went to the pharmacy with his mom. He wanted a snack from his bag. He sat on the bench next to the sink. His hands felt sticky and sandy.

Mom turned on the water. It was warm, not hot. Hayden put his hands under it. The water ran like rain over his fingers. Mom gave him one pump of soap. The bubbles were white and small. They counted together. One, two, three, four, five. The bubbles turned gray. Six, seven, eight, nine, ten. The gray ran down the drain. Eleven, twelve, all the way to twenty. Now the bubbles were white and clean.

Hayden rinsed off the soap. He looked at his hands in the mirror. His shadow waved back at him. He held his hands up. "Clean!" he said. Mom opened his snack bag. Hayden ate his crackers, one by one. Then he wiped his hands on the towel. "Twenty next time too," he said, and jumped off the bench.

Weston ran into Grandma's kitchen. He saw a big bowl of white snow. "Is it cold?" he asked. Grandma laughed. "It is ice cream. You can help."

Weston sat on his tall stool. He wanted to make his favorite color, blue. Grandma gave him little bottles. Each bottle had a color inside. "One drop," said Grandma.

Weston squeezed one drop of blue. The white snow turned blue like the sky! He clapped his hands. Then he dropped yellow. Green spread out like grass! "How?" said Weston. He made a puzzle face.

Grandma held up a spoon. "Try red and yellow," she said. Weston tried. The ice cream turned orange like a pumpkin. He dropped red and blue too. Purple swirled around and around.

Grandma scooped it into a bowl. Weston took one little bite. "It tastes like berries and sun!" he said. Grandma smiled and gave him a red spoon.

Jackson ran to the park with his red ball. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Jackson wore his t-shirt and shorts.

Then the wind began to blow. It was windy now. The wind pushed the last leaf off the big tree. The leaf flew up, up, up. "Come back, leaf!" Jackson called. The wind pushed his ball too. The ball rolled far away.

A girl named Mia chased the ball for him. She wore a jacket because she was cold. Jackson rubbed his arms. "Here," Mia said. "My mom has a spare sweater." Jackson put it on. Then clouds came. Big drops fell. It was rainy now. Mia opened her umbrella. Jackson stood under it with her. They watched the rain color the gray path dark. "Want to share a snack?" Mia asked. Jackson smiled and held out his hand for a cracker.

Wren sat at the big table. She had a pencil and some paper. "I want to write my name," she said.

Mama sat next to her. "Let's try," said Mama. Wren grabbed the pencil in her whole fist. She pushed hard. The letters came out fat and wobbly. The W looked like a squiggle. The R fell over on its face.

"Why do my letters fall down?" asked Wren.

"Hold the pencil like this," said Mama. She showed Wren how to pinch it with two fingers, nice and light.

Wren pinched the pencil. She touched the paper soft and slow. The W came out pointy. The R stood up tall. "It works!" said Wren.

She wrote W, then R, then E, then N. "Wren!" she said. She wrote it again. Then she wrote it all alone, with no help at all.

Mama taped the paper to the fridge. Wren smiled at her name, standing up straight. "I can write my name," said Wren, "all by myself."

Eva sat on the red rug at school. Miss Jo held up her hands. "Today we will sing a song," she said. Eva wanted to sing the whole song by herself. But she did not know it yet.

Miss Jo clapped her hands. clap, clap, clap. Eva watched. When Miss Jo clapped, her hands made a sound. When she stopped, the room was quiet. Eva tried to clap too. Her hands went fast, fast, fast. "Too fast," said Miss Jo with a smile. "Try to help me. Watch my hands first." So Eva watched. She waited. Then she clapped when Miss Jo clapped. clap, clap, clap. Now the sounds went together.

Then Miss Jo sang the rhyme. "Hickory dickory dock." She sang it two times. Eva listened with her big ears. She asked herself, "Can I remember the words?" She took a big breath and tried. "Hickory dickory dock, the mouse ran up the clock." The words came out. All of them! The class clapped for her, one clap, then a huge round of claps. Eva stood up tall and sang it one more time. "The clock struck one," she sang, "the mouse ran down. Hickory dickory dock."

Jasmine skipped into the school cafeteria. It was her first day of school. She held her lunch tray with two hands. On the tray was a tasty cheese sandwich and a little juice box.

Jasmine wanted her juice. But the straw was tricky. She pushed the straw down. Then she squeezed the box hard. Squirt! Juice went right up her nose. A boy named Ben laughed. "Do juice boxes bite?" Jasmine asked. "No," said Ben. "They just squirt if you squeeze them."

Jasmine tried again. She held the box soft and gentle. She took a little sip. No squirt! The juice was sweet and cold. From the kitchen door, a cook waved a big spoon at her. Jasmine held up her juice box and took a proud, tiny sip.

Ellie sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. "Will the shot hurt?" she asked. "Just a tiny pinch," said Mom. "Then we get ice cream." The nurse came in with a little bandage and a small needle. "Look at me," said Mom. "We can count together."

"One, two, three," they counted. Ellie squeezed Mom's hand. The nurse said, "All done." Ellie looked at her arm. The pinch was over already. The nurse pressed a round bandage on it. The bandage was pink with little stars. "You were so smart to sit still," said Mom.

Outside, the clouds began to rain. Ellie and Mom ran to the ice cream shop. Ellie licked a cold, sweet strawberry cone. Rain tapped on the window. Mom wiped Ellie's sticky chin. "My arm is all better," said Ellie. She held up her star bandage for Mom to kiss.

Muhammad sat at the dinner table. His bowl was empty. He wanted more soup, but the big pot was far away.

"Mama, more please," he said. Mama picked up the ladle. She turned the pot slowly. Hot steam rose up, so Muhammad stayed in his chair and watched. Mama filled his bowl. The soup went up, up, up, to the top.

Muhammad ate his soup. Then he ate bread. Then his tummy felt round like a ball. He yawned a big yawn.

Papa said, "Bath time first." Muhammad ran to the bathroom. Papa turned the tap and the tub filled with bubbles. Muhammad splashed and washed his toes.

After the bath, Muhammad put on his soft pajamas. The buttons were small, so he pulled them through one by one. Then he brushed his teeth at the sink.

He went to his room. His lamp was still on. He climbed into bed and pulled the blanket up. Papa turned the lamp off. The room went dark and quiet. Muhammad closed his eyes. "Good night, stars," he whispered.

Aiden sat on Grandpa's lap. The big game was on TV. "Red team, blue team," Aiden said. "Red team, blue team." Grandma laughed and clapped.

Grandpa had a little pot of face paint. "Hold still," he said. He painted a small red star on Aiden's cheek. Aiden looked in the mirror. The star was red and shiny. He pointed one finger at it. "Star!" he said.

The whistle blew. It was a sharp sound. Everyone jumped up. "Go, go, go!" they shouted. Grandpa waved his arms. Aunt Mei stomped her feet. Aiden clapped his hands too. Then the baby cousin woke up. She cried and cried. The room got very quiet.

Aiden slid off the lap. He found the baby's soft blanket. He gave it to her, very gently. The baby stopped crying. She grabbed one of his fingers and held on tight. On the TV, the crowd cheered again, but this time the family clapped softly, quiet as mice. The baby smiled at Aiden. "More game," Aiden whispered.

Arthur ran up the steps to Milo's house. He carried his blue teddy bear under one arm. Milo opened the door with a big smile.

"Let's play house!" said Milo. He pointed to a blanket over two chairs. "This is our home. My doll is the baby." But the baby doll had no bed. Milo looked and looked. No box was big enough.

Then Arthur saw something. He put his teddy down in a basket. The basket was round and soft, like a nest. The teddy fit just right! "Can the baby sleep here too?" Arthur asked. Milo nodded fast. "Yes! It is a perfect bed."

The baby doll went into the basket next to the teddy. Milo whispered, "Shh, the baby is sleeping." Arthur whispered too. He tucked the blanket up to the doll's chin.

Milo's mom came in with two cups of warm milk. "How is the baby?" she asked quietly. "Sleeping in her nest!" said Arthur. He picked up a toy spoon and fed the teddy a pretend snack. Milo laughed and clapped.

"Now the baby needs a hat," said Milo. He ran to get a small sock. Arthur held the doll still while Milo pulled it on.

Maya was four today. Her party was at the park. There was a big table with a cake on it. Grandma had put four candles on top. Dad lit the candles with a match. Maya stood back and watched.

Then the wind blew. The candle flames bent and wobbled. Maya gasped. One flame went out. Then another flame went out. The wind had blown them out. Maya had an idea.

"Can the wind blow out all of them?" she asked.

Grandma smiled. "You can try," she said.

Maya took a big breath. She puffed hard like the wind. The last two flames went out. A little smoke curled up. Everyone clapped and cheered.

"Now we sing," said Mom. The family sang the birthday song. Maya's cup tipped over and juice began to spill. Grandma caught it with a napkin. "No problem," Grandma said.

They ate cake on the grass. Maya said, "The wind puffed, and I puffed, and the candles went out." She took another big bite.

Hazel held her bunny in the store. Then she let go to grab a big red apple. The apple went into the cart. But bunny was gone.

"Where did bunny go?" Hazel asked.

Mama made the cart go slow. They looked down each aisle. They saw bread and milk and jam. No bunny.

Then Hazel stopped. She put her apple on the floor. She gave it a little push. The apple rolled far, under the shelf. The round apple made it all the way to the wall.

"Bunny might roll too," Hazel said.

She got down on her knees. She peeked under the shelf. It was dark in there. She saw a soft gray ear.

Mama reached in with her long arm. Out came bunny, with a bit of dust on his nose.

Hazel gave bunny a hug. Then she put him deep in her pocket, where he could not fall out.

"My apple found you," she whispered.

Athena was playing in the backyard. Her toy train sat on the grass. Grandma was by the grill at the far end.

A butterfly flew by. It was orange. Athena wanted to follow it.

"Stay close to Grandma," said Grandma. Athena counted her steps. One, two, three. The butterfly landed on the fence. Athena wanted to go to the fence.

Grandma held her hand. "The grill is hot," said Grandma. Athena looked at the grill. It was silver and big. It made a sizzling sound. Grandma put a bun near it with a long spoon. Athena saw the spoon. It was not for touching. That was the rule.

The butterfly flew again. It landed on Grandma's shoulder. "Look," said Athena. "It stays close too." Grandma laughed. "That butterfly is neat," she said.

The buns were ready. Grandma put the hot food on a plate. Athena waited on the grass with her train. She pushed the train. Choo, choo. The butterfly sat nearby.

Athena ate her bun at the little table. The bun was warm and good. The butterfly sat on the fence in the sun. Grandma poured cold water into a cup. Athena touched the cup. It felt cool on her hands.

"Stay close, stay safe," said Grandma. Athena snuggled next to her. The train went choo, choo, round and round.

Ayla was at Grandma's house. It was a cloudy day. "Let's play a game," said Grandma. She held up a card with a big letter on it.

"Can you find this letter in the room?" asked Grandma. The card had a big B on it. Ayla looked around. She saw a book on the table. She pointed at it. "B!" she said. Grandma smiled. "And B makes a buh sound," she said. "Buh, buh, book."

Ayla wanted to find more. She looked at the basket by the chair. "Ball!" she said. It started with B too. She touched the ball. It was smooth and bouncy. "Buh, buh, ball," she said all by herself.

Then Grandma held up a card with a big M on it. Hmm. Ayla looked and looked. Where was an M? Then she saw the milk glass on the tray. She ran over and put her little hand on it. The glass was cold. "Mmm, milk!" she said. Grandma clapped her hands. Ayla laughed and held the M card up high. "More letters, Grandma! More!"

Lea stood at the gate of the school playground. She held her mama's hand very tight. "I want a friend," she whispered. Mama smiled. "Let's look around."

A boy was pouring sand down a slide. The sand made a little pile at the bottom. Lea watched. He poured more sand. The pile grew high. Lea let go of mama's hand. She grabbed a small cup. She scooped her own sand. She poured it next to his pile. Now the pile was bigger.

"More sand, more pile," said the boy. He laughed. Lea laughed too. "I am Tom," he said. "I am Lea," she said. They made the pile big and round together. Mama sat on a bench close by. She waved. Lea waved back. Then she poured one more cup of sand.

Nathan held his lantern at the festival. Papa held his lantern too. It was dark outside. The lanterns were small paper balls with a light inside.

Nathan wanted his lantern to glow like the moon. But his lantern stayed dim. "Why is yours so bright?" he asked. "Let us walk up the hill," said Papa. "We will see."

They walked slowly. Nathan held his lantern with two hands. The grass by the path was wet. Nathan's shoes went squish, squish. Up they went, one step at a time.

At the top of the hill, Papa stopped. He turned the little stick on the lantern. Click. The lantern grew bright. "It was turned down," Papa said. "Now it is up."

Nathan looked at his own stick. He turned it. Click. His lantern glowed too. "Mine is like the moon!" he said. Down the hill, all the lanterns bobbed like little stars. Nathan walked with his, glowing all the way home.

The bookmobile came to Luna's street. It was a little truck full of books. Luna held her mama's hand. "Can I take one home?" she asked. "Yes," said Mama. "First you get a card."

A kind man gave Luna a small card. It had her name on it. It felt like a gift in her hand. Luna picked a book about a red bird. The man stamped the back of it. The stamp made a mark. The mark told the day to bring the book back.

"I want to keep it forever," Luna said. She moved the book behind her back. The man shook his head, soft and kind. "Others need to read it too," he said. "Bring it back, and you can take a new one."

The shelf was empty where the bird book had been. Another girl was looking there. Luna saw her. She gave the book back to the man. "Can I take the moon one?" she asked. He smiled and stamped it.

Emile went to the vet with his dad. There was a small gray rabbit in a cage. Emile wanted to take him home. The vet opened the cage. She put the rabbit on the table. The rabbit's nose went up and down, up and down.

The vet gave Emile a soft brush. Emile brushed the rabbit's back. The rabbit pushed his head under Emile's hand. "He likes that," said the vet. Emile gave the rabbit a green leaf. The rabbit took it in his teeth. He chewed and chewed.

Dad put the rabbit in a box with holes. At home, Emile put water in a little bowl. The rabbit drank. Then he sat still and closed his eyes. Emile gave him one soft kiss on his head. "Good night, rabbit," said Emile. The rabbit's ears went down, slow and sleepy.

Jasmine wanted to get the beanbag into the hoop. She threw it. It went low and fell on the grass. Her dog Max ran over and gave the beanbag a lick. "Yuck, Max," said Jasmine. She wiped it on her pants.

Dad rolled her a big red ball. Jasmine held out one hand. The ball bounced off her fingers. She tried again. One hand, and the ball fell again. Then Dad said, "Try two hands." Jasmine made two arms like a big bowl. The ball went in. "I got it!" she said. Max wagged his furry tail.

Then Jasmine looked at the hoop. She held the beanbag up high. She threw it high. The beanbag went in. "One, two, three!" she counted, jumping. Max barked, and Jasmine hugged the ball with both hands.

Julia could not find her bear. She looked under the bed. She looked in the toy box. No bear. Julia felt sad. Her lip went down, down, down.

Then she heard a bump. It came from the laundry basket. Julia felt a little scared. She held her mama's shirt tight. "Mama, something is in there," she said.

Mama lifted the towel. Out popped bear! Julia felt so excited. She jumped up and clapped. "Bear!" she shouted. Then she felt angry too. "Bad bear! You hid from me!"

Bear's fur was warm and sweet, like sunshine. Julia gave him a big hug. She stuck him under her arm, where he fit just right. "Bedtime, bear," she said. She turned off the light switch with Mama's help. Julia felt happy now. She closed her eyes and whispered, "Sleep tight, little bear."

Clara sat at the big art table. She was making a butterfly with paper and glue. She wanted it to look cute, with shiny wings. First she spread glue on the wings. Then she took the glitter jar. She sprinkled glitter all over the paper. She shook off the extra glitter. Where had the glitter gone? Some fell off onto the table. But the wings were still shiny. Clara looked closely. The glitter stayed only where the glue was. The dry parts were plain paper. Was it the glue that held it? She drew a fish on a new paper. She put glue only on its tail. She sprinkled glitter again. She tipped the paper sideways. The loose glitter slid off, like snow. The tail sparkled. "Look," said Clara. "Glue first, then sparkle." She held up her shiny fish.

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Maeva wanted to show him her park. She put bread in her little bag. "We can feed the ducks," she said.

The park smelled like grass and flowers. Grandpa sat on a warm bench. Maeva stood by the pond. It was quiet. No ducks came. The ducks were far away on the other side. Maeva waited. Her arms felt tired of holding the bag.

Then she tore a piece of bread. She dropped a tiny bit in the water. Plip. One duck turned its head. Maeva dropped another bit. Plip. The duck swam fast. Then more ducks came. They came and came. "Grandpa, look!" Maeva yelled. "My bread brought them!"

Grandpa laughed and helped her tear more pieces. The ducks ate from the edge of the water. Then Maeva saw something small and fluffy. A line of ducklings paddled behind one big duck. "Babies!" said Maeva. She dropped one last soft piece. The littlest duckling grabbed it first.

Jack walked home with Daddy. He held a small box. Inside was a bunny. Her name was Pip.

Pip was hungry. She bit the box. She made a funny hole.

"She needs food," said Daddy. They got a shiny spoon. Daddy put bunny food in Pip's bowl. Jack gave her a leaf of lettuce.

Pip ate the lettuce. Then she stopped biting. She sat down and got very still. Her ears went soft.

"Is she sad?" asked Jack.

Daddy put his hand near Pip. Pip hopped onto Jack's lap. She nuzzled his hand.

Pip was not sad. She was happy and full.

Jack stroked her soft fur. Pip closed her eyes. The birds began to sing outside.

Jack held her gently all the way home. "I will feed you every day," he said.

Jacob wanted to find his brown ball. It had rolled into the backyard. He held Grandpa's hand and went out the door.

Grandpa was cooking at the grill. The grill was hot. It made sizzling sounds. "Stay here with me," Grandpa said. Jacob sat on the step, close to Grandpa.

Jacob saw something round near the fence. It was under a spiky bush. He stood up. "I see my ball!" he said. Jacob took one step toward the bush. Grandpa caught his hand fast. "Not there. The bush has sharp sticks. I will get it."

Grandpa got a long stick. He pushed the ball out with it. The ball rolled to Jacob's feet. Jacob picked it up. It was warm from sitting in the sun. His hands felt the warm. Then he touched the cold step. Cold!

"Can we share the ball?" Grandpa asked. Jacob rolled it to Grandpa. Grandpa rolled it back. They played until the food was done. Then they sat together and ate warm food at the little table.

Brooks was on the swim team this summer. Every Tuesday he went to the big pool. His team was called the Little Fish.

Brooks wore goggles. The goggles hid his eyes. "Ready, Little Fish!" said Coach Mia. Brooks held the wall. He kicked his legs fast. Splash, splash, kick, kick. The water went up and up. Then Brooks felt himself move! His fast kicks made the water fly, and the water pushed him forward. Splash, splash, kick, kick. He moved some more.

Brooks counted the wall marks. One, two, three. Then he touched the far wall. Coach Mia clapped. Brooks climbed out and wrapped up in his big white towel. It was soft and snowy like a cloud. He sat by the sheep float bobbing in the shallow end. "I kicked hard," Brooks said, "and I went fast!"

Charles sat at the dinner table. He wanted the big red cup. It was the cup with paint on it, little blue stars painted by his sister May.

"Can I have the red cup?" asked Charles.

"You had it last night," said May. "Tonight it is my turn."

Charles looked at the plain white cup in front of him. He looked at the red cup. He reached out his hand.

Dad put his hand on top of Charles' hand. "One cup each," said Dad. "We all take a turn."

Charles frowned. Then he saw May sip from the red cup. She made a happy sound, a little "mm" sound.

"Is the red cup the best cup?" asked Charles.

"No," said May. "The milk tastes the same."

Charles picked up his white cup. He took a sip. The milk was cold and sweet. May was right. It tasted the same.

"Your turn tomorrow," said May. "I promise."

Charles smiled. "Okay. You can have my blue plate too."

"You want to share?" asked May.

"Yes. Fair is fair," said Charles.

Mom laughed. "Good sharing, Charles."

After dinner, Charles felt sleepy. The dog was asleep under the table. Charles patted his soft ears.

"Tomorrow," said Charles, "I get the red cup."

"Tomorrow," said May, and she laughed again.

Aiden put on his red boot. Then he put on the other one. "We need to go," said Mama. "The big meal is at the hall."

At the hall, everyone held hands. But Aiden did not know the words. "Say them with me," said Grandma. She squeezed his hand. Aiden squeezed back.

Grandma said the blessing. Aiden said it too, word by word. When he said the last word, everyone smiled. Then everyone picked up a fork. "The food waits for the words," said Grandma. "Is that true?" asked Aiden. "Watch," she said.

Aiden watched. No fork moved. Then Grandpa said, "Amen!" and every fork went down at once. The plates went clink, clink, clink.

Next month, Aiden ran in with one boot on. He held out his hands first. "Wait, wait!" he said. "The food needs the words!" Grandma laughed and laughed. "You say them, Aiden."

Aiden said the blessing all by himself.

Paisley ran to the circle rug at daycare. Miss Dana was holding her guitar.

"We need one more friend to sing," said Miss Dana. Ben sat in the corner. He was sad because his toy car was missing.

Paisley waved to him. "Come sing with us!" Ben came slowly and sat down.

Miss Dana played the counting song. "One, two, three, four, five." Everyone clapped on each number. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Paisley clapped loud on ten. Ben clapped too, just a little.

Then it was snack time. Miss Dana asked, "Who wants to pass out the cups?" Paisley raised her hand high.

She counted the cups as she set them out. "One, two, three." The cups made a little click on the table each time. "Four, five, six, seven, eight." Now everyone had a cup but Ben.

"Nine," said Paisley, putting one at his spot. Ben smiled.

At the art table, Paisley found a crayon with a sharp point. She used it to draw ten circles. "Look, Ben! I can count them!" She tapped each one. Ben laughed at her tapping joke and tapped some too.

Then he held up his drawing of a red car.

"Is that your toy car?" Paisley asked.

"Yes," said Ben. "I can make a new one."

Theodore went to the library with his mama. He found a book about a spider. The spider had eight little eyes. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight," said Theodore. He counted every eye.

He opened the book. The front was the part with the spider. He turned a page. The spider spun a web. He turned another page. A fly fell in. "Mama, the words tell me what happens!" said Theodore. His mama smiled.

Theodore wanted to keep the book forever. He hid it under his coat. A kind librarian knelt down beside him. "You can take it home," she said softly. "One, two, three weeks, then bring it back." Theodore gave back the book at the desk. He got a stamp on his hand. Then he picked out one more book, all by himself.

Blake wanted to fill the big water table at daycare. She turned the small faucet on top. Only a little water came out.

"Try the big faucet," said her teacher, Ms. Ruiz. "The big one is fast. The small one is slow." Blake turned the big faucet. Whoosh! The water ran fast. Soon the table was full. "That was fast," said Blake. "The small faucet was slow."

Then Blake touched the water. "Brrr, it is cold," she said. Ms. Ruiz brought a kettle. "The water in here is hot. I will pour it. You watch." She poured a little hot water in. Blake touched the side of the table. "Now it is warm. Not too hot. Not too cold."

"Time to play," said Ms. Ruiz. Blake dropped in a big boat and a small duck. She pushed the boat. It went fast. The duck floated slow. "Talk like a duck, Daisy duck," said Blake. Daisy laughed and clapped.

"You did it all alone," said Ms. Ruiz. "Big and small. Hot and cold. Fast and slow." Blake pushed the boat again. The small duck bobbed behind it, all the way to the bottom of the table.

Kayden wanted warm cookies. It was cold winter outside. Mom said, "Let's bake." Kayden helped from his chair. He had two eyes to see the flour. It looked white and soft like snow. He had two ears to hear the mixer. It went round and round. The dough got smooth.

Then Kayden had a problem. "How do I know when cookies are done?" he asked. Mom said, "Use your body. It knows." Kayden used one nose to smell. Mmm, sweet! The smell filled the kitchen. He waited. His nose smelled warm butter and sugar. "Done!" said Mom. She used the big oven mitt. Kayden touched a cooled cookie with one hand. It felt bumpy. He tasted it with his tongue. Sweet! "I will remember this," said Kayden. He counted his helpers: two eyes, two ears, one nose, one tongue, two hands. Mom laughed and ate one too.

Clara saw her friend Ben cry at school. His face turned down. Clara made the same face. Then she felt sad too. Her teacher, Miss Kim, gave Ben a purple truck. Ben smiled big. Clara made the same face. Now she felt happy too. Clara wanted to know why. She tried it again at play time. Mia ran fast and looked excited. Clara made the same face. Her tummy felt jumpy. Then Sam fell down and looked scared. Clara made the same face. Her eyes got wide. Faces were like a magnet, Clara thought. One face pulled another face to it. She went to Sam and held his hand. "You are okay," she said. Sam stood up. His scared face went away. Clara's went away too. Then Miss Kim put music on. Everyone danced. Ben filled his truck with blocks and laughed. "You laugh, I laugh," said Clara. Sam laughed with her.

John sat in his car seat. He was going to see Grandma. She had a big dog named Max. Max was hungry and had no bone.
The car went fast on the big road. Then it went slow on the small street. The sun was hot on the window. John rolled it up. The air inside turned cold.
A big truck went by. It was bigger than ten cars. A small bug sat on the glass. It was smaller than John's thumb.
At last they got to Grandma's house. Dad turned the car off. Grandma held a clean bowl of water. She gave Max a big bone. Max wagged his tail.
"Max was so hungry," said Grandma.
Max put his soft head on John's lap.

Sofia stood in the school hallway. She held her red backpack with both hands. Her backpack had a sheep on it, a soft white sheep with a bell. The big classroom door would not open. Sofia pushed it. Nothing happened. She pulled it. Nothing happened. "How do doors like this open?" she wondered.

Then she saw a small round button. It was red, like her backpack. Sofia pressed the button with one finger. Whoosh! The door slid open all by itself. Sofia's eyes went wide. She stepped back, and the door slid shut again. She pressed the button once more. Whoosh! The door opened again. "The button makes the door move," she whispered.

Inside, a teacher was mixing paint at a little table. Yellow paint went in. Blue paint went in. The teacher stirred and stirred. Now the paint was green! Sofia hung her backpack on a low hook and walked closer to watch. "Can I mix too?" she asked. The teacher gave her a stick and a small cup.

Maya ran into the garage. Dad had a big surprise there. It was a drum, red and shiny. Maya wanted to play it fast.

She tapped with one finger. The drum made a tiny sound. Tap. Tap. So small!

Then Dad put a drumstick in her hand. "Try this," he said. Maya hit the drum with the stick. BOOM! The drum made a big, big sound! Maya jumped. "Again!" she said. BOOM! BOOM! The whole garage rumbled. Her hair even wiggled.

The stick made the big sound. Her finger made the small sound. Maya tapped her finger again. Tap. Then she used the stick. BOOM! Tap. BOOM! She kept going back and forth.

"Listen, Dad!" she shouted. "I can make it big! I can make it small!" Dad laughed and covered his ears. Maya hit the drum one more time. BOOM!

William was on the swim team. Every Saturday morning he went to the big pool. His team was called the Blue Fish. William could not swim the whole lap yet.

Coach Maya said, "Kick your legs, William." William kicked hard. He splashed a lot. But he stayed in one spot. The water was cool and tickly. William felt stuck.

Then William watched his friend Mia. Mia kicked small kicks. Her legs went up and down, up and down. Mia moved fast through the water. William looked and looked.

William tried small kicks too. He kicked like Mia. Up and down, up and down. His body slid forward in the water. He moved past the rope. He moved all the way to the wall!

"Coach, look!" William called. Coach Maya clapped. Mia swam over and gave him a high five. "Good kicking," she said. William smiled big.

At the end, the team sat on the steps. Coach Maya handed out juice. William took two cups. He gave one to Mia. "Thank you," said Mia. William took a big sip of his juice and said, "Same time next Saturday?"

Ethan wanted the red crayon. It sat high on the art shelf. His paint dragon needed red fire, and the red crayon was the magic fire holder.

Ethan jumped. His hand could not reach. He tried a big stretch. Still no crayon. He almost pushed a chair over to climb. His teacher, Miss Amy, came fast. "No climbing, Ethan," she said. "Ask me for help instead."

"Miss Amy, please get the red crayon?" Ethan asked. Miss Amy smiled. She took it down with one gentle hand. "Thank you," said Ethan. He ran back to his dragon.

Then Ethan bumped the table. Lily's paint cup tipped. Blue paint ran across her paper cat. Lily began to cry. "Sorry, Lily," said Ethan. He grabbed a paper towel. Together they wiped the blue away.

The paint made a big blue lake. Lily laughed. "Now my cat can swim," she said. Ethan drew red fire over the lake. The dragon flew above it. "Roar," said Ethan. "Thank you for my lake," said Lily.

Lily stood in the reading corner. She had a brand new library card. It was red with her name on it.

"I want this one," said Lily. She held up a book about fire trucks. The cover was rough like sandpaper.

"Good choice," said the librarian, Miss Jo. She stamped the card. Then she stamped a little paper in the book.

"What is that?" asked Lily.

"That paper tells you the day the book comes back," said Miss Jo. "Then other kids can read it too."

Lily frowned. "But I want to keep it forever."

Miss Jo smiled. "You can borrow it again later."

Lily took the book home. She read it six times. She read it to her bear. She read it to her socks.

At bedtime, Mom said, "We can hang your new library card on the wall by your bed."

"Okay," said Lily. "But the book goes back on Sunday. My friend Ben wants the fire trucks next."

On Sunday, Lily carried the book all by herself. She set it on the desk, nice and flat.

"Here," she said. "But can I borrow it again?"

"You sure can," said Miss Jo. She stamped the book once more.

Lily grinned. "Ben, don't bend the rough cover," she whispered. "I need it back."

Zayn ran onto the big field at the community center. One coach, one whistle, one bouncy ball. "Time for soccer, Zayn!" Zayn kicked the ball with his red shoe. The ball went far. Then it stopped. Why did it stop? Zayn looked down. The grass was wet from the morning rain. He touched it with his hand. Cold! Wet and cold, like a splash.

Zayn tried again. On the dry grass, the ball rolled fast. On the wet grass, the ball went slow. He tried once more. Slow again on the wet part. Hmm. So that was it. Wet grass made the ball slow down.

His teammate Sam came running. Sam slipped and took a big fall. "The grass is slippery!" said Sam. Zayn waved to Coach Maya. "Watch this part," he said. He kicked the ball on the dry grass. It rolled and rolled, all the way to the net.

Colton ran to the snack table at daycare. His eyes saw a big orange basket. Teacher Mia lifted the lid. "Guess what is inside," she said.

Colton used his nose to sniff. "I smell apples!" he said. It was true. A pile of red apples sat in the basket. Everyone clapped.

Teacher Mia gave each friend one apple slice. Colton touched his slice. It felt cool and smooth. He took a big bite. His tongue tasted sweet apple juice. Yum!

Then Colton heard a loud crunch. He looked over. His friend Zoe was biting her apple. Crunch, crunch! Colton bit his apple too. His bite made a big crunch as well. The two friends crunched back and forth. Crunch! Crunch! Crunch!

Zoe laughed so hard that apple bits fell on her shirt. "You are messy," Colton said. He looked down at his own shirt. His shirt was messy too. Teacher Mia helped them wipe off the apple bits.

Then Colton held up his last piece of apple. He waved it in the air. "One more big crunch!" he said.

It was Ellie's birthday. Everyone came to her classroom. Mama hung three balloons by the window. One balloon had a big owl on it. Ellie's friend Sam pointed. "The owl is upside down!" The owl balloon looked silly with its feet in the air.

Then the owl balloon came loose. It floated up and up. It was lost near the ceiling. Ellie could not reach it. Grandpa got a chair. He stood on the chair. He caught the owl. Now the owl hung right again, with its feet down. "Hoot hoot!" said Sam, and everyone laughed.

Next came the cake. Miss Tara, the teacher, lit three little candles. One candle, two candles, three candles. "Make a wish," said Mama. Ellie took a big breath. She blew and blew. One candle went out. Two candles went out. Three candles went out. "Again!" said Sam. "Not yet," laughed Miss Tara. "First we eat the cake."

Everly sat in the big red seat. Mama sat next to her. A lady on stage held a violin. The lady played a song, and the song had a beat.

Everly wanted to clap too. She clapped fast, fast, fast. Her claps did not match the song at all. The boy next to her covered his ears. Everly put her hands in her lap.

Mama leaned close. "Try one clap, then wait," she said. "Then one more." Everly watched Mama's hands. Mama clapped, then waited, then clapped. It looked like a slow game. Everly watched and watched. Then she tried.

Clap, wait, clap, wait. Now her claps sat right on the beat. The song and her hands went together. The boy uncovered his ears and clapped too. Everly smiled so big her cheeks felt salty from the snack she had eaten before.

At the end, the violin got quiet. Everly stood up and sang her whole rhyme from memory. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." She did not miss one word. The lady on stage looked at Everly and clapped for her. Everly clapped back, clap, wait, clap.

Jordan dug a small hole with his hands. His teacher, Miss Ana, made the holes deep enough for seeds. Jordan dropped a carrot seed in each one. Then he patted the soil down, soft and flat.

Every day Jordan ran to the garden circle. He watered the dirt with a little blue can. But nothing came up. "Where are my carrots?" he asked. Miss Ana smiled. "Seeds need water every day," she said. Jordan saw that his friend Mia had forgotten to water her spot. Mia's dirt was dry and cracked. Jordan shared his water can with her.

Soon little green leaves popped up. Jordan's leaves came first. Then Mia's leaves came too, right after Jordan gave her water. Jordan clapped his hands. "Look, Mia! Water makes them grow!" Mia laughed and filled the can again.

Michael was at Grandma's house. He wanted to make a picture for her. Grandma put red paint, yellow paint, and a brush on the table. Michael dipped the brush in the red paint. He made a big red circle on the paper.

Then he wanted a sun too. Grandma said, "Try the yellow paint next." Michael put the brush in the yellow paint. He touched the yellow onto his red circle. The red circle turned orange! Michael looked and looked. His eyes got very big.

"Grandma, come see!" he said. Grandma came to the table. "What a pretty orange sun," she said. Michael made another circle. He put red, then yellow, and watched the orange grow again. "This one is for you," he said, and he held it up high.

Margot sat on the couch with Daddy. The big game was on TV. Everyone wore red shirts.

"Go, go, go!" they all shouted. Margot shouted too. "Go, go, go!"

Then baby Sam began to cry. The shouting was too loud for him. Aunt Jen picked Sam up. "He needs it quiet," she said.

Margot wanted Sam to feel better. She tried something. She clapped her hands very softly. Sam stopped crying. He looked at her leg, kicking slow and lazy on the couch. He made a little smile.

"Does he like soft claps?" Margot asked. "Yes, he does," said Aunt Jen.

So Margot clapped softly again. Sam smiled bigger. Now when the game got loud, Margot did not hurry to shout. She clapped her soft clap, just for Sam, and he giggled.

Nathan sat at the big table in writing club. He had a new hat on. It was too wide and slid over his eyes. He pushed it back.

Nathan wanted to write his name. He held the pencil in his whole fist. He made a line. The line sank down into a squiggle. It did not look like a letter at all.
