The teacher, Miss Ada, sat next to him. "Do you want to try my way?" she asked. "Yes," said Nathan. She showed him how to pinch the pencil with two fingers. Nathan tried it. He made a tall N. Then an A. Then a T. "NAT!" he said. "That is me!"

Miss Ada clapped. Then Nathan saw a small H at the end of her card. He copied it. Now the card said NATH. Nathan laughed. "One more letter tomorrow," said Miss Ada. Nathan drew a wide smiley face next to his name.

William sat in his car seat. He was going to Grandma's house. "Are we there yet?" he asked.

Mom said, "Play a game. Look out the window." William looked. He saw a cow! Then he saw a sheep. Then a dog by a fence. "Animals!" he shouted. Mom laughed.

William reached into his bag. He wanted his red crayon. He wanted to draw the cow. But the crayon was missing! "Oh no," said William. He looked under his coat. He looked by his feet. No crayon.

Then he saw his toy truck on the seat. He pushed the truck. The truck rolled. The crayon rolled out from under the truck! "Found it!" said William. He picked it up. He drew a cow on his paper. He drew a sheep too.

"I'm hungry," said William. Mom gave him a banana. William ate it up. Then he drew a big yellow banana. Outside, a horse ran by. William drew the horse fast, fast, fast.

The car stopped. "We are here!" said Mom. William held up his paper. "Look, Grandma! Animals and foods!"

Lucy went to the park with her dad. She saw a red balloon tied to a bench. A boy stood near the bench. He was crying.

"Are you sad?" Lucy asked. The boy nodded. His balloon had a small hole. It got small and small. Soon it was just a flat piece of rubber.

Lucy had chalk in her bag. She took out the yellow one. "I can color you a balloon," she said. She drew a big yellow circle on the ground. She drew a string on it too.

The boy stopped crying. He looked at the yellow circle. "A balloon that never pops!" he said. Now he was happy.

A big dog ran by. It was loud. Lucy felt scared. She held her dad's hand. The dog's owner called it back. The dog sat down and wagged its tail.

Lucy patted the soft dog. "Nice dog," she said. The boy patted it too. The dog licked the chalk circle. It left a wet mark that looked like a smile.

"I want to draw more," said the boy. Lucy gave him the blue chalk. He drew a blue balloon next to the yellow one. Then he drew a green one. Lucy clapped her hands. She was so excited.

A girl came by with a ball. She grabbed the blue chalk without asking. Lucy felt angry. Her face went hot. "That's his chalk," she said.

The girl gave it back. "Sorry," she said. "Can I draw too?" The boy said yes. She drew a pink balloon with a bow.

Four balloons sat on the ground, all in a row. Lucy squinted one eye and looked at them. They seemed to shine in the sun.

The boy looked at his flat red balloon. Then he looked at the four chalk balloons. He smiled a big smile. "These are better," he said. "They can't fly away, and they can't pop."

Lucy drew one more thing. She drew a small hand holding a small hand. "That's us," she said. "Friends at the park."

Ethan had a library book about a dog. It was time for bed. He held the book tight. "I want to keep this book forever," he said.

Dad sat on the bed. "Time to read," he said. "Open the front cover. That is where we start." Ethan turned the pages one by one. He saw the dog bark at a cat. Then the cat ran up a tree.

Ethan pointed at the letters. "What do these say?" he asked. Dad read the words out loud. Ethan looked at the page. The words told about the dog. The words and the picture went together.

At the last page, Ethan frowned. "Can we read it again?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "But on Friday we take the book back. Someone else wants to read it too." Ethan held the book to his chest. He was not sure.

On Friday, Ethan carried the book to the library. He set it on the desk. Then he saw a girl pick it up. She hugged it just like he had. Ethan waved at her. "The dog barks at a cat," he told her. She smiled and opened the front cover.

That night, Dad gave Ethan a new library book. It had a long, long train on the cover. Ethan opened the front page. "This one is mine for a while," he said. "But not forever." He patted the cover gently and turned the first page.

Hailey wanted to blow the bubbles. But her brother Sam had the wand. Sam blew one bubble. Then he blew two more.

"Next it is my turn," Hailey said. Sam gave her the wand. Hailey dipped it in the cup. She blew a big, round bubble. Sam smiled and clapped.

Then Hailey saw Sam's face go sad. He sat down on the step. Hailey looked at the wand in her hand. She held it out to Sam. "Your turn now," she said.

Sam took the wand. He blew a bubble that floated over the street. It popped in the air.

Mom called, "Snack time!" They ran inside. Two apple slices sat on each plate. Same for Hailey, same for Sam. They sat down side by side. Hailey took a big bite of her apple and smiled.

Yesterday Grandma made cookies with Madelyn. They were warm and sweet. Today all the cookies were gone. Madelyn wanted more cookies now.

"Can we bake cookies today?" she asked.

"Mixing comes first," said Grandma. "Baking comes later."

Madelyn helped mix the dough. She dropped one spoon of dough onto the pan. Plop. Then she dropped another. Plop. Soon the pan was full.

Then the doorbell rang. It was the mail carrier with a letter. The letter was for Grandma. It was stuck a little in the door, and Grandma pulled it out. The letter was from Aunt Jo. It said, "I will visit tomorrow."

"Tomorrow," said Madelyn. "That is after today."

"That is right," said Grandma.

Grandma put the pan in the oven. Madelyn watched from her chair. The kitchen began to smell sweet. The dough puffed up into round cookies.

"Now we wait," said Grandma. "Waiting comes before eating."

Madelyn waited. She looked at the oven. She looked at the letter.

At last the cookies were ready. Grandma put one on a plate for Madelyn. It was warm and sweet, just like yesterday's.

"Tomorrow Aunt Jo can have one too," said Madelyn, and she took a big bite.

Blake wanted a big tomato of her own. She held a tiny plant in her hand. "This one is too little," she said. Dad smiled. "Watch what water does."

Blake put the plant in a pot. She patted the dirt down soft. Then she gave it water from a small can. The dirt turned dark and wet.

Every day Blake came back. She counted the leaves. The number got bigger and bigger. One, two, three, four! The little plant grew tall like her knees.

Then one morning Blake saw something red. A tomato! It was round and shiny. Dad picked it and washed it. Blake took a taste. "Yum," she said. "Water made it grow." Dad laughed. "And you helped."

Matteo wanted to see the snow again. Yesterday the snow had fallen. Today the snow was melting. Little pools of water sat on the path.

"Will it snow again?" Matteo asked. Mom smiled. "Later," she said. "First comes bedtime, then comes tomorrow."

Matteo looked out the window now. The sky was dark. The melting snow shone in the light. He could not see new snow yet.

Mom helped him put on his warm pajamas. He brushed his teeth. He picked a book about a bear. Mom read it in her soft voice.

Matteo's face felt sleepy. He yawned a big yawn. "Sleep now," Mom said. "Snow later."

He closed his eyes. He waited and waited. Then he fell fast asleep.

In the morning, the sun came up. Matteo ran to the window. The sky was white. Snow was falling again! It fell on the trees. It fell on the path. It covered the old melting snow.

"Mom! Mom!" Matteo called. "Tomorrow came! And the snow came too!" He pressed his warm hands on the cold glass. "Today it snows!"

Carter wants to build a big tower at daycare. He finds the big blocks first. Big blocks go on the bottom. Then he finds the small blocks. Small blocks go on the top.

The tower grows tall. Carter pats each block. "Slow and steady," says his teacher, Miss Jo. Carter goes slow. One block. Then one more.

His friend Mia runs by fast. Her feet go stamp, stamp, stamp. The big tower wiggles. It falls down with a crash. All the blocks are on the floor now. They look dirty, so Miss Jo wipes them with a wet cloth.

Carter waits. He waits until Mia stops running. Then he starts again. Big blocks on the bottom. Small blocks on the top. Slow and steady. Slow and steady.

At snack time, Miss Jo brings warm muffins. "Hot, hot," she says, and blows on each one. Carter waits for his muffin to cool. He takes a small bite. Not hot anymore. Just right.

After snack, Carter builds his tower again. Nobody runs this time. The big tower stands tall. It does not wiggle. It does not fall.

"Look, Miss Jo!" says Carter. "My tower is so big!"

Gabriel wanted to find something red at Grandma's house. He looked in the big kitchen drawer. He found a blue spoon. He looked under the little table. He found a yellow cup. He looked in the toy box. He found a green ball.

"Grandma, I can't find red," said Gabriel. Grandma smiled. "Come to the window," she said. Gabriel looked out. Grandma's red bike was leaning by the fence!

Then Grandma held up a red apple. "Will you share it with me?" she asked. Gabriel nodded. Grandma cut the apple with her safe knife. Gabriel chewed his piece slowly. It was sweet and juicy. He put the green ball next to the blue spoon and the yellow cup.

"Look, Grandma," said Gabriel. "All my colors, in a row!" Grandma laughed and took a big bite of her apple.

Harper went to the pharmacy with Dad. She saw a little bottle of soap. It had a duck on top. "Can I hold it?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. Harper squeezed the duck. Soap came out. She squeezed again. More soap came out.

Then Harper saw a boy by the sink. He put soap on his hands. He rubbed and rubbed. He sang a song while he rubbed. "Why does he rub so long?" Harper asked. "Watch," said Dad. The boy held his hands under the water. The bubbles ran off. His hands came out shiny and clean.

Harper wanted shiny hands too. She put soap on her hands. "What if I rub quick?" she asked. "Try it," said Dad. She rubbed quick and rinsed. Her fingers still looked dull. "No shine!" she said. So she rubbed and rubbed. She sang the song too. The water carried the bubbles away. Harper held up her hands. They shined in the light. "Duck soap, you are my best friend," she said, and she squeezed the duck one more time.

It was Diwali night at Eleanor's house. Mama lit the little lamps with a match. Eleanor watched from her chair. "Can I help?" she asked. "Yes," said Mama. "You can put out the flowers."

One lamp, two lamps, three lamps. They made circles of light on the table. Eleanor put a flower by each one. The lamp made the flower glow. "Mama, look! The light touches the petals!" The petals looked like fire, but soft and orange.

Then Eleanor found one lamp with no flower. "Who lives here?" she asked. "Nobody yet," said Mama. Eleanor ran to the kitchen. She came back with a marigold, a rose, and a messy handful of petals. She made a little pile, red and yellow. Papa set the lamp on top. The whole pile glowed. "More light!" said Eleanor. "More flowers!" said Mama, and she hugged her tight.

Eliana went to the art gallery with her grandma. Eliana wanted to paint a picture of her toy monkey. The paint corner had little pots of colour.

"I need orange," said Eliana. "My monkey has an orange tummy."

But there was no orange pot. There was red. There was yellow. There was blue. Eliana looked and looked. No orange anywhere.

Eliana picked up a brush. She put red on the paper. Then she dabbed yellow right on top of the red spot. She swirled her brush around and around.

The red spot turned orange! Eliana gasped. The paint had made a new colour, all by itself.

"Grandma, look!" said Eliana. "My monkey can have his tummy now."

She painted a big orange tummy. Then she painted a blue tail and a red hat. Her monkey looked warm in his new colours.

Eliana was thirsty after all that painting. Grandma brought her water in a small paper cup.

Eliana looked at the cup. "Yellow cup, blue water," she said. She tipped a little blue paint towards the yellow cup. Then she stopped. "Not for drinking," she told her monkey. She put the paint down and took a big sip of water instead.

Hannah sat by the train window. She was going on a big family trip. Her bear, Mr. Buttons, sat on her lap.

"I want to see Grandma now," said Hannah. "Is the train slow today?"

Daddy looked out the window. "Rain," he said. "Lots of rain on the glass."

Hannah watched the rain. One drop slid down the window. It bumped into a little drop. Then the two drops made one big drop. The big drop slid down fast, like a race car.

Hannah gasped. She put her finger on the glass. The drop followed her finger! She moved her finger. The drop went that way too. It was a rain puppy.

"Look, Daddy!" she said. "I can lead it!"

She led the drop all the way down. Then it fell off the edge. Hannah laughed.

"Where did it go?" asked Daddy.

"It went to find Grandma," said Hannah. "It will tell her we are coming."

Then the train went around a bend. The sun came out. The rain stopped. And outside, Hannah saw one big yellow thing in a field.

"Daddy! A giant banana!"

"That is a moon bounce," said Daddy, laughing. "Maybe Grandma has one too."

"Maybe!" said Hannah. She hugged Mr. Buttons tight.

Ethan stood at the snack table at school. There were two plates of crackers. He wanted the plate with more crackers. But which plate had more?

His teacher, Miss Kim, said, "Count them." Ethan pointed at the red plate. He counted, "One, two, three, four, five." The last number was five. Then he counted the blue plate. "One, two, three, four, five, six." The last number was six. Six was more. Ethan picked the blue plate.

His friend Milo said, "Count again. Start at the other end." Ethan watched his own finger. He started from the last cracker this time. "One, two, three, four, five." The red plate still said five. He counted the blue plate backward. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six again!

Ethan counted both plates two more times. Each way gave the same numbers. Miss Kim smiled. Milo tried counting his own crackers from both ends too.

"Naughty crackers," said Milo. "They keep moving around." But the numbers stayed the same.

Ethan took his blue plate to the little line by the window. "Six crackers," he said. "I counted them every way."

Sophie wanted a big carrot of her own. Grandma gave her three little seeds. Sophie dug a small hole in the dirt. She dropped the seeds in and patted the soil. Then she poured water from her small blue can.

The next day, nothing grew. Sophie looked and looked. "Where is my carrot?" she asked. "The seeds are still working," said Grandma. So Sophie watered the dirt each day. She pulled one tiny weed that came up close.

One morning, green leaves popped out of the soil. Sophie clapped her hands. A pig in the next pen turned its head to look. Day by day, the leaves grew tall. At last, Grandma pulled up a fat orange carrot. "Wash it first," said Grandma. The water turned muddy. Sophie took a big crunchy bite.

Sara wanted to play the senses game. She had five picture cards on the floor. Each card had a body part on it. She did not know which card went first.

She looked at her hand. She touched the cat's soft fur. "Hands touch!" she said. She put the hand card up high on the wall.

Next she shook the rattle by her ear. She heard the sound. "Ears hear!" She hung the ear card up too.

Then she sniffed the apple on the table. "Nose smells. It smells sweet." The nose card went up.

She took a bite. "Tongue tastes!" Four cards were up now.

One card was left. Sara sat still and waited. She looked out the window. She saw a green snake in the grass! She saw it with her eyes. The eye card went up on the wall last.

All five cards hung in a row. Sara clapped her hands. "I did it! Five senses, all by myself."

Elias went to the big kitchen with his dad. Tonight the whole family would eat there. Elias wanted to help make the bread.

His dad gave him a bowl. Elias poured in flour. He added warm water from a big jug. He mixed it with a wooden spoon. The dough was soft and sticky.

Then his dad sprinkled in a little yeast. "Watch," his dad whispered, like a small mouse was listening. They put the bowl by the sunny window. Elias waited. Soon the dough began to puff up. It got big and round. It grew and grew, like a soft pillow.

"The bread is ready," said his dad. He put the dough in the oven, because ovens are hot. Elias watched from his safe spot. The kitchen began to smell warm and sweet.

Soon Mom came with the baby. Grandma came too. They all sat down at the long table. The bread was warm and soft. Elias tore a piece for everyone. "I made it grow," he said. Grandma took a big bite and smiled.

Isla ran to the big slide. The sun was on it. Dad put his hand on top. "Hot," he said. "Let's find a cool one." The small slide sat in the shade. Isla touched it. It felt cold. She slid down fast. Then she climbed up slow, slow, slow, like a sleepy turtle.

Isla wanted her juice pop next. It had been in the sun. It dripped onto her hand. The sun had made it melt! Dad held out his towel. "Sun makes pops go runny," he said. Isla wiped her sticky fingers.

She moved her cup to the shady bench. Then she stood very still. A little bird landed by her shoe. It hopped close. It pecked at a crumb. Isla whispered, "Hello, tiny friend."

The swing called her next. She pumped her legs fast. The wind rushed past her ears. Then she let the swing go slow. It stopped. "My legs did that," said Isla. Dad laughed. "Fast legs, big swing. Slow legs, little swing." Isla yawned. She was still awake, but only a little. On the walk home, she held the towel like a cape. "Look at me," she said. "I am flying."

Olivia wanted to blow bubbles on the porch. But her brother Sam had the bubble wand. He blew and blew. "My turn now?" Olivia asked. "You had a big turn," said Sam. He looked at her sad face. So he gave her the wand. "You can have a turn too," Olivia said.

Olivia blew one bubble. Then two. Then three! "Why did you share?" she asked Sam. "Because you let me go first," he said. The bubbles floated up to the cloudy sky. One bubble landed on the wall. It popped with a little pop.

The bubble juice tipped over. "Oh no," said Olivia. "It spilled." Mom came out with a towel. "Let's fix it together," she said. Olivia held the cup steady. Sam wiped the floor. Then Mom made more bubble juice. Sam took a turn. Olivia took a turn. "One for you, one for me," said Olivia. Sam smiled and blew a very big bubble.

Samuel hung his coat on the square hook. Then he looked for his name card. It was gone!

Miss Jo held up a box of shapes. "Find the shapes that match your name card," she said. "Then the card comes back."

Samuel looked around the room. He saw a clock. It was round like a circle. He saw a window. It had four sides like a square. He saw a slice of toast on the snack table. It was a triangle, with three pointy corners.

Samuel found a red rectangle under the chair. It had four sides. Two sides were long. Two sides were short. "Look!" he said. "A rectangle!"

On the back was his name. His card! Samuel heard a quiet pop. Miss Jo clapped. "You found it with shapes."

Then she pointed at the door. It was a big rectangle too. Samuel laughed and traced it in the air with his finger.

Ellie plays soccer at the park. Her team wears blue shirts. The ball is white and round.

Ellie wants to kick the ball. She runs to it. She kicks it with her foot. The white ball rolls and rolls. It goes into the net. The coach claps. "Hooray, Ellie!"

But then the ball rolls far away. Oh no. It rolls toward the shed. It stops at the big door. Ellie feels worried. The ball is far from her.

Dad is close by. He holds her hand. Together they walk to the shed door. Dad picks up the ball. He gives it back to Ellie.

Ellie kicks the ball again. It rolls to her friend Sam. Sam kicks it into the net. The team jumps up and down. Ellie's team will win the game today.

Ellie smiles at Dad. Dad smiles back. "Kick it one more time," he says.

Logan ran into the baby store. "I want to pick the blanket!" he said. Mom smiled. "Okay, you pick."

Logan looked and looked. A red blanket. A blue blanket. A blanket with ducks on it. Then he found a soft gray one. It was very cozy. Logan hugged it tight.

Next they found little shoes. "Babies can't walk," said Mom. Logan frowned. "Then why shoes?" Mom put a tiny shoe on Logan's hand. It flopped over, all soft. "Just to keep feet warm," she said. Logan laughed. "Silly shoe!"

At the big shelf, Logan pulled the blanket down. The whole pile fell! Blue, green, yellow, everywhere. Logan giggled. One blanket made them all fall down.

A worker helped stack them back. Then she held up a small hat. "This matches your gray blanket," she said. Logan gasped. It was gray too, with a bear on top.

"The baby will love it," said Logan. He put the hat on his own head. It was too small. It just sat on top like a little cup. Mom laughed and laughed.

At home, Logan put the blanket in the crib. He set the tiny shoes beside it. He put the bear hat on top. "All ready," he said. Then he patted the blanket, once, twice.

"Come soon, baby," he whispered. "I will follow you home."

Brooks ran to the playground. He wanted someone to play with. The swings were empty. The slide was empty too. Then he heard a small voice near the sandbox.

A girl sat in the sand. She held a doll in a leaf. "My baby is cold," she said.

Brooks thought fast. He found a big leaf. He put it over the doll like a blanket. The girl smiled. "Now baby is warm," she said. "One blanket, one hat, one bed."

They made a bed from a box top. Brooks patted the sand under it, soft and smooth. "Shh," he said. "Baby is sleeping." The girl rocked the box slowly, side to side.

Then they made a house. One bench was the wall. One mat was the floor. One bucket was the stove. Brooks stirred sand in the bucket. "Soup is ready," he called. The girl fed the doll one tiny spoonful.

The sun went down low. Brooks waved goodbye. "See you, baby," he said. The girl hugged her doll tight. "Bye, Brooks," she said. "You make good soup."

Mila sat at the little table in the art classroom. She wanted to paint a big apple for her grandma. She had red paint and yellow paint and blue paint.

Mila painted the apple red. Then she wanted leaves. "What color should the leaves be?" she asked her teacher.

"Try green," the teacher said.

"But I have no green paint," said Mila.

The teacher smiled. "Look at your tray."

Mila dipped her brush in the yellow paint. She dipped it in the blue paint too. She stirred them on the tray. The paint turned green! Yellow and blue made green. Mila laughed out loud.

She painted two green leaves on her apple. Then she painted a stem. Her teacher helped her send the painting to the drying rack.

At home, Mila gave the painting to grandma. Grandma hugged her. "What a big, beautiful apple," grandma said. Mila pointed at the leaves. "I made the green all by myself," she said.

Clara went to the community centre with her dad. There was a play corner with a tall shelf of toys. On the table sat two plates of crackers.

Clara wanted the plate with more crackers. But which plate had more? One plate looked big. One plate looked small. She was not sure.

Her friend Sam came over. "Let's count," he said. Clara pointed at the first plate. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. The last number was five. Then she counted the other plate. "One, two, three," she said. That one had three.

Sam counted the five plate too. He started at the other end. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. Clara put her finger on her chin. Sam started at the other end, but he said five too. She counted again from her end. Five again. She laughed. It was five both ways.

Dad came by with the keys to the car. The bell at the desk began to ring. Time to go home. Clara picked up the plate with five crackers. "This one has more," she said. She shared one with Sam, and they munched all the way to the door.

Lena sat in the big chair. She was waiting for the dentist. It was her very first visit.

Mama held her hand. Lena wanted to feel brave. But her tummy felt jumpy.

A lady at the desk gave Lena a card. The card had a smiling tooth on it. Lena pushed the card into her pocket.

In the corner there was a fish tank. Lena walked over to look. She pushed one finger on the glass, very soft. A little orange fish woke up. It swam right to her finger. Lena pushed the glass again. The fish came again. It liked her finger.

"Lena," a kind voice called. It was the dentist. Lena stood up tall. She held the card in her hand. The fish followed her finger all the way to the door.

The lights went out. Matthew stood in the backyard with Dad. Everything looked dark.

"The power is off," said Dad. "We must stay outside for a bit."

Matthew could not see his toy bus. He could not see the swing. He felt sad.

Then Dad clicked a big torch. A bright circle jumped onto the grass. Matthew gasped. Where did the light go? He pointed at the fence. Dad moved the torch. The bright circle moved too! It ran up the fence like a yellow cat.

"Can it find my bus?" asked Matthew. Dad swept the light around. It found the red bus by the flowers. Then it found Matthew's shoes. Then it found Mom at the door.

Mom held three glow sticks. She shook one and it turned green. Matthew held his new glow stick tight. It made his hands look green too.

The lights came back on. The house was bright again. But Matthew held up his torch. "Make the dark spot," he said. Dad turned the torch on. A bright circle sat on the grass, and Matthew laughed.

Raphael stood at the edge of the little pool by the lake. His mom held his hand. "Can I go in?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "The water is cool and nice."

Mom held him under his arms. Raphael let his legs hang down. He gave one small kick. Plop. A tiny splash came up. He kicked again, harder. Splash! Water flew onto his nose. "Hey!" he laughed. "My feet make the water jump!" Mom smiled. "Kick, kick," she said. Raphael kicked his fastest. Splash, splash, splash! His hair got wet. A duck on the lake turned to look.

After swimming, they sat on a towel. Dad helped Raphael tie the strings on his shorts. Then they walked home. "Time for a bath," said Dad. "Will there be soap bubbles?" asked Raphael. Dad laughed. "Big ones," he said. Raphael clapped his wet hands.

It was library morning at daycare. Miss Dana put three books on the rug. "One, two, three books," said Zoey. She patted the cover of the sweet bunny book. The cover said Zoey's name for bunnies, but Miss Dana read the words out loud. "The words say Sleepy Bunny," she said. Zoey turned the pages from the front to the back. "Read it again!" said Zoey. Miss Dana read it three times.

At home time, Zoey hugged the book. "I keep it forever," she said. Miss Dana shook her head. "We borrowed it. We take it back next time. Then other kids read it too." Zoey made a sad face. Then she made a big idea. "I borrow it lots of times!" she said. "One, two, three, four, five times!" Miss Dana laughed. "Deal," she said.

Aubrey woke up hungry. She wanted toast and milk. She wanted to make them herself.

Daddy made the toast. The toaster was too hot for Aubrey. She waited at the table.

Daddy put the toast on her plate. He gave her a small knife. It was dull and safe. Aubrey scooped soft butter. She spread it, and the toast tore. "Oh no," she said. A big hole showed.

Daddy brought new toast. This time Aubrey used less butter. She spread it slow and soft. The butter slid all over. The toast stayed whole. "I did it!" she said.

Next came the milk. Aubrey lifted the jug. It was heavy. Milk splashed over her cup and her hand. It ran onto her foot. Biscuit the dog trotted in. He licked the milk off the floor. "Biscuit, that milk is stinky now," Aubrey said. Biscuit barked once and sat down.

Daddy found a smaller cup. Aubrey poured again, slow and low. She watched the milk go up the side. It rose to the top. Not one drop fell.

Aubrey ate her toast and drank her milk. She patted Biscuit's head. "You can have a real treat later," she told him. Biscuit wagged his tail.

Edouard held his new library card. It was blue and had his name on it. He wanted a book about trucks.

He found a big book with a red truck on the cover. "This one," he said. The librarian stamped the book. "You can take it home," she said. "Bring it back soon so other kids can read it too."

At bedtime, Edouard read the truck book with Mama. He read it again in the morning. Then he put the book under his bed. "I want to keep it forever," he said.

Mama shook her head. "It is a library book. It goes back so other people can read it too." Edouard frowned.

Then he had an idea. He took his crayons and began to draw the red truck. He drew it big, with a blue sky and a garden beside it.

The next day, Edouard gave the book back. "Can I get another one?" he asked. The librarian smiled and stamped a new book. Edouard hugged it tight.

Lillian wanted her red balloon. It was in the toy box. She opened the lid. The balloon was not there!

Lillian felt sad. Her lip turned down. "Where did it go?" she asked. She looked under the table. No balloon. She looked behind the chair. No balloon. Then she heard a soft tap, tap, tap. Was it coming from the window?

Lillian felt a little scared. Slowly, slowly, she peeked around the curtain. There was her balloon! It was floating near the glass. The window was open a tiny bit. The wind had pushed the balloon there. Lillian laughed out loud. She felt so happy!

She reached up on her tiptoes. Daddy came to help. "I found it first!" Lillian said. She was excited. She hugged the red balloon tight. The balloon felt smooth and cool. Tap, tap, tap, it bumped her nose. Lillian giggled and held on.

Eliana sat in the car with Mama. They were going to the dentist. Eliana had never been to a dentist before.

"Will the dentist look at my teeth?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mama. "She will count them and make them shiny."

Eliana wanted her teeth to be shiny. But her mouth felt small. How could anyone see inside?

At the dentist's office, there was a big chair. It went up and down. Eliana climbed in with help. The dentist smiled a big smile. Then she opened her own mouth very wide. "Ahhh," she said.

Eliana watched. The dentist opened her mouth wide, so Eliana could see all her teeth. What a big view!

Eliana opened her mouth wide too. "Ahhh," she said. Now the dentist could see all of Eliana's teeth.

"Let me count," said the dentist. "One, two, three." She counted every tooth. She brushed them with sparkly paste. It had a happy taste, like strawberries.

"There," said the dentist. "All clean."

Eliana looked in a little mirror. Her teeth were shiny and white. In the car, Mama said, "Are you hungry now?"

Eliana nodded. On the way home, they shared a crunchy apple. "My teeth feel strong," said Eliana. She took another big bite.

Eliana stood at the gate. It was her first day of school. She held a little red truck. She did not know anyone yet. A boy ran by and did not look at her. Her face felt stormy, like a rain cloud.

A girl sat alone in the sand. Eliana pushed her truck near the girl. Beep, beep, she said. The girl smiled. She put a sand cake in the truck. Eliana drove it back to her. "Cake delivery!" said the girl. They laughed and laughed.

Then a small dog walked past the fence with its owner. The dog stopped to look at the truck. "No cake for you," said the girl. The dog wagged its tail anyway. Eliana made another sand cake. "This one is for the dog," she said, "just to look at."

Brooks sat in his cozy car seat. He was going to the dentist for the first time. His tummy felt funny. He held his toy plane tight.

"Will it hurt?" he asked.

"First we look," said Mom. "The dentist counts teeth. That is all."

A big truck went by. Its horn made a loud sound. Brooks jumped in his seat. His plane fell to the floor. It slid far, far away under the seat. His arms were too short.

"I can't reach it," said Brooks. He wanted to cry.

Mom unbuckled her belt and leaned back. She reached down. Her hand came up with the plane.

"There," she said. "Safe again."

At the dentist, Brooks sat in a big chair. It went up and down. The dentist smiled and counted. "Ten teeth up top," she said. "Ten teeth down low."

Brooks held his plane up high. "This flies to the moon," he said.

The dentist laughed. "Good flying, Brooks."

Parker wanted the big red truck. His friend Mia had it. Parker grabbed the truck. Mia cried loud. The teacher, Miss Jo, knelt down. "One truck, two friends," she said. Parker gave Mia the truck back. Then Mia rolled the truck to Parker. "Your turn," she said. Parker watched the wheels spin. Vroom! He rolled it back to Mia. Now it was a game. The truck went back and forth, back and forth. Parker clapped his hands. Then Max came over with blocks. Parker put a block in the truck. Mia put a block in the truck too. They made one tall tower together. Miss Jo turned off one lamp. The corner went dark. "Camp time," said Parker. He made a tent with a blanket. All three friends sat inside. "Welcome to our truck park," said Parker, and he rolled the truck again.

Sophia put on her party shoes. Today was her birthday! The bowling alley was loud and bright. The big shiny balls looked like giant striped eggs.

Mama helped Sophia pick a small blue ball. Sophia pushed it with both hands. The ball rolled slow, slow, slow. Then it bumped one pin. The pin wobbled and fell down. Boom! The pin fell into another pin. That pin fell too! "Look, look, look!" Sophia shouted. "My pin made the pin fall!"

Daddy clapped. Grandma clapped. Her friend Leo clapped too. "Do it again!" said Leo. Sophia pushed the ball again. This time it was fast, fast, fast. Three pins fell down, one by one by one.

Then the lights went dim. A big cake came out. Papa held the cake. On top was one real candle, glowing warm. "Make a wish," said Mama. Sophia puffed out her cheeks. She blew once. The little flame went out. The room went dark for a second. Papa turned the lights back on. Everyone cheered.

They ate cake with a spoon. Sophia did not forget one bite. "Best birthday," said Sophia. Leo licked his spoon and said, "Happy birthday, Sophia!" Then the pins went up again, all ten of them, standing tall and ready.

Hailey wanted to make a house for her pet rabbit. The rabbit could not sleep in her dollhouse. It was too small.

So Hailey found a big cardboard box. She cut a little door with help from Dad. Dad held the box. Hailey drew a circle for the door hole. Dad cut it out. The circle door was just right.

Next Hailey drew a square window. She drew a triangle on top for a roof. She drew a long rectangle for a ramp. The rabbit could hop up the rectangle and go in.

At first the rabbit would not go in. "Too scary," Hailey said. She put a carrot near the door. The rabbit came. It nibbled the carrot. Then it went inside the box.

Hailey gave the ramp a little pull to make it flat. The rabbit hopped out and hopped back in again.

"Good house," said Dad.

Mila wanted to find her little blue ball. It had rolled under the big teddy bear. She pushed the big teddy. It was too heavy. She found her small rabbit instead. The rabbit was light and soft.

"Rabbit, will you help me?" she asked. "Yes, let's go," she said in a small rabbit voice. Mila made the rabbit hop fast, fast, fast across the playroom. Then she made it go slow, slow, slow. She reached the big teddy and peeked behind it.

There was the blue ball. It had rolled into a sunny spot. Mila touched the floor there. It felt warm like soup. She touched the floor by the door. That spot was cold. She sat in the warm spot and held her ball. "We found it, Rabbit," she said. Then she rolled the ball slow across the cold floor, and fast all the way back.

Parker looked for the red truck at school. He could not find it. "Where did it go?" he said.

Miss Amy smiled. "Look by the old slide," she said. Parker ran to the slide. The red truck was under it. Next to it was a blue ball.

Parker pushed the blue ball. It rolled down the hill. Parker ran after it. The ball stopped in the yellow sandbox.

"My turn!" said his friend Mia. She rolled the ball back up. Parker tried too. The ball rolled down again. They kept rolling it. "Again!" said Parker.

Then they sat in the green grass. Parker held the red truck up high. Mia held the blue ball. "We found everything," said Parker. Miss Amy clapped. "Good looking, Parker!" she said.

Parker drove the red truck across the green grass. "Beep, beep!" he said.

Isla's class had ten crackers to share. But the crackers were all in one big pile. "How many do you get?" asked her friend Tom. Isla did not know yet.

Then Miss Pete began to sing. "One, two, three, four, five." She tapped the crackers as she sang. Isla watched her finger. Each tap moved one cracker to a small plate. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten," sang Isla, tapping too. The pile got small. The plate got full. "Ten crackers for you," said Isla. Tom laughed. "Ten for me too!"

At play time, Isla pretend-fed a toy cow. She counted the hay pieces out loud. "One, two, three." The cow looked very hungry, so she counted more. "Four, five, six." Tom sat far away at first. Then he ran over. "I can count to ten too," he said. "Show me," said Isla. Together they sang, "Seven, eight, nine, ten." Miss Pete clapped from the door.

Natalie had a blue team shirt. Today was her first soccer game in the backyard. Dad set up two small nets in the grass.

Her friend Mia came to play too. Natalie wanted to score a goal. She ran to the ball. She kicked it very, very soft. The ball went tap, tap, and stopped. "Why did the ball stop?" she asked.

Dad smiled. "Try again. Watch the ball." Natalie looked at her foot. She looked at the ball. Then she kicked it hard. The ball flew into the net! The net went swish. "It went in!" said Natalie. A big kick makes the ball go far.

Dad blew the whistle for snack time. Natalie sat on the crunchy leaves by the fence. A feather fell down next to her shoe. She put it in her pocket. Then she ran back and kicked the ball again.

Levi wanted to be the line leader at school. But Miss Kim said the line leader had to be neat and clean. Levi looked down at his shirt. It had orange paint on it. It had jam on it too. At snack time, orange juice dripped onto his shoe.

"Levi, you are a sticky boy," said his friend Poppy. She laughed a gentle laugh. Levi laughed too. Then he had an idea.

Miss Kim took him to the little sink. Levi pushed up his sleeves. He washed his hands with soap. The soap smelled like lemons. He tried to lift his wet shirt, but it stuck to his tummy. Miss Kim helped him put on the spare shirt from the box. It was blue and soft and clean. Poppy gave him a big hug. "Now you are a clean boy," she said.

At nap time, Levi lay on his mat and smiled. When the lights came on, Miss Kim said, "Line leader today is Levi." Levi stood up tall. He held the door handle. "Follow me," he said. "No jam allowed."

Jack ran to the red slide at the park. But a girl was already at the top. Jack stopped and waited at the bottom. The girl slid down, laughing. Then Jack took his turn. Whee! The slide was fast.

Next, Jack saw the round sandbox. Two boys were digging there. Jack had no shovel. One boy saw Jack's sad mouth. The boy held out a small blue shovel. "You can use it," he said. Jack took it and dug a big hole. They filled it in together.

Then the teacher blew a whistle. Everyone ran to the picnic table. The rule was water and crackers first. Jack sat with the other kids. Each child got one cup and two crackers. Jack saw that every plate looked the same. No one got more. No one got less.

After the snack, Jack went back to the slide. He let a little girl go first. She slid down and waved at him. Jack waved back and climbed the ladder.

Declan sits in his car seat. He holds his teddy bear tight. Today they will stop for fresh apples at the farm stand.

Mama parks the car. The sun is hot on the door. Declan touches the window. "Ouch," he says. He pulls his hand back fast. The window is too hot to touch.

"Stay close to me," says Mama. Declan holds her hand. They walk to the apples together. A big yellow sign stands by the road. Declan wants to touch it. It is sharp at the corner. "Not that one," says Mama. She turns his hand away.

Then Declan spots the water bottle. He presses the cold bottle to his knee. It feels good after the hot sun. He laughs.

"Good thinking," says Mama. She buys red apples. Declan carries one small bag. He does not let it slip.

Back in the car, Declan holds the cold bottle. "Nice and cold," he says. Mama smiles and starts the engine.

Levi wanted to play house with his teddy bear. But teddy was hiding somewhere. He looked under the table. No teddy. He looked in the toy box. No teddy.

Then Levi remembered the big block basket. He had put teddy there yesterday. He lifted one block. Then another block. At the bottom, teddy was smiling up at him.

"There you are!" said Levi. He hugged teddy tight. "Are you hungry?" he asked. Teddy said nothing, so Levi made a pretend cake. He put crunchy crackers on a plate too.

Papa came to help. Papa used the real kettle for warm water, and Levi stirred his pretend tea. Levi fed teddy a cracker bite. "Yum," Levi said in a big teddy voice. "More cake, please!"

"Coming right up," said Levi.

Beau sat on the small stage in the school auditorium. A big drum sat in front of him. His teacher, Miss Jo, handed him two soft sticks.

"Tap it," said Miss Jo.

Beau tapped the drum. It made a sound. Tum.

He tapped harder. The sound got bigger. TUM!

Beau tapped soft again. The drum went quiet. He tapped hard. The drum went loud.

"Soft stick, small sound," said Miss Jo. "Hard stick, big sound."

Beau looked at the drum. It was like a puzzle. And the answer was true. He held the sticks himself.

"I can make it big," said Beau.

He lifted his arm high and hit the drum. TUM! TUM! TUM!

The sound flew all the way to the back seats. Miss Jo smiled and clapped her hands.

Jack came home with a little white rabbit. Her name was Rosie. Jack held the box very carefully.

"Can I feed her now?" Jack asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Rabbits love carrots." Jack gave Rosie a small carrot. Rosie munched it fast. Her nose went up and down.

Then Jack saw something. Rosie left little round balls in her cage. "Mom, look! What is that?" Jack asked. "That is how rabbits make their potty," said Mom. "So we must clean her cage."

Jack helped Mom sweep the cage. He put in fresh soft hay. Then he gave Rosie more carrot. Rosie hopped in her clean cage. She looked very happy. She stretched out her legs and closed her eyes.

Jack clapped his hands. "Clean cage, happy rabbit!" he said. Rosie twitched one long ear. Jack ran to get his crayons. He wanted to draw her picture.

Elijah held Papa's hand at the ice rink. The game was big and loud. "Go, go!" the crowd shouted. Elijah's friend Mia waved from the next seat.

Elijah wanted to see the puck. But a tall man stood in front of him. He could only see the man's big red coat. Elijah stood on his tiptoes. Still no puck. He waited. The man stayed tall.

Then Elijah clapped his mittens together. The tall man turned around to look. He looked down and saw Elijah. "Oops, sorry, little guy," the man said. He moved one step to the side.

Now Elijah could see the fresh, shiny ice. He could see the puck slide and zoom. One player scored a goal! The crowd jumped up. Papa gave Elijah a kiss on the cheek. Mia gave him a high five.

Elijah clapped his mittens again, just for fun. This time nobody turned around. They were all watching the game. Elijah laughed and clapped anyway.

Arlo had a big game today. His team played in the backyard. Arlo wore his red shirt.

"Kick the ball, Arlo," said Dad. Arlo ran to the ball. He kicked it with his toe. The ball went a tiny bit. Hmm. Why did it stop so fast?

Arlo looked down. The grass was tall and thick. Did the tall grass hold the ball? He tried again. Yes! The tall grass grabbed the ball. Then Dad rolled the ball to the short grass. Arlo kicked it there. The ball rolled and rolled and rolled. It went all the way to Sam!

"Kick it to me," Sam called. Arlo kicked hard on the short grass. The ball zoomed past Sam. It went right into the net. The net caught the ball. Goal!

"Nice kick," said Sam. Arlo clapped his hands. The net stopped the ball. The short grass let it go. What a fun game this was.

After the game, they sat under the tree. Mom brought orange slices. Arlo took a big bite. "Juicy," he said. "So juicy!" Juice ran down his chin. Sam laughed and ate one too.

The end of the season was coming soon. Arlo hoped they would play one more game. "Can we play again?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Same short grass." Arlo grinned and kicked his feet in the air.

Isaac sat at the dinner table. He wanted his carrots cut into little stars. He loved little stars.

"Carrots are cooking," said Mom. "They need a wash first." Isaac watched Mom wash the carrots in the sink. The water made a splashy noise.

"Can I count them?" Isaac asked. "Yes," said Mom. "One, two, three carrots." Isaac tapped each carrot with his finger. "One, two, three!" he said.

Mom cut the carrots into stars. Some stars fell off the cutting board and rolled onto the table. Isaac counted the rolling stars. "One, two, three, four, five!" The stars stopped rolling when they bumped his plate.

Then Isaac saw something. When he blew on a star, it slid away. When he blew again, it slid back. "Mom, look!" said Isaac. He blew one, two, three times. The star slid one, two, three times.

Mom laughed and put the stars on his plate. Isaac ate one star. Then he ate two more. Dad came in early from work and sat down too.

"Do you want to count my peas?" asked Dad. "Yes!" said Isaac. He tapped each pea. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Dad clapped his hands. Isaac grinned and ate a star.

Margot had a library book. It was about a little bear. On the cover, the words said "Bear". Mama pointed at them. "That says Bear," said Mama. Margot tapped the words. "Bear," she said. The marks on the page had a name inside!

Margot opened the book. She turned page one, page two, page three. "Front to back," said Mama. Margot turned the last page. "The end!" she said. Then she hugged the book. "My bear book stays with me."

"It goes back to the library," said Mama. "Other kids want to read it too. We bring it back by Friday." Margot held the book tight. "But I love the bear!" She put the book under her pillow. The book made a big bump. Her head could not sink down. "Stinky plan," said Mama, laughing. "Books need air, not pillows."

So Margot packed the book in her bag. She counted what went in. "One book, one crayon, one snack." At the library, she gave the book to the lady at the desk. Then she found a new bear book on the shelf. "This one says Bear too!" said Margot. She held it up high. "We take this one home, and bring it back by Friday." The lady smiled and stamped the card. "See you on Friday, Margot."

Theodore went to the store with Mama. He wanted the bread with seeds on top. Yesterday they had no bread at home. Today they could buy some.

"Can we get it now?" Theodore asked.

"Now we shop," said Mama. "Bread comes last." First they got apples. The apples sat in the middle of the cart. Then they got milk. Then Mama picked up the dark bread with seeds. Theodore put it in the cart all by himself.

At home, Mama cut the bread. Theodore helped by putting slices on the plate. The bread was gone by the end of lunch. All the seeds were gone too.

"More bread tomorrow," said Mama.

"Tomorrow," said Theodore. He gave the empty plate a little kick under the table. Then he ran to look at the calendar on the wall. "Show me tomorrow, Mama!"

Gabriel was drawing at the big table. He drew a red balloon. "I need one more crayon," he said. Mom gave him the blue one. Gabriel smiled a big smile. He was happy.

Then his little dog ran by. The dog jumped up. The paper fell on the floor. Gabriel's face got hot. He stamped his foot. "Bad dog!" he shouted. He was angry.

Mom picked up the paper. "It is not broken," she said. "Look. You can fix it." Gabriel looked. The balloon had a small rip. He put tape on it. "All better," he said.

Just then the door opened. It was Grandma, the kind woman next door. Gabriel jumped up and down. "Grandma!" he yelled. He was so excited. But then the dog barked loud. Gabriel hid behind Mom's legs. He was scared.

Grandma bent down. "The dog is happy to see me," she said. "She barks hello." The dog licked Gabriel's hand. Gabriel laughed. He showed Grandma his red balloon. Grandma clapped. Gabriel drew her a cat. His happy smile came back. "I did it!" he said.

Noah had a red jersey. His team was the Little Bears. Today they played in Coach Dad's backyard. The goal was between two plastic cones.

Noah wanted to score one goal. He kicked the ball. The ball rolled and stopped. It did not reach the cones. "I guess I need a big kick," Noah said.

He ran to the ball. He kicked it hard with his whole foot. The ball flew past the cones and into the flowers. "Goal!" Noah shouted. Coach Dad clapped his hands. A big horse stood by the fence. It looked up from the grass.

The sky turned orange. It was getting late. "One more kick," said Coach Dad. Noah set the ball down by the cones. He tapped it with his toe. The ball rolled slowly, slowly, and stopped right in front of the horse. The horse sniffed the ball. Then the horse pushed it back with its nose. The ball rolled all the way to Noah's feet. "Thank you!" said Noah. He hugged the ball under his arm and waved to the horse.

Luca ran to the backyard with his red ball. He wanted to paint a big picture on the fence. He had blue, yellow and green paint cups. Dad set them on the grass.

Luca dipped his brush in the yellow cup. He made a big yellow sun on the fence. Then he dipped the same brush in the blue cup. Oh no! The blue cup turned green! The yellow paint had hopped on the brush.

Luca looked at his green paint. He made green grass under the yellow sun. He laughed and clapped. Then he found a clean brush for the blue sky. Dad gave him a happy thumbs up.

"Look, Dad! Yellow and blue made green!" said Luca.

Wesley stood in the band room. He held a big drum. He wanted to make it boom.

"Hit it hard," said Miss Kay. Wesley swung his arm. He hit the drum. It made a tiny sound. Tap. That was all.

Wesley frowned. He wanted a big boom. He tried again. Tap. Tap. Too small!

Then he looked at his drumstick. The soft round end was hitting the drum. He turned the stick around. Now the hard little end was down.

He swung his arm. He hit the drum. BOOM! The drum went boom so big, it made a cymbal wobble on the shelf. The cymbal fell over with a crunchy crash.

"Oops," said Wesley.

Miss Kay laughed. "Big boom," she said. "Maybe not that big."

Wesley hit the drum again. Boom. Boom. Boom. Just right. Then he played a song for his mom at pick-up time. She clapped very loud.

"Play the boom part again," she said. Wesley grinned and swung his arm.

Myles ran into the sunny backyard. The sun warmed his back. He took off his big coat. "Too hot!" he said.

Then the wind began to whoosh. The wind lifted his hat right off his head. The naughty wind sent the hat under the bush. "Come back, hat!" Myles called.

Dark clouds rolled in. Rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip. The rain made little ponds on the stones. Myles put his hat back on and pulled up his hood. Now the rain could not wet his hair.

In winter, snow would fall here. Snow could freeze the pond hard. Myles would wear mittens and boots.

A little turtle sat by the pond. It did not mind the rain at all. "Do you like the rain, turtle?" Myles asked. The turtle slid slowly into the water.

Camille wanted warm milk before her nap. "Stay close to me," said Grandma. Camille stayed right by the table.

Grandma turned on the stove. Blue flames jumped up. Camille saw the pot. Steam rose from the pot like little clouds. Grandma held up her hand near the steam. "Hot," she said softly. Camille held up her hand far away. She did not feel hot. Far was safe.

Camille counted the safe things she could touch. "One, the cup. Two, the spoon. Three, my napkin." Grandma poured the warm milk. She poured and poured, until the cup began to fill. Camille wrapped both hands around the cup. Warm, not hot. Just right.

Camille sipped her milk. It tasted like a sweet dream. "I was brave," she whispered. Grandma kissed the top of her head. Camille counted again. "One, warm cup. Two, soft kiss. Three, sleepy girl."

Madison wanted to find colors for her magic jar. She ran out to the backyard with the jar in her hands. First she found one red leaf by the fence. She dropped it in. The leaf spun round and round.

Next she heard a buzz. A yellow bee flew to a flower. The flower was yellow too. "I see yellow," said Madison. But the bee flew away fast. Madison looked down and found yellow pollen on her finger. She wiped it into the jar.

Then she saw green grass and picked one blade. She saw blue sky and shut the lid tight. "Now my jar has the sky," she said. She held the jar up high. The colors mixed in the sun and glowed. A little snake slid by and looked up. Madison waved. "Hello, snake. Want to see my rainbow?"

Leon sat on the big red couch at Mr. Rosa's house. Everyone was watching the big game on TV. Uncle Sam held a plate of pizza bites. Mrs. Rosa said, "Watch this part!"

Then the TV picture went frozen. It just stopped. The players stood like statues. "Oh no," said Uncle Sam. "Not now!"

Leon wanted to see the goal. He looked all around. Then he saw something. The dog, Biscuit, had a string from the curtain in his mouth. Biscuit pulled the string. The string was tied to the little black box behind the TV. When Biscuit pulled, the picture wobbled!

"Biscuit, drop it!" said Leon. Biscuit dropped the string and wagged his tail.

Mr. Rosa knelt down and fixed the little black box. "All safe now," he said. "You have sharp eyes, Leon." The picture moved again. The players ran!

Uncle Sam took a big bite of his pizza bite and cheered. "Go, go, go!" he shouted.

Biscuit jumped on the couch next to Leon. Leon held the curtain string up high, far from the dog. "This is my job," Leon said. "You watch the game."

Biscuit licked his nose just as the crowd on TV shouted, "Goal!"

Daniel put on his little white hat. He was baking bread for his family. "I will make the biggest bread ever," he said.

He mixed flour and water in a big bowl. Then he added more and more flour. The spoon got stuck. The dough was stiff like a rock. "Oh no," said Daniel. "My dough will not move."

His teacher laughed softly. "Try a splash of water," she said. Daniel poured in a splash. He mixed. The water made the dough soft and squishy. "It moves again," he shouted. He squished it with his hands. It felt like play dough.

The teacher put the pan in the hot oven. Daniel stayed at the safe table and helped clean the big bowl. Soon the bread came out, big and golden.

At home, everyone ate it up. "More bread, Daniel," said Dad. Daniel grinned and said, "I will need a bigger bowl."

John sat at the little table in art class. He wanted to paint a house. But his brush made a blob. "That is not a house," said John. His friend Mia showed him her paper. She had cut a square for the house. She had cut a triangle for the roof. "Cutting makes shapes," said Mia. John got the safe paper and the kid scissors. He cut a square. He cut a triangle too. He cut a small rectangle for the door. Then he cut a circle for the sun. He glued them all on.

Miss Amy held the glue gun. "Only I use this," she said. "It can burn your finger." John watched from his seat. The hot glue held the roof on tight. He pressed the paper shapes with his clean hand. Then he drew curly lines by the door. "Look, curly smoke from my chimney!" said John. Mia smiled and gave him a yellow crayon. John drew rays all around his circle sun. "A square, a triangle, a rectangle, and a circle," he said. "My house is done!" Miss Amy hung it on the wall, up high where everyone could see.

Benjamin wanted to play house at daycare. But the baby doll was missing. "Where is Baby?" he asked. Mia pointed at the big toy box. Benjamin dug deep. He pushed teddy bears aside. Then he found the doll, all wrapped in a sock.

The sock was Baby's blanket. Benjamin rocked Baby in his arms. "Time to eat," he said. He gave Baby a wooden bowl. Mia was the cook. "Soup is ready," she called. The soup was just green blocks in a cup.

Benjamin fed Baby one spoonful. Baby fell over. Benjamin gasped. "Baby is scared of the spoon!" he said. He tipped the bowl to Baby's mouth instead. Baby stayed sitting up. "Baby likes the bowl better," Benjamin laughed.

Then Mia built a mountain of pillows. Baby slid down the mountain. Whee! Benjamin clapped and picked Baby up. "Again, again!" said Mia, pushing the pillows higher.

Violet put on her special dress. Her family was going to a big house of prayer. Today there was a festival with songs and food.

Violet wanted to see the lamps. There were many little lamps at the front. They looked like tiny stars. But the lamps were far away, and she was small. The tall people stood all around her. She could not see anything but coats and sleeves.

Mama knelt down beside her. "You can sit on the step," Mama said. It was a wide stone step. Violet climbed up all by herself. Now she was taller. She could see the whole row of lamps. Each little flame stood up straight and warm. Grandma lit one more lamp with a long match. The new flame came up, and then a new smell of sweet smoke floated over.

"Do you see it, Violet?" Grandma asked.

"Yes," said Violet. She planted her hands on her knees and watched. One flame. Then sweet smoke. Again and again, like magic that was not scary at all.

Aurora ran into Grandma's kitchen. The whole family was coming today. There were big breads on the table and cups of juice.

"Can we eat now?" Aurora asked.

"Not yet," said Grandma. "First we hold hands. Then someone says the special words."

Aurora wanted to say the words. She asked, "Can it be me?"

"You need to learn them first," said Grandma.

Grandma said the words slow. Aurora tried to hurry. She mixed them all up. Everyone laughed, but it was a nice laugh.

Then Aurora had an idea. She found a pencil. Daddy wrote the words on a card. Aurora drew a sun on it too.

Everyone sat down at the big table. They all held hands. Aurora stood up tall. She looked at her card.

"Thank you for our food and our family," she said. "Bless everyone here."

Everyone smiled at once. Then everyone picked up their bread at the same time. Grandpa winked at her.

"You did it!" said Mommy. "Now we can eat."

Aurora bit into her warm bread. She was a lucky girl.

"Can I do it again tomorrow?" she asked.

Grandma squeezed her hand and said, "Yes, every day."

Violet ran to school. She was almost late. She had eaten her breakfast fast.

In the music room, Miss Ana sat at the piano. "Let's sing our counting song," she said. Violet loved that song. "One, two, three, four, five," they all sang. Then they sang more. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

Then Miss Ana dropped the rhythm sticks. The sticks rolled under the shelf. Ten little sticks rolled far, far away.

"Can you help, Violet?" asked Miss Ana. Violet got down on her knees. She reached under the shelf. She pulled the sticks out one at a time. "One," said Violet. She pulled again. "Two." She kept pulling. "Three, four, five."

Miss Ana put each stick back in the box. Violet pulled out more. "Six, seven, eight, nine." One stick was still hiding. Violet reached way in. Her fingers found it. "Ten!" she said.

Miss Ana closed the box. All the sticks fit just right. "You found them all," said Miss Ana. "Now we can play the song." The sticks tapped one, two, three, four, five. They tapped six, seven, eight, nine, ten.

Violet smiled and tapped along. "Again, again!" she said.

Sophie sat in the family car. She buckled her seat belt all by herself. Today was a big day. They were going to get the new baby.

"Who is in our family?" asked Daddy.

"Mama, Daddy, me," said Sophie. She held up one finger, two fingers, three.

"Now there will be four," said Daddy.

The baby was small and light as a loaf of bread. Daddy carried him out and put his seat in the car. Then the baby began to cry. He cried loud and long. Sophie covered her ears. She wanted the baby to like the car. She wanted him to stop.

Sophie had an idea. She took her deep blue blanket from her bag. She could not reach the baby. But she could reach her own teddy. She held teddy up so the baby could see it. She sang her quiet song, the one Mama sang at night. "Sleep, baby, sleep," she sang.

The baby looked at teddy. The crying got small. Then the crying stopped. The baby made a soft sound and closed his eyes. He fell asleep because of her song. Sophie had made that happen.

"Who is in our family?" asked Mama, smiling in the mirror.

"Mama, Daddy, me, and baby," said Sophie. One finger, two fingers, three fingers, four. When they got home, they would sit together on the couch. Mama had cookies waiting, one for Sophie and one for Daddy, and the baby would sleep in his blanket.

"Good work, big sister," said Daddy.

Sophie sang her quiet song all the way home.

Clara wanted to help at school. She wanted to make snack time come fast. Her teacher, Miss Rose, said, "First we wait for the bread."

Clara looked at the big oven. Miss Rose put the bread in. "It is hot," said Miss Rose. "You stay way back here." Clara stood back. The oven was hot. Her juice box was cold. She held it in her hands.

A little bird landed at the window. It had one wing up, then both wings out. It was small. Clara was big next to it. The bird flapped fast. Clara waved slow. The bird came closer. Then it flew away. "Come back, little bird," said Clara.

She waited and waited. Miss Rose took the bread out. It smelled good. Miss Rose cut it, one, two, three. The bread steamed. Clara blew on her piece. She blew slow. The steam went away. Now the bread was just warm. Clara took a bite. "Yum," she said. "The little bird missed this."

William was at summer camp. There was one big red truck on the toy shelf. William wanted that truck more than anything.

Ben grabbed the truck first. William grabbed it too. The truck went squeak, squeak. Both boys pulled. Then the wheel fell off. It rolled under the table.

William got down on his knees. He reached for the wheel. He pushed it back on. The wheel made the truck roll again. William held the truck out to Ben. "Your turn first," he said.

Ben drove the truck in a circle. "Your turn now," said Ben. William took the truck and drove it to the sandbox. The sand felt warm on his toes.

Then William filled a bowl with sand. He tipped it over. The sand made a round, friendly hill. Ben laughed and clapped. "Make another one," said Ben. So William filled the bowl again, and Ben waited, with his hands in his lap, until it was his turn.

Rehmat went to the bank with Mama. It was cold outside. Rehmat wanted to wear her red coat all by herself.

She pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. The coat sat crooked on her shoulders. One sleeve hung down empty. "Silly sleeve," said Rehmat. The sleeve flapped like a wing when she moved.

Mama smiled. Rehmat tried again. Arm in, arm in, and pull. The coat sat straight now. Time for the zipper. Rehmat pulled it up, but the zipper slid back down. She frowned at it.

Then Rehmat looked down. The two sides of her coat were apart. She pushed them together at the bottom. She pulled the zipper again. Zip! It went all the way up to her chin. "I did it!" said Rehmat. Mama clapped.

The bank man gave Rehmat a red apple for being so patient. Rehmat held it with her warm hands. "My coat is on, and it will not come off," she said. She marched to the door, and the zipper gleamed in the light.

Luka sat at the paint table at summer camp. He wanted to paint a sun, but there was no orange paint. He looked in the cup. Only red, yellow and blue.

Luka felt shy about asking. He watched the red paint. He watched the yellow paint. Then he tried something. He dipped his brush in red. He made a red dot on the paper. He dipped the brush in yellow. He put yellow right on the red dot.

The two colours touched. They moved together. The dot turned orange! Luka blinked. He made another dot. Red, then yellow. Orange again.

"Look, Mother," he said at pick-up time. He held up his orange sun. His mother smiled big. "That sun looks warm," she said. Luka touched the wet paper with one finger. His fingerprint came out orange too.

Joshua ran into the cooking classroom. Today he would make muffins for his whole family. "Blueberry muffins for Mama, Daddy, and Baby Ruth!" he said. "One, two, three muffins, and one for me. Four!"

He put flour in the big bowl. He cracked an egg. He poured in milk. Then he began to stir. Round and round went the spoon. The batter was thick and lumpy, like mud. "Silly, naughty lumps," said Joshua. "Go away!" He stirred and stirred. The lumps went away. Now the batter was smooth and shiny.

But wait. Joshua had forgotten the blueberries! He dropped them in. He stirred again. The white batter turned purple, purple, purple. Joshua laughed. "The blueberries make it purple!"

Miss Amy put the pan in the hot oven. Joshua watched from far away. Soon a yummy smell filled the room. Then the timer rang. Out came four big muffins, warm and blue.

Joshua carried them home in a basket. "Muffins!" said Mama. "For you, and you, and you," said Joshua. Baby Ruth clapped her hands. Joshua took a big bite. "Purple inside!" he said.

Miles sat in the car with his blanket. They were going to the salon for his first haircut. "I want my hair to stay," said Miles.

At the salon, the hairdresser put a cape on him. She sprayed his hair with water. Miles felt the wet drops. "Cold!" he said. The hairdresser laughed kindly. Then she began to snip. Little pieces of hair fell down. They landed on the cape like tiny dark snow.

Miles watched one piece fall on his arm. He blew on it. The hair jumped up and slid away. He blew again. Another piece slid off. "Look, Mom!" said Miles. He kept blowing, and the hairs kept sliding. When it was done, Miles marched to the car. His hair was short and soft. He touched it all the way home.

Yesterday Parker painted a picture at school. It was a gift for his mom. But paint takes time to dry. His paper was still wet at home time.

Today Parker looked for his picture on the shelf. It was missing! "Where did it go?" he asked. His teacher said, "Let's look for it." They looked in the paint corner. They looked by the window. The sun was shining there.

There it was! The warm sun had touched the wet paint all night. Now the paper was dry and flat. Parker touched it with one finger. "All dry," he said. "Now it can be a gift."

"Can I take it home now?" he asked.

"Yes," said his teacher. "Take it now."

Parker held it all the way to the car.

Anna lost her bunny at school. She looked and looked. "Where is bunny?" she said.

Anna looked by the slide. No bunny. She looked by the swings. No bunny. Then the wind blew. The wind lifted a short red scarf on the ground. Under the scarf was bunny!

"Bunny! I found you!" said Anna. She gave bunny a big hug.

The wind blew again. It lifted the scarf up high. Anna laughed. She watched the wind fold the scarf right back down.

"Time to go," said Mama. Anna held bunny close. They walked past the park gate together.

"Goodbye, wind," said Anna. "Thank you for showing me bunny." The scarf fluttered softly, like a little wave goodbye.

Milo went to the park with his dad. He saw a hoop on the grass. Dad held out a beanbag. "Throw it in," said Dad.

Milo threw it. The beanbag went low. It hit the rim and fell out. Milo got the beanbag. He stood very close to the hoop. He threw it high. The beanbag went up and then down. It fell in! "It went in!" said Milo. Dad clapped.

Then Dad rolled a big ball to Milo. Milo held out one hand. The ball hit his hand and fell. Milo sat down in the grass. He felt dizzy from turning to chase it. Dad came close. "Try two hands," said Dad. He showed Milo how to hold both arms out. Dad rolled the ball again. Milo made a cup with both hands. The ball landed right in them. Milo held it tight and did not let go.

"My turn to throw it," said Milo. He filled his arms with the big ball and hugged it all the way home.

Eli sat on the little red mat at daycare. Miss Ana held up a book. "This book is from the library," she said. "We can take it home, but we must bring it back."

Eli loved the book about the big red truck. He read it with Miss Ana. She opened the top page first. She turned each page one by one. The words on the page told her what to say. The words said, "The truck goes fast!"

"I want to keep this book forever," said Eli. "Can I keep it?"

"No," said Miss Ana. "Someone else wants to read it too. But you can borrow it again."

Eili frowned. Then he had an idea. "Can I hold it one more time?"

"You can," said Miss Ana.

Eli held the book. He turned the pages, front to back. He pointed at the words. "Truck!" he said.

Tomorrow, his friend Mia would read it. And after that, Eli would borrow it again.

"Fast truck," said Eli, and he turned to the top page one more time.

Charlie was at Sam's birthday party. There was a big red ball in the toy box. The ball was bumpy all over. Charlie wanted to hold it.

A boy named Ben had the ball first. Charlie ran over fast. She reached out to grab it.

Her grandma put a hand on her arm. "Let's wait," Grandma said softly. Charlie sat on her leg and folded her hands. It was hard to wait. She watched Ben roll the bumpy ball on the floor.

Then Ben rolled the ball right to her. "Your turn," he said. Charlie caught it. It felt funny in her hands, like tiny bumps on her skin.

Ben sat down to wait, just like Charlie did. A bug crawled near his shoe, and he stopped to scratch his leg. While he scratched, Charlie rolled the ball back to him.

Ben laughed and rolled it again. "We can both play," he said.

Charlie clapped her hands. The party had cake next. Grandma held the candle, and everyone sang. Ben sat right next to Charlie.

"Best party," said Charlie, holding the bumpy ball in her lap.

Lillian went to the big party with Mama and Papa. The room was noisy. There were drums and songs and lots of people. Lillian wanted to light a little lamp like the big kids. But she was too small.

Mama held her hand. "Watch first," Mama said. A big girl put a candle in a cup. The wick caught the flame. Then the cup glowed all around. Lillian looked and looked.

"Now you," Papa said. He lit a long stick for her. It was safe in his hand. Lillian touched her candle to the big girl's candle. The wick made a little spark. Then her candle had a flame too! The cup began to glow.

Lillian put her cup on the table. It sat with all the other cups. So many little lights. The room looked warm and gold. The big girl smiled at her. "Good job," the girl said.

Lillian waved her hand behind the cup. The light made a big shadow on the wall. The shadow danced when she moved. Lillian laughed and made it dance again.

Lena wanted to make pancakes for her family. "Can I help?" she asked. Mama said, "Yes! You can mix." Lena stirred the bowl. Flip, flip, flip went the spoon. The batter was lumpy, then smooth.

Mama put the pan on the stove. Lena stood back, safe and far. Mama held up a cold pat of butter. It was hard. Lena asked, "What will the warm pan do to it?" Mama dropped the butter in. Sizzle! The hard butter turned soft. Then it turned to a shiny puddle. "It melts!" Lena yelled. "The warm pan makes it melt!"

Mama poured the batter. Bubbles popped up, pop, pop, pop. "Flip it now," said Mama. The pancacake turned golden. Lena wore her fox apron. The fox had a happy face, just like Lena.

Soon there was a tall stack of pancakes. Daddy came in and said, "Wow!" Lena set the table. Everyone ate and ate. "Best pancakes ever," said Daddy, with syrup on his chin. Lena clapped her hands. "More butter, please!" she yelled. Mama laughed and held up the dish. The butter was soft now, sitting in the warm, sunny spot on the table.

Ibrahim wanted to dress his robot. But the robot had no clothes at all.

Ibrahim looked out the big window. The sun was shining. "It is sunny," he said. He put a little hat on the robot's head. Sun hats are good for sunny days.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain fell, drip drip. "It is rainy," said Ibrahim. He put little boots on the robot. Rain boots are good for rainy days.

The wind blew hard. "It is windy!" said Ibrahim. The wind pushed the hat right off. He held the hat and put it back on. Then he remembered the coat. He wrapped a tiny coat around the robot.

Mama came to the window. "What about snow?" she asked. She opened her hand. A white mitten fell out, soft as snow. "A surprise for your robot," she said.

Ibrahim put the mitten on the robot's hand. "Now you are ready," he said. He hugged the robot tight. Outside, the rain went drip, drip, drip.

Kinsley ran to the swings at the park. The big swing was wet from the rain. "Slippery," said Mama. Kinsley touched it. Her hands slid down. She wanted to swing so much.

Kinsley saw a boy on the dry swing next to her. "Can you please help me get a dry swing?" she asked Mama. "Yes," said Mama. She wiped the wet swing with a towel. "Thank you," said Kinsley. She climbed up. The swing was dry now. She pumped her legs. Up she went!

Then the boy fell off his swing. He sat on the ground. "Sorry," said Kinsley. "Are you okay?" The boy nodded. His dad came fast and picked him up. Kinsley kept swinging. Mama waved from the bench. Kinsley waved back, way up high.

Georgia put on her big sun hat. The hat was too loose. It fell over her eyes. "I can't see!" she said. Papa laughed softly. "Then push it up."

Georgia pushed up the hat. Now she could see the farm. She saw a red barn. She saw a fluffy white sheep. "My eyes see the sheep!" she said.

Papa gave her a soft piece of hay. Georgia touched it with her fingers. "My hands feel the hay. It is prickly." Then the sheep went "Baa!" Georgia giggled. "My ears hear the sheep." A warm breeze came by. It smelled like apples. "My nose smells apples," Georgia said.

They walked to the apple tree. Papa picked a small red apple. He washed it and cut it with his knife. Georgia waited. Then she took a little bite. "Yum! My mouth tastes the apple!" Papa smiled. "You found all five," he said. Georgia clapped her hands. Her hat slipped down again. She pushed it up and laughed. "Eyes again!"

Henry got in the family car. They were going on a big trip to Grandma's house. Henry had his own little bag. Inside were his teddy bear, his blocks, and one shoe.

Dad looked at the bag. "It is too full," said Dad. "The zipper will not close."

Henry tried to pull the zipper. It would not move. The bag was stuffed like a big round ball.

"Why will it not close?" Henry asked.

"Too many things are inside," said Dad.

Henry looked in his bag. He took out one block. He tried the zipper again. Still stuck! He took out the shoe. Now the bag was soft and squishy. Henry pulled the zipper. Zip! It closed all the way.

"My bag closed!" Henry shouted.

Dad put the bag in the car. Then they drove off. The sky got dark and stormy on the way. Henry held his teddy tight. Soon they would see Grandma's front door.

"Are we almost there?" Henry asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Look out the window."

Henry saw Grandma waving by her gate.

Evelyn wanted to sing the whole song. But she forgot the words in the middle. Mommy sang "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Evelyn sang "Twinkle" and then stopped. She frowned.

Mommy clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. "Try clapping with me," said Mommy. Evelyn watched Mommy's hands. They went up and down like a little bird. Evelyn clapped too. Her claps were fast, fast, fast. "Too speedy," laughed Mommy. "Slow your hands down." Evelyn watched the red block on the floor. It sat still. She thought of slow, still things.

Evelyn made her hands go slow. Clap, clap, clap. The claps matched Mommy's song. Then the words came out too. "How I wonder what you are." She did not stop. She sang it all the way to the end. Baby brother woke up from his nap and cried. Evelyn clapped slow claps and sang again, soft this time. Baby stopped crying. He watched her hands go up and down.

"Again," said Evelyn. "Up above the world so high." Baby kicked his feet and made a happy sound.

Axel sat down at the dinner table. He saw a big bowl of green peas. "I want peas!" he said. Mama said, "Let's count them first."

Axel clapped his hands. Mama put peas on his plate. "One, two, three," she said. Axel tapped each pea with his spoon. "Four, five, six!" he said. The peas rolled a little. He laughed.

Then Axel saw one pea near the edge. He pushed it with his finger. It rolled right off the plate. It dropped under the table. "Oh no!" said Axel. "My pea is missing!"

Papa bent down and looked. "I see it," he said. He picked it up. "Let's not forget this little pea." Axel giggled. Papa put it back on the plate.

"Now count again," said Mama. Axel pointed at each pea. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven!" He counted so fast. Then he ate one pea. "Now six!" he shouted.

Papa said, "Count to ten and eat them all." Axel grinned. "Seven, eight, nine, ten!" Then he opened his mouth wide. "Yum, yum, yum," he said.

Olivia's class was going outside. Teacher Sam said, "Coats on!" Everyone ran to the hooks. Olivia grabbed her purple coat.

She pushed her arm in one sleeve. Then the other arm. The coat hung behind her, funny and low. Teacher Sam said, "You can fix it. Take your time."

Olivia looked at the tag inside the collar. The tag was by her knees. She wiggled the coat off. She turned it around. Now the tag was at her neck. She pushed her arms in again. This time the coat sat just right on her back.

Next came the zipper. Olivia held the bottom part. She pushed the zipper down into it. Click. It caught! She pulled the slider up, up, up. The coat closed all the way to her chin.

Teacher Sam looked at the clock. "Still time before outside," he said. Olivia smiled and pulled the zipper down, then up again, just to see it open and close.

"Look at me!" she said.

Paisley had a new pet. It was a small orange fish. His name was Pip.

Pip swam in his bowl by the window. Paisley wanted to touch him. She tapped on the glass. Tap, tap. Pip hid behind the little green plant. He did not come out.

"Poor Pip," said Mama. "Watch and see." Mama did not tap. She sat very still. Soon Pip peeked out. Then he swam in a big slow circle.

Paisley tried too. She sat very still, just like Mama. Her hands stayed in her lap. Pip came out of the plant. He blew a tiny bubble.

Paisley fed Pip one small pinch of food. The flakes looked like yummy little stars to her, but they were fish food. Pip gobbled them up.

Outside, the moon came up. It was big and round. The moonlight shone on the fish bowl. Pip swam past the light and back again.

Paisley did not tap on the glass anymore. She just sat and watched. Pip swam right up close to her. He waved his little fin.

"Night night, Pip," said Paisley.

Milan wanted to plant a seed at school. Yesterday, his teacher had shown the class a bean. She said they would plant it today. Today was now. Milan held his little pot.

"Can we plant it now?" he asked.
