"Not yet," said Miss Ada. "Now we will put the bean in the dirt. Later, we will give it water. Tomorrow, it might look different."

Milan pushed the bean into the dark dirt. He patted it down, pat, pat, pat. Then he waited his turn for the watering can. He poured the water, drop by drop. The dirt turned dark and wet.

"Where is my plant?" he asked.

"Tomorrow," said Miss Ada. "You must wait."

Milan put the pot on the bright windowsill. He looked at it all day. At story time, he looked again. The pot sat still.

The next day, Milan ran to the window. He leaned in close. A tiny green tip was poking out of the dirt. "It came!" he shouted. "The bean grew in the night!"

Miss Ada smiled and gave him a shiny coin sticker for his pot. "Look what waiting can do," she said.

Milan tapped the glass. "Grow more tomorrow," he whispered to the little green tip. "I will come back and see you."

Jaxson woke up in his soft bed. The sun made a warm spot on his blanket. He rubbed his eyes and called, "Mama, I'm up!"

First came breakfast. Jaxson ate one egg, one piece of toast, and one banana. He counted them on his plate. "One, two, three," he said. His tummy felt happy and full. The banana tasted sweet on his tongue.

Then Jaxson played in the sandbox outside. His sister, a big girl named Mia, played too. They dug and patted and poured. Soon Jaxson's hands were dirty. His feet were dirty. Even his nose had a smudge of dirt. "Time for a bath," said Mama. She filled the tub with warm water. Jaxson stepped in carefully. The water turned brown and cloudy. "Look, Mama! The dirt left my feet!" Mama smiled and let the dirty water go down the drain. Jaxson came out clean and pink.

He put on one shirt, one sock, one sock, and one cozy sleeper. He counted again. Then he found a surprise under his pillow. It was his little rubber duck, hiding there all day. "Quack," said Jaxson. Mama laughed and kissed his head. Jaxson hugged the duck and closed his sleepy eyes.

Hayden wanted to wash his toy lion. The lion had jam on its mane. Hayden held the lion in the bathroom. He reached for the shiny tap.

Mama put her hand over his. "Let me do the tap," she said. Mama turned it a little. The water ran warm, not hot. Hayden put his fingers in. It felt nice. He put the lion's paw in too. The jam began to melt away.

Then Hayden saw the little bottle by the sink. He reached for it. "That one is for grown-ups," said Mama. She moved it up high. Hayden looked at his lion instead. He rubbed the mane with a soft cloth. Round and round he went. The jam came off. The lion was clean and special again. Hayden gave the lion a big hug. "All done," he said.

Billie stood in the kitchen. Her mom was cooking soup on the stove. Billie held her mom's leg and stayed close. The pot made steam. The steam went up, up, up.

"Is the soup hot?" Billie asked.

"Yes, very hot," said Mom. "Only I touch the pot."

Billie touched a spoon on the counter. The spoon was cold. The spoon did not make steam. The pot was hot, and the pot made steam. So Billie could tell which one was which.

"I need to stir," said Mom. "You can sit on your swing outside."

The sun was bright in the yard. Billie sat on her swing. Through the window, she watched Mom stir the hot soup. She swung her legs and waited for lunch.

Zoe packed her little red bag. "We go on a trip today!" said Mama. They drove a long, long way to the big park.

At the park, Daddy set up the tent. Zoe wanted her teddy bear. She looked in the car. She looked by the tree. No teddy. Zoe's lip went wobbly.

"Let's open your bag and look," said Mama. Zoe unzipped the bag. There was teddy, under her socks! Zoe had packed him herself. She hugged him tight.

Later, they walked on a bumpy path. Zoe saw a wheel on Daddy's cart. Daddy pulled the cart, and the wheel turned. When the wheel turned, the cart rolled. When Daddy stopped, the wheel stopped too. Zoe laughed and patted the wheel.

At night, Daddy made a fire far away. Zoe sat with Mama on the big log. An owl made a sound, "Who, who." Zoe held teddy close.

"It's just an owl," said Mama. "We are all here together."

Zoe yawned. She snuggled into her warm sleeping bag. "Night night, teddy," she said.

Asher ran to the snack table at summer camp. He wanted the watermelon so much. But Miss Jo put up her hand. "Wash first, sweet pea," she said.

Asher looked at his hands. They had sand on them. He put one finger in his mouth. Yuck. Sand was gritty and bad. So he went to the little sink. He pushed the soap pump. Bubbles came out, big and white. Miss Jo sang a song while he rubbed. "Bubbles, bubbles, up and down. Bubbles, bubbles, all around." Asher sang too. The bubbles carried the sand away. He watched the sand go down, down, down the drain.

Then the team sat together on a cozy blanket. Asher held his watermelon slice. It was clean and sweet. "No sand today," said Asher. He smiled and took a big bite.

Aaron lost his blue toy car. He loved that car. He looked for it at school, on the big playground.

"Where is my car?" said Aaron. His friend Mia came to help. "Let's look by the slide," she said. They looked there. No car. They looked by the swings. No car. The sky was cloudy, and everything looked gray.

Then the sun came out. The clouds moved away. The slide got bright. The sandbox got bright too. Something in the sandbox shined. It was a little blue shine! Aaron ran to the sandbox. He dug in the sand with his hands. Out came his blue car!

"The sun helped me find it," said Aaron. "The light made it shine!"

Mia clapped. "Good looking, Aaron!"

"Want to make it ride down the slide?" said Aaron. "Yes!" said Mia. The little blue car zoomed down, and the two friends laughed.

Luka sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted the fish sticker on the wall. But first, Doctor Amy said, "I need to check you." Luka looked at the sticker with his eyes. "Fish can swim," he said. "Can I have that fish?"

"One thing at a time," said Doctor Amy. She held up a small light. "Tell me what you see." Luka saw the light with his eyes. It blinked on and off. He covered one eye. The light looked the same. He uncovered it. Then the light looked different. Covering made it change! He tried both eyes. Now he saw two lights.

Next came the sounds. Doctor Amy rang a tiny bell. Luka heard it with his ears. Then he sniffed with his nose. "I smell soap," he said. He tasted an apple slice with his tongue. He touched the cool table with his fingers. "Eyes, ears, nose, tongue, fingers," he counted. "Five helpers." Doctor Amy smiled. "All five work great. Now look what I have." She held out the fish sticker. It was a fish by a tree, with brown roots under the ground. "For my best helper," she said. Luka stuck it on his shirt. "My fish can swim on me," he said.

Madison stood at the running track. She held a red beanbag. A hoop lay on the ground far away. She wanted the beanbag to land inside it. She threw it. The beanbag fell to the left. It missed the hoop. Madison frowned. She asked, "Where did it go?" Her dad said, "Try again." She looked at the hoop. She stood straight and faced it. She threw the beanbag straight ahead. It landed inside the hoop. "It went in!" she said.

Next, Dad rolled a big ball to her. She used one hand. The ball bounced off and rolled away. She asked, "Why did it fall?" She looked at her hands. She held out both hands. Dad rolled the ball again. She caught it with both hands. "I got it!" she said. Dad clapped. On her shirt was a little pig, and it bounced up and down as she jumped. "Can we go now?" she asked. Dad said, "Yes. Let's go home and swim."

Mya went to the library with her dad. The storytime room had soft blue mats. A lady named Miss Jo held up a card. "This is a library card," she said. "It lets you take books home."

Mya wanted a card so much. She waited in the line. One friend went first. Then another friend. Then it was Mya's turn. Miss Jo wrote Mya's name on a little card. Mya clapped her hands.

Mya picked a book about a striped cat. The cat had red stripes and yellow stripes. She held it tight. "This book is mine forever," she said.

Miss Jo shook her head. She showed Mya a paper pocket in the book. "The book goes home with you," she said. "Then you bring it back. Then Tom can read it too."

Tom was the boy with the blue shoes. Tom looked at the striped cat book. He wanted it too.

Mya looked at the book. She looked at Tom. She gave the book a big hug. Then she set it in her bag.

"Seven sleeps," said Miss Jo. "Then the book comes back."

At home, Mya counted the sleeps. One sleep. Two sleeps. Three sleeps. Four sleeps. Five sleeps. Six sleeps. Seven sleeps!

Mya carried the book back to Miss Jo. She set it in Miss Jo's hands. Then something surprising happened. Tom clapped for her. And on the table sat a new book. It was about paint. Bright paint, red and yellow, just like the cat.

"Ready for the next one?" asked Miss Jo.

"Yes," said Mya. "And Tom can have it after me."

Iris wanted to wash her hands all by herself. She stood by the sink and looked up at the faucet. The faucet was shiny and silver. It had a red dot on one side and a blue dot on the other side.

"Can I turn it on?" she asked.

"Yes, but wait for me," said Dad. Dad came and stood close to her. He put his hand under the water first. "Let me check it," he said.

Iris waited. She saw Dad touch the water and nod. "Now it is warm, not hot," he said. "Cold, then warm. Hot water can hurt you."

Dad turned the shiny handle a tiny bit. First the water was cold. Iris touched it with one finger. Then Dad turned it more, just a little. The water got warm. Iris put both hands in. She rubbed the soap and made white bubbles.

She saw that the little red dot made hot water. She did not touch that side. Dad turned the red side for her, slowly and carefully.

"I can learn the dots," said Iris. She pointed to the blue dot. "Blue is for me."

"That's right," said Dad. He handed her the small towel. Iris dried her hands and hung the towel on the hook, all by herself.

"Good helper," said Dad. He lifted her down and held her hand as they walked out.

Liam stood in the school computer lab. He wanted to draw a big sun. But the tablet was dark and still. He touched the black screen. Nothing happened.

Miss Rosa knelt down next to him. She held his hand gently. "Push the round button," she said. "It lives at the bottom of the tablet." Liam found the round button. He pushed it with one finger. The screen lit up, all bright and yellow and blue. Liam laughed out loud.

Now he needed the drawing app. Miss Rosa showed him the little picture of a paintbrush. Liam tapped it once. Nothing. He tapped it again, slower this time. The white page opened. Liam dragged his finger across the glass. A thick green line followed his finger. He made a circle. He made rays, one by one. The tablet felt smooth and warm under his hand.

Then the bell rang. Time to go. Miss Rosa did not grab the tablet. She waited. Liam looked at his sun. He pressed the round button again. The screen went dark. He slid the tablet into its soft blue bag. He pulled the zipper. It was a tight fit, but he tugged it to the top.

Liam carried the bag with two hands. He set it in the basket by the door. "My sun is sleeping," he told Miss Rosa. She smiled and patted the bag. "See you tomorrow, sun."

Jordan was at a restaurant with Mom and Dad. A big game was on the big screen. Everyone wore the team color, red. Jordan had a red hat and a red scarf. Even his boots were red.

Then the screen went dark. The game was frozen. The players did not move. "Oh no!" said Jordan. The whole room went quiet.

A waiter came by. He pressed a little button on his remote. The screen lit up. The players ran again. Jordan clapped and clapped.

Later, the screen froze one more time. Jordan waved his hand high. "Press the button!" he called. The waiter smiled and pressed it. The game came back, and everyone cheered. Dad lifted his cup. "Way to go, Jordan!"

Arlo woke up and looked out the window. The backyard was white. "Snow!" he shouted. "No school today," said Mom. "It is a snow day."

Arlo wanted to build a snowman. He put on his boots. Mom helped him tie his boots. She pulled the laces tight. Then they went outside. The snow was cold and soft. It squeaked under his feet.

Arlo patted a big snowball with his mittens. He patted it and patted it. "Why is it getting smaller?" he asked. Mom said, "Your hands are warm. Warm hands make snow melt." Arlo held his mittens on the snow. Drip, drip, drip. Little wet spots appeared. He gasped. His mittens made water!

Arlo took off one mitten and made a face in the snow. He pressed his warm thumb here and there. The snow melted into two eyes and a smile. Mom knelt down and gave the snowman a gentle pet on his cold head. "Good snowman," she said. Arlo laughed. Then he put his wet mitten back on and patted more snow.

Leon sat in a big chair at the hair salon. The chair was too big for him. His dad stood right beside him and held his hand.

"I don't want a haircut," said Leon. "I want my hair to stay on my head."

The hairdresser, Mia, smiled. "Watch what my scissors do," she said. "Snip, snip. One piece falls. Snip, snip. Two pieces fall."

Mia snipped near Leon's ear. A little piece of hair dropped down. It fell on the cape like a soft brown string. Leon watched it fall.

"Another one!" he said. "Snip, snip, three!"

Mia snipped again. More hair fell. It made a little pile on the floor. Leon saw that each snip made one piece fall. He turned his head to see better.

"Look, Dad! Snip, snip, four pieces!"

Dad laughed. "You are watching so well."

Soon the snipping stopped. Mia brushed Leon's neck with a soft brush. Leon looked in the mirror. His hair was short now. He touched it with his hand. It felt fuzzy like a peach.

"I have a new head," said Leon.

"You have the same head," said Dad. "Just less hair on it. You look so big."

At home, Mom was going to cook dinner. Leon ran to her. "Mom! My hair fell down, snip by snip!"

Mom hugged him close. "My big boy," she said.

Leon yawned. All that watching had made him tired. He leaned his fuzzy head on Mom's shoulder.

"Snip, snip," he said softly, and closed his eyes.

Claire loved the bean game at daycare. Yesterday she planted a bean in a little cup. She gave it water and set it on the sunny windowsill.

Today Claire ran to the window. "Look, look," she said. The bean was still brown and round. Nothing had grown. Miss Pat smiled. "Not yet. Roots grow first, under the dirt. That takes time. Let's wait."

So they waited. Claire played blocks with Ben. Later she looked at the cup again. Still brown. Still round. The sky outside was cloudy. "Tomorrow," said Miss Pat. "Come back tomorrow."

Tomorrow came. Claire ran to the window. A small green sprout stood up out of the dirt! "It grew!" said Claire. She tapped the cup gently. Miss Pat brought more water. "Now we wait again," she said.

Claire grinned. "More tomorrow," she said, and set the cup back in the sun.

Edouard sits on the soft red rug at school. He holds a book about a pet dog. The pages feel smooth. The book smells like paper and glue. Edouard opens the cover. He sees small black marks on the page. "What are those marks?" he asks. "Those marks are words," says his teacher, Miss Lily. "Words tell the story."

Edouard turns the pages. He starts at the front. He goes to the back. One page, two pages, three pages. The dog finds a tight little hole. The dog digs. The dog is happy. Edouard hugs the book. He wants to keep it forever.

"Can I take this book home?" he asks. "Yes, you can borrow it," says Miss Lily. "But we must bring it back on Friday." On Friday, Edouard puts the book in the basket. His friend Sam picks it up next. "New reader!" says Edouard, and he claps his hands.

Zoey wanted to build a house for her toy fish at daycare. But the blocks kept rolling away. Why did they roll? Zoey looked closely. Those blocks were round like balls. Round things roll!

She needed blocks that would stay still. She found a block with flat sides. It had four sides, all the same. She stacked it. It did not roll. "Square, square, stay right there," she said.

Next she found a long, flat block. It had four sides too, but two were long and two were short. She stacked it on the square block. It sat nice and still. Then she found a block with only three sides. It looked like a little roof. On it went, up on top. Pointy side up!

Zoey patted the tower. "My fish has a house," she said. Miss Ana smiled and pulled a cushion over. "Here is a round pond for your fish." The round cushion did not roll. It was soft and flat. Zoey placed the fish on top. "Round like you," she whispered. "But you stay still too."

Elizabeth wants to paint a butterfly at daycare. She sees the paint jars on the high shelf. They are too far up. She jumps. She jumps again. No paint.

She walks to Teacher Nan. "Please help me get the paint," she says. Teacher Nan smiles. She brings the jar down. "Thank you," says Elizabeth.

She paints one wing. She paints two wings. Then paint drips. It lands on Ben's paper. His paper has a big red spot now. "Sorry, Ben," says Elizabeth. Ben makes a face. Then he laughs. "It looks like a red sun," he says. He adds yellow all around it.

Elizabeth makes the wings straight and purple. One, two, three, four spots on each wing. "It is a magic butterfly," she says. "Let's pretend it can fly." She holds it up. It waves in the air. "It says please and thank you too," says Ben. Elizabeth giggles. The butterfly flaps around the table and lands on her nose.

Alexander stood at the bus stop with Grandma. The big yellow bus would come soon. But Alexander's coat was not on yet. It sat on the bench like a sleepy turtle. "Can I do it myself?" he asked. Grandma smiled. "Try," she said.

Alexander pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. The coat hung crooked. Why? He looked down. One side was inside out! He pulled it off and shook it. Now the coat looked right. He pushed his arms in again. This time it fit. He found the zipper pull and pushed it up, up, up. Zzzzzip! It closed all the way to his chin.

"Look, Grandma!" said Alexander. "I did it!" Just then the bus came around the corner. Alexander was not too cold, and not too tired of waiting. He climbed the steps holding Grandma's hand. The turtle coat on the bench was gone. Alexander was wearing it. He had won the zipper all by himself.

Anna sat at the table. The soup was hot. She wanted to eat it now.

Papa held up his hand. "We say our words first," he said. "Then we eat."

Anna pouted. The steam went up, up, up. "I want soup," she said.

Mama pointed at the steam. "Watch the steam," she said. "It rises like our words."

Anna watched the steam. It went up in little curls. Papa put his hand out. Anna put her small hand in it. Mama held Papa's hand too.

Then they said their words. "Thank you for our food. Thank you for our family." Anna said the parts she knew. "Thank you for soup. Thank you for cow milk."

Papa laughed. "Yes, thank you for cow milk," he said.

Then something surprising happened. A voice said, "Thank you from Grandma too!" Grandma was on the phone!

Anna clapped her hands. "Grandma said it too!"

Now every night, Anna held hands first. Then she said the words. Then everyone ate together.

"Bless our soup," Anna said. "Bless Grandma far away."

"Grandma can hear us," said Mama. "Listen."

The phone made a happy sound. "I hear you, young lady," said Grandma. "Amen!"

Eleanor ran to the swing. But the swing was wet. Rain had made a big puddle under it.

Eleanor looked with her eyes. The water shone in the sun. She touched it with her hand. It was cold and shiny. She sniffed with her nose. The wet slide smelled like rain. A bird sang, and she heard it with her ears.

Then a curly dog ran by. It shook its fur. Water flew everywhere. The water landed on the swing. The swing dried in the sun.

Eleanor waited. She touched the swing again. It was dry now. "Mama, look," she said. "The sun dried it." A small child sat alone by the sandbox, looking sad. Eleanor gave the child her hat. Then she climbed on the swing. "Whee," she said.

Owen did not want to go to the doctor. He was grumpy all morning. "No doctor," he said. "No shot, no cold thing."

Mom drove anyway. "We will get bread after," she said. "Warm bread."

At the office, Owen sat very still. He wanted to hide.

The doctor came in. "Hello, Owen!" she said. "Let's play a game. We use our body parts to find things out."

First she held up a card. "Close one eye. What do you see?" Owen looked with his eyes. "A duck!" he said. "A silly duck with a hat!"

Next she turned a knob. Beep, beep. Owen heard it with his ears. "I hear it!" he said. "It goes fast!"

Then she held a little jar. "Sniff this." Owen smelled it with his nose. "Yuck! That smells like socks!"

The doctor laughed. "Open wide." Owen stuck out his tongue. She looked, but he did not taste anything. "Say ahhh." "Ahhh!"

Last came the cold circle. Owen touched it with his tummy. "Brrr!" he said. "That is cold as snow!"

Then the doctor gave him blocks. "You can build a tower while we talk." Owen built it tall. Too tall. It fell down. Boom!

"Uh oh," said Owen.

"That is okay," said the doctor. "Now watch this." She spun the top block. It wobbled. Then the whole tower wobbled. Then it tipped.

Owen gasped. He built it again. This time he made a wide bottom. He spun the top block. The tower wobbled. But it did not fall.

"Look, Mom! Wide bottom, no fall!"

Then the doctor said, "All done, Owen." No shot today.

Owen got a dinosaur sticker. "I like the doctor," he said. "Can we come back tomorrow?"

Mom laughed. "Let's go get that bread. You can smell it all the way home."

Grandma was coming to stay! Anna ran to the kitchen. "One week," said Mama. "Seven whole days."

Anna wanted to make Grandma a surprise. She took out paper and glue. She made a card. It was messy. Glue was on her hands. Glue was on the table. Glue was on one cup!

Then Anna saw something. The glue dripped down. It dripped onto the floor. Papa slipped a little. "Whoa," said Papa. "The floor is sticky!"

Anna looked at the sticky spot. Her messy glue did that. Papa wiped it with a wet cloth. The stickiness went away.

"I can fix it too," said Anna. She wiped the cup. She wiped the table. Clean, clean, clean.

The doorbell rang. Grandma was here! Anna held up her card. "For you," said Anna. "One card, seven days."

Grandma gave her a big hug.

Henri stood by the big table at the hall. Everyone held hands in a circle. Papa held Henri's little hand. Henri wanted to say the words too, but he did not know them yet. The words felt too long and too thick, like a big sandwich he could not bite.

Papa said the blessing, one line at a time. "Thank you for our food." Henri listened close. "Thank you for our family." Henri opened his mouth. "Thank... you," he said. Mama smiled at him. Grandpa squeezed his hand.

Then it was time to eat. But Grandpa did not pick up his spoon. He looked at Henri and waited. Henri took a big breath. "Thank you for our food," he said. "Thank you for our family." Then Grandpa picked up his spoon. Then Mama did. Then everyone ate together.

Henri looked down the long table. When he said the words, the food started. It was like pushing a swing and the swing went. Papa put warm bread on Henri's plate. Henri took a bite. "Again next time," said Papa. "Yes," said Henri. "Me first."

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Olivier wanted to show him the park. "We will go every day," said Olivier.

On Monday they went to the big slide. On Tuesday they fed the ducks. But on Wednesday, rain fell. Olivier looked out the window. "The park is all wet," he said. "What can we do now?"

Grandpa smiled. "We can cook," he said. Grandpa cracked the eggs. Olivier stirred the bowl from his tall chair. Then Grandpa held the pan, and Olivier watched the pancakes puff up. "The pan made them big," said Olivier. "How does it do that?"

On Thursday the sun came back. Off they went to the park. Olivier found a big puddle. He dropped in one little stone. Plip! The water made rings. Then he dropped a big stone. Sploosh! The rings got big too. "Grandpa, come see!" he called. "Big stone, big rings!"

On Friday they made a sign for Grandpa's door. It said "Olivier's Grandpa" with a drawing of the park. Grandpa hung it up with a nail and his hammer, and Olivier held the sign steady.

On Sunday night Grandpa packed his bag. "Next time," said Olivier, "we drop the big stone first." Grandpa laughed and zipped the bag closed.

Bennett ran into the pool changing room. His swimsuit was all wet. Drip, drip, drip went the water on the floor. It made a little puddle by his feet.

Bennett looked down at the puddle. Where did the water come from? He stood very still. The drips came from his wet suit. When he moved, the drips moved too.

Bennett was sad. His clothes were in his bag. If the wet suit went in the bag, the bag would get all wet inside. He thought and thought.

Then he had an idea. He squeezed his swimsuit with both hands. Water ran out of it and down the drain. He squeezed until it stopped dripping. "All done," he said. Now the suit could keep the bag nice and dry.

Bennett put the suit in the bag. He picked it up. Not one drip fell. He smiled and ran out to find Daddy. "Look, my bag is dry," he said.

Sofia carried her swim bag down to the beach pool. Her towel had furry stripes on it. It was soft and warm.

A boy named Max was already in the pool. He kicked his legs fast. Then he zoomed forward like a little boat. Sofia watched him with wide eyes.

"I want to zoom too," she said. "How did you do that?" Max laughed. "Kick hard and see!"

Sofia held the pool wall with both hands. Then she kicked her legs. Splash, splash, splash! Her feet made white bubbles. And she felt herself slide forward through the water!

She kicked some more. She slid even farther. The water pushed her along, all the way to Max. He clapped his hands. "You zoomed!"

Sofia turned around and kicked back the other way. She zoomed to the wall. She zoomed to Max. She zoomed again and again.

"Look, Dad!" she called. Dad waved from his beach chair. Sofia kicked her fastest kick of all. The bubbles flew up around her like snow.

"Race you to the steps!" said Max. Sofia grinned and kicked.

Eliana was three today. The community hall had balloons and paper snowflakes on the walls. They looked like soft white snow. There was a cake with thick pink frosting. Everyone sang the birthday song. Daddy lit three little candles with a match. He stepped back and stood by Eliana.

Then one candle went out. Eliana looked. A big fan was blowing on the cake. The fan made air move. The moving air blew out the candle. "Why did it go out?" Eliana asked. Grandma pointed at the fan. "The wind from the fan did it," she said. Daddy turned the fan off. He lit the candle again. This time it stayed lit. All three candles glowed.

Eliana took a big breath. She blew out all three candles herself. Everyone clapped. Then Eliana slid her fingers through the thick frosting and licked them. "Best cake ever," she said.

Riley went to the park with her dad. She wanted to find something special for show-and-tell. What could she find?

First she used her eyes. Her eyes saw a red leaf by the bench. She picked it up. Then her ears heard a sound. "Tweet, tweet!" A little bird sat in the tree. "Hello, bird," said Riley.

Next her nose smelled something sweet. Mmm! Dad was holding a picnic bag. Inside were strawberries. Riley used her tongue to taste one. Sweet and juicy! Her hands touched the grass. It was soft and a little dirty. Her hair got dirty too when she rolled down the hill. "You need a bath tonight," said Dad, and he laughed.

Riley put the red leaf in her pocket. Then the wind began to blow. The leaf went up, up, up! It flew right onto the bird's branch. The bird hopped onto the leaf. "Look, Dad!" said Riley. "The bird likes my leaf too."

Isaiah went to the store with Mama. He held her hand on the busy street. At the door was a big bin of apples. Isaiah wanted a red one.

A girl was already at the bin. She picked apples one by one. Isaiah stood and waited. Mama said, "She goes first. Then it is your turn." So Isaiah kept waiting. The girl looked up. She said, "You can have a turn now." Isaiah picked a big red apple. The bin was full of apples, so there were plenty for both.

At the checkout, the line was long. Everyone stood one behind another. Isaiah stood behind a man with a full cart. Nobody pushed. Nobody ran. The line moved, step by step, all the way to the front. Isaiah put the apple on the belt all by himself.

Then the man with the full cart turned around. He held out a small sticker. "A star for waiting so nicely," he said. Isaiah pressed it onto his shirt. It was shiny gold. Isaiah smiled all the way home.

Elliot wanted to play house. He had a soft gray duck under his arm. "You be my baby," he told the duck.

He set the duck in a box. The box tipped over. The duck fell out! "Oh no," said Elliot. He tried again. The box tipped again. The duck fell on the rug.

Elliot looked around the room. He saw his big blanket. He pulled it into the box. The blanket made the box soft and full. He laid the duck on top. The box did not tip now. "There," said Elliot. "A bed for baby duck!"

Next, baby duck needed lunch. Elliot found a red play apple. "Juicy apple for you," he said. He held it to the duck's beak. Then he patted the duck's back, very gently. He sang a small song, "Sleep, baby, sleep."

Mom peeked in the door. "Is the baby sleeping?" she asked. "Shh," said Elliot. He covered the duck with a tiny sock. "Baby duck likes the sock," he whispered. "I like playing house, Mom. Come play too!"

Grayson got in the big car. "Campsite, campsite, campsite!" he yelled. Dad drove a long, long way. Mom said, "One tent, two bags, three snacks." Grayson counted too. "One, two, three!"

The tent went up. It was red and spotted. Grayson peeked inside. "My sleeping bag goes here!" But the wind began to blow. The tent's paper map flew off the table. It went up, up, up.

"My map!" Grayson yelled. He ran to Dad. Dad picked up a big rock. He put the rock on the corner of the map. The wind blew again. The map stayed still. The rock held it down.

Grayson found a small stone. He put his stone on the other corner. "I can help too!" The wind blew and blew. The map did not move at all. Grayson clapped his hands. Then he ran to get one more stone for Mom's hat, just in case.

Brielle woke up and wanted to play outside. But first she had to pick her clothes. She did not know what to wear.

She looked out the window. The sun was shining. It was sunny. So she put on a little hat. The sun was bright on her nose.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. It was rainy now. Brielle took off her hat. She put on her rain boots instead. She met her boots by the door. They were yellow and shiny.

The rain stopped. The wind began to blow. It was windy! The wind blew the leaves fast across the yard. Brielle's hat flew off the hook. She laughed and put on her warm coat.

Then something soft and white fell from the sky. It was snow! Brielle put on her mittens. She put on her big puffy coat.

Mom opened the door. "Brr, look at you," said Mom. Brielle ran outside. She made one small snowball and held it up high. "It's snowy!" she said. Mom took a picture of her in the soft white yard.Brielle woke up. She looked out the window. The sun was shining. It was sunny today.

She wanted to wear her yellow hat. But where was it? She could not find it. Brielle met her cat, Mila, near the couch. Mila was sleeping on something soft. It was the yellow hat!

Brielle put on the hat. She went outside. The sun felt warm on her nose. She did not need a coat.

Then the wind came. It was windy. The wind blew her hat away. The hat flew fast across the grass. Brielle chased it. She caught it and held it tight.

Then rain began to fall. It was rainy now. Brielle ran inside. Mom gave her red boots and a raincoat. Brielle stomped in small puddles. Splash, splash.

Next, soft white snow fell down. It was snowy. Mom put warm mittens on Brielle's hands. Brielle patted the snow. "More hat," she said, and put the hat back on her head. The wind could not take it now.

Jayden sat at the paint table at summer camp. His teacher Mia gave him three cups. "Red, yellow, blue," she said. Jayden pointed. "Red, yellow, blue," he said back. He tapped each cup as he named it. Red. Yellow. Blue.

Jayden wanted to paint a big green hill for his picture. But there was no green paint. He looked and looked. His lip wobbled. "No green," he said. "My hill is stuck." Mia sat down next to him. "Try mixing," she said. Jayden dipped his brush in the yellow. He dipped it in the blue. He swirled them together on his paper. The paint was cool and smooth under his brush. It made a big green blob!

Jayden clapped his hands. "I made green!" he said. He painted a big green hill with a red sun above it. His brush went swish, swish. "Look, Mia!" he said. Mia smiled. "That is a fine hill, Jayden."

Luke woke up early. Today was the big family party! Grandma was coming, and Aunt May, and baby Sam too. Luke wanted to help make the bread. But the kitchen table was empty. "Where is the dough?" he asked. Mom laughed. "It is hiding," she said. "Come and see." She lifted a towel on a bowl. The dough had grown big and puffy! It had pushed the towel up like a little hill. "Wow!" said Luke. Mom said, "Now we can fold it." Luke patted the soft dough. It felt squishy like a pillow. He folded one side over. Then he folded the other side. "I did it!" said Luke. Grandma arrived with a big smile. "Something smells good!" she said. Luke jumped up and down. "I made bread! Come and see!" The oven was hot, so Dad put the bread in. Luke watched from his chair. Soon the bread was golden. Dad set it on the rack. Everyone sat down together. Luke tore a piece for Grandma. She took a big bite. "Mmm," said Grandma. "This is the best bread ever." Luke grinned. "More bread, please!"

Hailey stood by the big door of the grocery store. The cold air whooshed in every time it opened. She held her coat in her little hands.

"Can you do it all by yourself?" asked Mama.

"I can try," said Hailey.

She pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. The coat sat crooked on her shoulders. The zipper dangled far, far down. Hailey pulled the little slider up, but it would not move. She pulled again. Nothing happened.

"Why won't it go?" she asked.

"Look at the bottom," said Mama. "The two sides have to sit together first."

Hailey peeked down. The zipper ends were apart. She pushed them snug into one point. Then she pulled the slider. Ziiiip! All the way up to her chin.

"Cold air, go away!" said Hailey.

Mama laughed. They walked out to the car. There was a tiny pocket on the coat Hailey had never seen before. She unzipped part of the way, poked a finger in, and found a peppermint.

"Is this true? A candy pocket?" said Hailey.

"It sure is," said Mama. "But you have to zip up first. Cold hands can't hold candy."

Hailey zipped it up fast. She held the peppermint tight all the way home.

Hudson stood at the little table in the art room. He had three pots of paint. One pot was red. One pot was yellow. One pot was blue.

"I want to paint a grape," said Hudson. "Grapes are purple." He looked and looked. There was no purple paint.

Miss Ana sat down next to him. "You can mix paints," she said. She put out a big clean tray. "Take your time."

Hudson dipped his brush in the blue pot. He made a blue spot on the tray. Then he dipped his brush in the red pot. He made a red spot on the blue spot. He stirred it round and round with the brush.

The paint turned purple. Hudson stopped stirring. He looked at it for a long time. Then he painted a big purple grape on his paper.

Next he wanted to paint a green leaf. He looked at his pots again. He put a yellow spot on the tray. He added some blue. He stirred slowly. The paint turned green.

Hudson hummed a little song while he painted. His brush went scratch, scratch on the paper. The purple grapes and the green leaves went home with him that day.

Alice sat in her car seat. The sun was warm on her lap. "Are we there now?" she said.

"Not yet," said Mama. "We are driving now. We will see Grandma later."

Alice looked out the window. A red truck went by. Then a cow went by. The truck was loud. Then the cow was loud too. Alice laughed and opened her mouth wide to moo.

Yesterday, Alice had picked blueberries with Grandma. The basket had been heavy to carry. Today, the blueberries sat in a big jar at home. Tomorrow, Mama would make jam. Mama would cook it, and Alice would watch from her chair.

"First we drive," said Mama. "Then we eat lunch. Then we see Grandma."

Alice held up one finger. "First the cow!"

Mama laughed. "Yes. First the cow. Now here comes the bridge."

The car went up, up, up. Then it went down. Alice's tummy felt funny and good. "Again!" she said.

"Later," said Mama. "The bridge comes again later."

Alice watched the road. She waited for the bridge. Then she saw it, far away, small like a toy. "Bridge!" she said, and pointed her finger all the way there.

Henri sat on the train with Mama. They were going to Grandma's house for a family trip. Henri held his little blue bear. The train went clickety-clack, clickety-clack.

Henri wanted to see the cows in the fields. He looked out of the window. But the window was foggy and white. "Where are the cows?" he asked. "I can't see them." The window felt cold and wet when he touched it.

Mama took his hand. "Try this," she said. She helped him rub the window with his sleeve. Round and round his hand went. The fog wiped away in one little circle. "Now look," said Mama. Henri peeked through the circle. He saw a green field. He saw a big cow! The cow looked back at him.

The window fogged up again, so Henri rubbed a new circle. Each time it turned white, he wiped it clean, and the world came back. "I did it!" said Henri. He waved to the cow through the clear round hole. Then Mama gave him his warm cup of milk. The train went clickety-clack, and Henri watched the trees go by, round and round, wiping the window whenever it turned white.

Charlotte got her first haircut today. Her mama held her hand. They rode past the park on their bike. Then they came to the barbershop.

The barber was named Sam. Sam made the big chair go up. The chair could roll across the floor. "Whee," said Charlotte. Sam rolled the chair a little bit. Then he rolled it back.

Charlotte looked in the mirror. Her hair was long and curly. It stood up like a fluffy cloud. Sam filled a spray bottle with water. He sprayed her hair. The water made the curls fall down. The curls went flat and shiny. Now Sam could cut the straight wet hair.

"Is my hair weak now?" asked Charlotte. "No," said Sam. "It is just wet. Wet hair lies down flat. That helps the scissors." Charlotte watched. Snip, snip. The scissors cut a little piece. Snip, snip. Another piece fell. The pieces dropped onto the cape like dark rain.

Sam brushed the little pieces away. He took off the cape. Charlotte jumped down. Her hair was short and neat. She spun around in front of the mirror. "Mama, look at me!" said Charlotte. Mama clapped her hands.

Everly wanted the moon. She saw it in the sky last night. "Moon," she said. "Moon is up now too," said Mama. Everly looked out the window. The moon was big and white. But it was bedtime. "Can I hold the moon now?" asked Everly. "Not now," said Mama. "Later you can look again."

Mama tucked Everly into bed. "Yesterday you saw the moon too," said Mama. "You waved at it." Everly remembered waving. Her hand went up and down. The moon stayed in the sky. Everly waved again now. The moon did not come.

"I will get it tomorrow," said Everly. "Yes, tomorrow," said Mama. "First we sleep. Then it is a new day." Everly closed her eyes. She waited. She heard the wind outside. She heard Mama hum.

In the morning, Everly ran to the window. The sky was light. The moon was small and pale. "Moon stayed all night!" said Everly. She got a cup of water. She tasted it. She made a sour face. "This water tastes funny," she said. Mama laughed. "Here is fresh water." Everly drank it all. Then she waved at the pale moon. "Bye, moon. Come back tonight."

Dylan ran to the park with his red kite. The sun was warm on his face. The grass smelled fresh and green. He felt so excited.

Daddy held the kite up high. "Ready?" said Daddy. Dylan began to run. He pulled the string. But the kite did not go up. It sat on the grass. Dylan felt sad. His mouth turned down.

Then the wind came. Dylan saw the leaves start to dance. The wind pushed the kite right up into the sky. The red kite went higher and higher. Dylan laughed. He felt happy all over. He jumped up and down. "Look, Daddy! Look!"

A big dog ran by. It barked loud. Dylan held Daddy's hand. He felt scared for a minute. But the dog was only chasing a ball. It wagged its tail. Daddy said, "See, he is friendly." Dylan smiled again.

The wind stopped. The kite began to fall. Dylan stomped his foot. He felt angry. He wanted the kite to stay up. Then he remembered. He waited. He watched the leaves. They began to dance again. The wind pushed the kite back up. The sky was full of kites and birds. Dylan pulled the string with both hands.

"Again!" said Dylan. Daddy smiled. They ran together across the soft grass. The red kite flew above them.

Sofia sat in the car with her teddy bear. "One bear, one Mama, one Sofia," she counted. They were going to the dentist for the first time. Sofia held teddy close. She was scared of the big chair.

The sun came through the window. It made a warm spot on her knee. Sofia moved her hand into the light. Her fingers turned bright and warm. She moved her hand away. The spot on her knee stayed warm.

"I can reach the sun spot," Sofia said. She reached out and patted teddy's ear. "The sun makes you warm, teddy." She put teddy in the light. Ted sat in the warm glow. Ted felt soft and cozy.

Mama parked the car. The dentist had a big wooden door. Sofia carried teddy inside. The chair was big, but she climbed up with help.

The dentist counted Sofia's teeth. "One, two, three," she said, all the way to twenty. Then Sofia held teddy up. "Count his teeth too," she said. The dentist smiled and gave teddy a little tap. Sofia grinned in the bright light.

Baby Mia was crying in the basket. She was little and red in the face. Lincoln wanted her to stop.

Mama said, "She may be cold." Lincoln touched Mia's tiny hand. It felt cool, like a small stone.

"I will fetch her blanket," Lincoln said. He ran to his bed. He grabbed his soft blue blanket. It smelled like sleep and warm milk. He laid it over Mia, very gently.

Mia stopped crying. She opened her eyes. She made a small sound, like a duck.

"She is warm now," said Mama.

Mia wrapped her hand around Lincoln's finger. Her hand was warm now too.

"You are not alone, Mia," Lincoln said. "I am here."

Mia yawned. Then she fell asleep under the blue blanket.

Ellie sat at the dinner table. Her bowl was empty. She wanted the special bread Grandma made.

"Yesterday we had Grandma's bread," said Ellie. "I want it now."

Mom smiled. "Grandma will bake a new loaf. But that is tomorrow. Today we have this bread."

Ellie looked at the bread in front of her. It was soft and white. She poked it with her finger. It did not look like Grandma's bread. Grandma's bread had seeds on top, like little brown boats.

Ellie pushed her plate away. "I don't want this bread."

Mom took a spoon of soup and poured it slowly. Drip, drip. Ellie watched the spoon. Then Mom tore the soft bread and dipped it in. The bread drank up the soup.

"You try," said Mom. "You can dip now."

Ellie picked up a small piece. She dipped it in her soup. It came out warm and wet. She took a bite. It was soft inside and good.

"Yum," said Ellie. She dipped another piece. Then another one.

Dad laughed. "Tomorrow, Grandma's bread. Today, dipping bread."

Ellie nodded. She kept dipping until her bowl was empty too.

"When is tomorrow?" she asked.

"After you sleep," said Mom. "First we sleep, then it is tomorrow."

Ellie yawned. She was not upset anymore. Her tummy was full.

"Can we have soup again tomorrow too?" she asked.

"We can have soup tomorrow too," said Dad.

Ellie rubbed her eyes and said, "Tomorrow, dipping bread and seeds."

Michael put on his coat all by himself. The zipper was hard. He pulled and pulled. Then the zipper went up. His teacher smiled. "Nice work, Michael," she said.

At school, Michael saw his friend Sam. Sam's shoes were on the wrong feet. Sam looked shy. He hid his feet under the rug. "I can't do the buckle," Sam said.

Michael sat down next to Sam. "Watch me," he said. Michael pulled the strap. He pushed the buckle. Click. The buckle was on. Sam tried the other shoe. He pulled the strap. He pushed the buckle. It did not click.

"Try again," said Michael. Sam pulled the strap slow this time. He pushed the buckle. Click. Sam jumped up. "I did it." Both shoes were on the right feet now.

The class went to wash hands for snack time. The soap smelled like lemons. Michael sniffed his hands. "Mmm," he said. Sam sniffed too. After snack, the class napped on little mats. Then they went outside to play.

At pick-up time, Michael's mom came. She pointed at his coat. "Who zipped that?" she asked. Michael puffed out his chest. "Me," he said. Then he bent down and buckled his shoes again, just to show her.

Yesterday, Anthony went to the library with Mama. He found a big red book about diggers. He took it home and read it three times.

Today, Anthony was hungry for more diggers. "Where is my red book?" he asked. He looked on the shelf. One blue book. One green book. One yellow book. No red book. "Maybe someone took it home," said the library lady. "It will come back later."

Anthony waited. He read a train book now. He stacked some soft blocks. Then he heard a bump. A red book slid down the return chute! It was the digger book. "It came back!" said Anthony. The library lady did smile. "You gave it back yesterday. Now it is here today." Anthony hugged the book tight. "Tomorrow I will bring it back again. And later, can we have cake?" Mama laughed. "Later, little one. Now let's check it out."

Charlie went to the basketball court with her dad. The sun made a long shadow by the net. Charlie held a red beanbag in her hands. She wanted to throw it into the hoop.

"Throw it high," said Dad. "One, two, three, up!" Charlie threw it. The beanbag hit the rim and fell down. She tried again. "One, two, three, up!" This time it went in. The net moved and made a soft swish. Charlie clapped her hands.

Then Dad rolled her a big blue ball. "Catch it with both hands," he said. The ball bounced off her arms. It rolled a long way across the court. Charlie ran after it and patted it, like patting a sleepy cat. "Nice pat," said Dad. "Now make your arms into a big bowl." Charlie held out both arms. "One, two, three, catch!" The ball landed right in them and stuck, like a magnet on the fridge.

Dad smiled and held up the beanbag. "Want to try both together?" Charlie nodded. She threw the beanbag into the hoop. Then she held out her arms. The big ball came, and she caught it. "I did both!" said Charlie. Dad picked her up and spun her around, and the net above them went swish, swish, swish.

Nora was at Grandma's house. Lunch was on the table. Nora wanted the crunchy carrots right now. Grandma said, "First we wash hands." Nora looked at her hands. They had dirt on them from the garden. She did not want to wait.

Grandma helped her at the sink. Grandma made the water warm. Nora rubbed the soap all over. "Now we sing the hand song," said Grandma. They sang it all the way through. The bubbles went down the drain. Nora looked at her hands. The dirt was gone. The soap made the dirt go away.

Nora marched to the table. She picked up a carrot. Crunch, crunch, crunch. "Yum," said Nora. Grandma smiled. "More carrots?" she asked. "Yes please," was Nora's answer.

Leah went to the pool by the beach. She wanted to swim like the big kids. But when she let go of the wall, she sank down. Water went over her mouth. She grabbed the wall again.

Leah watched her teacher, Miss Jo. Miss Jo took a big breath. Then she lay flat on the water. She floated like a leaf. Leah had a question. "Do I float if I hold my breath?" "Try it," said Miss Jo.

Leah filled her lungs with air. She held it. She lay back in Miss Jo's arms. Her belly went up, up, up. Her toes came up too. She was floating! After the pool, Mom shared a crunchy apple with her. "You swam today," said Mom. Leah kicked her feet in the sand and smiled.

Riley wanted to find her lost red sock. Grandma said, "Let's count the places we look."

"One," said Riley. She looked under the big blanket. No sock there.

"Two, three," said Grandma. They looked in two shoes by the door. No sock. "Four," said Riley. She peeked in the quiet corner by the chair. No sock.

Grandpa sang, "Five, six, seven!" They looked in the toy box, the basket, and the big pot. Still no sock.

"Eight," said Riley. She looked by the drying rack. The wet clothes were hanging there. They would dry soon.

"Nine," said Grandpa. He looked under the bed. "Ten!" he shouted. He held up the red sock.

Riley laughed. "The sock was hiding!"

Grandpa put the sock on his own ear. "Does it fit me?"

Riley giggled. "No, Grandpa! That is my sock!"

Grandma smiled and hung the sock on the rack to dry.

Hazel wanted a picnic. But her basket was empty. "I need food," she said.

She went to the kitchen. Mom cut an apple and a cheese square. Mom put in two crackers too. Hazel looked at them. "These are all foods," she said. She put the foods in her basket.

Outside, Hazel saw her toy bunny on the grass. Bunny was hungry, she thought. She gave bunny a pretend bite of apple. Then her dog Bingo ran up. Bingo made a happy sound and wagged his tail. "You are not a toy," Hazel told him. "You are an animal." She gave Bingo a real crumb. He ate it fast.

A bird flew down. It pecked at a cracker bit. Hazel laughed. Now bunny, dog and bird all sat on the blanket with her. Hazel clapped her hands. "Welcome to my picnic, friends," she said.

Emmett wanted a snack before his nap. Mom was baking bread in the kitchen. Emmett used his nose to sniff the air. "Mmm, it smells sweet," he said. "What is that smell?" He answered himself: "Bread!"

He used his ears to listen. He heard a bump, bump, bump. "What is that sound?" he asked. Mom laughed. "That is the dough in the bowl. It is rising like a balloon." Emmett touched the bowl with one finger. It felt soft and warm, like a cat's tummy.

"I want to taste it," said Emmett. "Not yet," said Mom. "It is still warm from the oven." She gave him a little crust on a plate. Emmett used his eyes to look at it. It was brown and bumpy. He took a big bite. "Crunch!" he said. "My ears hear my own snack!"

Emmett helped Mom sweep the crumbs off the table. "One crumb, two crumbs, three crumbs," he counted. Then he patted his tummy. "My tummy says thank you." Mom kissed his wild, messy hair. "Nap time now, bread boy." Emmett yawned and hugged his bear tight.

Lincoln ran to the school garden. Today was planting day! He held three little seeds in his hand.

"I will plant a carrot," he said. His teacher, Miss Ana, helped him dig a small hole. Lincoln dropped the seed in. He patted the dirt down. Then he watered it with a tiny blue can.

Every day Lincoln ran to look. One morning, a green sprout peeked out! Lincoln jumped up and down. But next to it, nothing grew. That spot had no sprout at all. It was a puzzle.

"Why did this one grow?" Lincoln asked. He looked and looked. Then he saw it. The empty spot was dry and cracked. His sprout had wet, dark dirt. He had poured water there every day. The water made the seed grow.

"Maybe more water will help!" Lincoln said. He gave the dry spot a big drink. He waited and waited.

Days later, a tiny sprout popped up there too. "It worked!" Lincoln cheered.

At last, a fat orange carrot grew. Miss Ana washed it at the sink. She cut it into round little coins. Lincoln took a bite. It was not salty. It was sweet and crunchy. Lincoln smiled. "Water next, then carrots," he said. "Every time!"

Victor wanted to build a house for his toy cat. He looked for the right blocks. The square block had four flat sides. It sat still on the rug. The triangle block had three sides and pointy corners. It sat on the roof like a hat. "Good," said Victor.

But the round block would not stay up. It had no flat sides at all. Victor pushed it on top. It rolled off. It rolled right under the chair. "Oh no," said Victor. His sister Mia came in. "Let it be a ball," she said. "Cats like to chase balls." She reached under the chair and got it.

Victor gave the round block a push. It rolled across the rug. The toy cat sat next to it. The long rectangle block became the door. Victor put the cat in. Mia blew him a kiss. "Nice house," she said. Victor waved and made the cat fly out for one more roll.

The lights went out. The whole house went dark. Jules stood still in the kitchen. "Mommy, where did the light go?" he asked.

Mommy found the big flashlight. She clicked it on. A bright beam lit up the room. "The power is out," she said. "We will use the flashlight now." She planted the flashlight on the table, standing up tall. The light shone on the wall.

Jules held his hand in the light. A big shape appeared on the wall. "Mommy, look! What is that?" he asked. "That is a shadow," she said. "Your hand is blocking the light. So the wall stays dark there." Jules wiggled his fingers. The shadow fingers wiggled too.

He made a bunny shape with two fingers up. The wall had a bunny now. He bent his fingers, and the bunny's ears flopped down. He laughed a soft little laugh.

Then Daddy came in with a small lantern. He set it on the floor. Now Jules had two shadows! One bunny on each side of him. "Two bunnies!" Jules said. He clapped his hands. Both bunnies hopped away.

Hunter wanted warm cocoa. He wanted it fast. Mom said the milk had to heat slow on the stove. Hunter stood far back and watched. The big pot sat on the fire. The little cups waited on the table.

The sky outside turned stormy. Rain hit the window fast. A small bird sat under the big roof. It was dry there. "Smart bird," said Hunter.

The milk got hot. Mom poured it slow into Hunter's little cup. Hunter blew on it. He blew slow. Then he blew fast. The steam danced away. Mom put one cold spoon in the cup. Hunter touched the handle. The cold spoon made his cocoa cool enough for a big sip. "Mmm," said Hunter. "Cold spoon, happy tongue!"

Aiden finds a red book at school. The cover has a picture of a sleepy bear. Under the bear are little black marks. "Those marks say Sleepy Bear," says his teacher. Aiden lifts the cover with both hands. He turns page one, then page two, then page three. The bear yawns on each page.

Aiden wants to keep the book forever. He puts it in his cubby. He hides his coat over it. "The book lives in our book corner," his teacher says. "It is like a library book. You can take it home. Then you bring it back so other kids can read it too."

Aiden feels upset at first. He hugs the book tight. Then he sees Mia waiting. She points at the sleepy bear. Aiden looks at the marks on the cover. He opens the book for her. "Sleepy Bear," he says. Mia smiles. Aiden turns the pages, one by one, all the way to the end.

Austin waited in a big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted to know if his ears were okay. He could not hear his mother when she whispered.

Dr. Amy smiled. She held up a little bell. She rang it near Austin's ear. Ding! Austin heard it with his ear. He turned his head. "I hear it!" he said.

Then Dr. Amy shined a tiny light. Austin saw it with his eyes. He saw the light go blink, blink. Next she held out a sticker. "Touch it," she said. Austin touched it with his fingers. It felt squishy. He sniffed a soap sample with his nose. It smelled like flowers. The nurse gave him a sweet candy. He tasted grape with his tongue.

Dr. Amy looked in Austin's ears. "Your ears are clean," she said. "I found a tiny marble in one." Austin's mother laughed. "My sock was squishy last night," she said. Austin grinned. He put the marble in his pocket. Then he rang the bell himself. Ding! His mother covered her ears. "Not too loud," she said, "or the baby will not sleep." Austin rang it very soft. Ding.

Nataly ran into the nursery. A new baby was coming today! The little crib stood by the window. It smelled like soap and clean sheets.

Natalie wanted to make the room ready. She found paper and glue. "I will make a picture," she said. She glued a big red heart onto the paper. She glued a yellow sun, too. The glue was cold and sticky on her fingers. Then she laid the blue blanket down flat in the crib. She patted it with both hands. Smooth and flat, just right for a baby.

Daddy made a road with tape on the floor. It was a long road for toy cars. "The road leads to the crib," he said. Natalie pushed a little car along the road. Vroom, vroom! The car rolled all the way to the crib and stopped.

Then they heard the door. Mommy came in. She carried a small bundle. A tiny face peeked out. "This is Baby Sam," said Mommy. Natalie touched his small hand. Baby Sam grabbed her finger and held on tight. Natalie laughed out loud. "He likes me!" she said. She taped her picture on the wall, right over the crib. Baby Sam looked up at the big red heart.

Raphael put on his big boy shoes. He was going to school with his teacher, Miss Kim. His tummy felt jumpy and excited.

At school, a boy named Ben was crying. His block tower had fallen down. Ben looked sad. Raphael had an idea. He picked up the blocks one by one. He stacked them up tall. Then he put a red block on top. "Look, Ben," he said. "It fits!" Ben stopped crying. He smiled a big smile. Now Ben looked happy.

A girl named Mia ran by too fast. She bumped the tower. Crash! It fell again. Ben's face turned red. He looked angry. "Do you want to build it again?" Raphael asked. Ben nodded. They built it together, taller than before. "Is this tower real big?" asked Raphael. "The biggest," said Ben. Miss Kim gave them each a paper star. Raphael stuck his star on his hand and waved it high.

Everett sat at the dinner table. He wanted the big red tomato. It sat far away, by Daddy's plate.

Everett used his eyes to look at it. It was round and shiny. He used his ears to listen. The pot went pop, pop on the stove. Daddy stirred it from far away.

"I smell it!" said Everett. His nose wiggled. "It smells like summer!"

Daddy slid the tomato closer. Everett touched it with one finger. It felt smooth and cool. But the bowl felt rough next to it.

"Try a bite," said Daddy.

Everett stuck out his tongue. He licked the tomato. He made a face. Then he froze.

"It's sour!" he said. "My tongue knows!"

Daddy laughed. Everett laughed too. He picked up the tomato with both hands. He took a big bite anyway.

Lennon wanted the red crayon. It sat on the far side of the table. Her friend Mia was using it.

"May I have the red crayon, please?" Lennon asked.

Mia smiled and gave it to her. "Thank you," Lennon said.

Then Lennon drew a big cat. She reached for the glue. The glue rolled off the table. It hit Mia's shoe and made a white spot.

"Sorry, Mia," Lennon said.

"It's okay," said Mia.

The glue bottle was too high to reach on the shelf. Lennon could not put it back. What should she do now? She walked to Teacher Rosa.

"Can you help me, please?" Lennon asked.

Teacher Rosa took the glue and put it high up. Then she picked up her phone and took a picture of the big cat.

"Wow," said Teacher Rosa. "What a spotted cat!"

Lennon looked at her cat. It had lots of spots. She started to draw another one.

"Can I have the blue crayon, please?"

Madelyn wanted her sheep to have a house. The toy barn had four doors. One door was a circle. One was a square. One was a triangle. One was a rectangle.

She pushed the sheep to the circle door. The sheep did not fit. She pushed it to the square door. It did not fit. She pushed it to the triangle door. Still it did not fit. The old sheep had one weak leg, so it could not jump or climb. "No door fits you," Madelyn said. "No door fits you at all."

Then Madelyn saw the roof. The triangle roof sat on top. She lifted it up, up, up. The barn was open now. She set the sheep down on the soft straw. She put the triangle roof back in place.

Madelyn peeked through the little circle window. The sheep peeked back and said, "Baa."

Cooper wanted his ball to roll fast. He gave it a big push. The ball zoomed across the playroom. Then he gave it a small push. The ball rolled slowly and stopped near his toe. "Hmm," said Cooper. "Big push, fast ball!"

Cooper found two cups on the little table. One cup was cold. He touched it with one finger. Brrr! Dad held the other cup. "This one is hot," said Dad. "Watch from here." Steam rose up in a curl. Cooper smelled the steam. It smelled like warm cocoa. He waited and waited. At last the hot cup turned cool too.

Then Cooper smelled something sharp. It was the orange Mom was cutting in the kitchen. She cut a big piece and a small piece. Cooper took the small piece. He chewed it slowly. Then he gave one big, happy jump. "Big jump!" he said.

Rowan wanted a sandwich. But Mom said, "First, find the bread."

Rowan opened the bread bag. The bag was closed with a twist. He turned the twist and turned it. Then the bag opened wide.

The bread was square! "Square like my blocks," said Rowan. Mom took a big knife. She cut the bread on the diagonal. Now there were triangles! Rowan clapped. "Two triangles!"

Rowan put cheese on one triangle. The cheese was a circle. "The circle sits on the triangle," he said. Mom cut a pickle into long strips. Rectangles!

Mom sang a little song while they worked. Rowan sang too. "Square, triangle, circle, rectangle, yum, yum, yum!"

Then Rowan reached for his milk. It tipped over. "Oh no, a spill!" But Mom wiped it fast. "Mistakes are okay," she said. "Clean up, then try again."

Rowan set his cup down slowly this time. No spill at all. He bit his triangle sandwich. "Mmm," said Rowan. "Triangles taste best!"

Jasmine wanted a party for her bear. She looked in the toy box. She found red cups. "Red for bear," she said. She marched to the kitchen with them. "More cups, please," she said.

Mama gave her blue cups too. Jasmine set them on the floor. She found a yellow banana. "Yellow for the party," she said. She put it on a green plate. "Green plate, yellow banana. So pretty."

But bear had no hat. Jasmine looked and looked. She found a red sock. Too big. She found a blue sock. Too big. She waited. She looked again. There, under the chair, was a tiny green sock. "Green hat for bear," she said. She put it on bear's head. It fit just right.

Jasmine clapped her hands. Mama brought milk in the blue cups. Bear got the green sock hat. The banana sat on the yellow... no, the green plate. Jasmine sat down next to bear. "Now we can eat," she said. "Our party can start."

Gabriella went to the community kitchen with her mama. She wanted to help make bread for the family. The big mixing bowl was old and blue. Mama let Gabriella pour in the flour. It fell like soft snow. Gabriella poked the flour with one finger. "Where did my finger go?" she asked. "It is hiding in the flour," Mama said.

Next came the warm water and the yeast. Mama stirred it slow. Then they had to wait. Gabriella watched the bowl. The dough sat still, like a sleeping cat. "Is it broken?" Gabriella asked. "No, we wait," said Mama. They washed the table. They set out cups. Gabriella waited some more.

Then she looked again. The dough was big now! It had grown up and up, like a puffy cloud. Gabriella poked it softly. It squeezed back through her fingers. "It got big!" she said. Mama smiled. She put the pan into the hot oven, and Gabriella stood back.

Soon the kitchen smelled warm and sweet. Mama took out the bread with big gloves. Gabriella tore a piece for papa and a piece for grandma. She took one bite. It was soft inside. "The little dough grew into this," said Gabriella. She hugged the warm loaf, right against her cheek.

Isla wanted to find her soap. It was bath time. Mama was there to help.

Isla used her eyes. She saw a yellow duck. She saw a blue pot. No soap yet.

Then Isla used her ears. She heard a drip, drip, drip. The water was running! When Mama turned the tap, the drips came. When Mama turned it off, the drips stopped. Isla clapped her hands.

Isla used her nose. She smelled something sweet. "That way!" she said. She walked to the shelf.

There was the soap. Isla touched it with her fingers. It felt smooth and slippery. She licked it with her tongue. "Yuck!" said Isla. "Soap is not for tasting." Her tummy was fine. She had only tried a tiny bit.

Mama laughed. "Good finding, Isla. Now let's wash." The water was warm and cozy. Isla rubbed the soap on her arms.

"I found it myself," said Isla. "And now the bathroom is all tidy."

The lights went out. The whole farmhouse went dark. Kai stood very still.

"Mama!" he called.

"I am here," said Mama. She took his hand. "The power is off. Let's find the big lamp."

Mama lit a candle on the table. The wick caught the flame. Then the little room was not dark anymore. The candle made the room glow.

Kai clapped his hands. "It works!"

"Want to help?" Mama asked. She held the candle up high. "Watch what happens when I step this way."

Mama took a step. Her shadow on the wall took a step too. It grew big, then small, then big again.

Kai giggled. He moved his arm. His shadow moved its arm!

"We are having a shadow party," said Mama.

Dada came in with blankets. They sat close on the rug. The candle flickered. The shadows danced on the wall.

"This is a pretty party," said Kai. He made a bunny with his fingers. The shadow bunny hopped.

Then the lights popped back on. The room was bright again. Kai waved at the candle.

"Bye bye, little flame," he said. "See you next time."

Colton stood in the restaurant kitchen. It was snowy outside the window. The cook, Mr. Bell, set down warm toast. "Can I help?" Colton asked. "Yes," said Mr. Bell. "Spread the butter. Then pour the milk."

Colton picked up a dull little spreader. He dipped it in soft butter. He slid it across the toast. The butter made the toast shiny. "Where did the butter go?" he asked. "Into the bread," said Mr. Bell. Colton slid again. More shiny spots.

Next came the milk. Colton held the cup on the table. He tipped the pitcher a little. Milk went in, drop by drop. He tipped it too far. Milk ran over the rim. "Oh no," said Colton. He wiped it with a cloth. Then he tipped just a little. The cup filled up. Not one drop fell.

A tiny turtle sat on the shelf by the cups. Its shell was shiny, like the butter. Colton laughed. "More milk," said Mr. Bell, and slid a new cup across the table.

Cooper sat in his car seat. His cup had rolled under the seat. He could not reach it. "Help, please, Daddy," he said.

Daddy reached back and got the cup. "Here you go." Cooper took a drink. "Thank you," he said. Daddy smiled in the mirror.

Then Cooper dropped his bear. The bear sat in the middle of the floor. Cooper's foot was on the bear's paw. "Sorry, Bear," he said. He moved his foot. He hugged Bear tight.

Outside, a big truck went by. It made a loud sound. Cooper held his ears. "Will it be quiet soon?" he asked. "Yes," said Mommy. "Watch." The truck drove away. It was quiet now.

Cooper counted what he had. One cup. One bear. One blanket. "Say it again," said Mommy, and Cooper laughed and counted. One, two, three.

The car turned onto their street. Home. Cooper waved at the house. "Hello, house," he said. Daddy parked the car, and Cooper held Bear all the way to the door.

Jordan ran to the window at daycare. Snow was falling outside. "Yesterday there was no snow," said Miss Ana. "Today the snow is here."

Jordan pressed his hands on the cold glass. The snowflakes landed one by one. Then they melted into little wet dots. Where did each flake go? Jordan watched another one land. It made a small wet dot too.

"Now we will go outside," said Miss Ana. "Later we will have warm soup." Jordan put on his boots. His boots were blue and good for snow.

Outside, Jordan found a shovel. He pushed the snow into a pile. The pile grew bigger and bigger. He patted it and made it tall. Then he tried to stack one snowball on top. The big pile held the snowball up. The tall pile did not fall down.

"When can we build more tomorrow?" Jordan asked.

"Tomorrow the snow will still be here," said Miss Ana.

Jordan looked at the tall white pile. Then he looked up at the sky. More snowflakes were coming down, one by one.

Julia wanted to play outside. She looked out the big window. The sun was out. It was sunny. "Hat!" said Julia. She put on her sun hat. One, two, she tapped it down.

But then the wind came. The tree bent and waved. It was windy. The wind took Julia's hat. The hat flew across the grass. Julia held her hat down with both hands. That did not work. The wind blew again.

Then rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip. It was rainy. Julia ran inside. Mama gave her boots and a raincoat. Julia put them on. One boot, two boots. "Now you can splash," said Mama.

Julia splashed in a puddle. The splash made a big circle. The rain made little circles too. Julia laughed. The rain stopped. The sun came back. Julia saw something in the sky. It was a rainbow. It made a big triangle of colors over the houses.

Then soft white flakes fell. It was snowy. Julia held out her hand. One flake landed on her mitten. It was tiny and white. Mama called, "Cocoa time!" Inside, Mama held the warm cup. Julia took a sip. "Tasty," said Julia. She looked out the window at the snow. "Snow again tomorrow?" she asked.

Connor sat at the dinner table. He was hungry. He wanted his favorite dinner.

"Guess what we eat tonight," said Dad. He put a bowl on the table. Connor peeked in. It was soup with carrots and noodles. Carrots were foods. Foods went in his tummy!

Connor held up his fork. "My monkey wants dinner too!" His toy monkey sat in his chair. "Monkey eats bananas," said Dad. "Bananas are foods too." Connor giggled. Monkey was a toy. Toys could not eat.

Connor gave monkey a pretend taste. Then he ate a big spoon of soup. Yum. He made a happy sound, "Mmm!" Monkey got soup on his fur.

Mom laughed. "Now monkey needs a bath." She wiped monkey's face with a napkin. Connor gave monkey a hug. Then he ate his noodles, one by one, all gone.

Henry wanted to ride the big red swing at the park. Yesterday the swing was wet from rain, so he could not ride it. Today the sun was out, and the swing was dry. But a girl was on it now. Henry had to wait.

Henry sat on the bench with Dad. He pulled his sweater tight because the wind blew. "When is later?" Henry asked. "Soon," said Dad. They watched the clouds move across the sky. The clouds went slow, then they went fast.

Then the girl jumped off the swing. "Now it is yours," she said. Henry ran fast. Dad pushed him up high. Henry laughed. Tomorrow they would come again, and maybe the clouds would bring rain. "Tomorrow I will wear my rain boots," said Henry, kicking his feet into the blue sky.

Felix loved the red truck book. Miss Dana held it up at story time. She turned the pages one by one. First page, then next, then next. The truck went beep on the last page. Felix listened to every beep.

After snack, Miss Dana said, "A librarian is coming." Felix ate his salty crackers and waited. He waited a long time. At last, a lady came with a big bag of books. Each book had little marks on the front. "Those marks are the name of the book," said Miss Dana. Felix looked close. "Truck," he said. Miss Dana smiled and nodded.

Felix picked the red truck book. "I want to keep it," he said. "It is mine now." The librarian shook her head. "You can take it home," she said. "But you need to bring it back on this day." She showed him a paper with the day on it. Felix held the book tight. Then he thought about his friend Sam. Sam liked trucks too.

"Sam can read it next," said Felix. He gave the book back on the right day. The librarian had a surprise for him. She held up another truck book. "This one is new," she said. Felix opened it, front page first, and sat down to look. "Beep," he said, turning the page.

Zoey sat at the dinner table. She had a big spoon in her hand. Tonight they were having soup.

Zoey wanted to scoop the soup all by herself. She tried. The spoon went in. The soup dripped out. Plop, plop, on the table. Her face turned sad.

"Keep trying," said her father. "Go slow."

Zoey tried again. She chased a carrot around the bowl. It kept sliding away. Her face felt hot and angry. She put the spoon down.

Then the ladle slipped. A big wave of soup splashed. Zoey jumped back, scared. "It's okay," said her father. "We can wipe it up." He used a towel.

Zoey picked up her spoon once more. She held it still. She scooped slow and steady. The soup stayed on the spoon. It went into her mouth!

"I did it!" said Zoey. Her smile was big and happy. She jumped in her seat, so excited.

"Zoey scooped the soup," said her father. He clapped. Zoey clapped too. Then she chased one more carrot, and this time she caught it.

Layla was building a tower with her blocks. She stacked one, two, three blocks high. "Tall!" she said. She felt so happy.

The cat jumped up. The tower fell down. Crash! Layla's lip wobbled. She felt sad. She wanted to cry.

Then the cat knocked her juice cup over too. "No, cat!" said Layla. Her face got hot. She felt angry. She stomped her little foot.

Mama came over. "Let's try again," said Mama. "The cat can watch from the chair." Mama put the cat on the soft chair. He curled up in a ball.

Layla had an idea. She would build a different tower. She made it short and wide. She put the blocks down slow, slow. She waited and patted each block.

The tower stood up. It did not fall! Layla clapped her hands. She felt excited. She jumped up and down.

The cat slept on the chair. Layla sat by her tower. She touched the top block very softly. "Stay," she whispered.

The blocks stayed still, and Layla smiled.

Evelyn sat at the little blue table. She was making a paper lion. First she glued on a round orange face. Then she wanted to add the mane.

Evelyn stuck on one yellow strip. It fell off. She stuck it on again. It fell off again. The strip dropped to the table.

Evelyn made a sad face. Her teacher Miss Jo came over. "Try this," said Miss Jo. She showed Evelyn how to press the strip down. "Now hold it. Count with me. One, two, three, four, five."

Evelyn pressed hard. She counted to five. Then she let go. The yellow strip stayed on! It did not fall. The glue worked when she held it first.

Evelyn clapped her hands. She took the next strip. She pressed and counted. On it went. Press and count, press and count. Soon the whole mane was on, all around the round face.

Miss Jo hung the lion on the wall. Evelyn pointed at it. "Look at my lion," she said. "I made it stay."

Stella loved book day at daycare. Miss Amy put a big bag of books on the rug. "These are library books," she said. "We can borrow them and take them home. But we must bring them back by Friday, so other kids can read them too."

Stella picked a book about a red fox. She held it in her hands. The front cover had the fox on it. She opened the front first, just like Miss Amy showed. She turned the pages one by one, all the way to the back cover.

"Look at these little marks," said her friend Ben. He pointed at the page. "Those are words," said Stella. "My mom reads them out loud. They tell you what the fox says." She ran her finger under the marks. Could the marks really talk?

Stella wanted to keep the fox book forever. She hid it in her cubby. But on Friday, Miss Amy said, "Time to bring the books back." Stella marched to her cubby and got the fox book. She gave it to Miss Amy. The book went into the big bag. Another kid would read it next.

"What will you pick next time?" Miss Amy asked. Stella smiled. "Maybe a bear book," she said.

The lights went out. The backyard went dark. "Mama, where did the light go?" asked Jules. "Away for a little nap," said Mama. She clicked a flashlight. Click. The light came back. Click. It went away. Jules laughed. "Do it again!" he said. Click went the light on the grass. "Look, a white spot," said Jules. "It looks like snow, but it is not real snow," said Mama. Jules touched the spot. Warm grass, no snow. He shone it on the wall. He shone it on his shoe. Click and spot, click and spot. Then they counted the stars. One star, two stars, three stars. "Can stars go out too?" asked Jules. "No," said Mama. "Those lights stay on all night." Jules waved up high. "Good night, stars. Good night, one white fish in the sky." "A fish?" said Mama. "Yes, that one," said Jules, pointing.

Victoria was at the beach with her dad. The big pool was next to the sand. Victoria wanted to swim like the big kids. Dad held her hands in the water. "Kick your legs," he said. Victoria kicked. But she stayed in the same spot. The wind blew a little wave past her face. She saw a slimy green leaf float by. It went fast when the water moved. So the water moving made the leaf go. Victoria tried again. She kicked her legs hard. Her feet made the water move. Then she moved too! She went forward, bit by bit. "Again," said Dad. Victoria kicked some more. The moving water pushed her to the ladder. "I went all the way there!" she said. Dad smiled and clapped. After swimming, they walked on the sand. Victoria found a shell. It had a little crack in it. "Don't break it," she told herself. She put it in her pocket, safe and soft. Then she looked back at the pool. "Same time tomorrow?" she asked. Dad said, "Same time tomorrow."

Aubrey woke up early at Grandma's house. She reached for her bunny. Bunny was not there.

"Where is bunny?" Aubrey asked. Grandma said, "Let us look." They looked under the bed. No bunny. They looked in the toy box. No bunny. Aubrey sat down. Her lip went wobbly.

Grandma went to the window. She opened the curtain. The sun came in. It made a bright spot on the floor. Aubrey saw something. The big blanket had a lump in it. The lump was bunny-shaped!

Aubrey pulled the blanket back. There was bunny! "You were hiding!" Aubrey said. She hugged bunny tight. Grandma laughed and clapped her hands.

"Time for breakfast," said Grandma. Aubrey sat at the table. Grandma gave her milk in a blue cup. Aubrey held bunny on her lap. She let bunny take a pretend sip. "Bunny wants to share," Aubrey said. Grandma smiled. The sun made a warm spot right on bunny's soft ears.

Mohamed sat at the kitchen table. He had paper, glue, and yellow paint. He wanted to make a flower for his mama.

First he had to sort his papers. He put the big ones here. He put the small ones there. Then he picked a clean white sheet for his flower.

Mohamed squeezed the glue bottle. Squeeze. Squeeze. Squeeze. The glue made a big puddle on the paper. He stuck on a green stem and yellow petals. But the paper felt funny. It turned soft and wrinkly. The corner tore a little when he touched it.

"Mama, look," said Mohamed. "Too much glue."

He tried again with a new sheet. This time he made small dots. Dot. Dot. Dot. He stuck on the stem. He stuck on the petals. The paper stayed flat and clean. The flower looked bright on the white page.
