Then Mohamed blinked. One petal had fallen into the paint. It came out yellow on both sides. Mama laughed and clapped her hands. Mohamed held up his flower, yellow and shiny, and turned it in the light.

Carter wanted to help make breakfast. Mom said, "Stay here by me." Carter stood close to Mom's legs. He could see the stove from there.

The pan sat on the stove. It made a sizzle sound. Steam went up, up, up. Carter wondered, was the pan hot or cold? He put his hand near it. The air felt warm. Mom moved his hand back. "The pan is hot," she said. "Only grown-ups touch it." Carter nodded. He looked at his toy pig on the floor. The pig was different. The pig stayed cold.

"Can I help a safe way?" asked Carter. Mom gave him a cold spoon. Carter stirred the eggs in a bowl. The spoon went round and round. Mom poured the eggs into the pan. Sizzle, sizzle!

The eggs turned from runny to fluffy. Carter saw that the hot pan had done that. "Breakfast is ready," said Mom. Carter clapped and hugged his pig.

Felix stood in the band room. He held a little drum. He wanted to make it sound big.

Felix tapped it with one finger. The drum went tap, tap. That was too small. He waited. Then he tapped with his whole hand. The drum went boom. A big sound came out! Felix tapped again and again. Boom, boom, boom.

Miss Ana smiled. "You made a big sound," she said. "Do it once more, slowly." Felix raised his hand high. He waited a moment. Then his hand came down. Boom. The sound was so big that a bird outside the window flew up into the sky.

Felix laughed. He looked at his hand. Then he looked at the drum. He lifted his hand one more time and said, "Boom."

Ruby went to the garden center with Dad. She wanted to grow her own vegetables. There were so many plants to pick. "Look at this one," said Ruby. She held up a small tomato plant. It had one tiny green leaf on top.

Ruby put the plant in her cart. She also got a little carrot seed packet. Dad got a big bag of soil. At home, Dad filled a pot with soil. Ruby made a small hole with her hand. She set the tomato plant in. She patted the soil down. Then Ruby dropped three carrot seeds in a second pot. She covered them with soft soil.

Ruby watered both pots. She put them by the sunny window. Every morning she looked. "Nothing yet," said Ruby. Then one day, a small green leaf popped up. "Dad, come see!" Ruby called. Dad came fast. More leaves came, one by one. The noisy cat next door meowed at the window. "Look, cat," said Ruby. "My plant grew!" She gave the plant more water. The carrot leaves grew tall and feathery. Ruby counted them with her finger. Then she smiled and whispered, "Grow, little plant, grow."

Logan held Daddy's hand at the hotel pool. The water was blue and cool. "I want to swim," said Logan. "I might sink down." Daddy held him close. "I have you," said Daddy.

Logan kicked his legs. He blew bubbles in the water. Then he saw a little pink ball float by. It sat on top of the water. It did not sink at all! Logan let go of Daddy's thumb and put his hand out. He pushed the ball down. The ball popped right back up. It floated again.

Logan lay back in Daddy's arms. His tummy went up, like the ball. His ears were in the water. He heard a swishy sound. "I float!" said Logan. Daddy smiled. "Yes, you float," said Daddy. Logan saw the pink ball bobbing next to him, right there by his cute toes.

Milo went to the library with his mom. He found a book about a big red fire truck. He opened the front of the book. The words ran one way, all the way to the back. Milo put his finger under the words. "That says fire truck," his mom said. Milo tapped the word. The page showed a fire truck. The words made the picture come.

"I want to keep it forever," said Milo. He held the book tight.

The library lady shook her head. "The book goes back," she said. "Someone else wants to read it too." She held up a small card. The card had a day on it. "Bring the book back on this day."

Milo looked at the card. He did not want to let go.

At home, Milo read the fire truck book every day. He read it front to back. He read it under the tree in the yard. He read it while the busy birds chirped outside.

Then the card day came. Milo carried the book back to the library. He set it on the desk. A girl picked it up right away. She opened the front cover.

"Fire truck," Milo said, pointing at the word.

The girl smiled and turned the first page.

Grayson ran to the playground with his mama. The sun was hot on his face. The slide was hot too. He put his hand near it and pulled it back fast.

"Too hot," said Mama. "Let's find the shady slide." Grayson touched the shady slide. It felt cool. He slid down, down, down. "Again!" he said. He slid again and again.

Then Grayson saw a shiny thing in the grass. It was a piece of glass. It sparkled in the sun. He reached out his hand. Mama came quickly and picked it up with her glove. "Not for touching," she said. She put it far away in a bin. Grayson waved bye-bye to the glass.

Next, Grayson saw a picnic table. A man was eating pizza there. The cheese was bubbly and hot. Grayson stood far away and watched. The man blew on his slice. He blew and blew. Then he took a little bite. Grayson held Mama's hand the whole time.

"Stay close," said Mama. Grayson stayed close. They walked to the swings together. The swing went up, and the swing went down. Grayson laughed. "One more push, Mama!" he said.

Grandpa came to stay at Jaxon's house. He would stay for a whole week. Jaxon wanted to make Grandpa laugh every day.

In the backyard, Jaxon found his rubber snake. It was long and green. "What does this snake do?" Jaxon asked. Grandpa smiled. "Watch," he said. Grandpa put the snake in the grass. Then he called, "Grandma, come look!"

But Grandpa had a trick of his own. He hid the snake under Jaxon's sand bucket. When Jaxon lifted the bucket, the snake popped out. Jaxon jumped. "You made me jump!" he said. Grandpa laughed and laughed.

The next day, Jaxon tried the trick too. He put the snake by the door. Grandpa opened the door. He jumped up high. "I am afraid of snakes!" Grandpa said. Jaxon laughed so hard. "The snake made you jump!" he said. "My turn again," said Grandpa, and he picked up the green snake.

Cooper was going to the big game! Dad held his hand. Aunt Mei carried hot cocoa. Cooper wore his red robot hat.

The ice rink was loud and bright. The skaters zoomed past. "Go, go, go!" shouted Cooper. But his team was losing. Cooper felt small in the big crowd.

Then Cooper saw something. When he clapped his mittens, the man next to him clapped too. Clap, clap! When Cooper stomped his feet, Aunt Mei stomped too. Stomp, stomp! Soon everyone was clapping and stomping. The noise grew and grew. The players skated faster and faster. His team scored a goal!

"That was so loud!" said Dad. "The smelly old rink smelled like popcorn," said Aunt Mei, "and it was the best game ever."

"Did you see that?" asked Cooper. "I started the clapping!"

Jacob skipped into the kitchen. The table was set for dinner. His bowl was red. Mama's bowl was big. Papa's plate was white.

"Can we eat now?" Jacob asked.

"First we hold hands," said Papa. "Then we say our thank you."

Jacob wanted his noodles. They smelled warm and good. But he put his little hand in Mama's big hand. He put his other hand in Papa's hand.

"Now we all close our eyes," said Mama. Jacob squeezed his eyes shut. The kitchen went dark behind his eyelids.

"Thank you for this food," said Papa.

"Thank you for our day," said Mama.

"Thank you for noodles," said Jacob. He peeked with one eye. Everyone was still holding hands.

They opened their eyes. They smiled at each other. Then they ate!

"Tomorrow we say it again," said Jacob.

"Yes," said Mama. "One family, two hands, three bowls."

Jacob looked at the window. "Look, snow!" The white flakes fell past the glass, and he waved his spoon at them.

Sienna's hair was in her eyes. Grandma brushed it. It fell right back. "We need a haircut," said Grandma. "A real one, at the salon." Sienna held Grandma's hand tight. She did not want the scissors near her head.

At the salon, a lady named Roz put a cape on Sienna. The cape was blue and shiny. Roz picked up her scissors. Snip, snip. Little pieces of hair fell down. They landed on the cape. They made a small pile. The pile grew and grew. Now it looked like a tiny mountain on Sienna's lap. "Look at that," said Grandma. "You grew a hair mountain!"

Sienna laughed. She wanted a bigger mountain. "More, please," she said. Roz snipped some more. The mountain grew taller. Then Roz spun the chair around. Sienna saw a girl in the mirror. The girl had short hair. She could see her eyes! "That's me," said Sienna. She waved at the girl. The girl waved back. "Bye bye, hair mountain," said Sienna.

Charlie woke up and looked out the window. Snow was everywhere. Snow on the road. Snow on the cars. Snow on the trees. "A snow day!" said Mama. "No school today."

Charlie put on his boots. He put on his big coat. He went outside with Mama. Charlie wanted to make a snowman. He patted the snow. He patted and patted. The snow got round. The snow got big. His pats made the snow stick together.

Then Charlie saw something. When he stomped his boot, snow fell off the tree. Stomp, and down it came. He stomped again. More snow fell on his hat. A little snow went in his ear. Charlie laughed. He stomped by the empty mailbox too, but that snow did not fall. Only the tree snow fell.

Charlie peeked up at the branches. He stomped one more time. The last bit of snow came down like a soft white hat. "Goodbye, tree snow," said Charlie. He waved at the tree and held Mama's hand.

Oliver walked home with a small box. Inside was his first pet, a little puppy. The puppy was brown and soft.

On the street, the puppy made a sad sound. "He is whining," said Mom. Oliver peeked in the box. The puppy licked his hand. "He likes you," said Mom. At home, Oliver put the puppy on the floor. The puppy walked around and around. Then he nosed his empty water bowl.

"Mom, the bowl is empty!" said Oliver. Mom held the bowl, and Oliver poured in fresh water. The puppy ran to the bowl. He drank and drank. Then his tail went wag, wag, wag. "You were thirsty," said Oliver. He patted the puppy's nice soft ears. The puppy gave his shoe a little chew. "No, that would hurt my toe," said Oliver, and he gave the puppy a bone instead. The puppy lay down with his bone and looked up at Oliver. "Good boy," said Oliver.

Florence ran to the shape wall at school. It had a circle, a square, and a rectangle. But the triangle spot was empty! "We need a triangle," said her teacher. "Can you help find one?"

Florence looked all around. The clock was round like a circle. The window was a square with four sides. The door was a tall rectangle. "Pay attention, triangle," she whispered. "Come out!" Then she looked out the window. A bird flew to a nest in the tree. The nest sat on top of the little wooden birdhouse. The birdhouse roof had three sides and three points!

"There you are!" Florence cried. She pointed and pointed. Her teacher came to look. "Yes! A triangle roof," she said. Florence clapped her hands. The bird was safe in its nest. Florence drew the triangle all by herself. She ran back and taped it on the empty spot. The shape wall was full at last. "Look, look!" said Florence. "Now it is done!"

Carter sat on the big soft rug. Everyone came to watch the game. Mama was there. Papa was there. Uncle Ben was there too. The room smelled like warm popcorn.

The game was close. Papa waved his arms. Uncle Ben jumped up. Carter wanted to see better. He clapped his hands. Then everyone clapped too. Carter stomped his feet on the floor. Then Uncle Ben stomped too. Carter blew a big breath. Mama blew one too. Each thing Carter did, the big people did after him.

Carter looked at the clock. Then he stood very still. He put one finger on his nose. The room went quiet. Everyone put a finger on a nose. Then Carter giggled, and everyone giggled. The team on the screen scored a point. "We win!" said Papa. "Thank you, Carter," said Mama. "You are a different kind of cheerleader." Carter took a deep bow.

Ruby went to the doctor with her mama. She wanted to know why her neck felt sore. "The doctor will look at you," said Mama.

First the doctor looked in Ruby's eyes. "I see you blinking!" she said. Then Ruby heard a beep. It was a little machine. "My ears heard that!" said Ruby. The doctor let Ruby touch a soft teddy bear. It was fuzzy on her fingers. Ruby smelled something sweet. A sticker smelled like strawberries! She stuck out her tongue. "I taste apple juice," said Ruby, because Mama gave her a sip.

Then the doctor said, "Turn your head." Ruby turned her neck, slowly, slowly. It did not hurt now! "You did it," said Mama, and she clapped. Ruby put the sweet sticker on her shirt. "Next time I want to do it again," said Ruby.

Jasper sat at the table. Daddy put a orange on his plate.

"Let's play a game," said Daddy. "What do your eyes do?"

Jasper looked at the orange. "My eyes see it! It is bright and orange."

"Good! Now close your eyes."

Jasper squeezed his eyes shut. He could not see the orange. But he could hear something. Snip, snip, snip. Daddy was peeling it.

"My ears hear that!" said Jasper.

"Good try," said Daddy. He held out his hand. "What is this?"

Jasper touched it. It was bumpy and cold. "My hands feel it!" he said. "Wait. My skin feels it!"

Daddy smiled. He put a piece of orange near Jasper's nose. Jasper sniffed. It smelled sweet. "My nose smells it!"

"Now open your mouth."

Jasper took a bite. Yum! It was juicy. "My tongue tastes it!" he said.

Jasper wanted to do one more thing. He stood up. He wanted to swing his arms like a big wind. He swung and swung. Then he hit his cup, and it tipped over. Milk ran across the table.

"Oh no!" said Jasper.

Daddy ran over with a towel. "That is okay," he said. "We can wipe it up. Mistakes happen when we learn."

Jasper helped wipe the milk. Then he had an idea. He picked up one small piece of orange. He held it out to the cat.

The cat sniffed it with her little nose. Then she turned away.

"Cats do not like oranges," laughed Jasper.

Joseph ran to the window at school. The sun was out. "It is sunny today," said Miss Kim. Joseph wanted to play outside.

Joseph put on his sun hat. Then he heard a sound. Drip, drip, drip. Rain fell on the window. "Now it is rainy," said Miss Kim. Joseph put his hat away. He reached for his rain boots and his rain coat.

Outside, the wind blew. "It is windy too," laughed Joseph. His hat flew off. Miss Kim caught it. She put it in her pocket. "Your family gave you warm clothes," she said. Joseph felt a cold spot on his nose. Small white flakes fell down. "Snow!" said Joseph.

"Snow means mittens," said Miss Kim. She pulled warm mittens from the box. Joseph held out his hands. "Now my hands stay awake and warm," he said. Miss Kim laughed. They made white footprints side by side in the snow.

Livia ran to the door when Mommy said, "Doctor day!" Livia loved the doctor's office. It had stickers and a fish tank. She wanted a dinosaur sticker next.

In the big room, the nurse said, "Time for your shot." Livia looked at her arm. She squeezed her teddy bear tight. "One little pin," said the nurse. The nurse pushed the tiny needle in. "Ow!" said Livia. Then it was done. "All done," said the nurse.

"Look, Mommy, look!" cried Livia. There was a small red dot on her arm. Mommy kissed the dot. Livia kissed her teddy bear's arm too. The nurse laughed and held out a basket. There were no dinosaur stickers. There was a shiny bandage with stars. "Stars for a brave girl," said the nurse. Livia stuck the bandage right next to the red dot and smiled.

Cooper ran onto the soccer field. His team wore blue shirts today. He wanted to score one goal this season. He had not scored yet.

The coach gave him a drink of water. "Go get the ball, Cooper," she said. Cooper kicked the ball. It went a little way and stopped. He kicked it again. It rolled more. Then Cooper saw it. When he ran fast, the ball rolled fast too. When he ran slow, the ball rolled slow. He ran fast, and the ball rolled fast all the way down the field.

The grass was pretty and green in the sun. Cooper kicked the ball toward the net. The ball went in! The blue team cheered loud. "I did it!" Cooper said. Then he picked up the ball and hugged it tight.

Penelope went out to the backyard. She wanted to find something red. She looked by the big tree. She saw green grass and green leaves. No red yet.

Then she heard a little buzz. A bee flew to a yellow flower. The bee sat on the yellow flower. Then it flew to a blue flower too. Penelope watched the bee go from flower to flower.

The bee dropped some yellow dust. The dust fell on Penelope's red apple. The apple sat on the clean table by her chair. Yellow dust made little dots on the red apple. Penelope laughed. Her red apple had yellow spots now.

Dad came out with a broom. He began to sweep the leaves off the patio. Penelope showed him the apple. "Look, Dad. Yellow dots on red," she said. Dad smiled and nodded. The bee buzzed by one more time, then went home to its hive.

It was Hudson's birthday at the bowling alley. Mom gave him a big red ball. He wanted to knock down all the pins.

Hudson pushed the ball. It went slow. The pins did not fall down. "Oh no," said Hudson. "That is a problem." Dad knelt beside him. "Push it fast this time," Dad said. "You are safe here. Just watch."

Hudson drew his arm back far. Then he pushed the ball fast. The ball rolled and rolled. It hit the pins. All ten pins fell down with a big crash! Everyone clapped. His friends jumped up and down.

Then the lights went dim. Mom carried a cake with three little candles. Mom blew out the candles, and the smoke curled up. Hudson got the first big slice. "Happy birthday, Hudson!" everyone sang. Hudson took a huge bite of cake.

Rosalie ran to the paint table. Three big pots sat there. One pot was red. One pot was yellow. One pot was blue.

"I want to paint a sun," said Rosalie. "The sun is yellow. Yellow is my best one!" She dipped her brush. She painted a big yellow circle.

Then she stopped. She wanted to paint an orange too. But there was no orange paint. She looked in all the pots. Red, yellow, blue. No orange anywhere. "Oh no," said Rosalie. She put her brush down.

Her teacher sat beside her. "Try your brush in the red," she said. Rosalie dipped her brush in the red pot. She painted red on top of her yellow circle. She stirred it round and round with her brush.

The circle turned orange! "Look, look!" said Rosalie. "It is a true orange now!" She held up her paper. Then she ran to the shelf to get more paper. She was going to paint one in every colour she could make. "I will paint a green apple next," she said. Her teacher handed her the blue pot.

Evan stood at the gate of the school playground. He held his new red truck tight. He did not know anyone yet. A boy sat by the sandbox all alone. The boy was crying.

Evan walked over slowly. He held out his red truck. "You can push it," Evan said. The boy wiped his eyes. He pushed the truck in the sand. The truck rolled down the sand hill. The boy laughed out loud. Evan laughed too.

Then more kids came to watch. The truck rolled again and again. Soon everyone was taking turns pushing it. A teacher smiled and sat nearby. Evan sat down in the warm light of the sun. One boy patted him on the back. "Push it to me," the boy called. Evan pushed the truck hard. It rolled right to his new friend's hands.

Naomi had a beautiful library book about a little red dragon. She wanted to keep it forever. At bedtime she hugged the book tight. "Mine," she whispered.

But Mama said, "Tomorrow is take-back day." Naomi frowned. She looked at the cover. The cover had words on it. The words said the dragon's name was Pip. Naomi pointed at the words. Mama read them out loud. Words could talk! Naomi turned page one, then page two, then page three. The dragon story went from the front to the back. She counted, "One, two, three, four, five pages left."

The next morning they went to the library. Naomi gave the book to the lady at the desk. Then the lady gave it back for one last hug, and put it on the shelf. "Goodbye, Pip," said Naomi. Then she chose a new book, all about a big blue whale. "This one goes front to back too," she said. "I checked."

Lena found a red book at daycare. It was about a spoon who loved soup. On the cover, Lena saw little marks. "What are those?" she asked.

"They are words," said Ben. "My mom reads them to me."

Miss Tia sat down. She held the book. She opened the front page first. She turned each page, one by one. Lena listened. The spoon jumped into the pot. Lena laughed.

"Again!" she said.

"You can take it home," said Miss Tia. "It is a library book. But on Friday, it comes back. Other kids want to read it too."

Lena hugged the book. At home, Dad read it twice. Lena kicked her feet with joy.

On Friday, Lena put the book in her bag. At daycare, Ben held it. "Now I read it," he said.

Lena patted the cover. "The spoon is sharp and funny," she said. "Read it to me too."

Jules was hungry. He wanted a snack. Grandma said, "Let's bake bread."

Jules watched with his eyes. Grandma mixed flour and water in a big bowl. Her hands went round and round. Then she put the dough near the warm stove to rise. "Can I touch it?" asked Jules. "Not the stove," said Grandma. "The stove is hot. But you can touch the dough later."

Soon the dough grew big. It looked like a soft cloud. Jules tapped the top with one finger. "Knock, knock," he said. The dough was squishy. His hands felt it. It was warm and soft like a pillow.

Then Grandma put the bread in the oven. Jules heard a click. He heard the oven hum. A yummy smell came out. Jules smelled it with his nose. "What is that smell?" he asked. "It is our bread," said Grandma. "Smells can tell us dinner is coming."

The timer went ding. The bread was not late after all. Grandma took it out with big mitts. She cut a slice and gave Jules a small piece. He tasted it with his tongue. It was warm and good. "Bread!" said Jules. "More, please."

Jaxon sat in the car with Mom. The car went past the egg shop. The car went past the big park. The car went past the yellow bus. "We are going to get your first haircut," said Mom. Jaxon held his toy truck. He did not want his hair cut.

At the salon, a lady named Rosa smiled at him. She put a soft cape on Jaxon. Then she picked up her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Jaxon watched the mirror. The scissors cut his hair. Then the little hairs fell down. Snip, then fall. Snip, then fall. They landed on the cape like tiny bits of string.

Jaxon pointed at the little hairs. "Look, Mom! The scissors make the hairs come down!" He turned his head to see. More hairs fell. Rosa laughed softly. She let Jaxon hold the little brush. He helped her brush the hairs off the chair. One sweep, two sweeps, three sweeps.

Then Rosa turned on a warm fan. It made warm air. The warm air made Jaxon's hair dry and soft. It made his head feel like sunshine. Rosa held up the mirror. Jaxon saw a boy with short, neat hair. The boy looked happy. "That's me!" said Jaxon. Mom hugged him tight. On the ride home, the sun did shine on his new hair. "Egg shop, park, bus," said Jaxon, looking out the window. Then he fell fast asleep.

Florence stood in the backyard. Dad put a red hoop on the grass. "Throw the beanbag in," said Dad. Florence threw it. The beanbag hit the rim. It fell out. "Try again," said Dad. Florence held the beanbag up high. She looked at the hole in the middle. She let it go. The beanbag dropped through the hoop. It landed in the grass with a soft plop.

"Now catch the big ball," said Dad. He blew a little puff of air and rolled the ball to her. Florence held out one hand. The ball bumped her fingers. It bounced away. The dog ran after it and fell asleep on the ball, like it was a pillow.

"No, silly dog," said Florence. She used both hands to pull the ball out. Dad rolled it again. This time Florence held out two hands, cupped like a little soup bowl. The ball landed right in them. She did not drop it.

"I caught it!" said Florence. She hugged the ball. Dad clapped. Then Dad threw the beanbag, and it bounced off the rim and landed on the dog's head. The dog woke up and ran in a circle. Florence laughed and laughed. She threw the beanbag one more time. It sailed right through the hoop.

Milo was at Grandma's house. He wanted to find the red ball. He looked under the blue chair. No red ball there. He looked behind the green plant. No red ball there either.

"Grandma, where is my red ball?" asked Milo. "Let's look together," said Grandma. They looked and looked.

Then Milo heard a funny sound. Pop, pop, pop. The sound came from the kitchen. Milo and Grandma went to look. Grandpa was at the stove. He was making popcorn. Grandpa moved the pot and kept it safe.

"Your red ball rolled in here," said Grandpa. "It rolled right under the yellow table." Milo hurried over. He got down on his knees. He reached under the yellow table. There it was! His red ball. It was smooth and warm from the sunny room.

"Thank you, Grandpa!" said Milo. He gave his grandpa a big hug. Then he saw the popcorn. It was white and fluffy, not red or blue or yellow. "Popcorn for you," said Grandpa. He put some in a small bowl.

Milo sat on the blue chair. He hugged his red ball. He munched the popcorn. The popcorn was all gone. "All gone!" said Milo. Grandma laughed. "Time for your nap," she said. Milo yawned a big yawn. He held his smooth red ball. He closed his eyes. "Sweet dreams, Milo," said Grandma.

Iris wants to wear her dress at school. But her dress is at home. It is in the wash. "Who will bring it to me?" she asks her teacher. "Your mama will bring it after lunch," says the teacher.

At lunch, Iris eats her crunchy carrots. Crunch, crunch, crunch. She drinks her milk. Then the door opens. It is Mama! She holds a small bag. Iris peeks inside. There is her clean dress. It smells like soap. The wash made it clean and soft.

Iris changes into her dress. The teacher helps her. "Now I have my dress on," says Iris. "Wash, wash, wash," she sings. "The wash made my dress new again!" She spins around and around. Her dress flutters like a butterfly.

Leo stood on the balcony with a big red pot. He wanted to grow tomatoes. His friend Mia lived next door. She grew tomatoes on her balcony too.

Leo put dirt in the pot. He made a little hole. He dropped in one seed. He patted the dirt down. Then he watered it with his small can.

Every morning Leo looked. Nothing came up. "Where is my tomato?" he asked.

Mia laughed. "Mine was little too. Then it grew tall."

Leo kept watering his pot. One morning he saw something green. A tiny sprout peeked out of the dirt. Leo clapped his hands.

The sprout grew and grew. It became a tall green plant. Round orange tomatoes hung on it. Leo picked one. It was warm from the sun.

He held it out to Mia over the wall. "A tomato for my friend!"

Aaron sat at Grandma's big table. He wanted to help make cookies. Grandma said, "First, tell me your five senses."

Aaron tapped his head. "Ears?" Grandma smiled. She shook a little bell. Ring, ring! Aaron covered his ears. "My ears hear the bell!"

"That's one," said Grandma. "Now what else?"

Aaron picked up a cookie from a plate. It was warm. Grandma had taken it from the oven, not Aaron. He sniffed it with his nose. "My nose smells it. It smells sweet!"

"Good," said Grandma. "Keep going."

Aaron touched the cookie. "My fingers feel it. It is warm." He looked at it. "My eyes see it. It has chips!" He bit it. "My mouth tastes it. Yum!"

Grandma laughed. "You said all five. But wait. Where does the nose go?"

Aaron pointed to his ear. Then he stopped. "That is wrong. The nose goes here!" He touched his nose.

Grandma gave him the answer with a hug. "Five senses, five body parts. You did it."

The bell rang again. Aaron shouted, "I hear it with my ears!"

Elizabeth wanted to wear her bear pajamas. But where were they? "Let's look," said Mommy.

First Elizabeth checked the bathtub. No pajamas there. The tub was empty now. Her bath was all done. Next she checked her chair. No pajamas there. Only a plate with crumbs. Her dinner was all done too. One place left to look.

Elizabeth ran to the big basket. There they were! The bear pajamas were waiting in the wash. "Can I have them?" she asked. Mommy said, "They are wet, so let's make them dry." Mommy put them in the dryer. Elizabeth watched the round door spin around and around.

At last the pajamas came out, warm and soft. Elizabeth pulled them on. She could zip the zipper all by herself. Then Mommy tucked her into bed. "One kiss for bear," said Elizabeth. "And one for me." Mommy kissed each sleepy eye. "Good night, safe and warm," Mommy said. Elizabeth hugged her bear tight.

Alexis was at Grandma's house. Mom came in with a little bundle. "This is your baby sister, Rose," said Mom. Alexis looked at Rose. She was tiny. She had little fingers and little toes.

Rose started to cry. She cried loud. "Wah, wah, wah." Alexis put his hands over his ears. "She is loud for someone so small," said Grandpa with a smile. "That is not a mean sound. That is how she talks." Alexis wanted her to stop. He wanted to be a good big brother.

Alexis found a rattle in the toy box. He shook the rattle near Rose. Shake, shake, shake. Rose stopped crying. She looked at the rattle. Her eyes got big. Alexis shook it again. Rose made a small gurgle. It sounded a bit like a giggle.

"That works!" said Grandma. "You found her favorite sound." Alexis felt proud. He shook the rattle slow. Rose watched it go back and forth. Her eyes followed every shake. She did not cry at all.

Then Alexis tried one more thing. He made a funny face, with his tongue out. Rose copied him! Her little tongue came out too. Mom laughed. "She is learning from you," said Grandma. "You are her first teacher." Alexis puffed up his chest. He shook the rattle one more time. Rose grabbed it with her whole tiny hand.

Jasper wanted the red truck. Tom had the red truck. Tom would not give it up.

Miss Lily stood by the toy shelf. She sang a little song. "One, two, three," she sang. "Four, five, six." Tom held the truck tight. "Seven, eight, nine." Tom looked up. "Ten!" said Miss Lily. "Now it is Jasper's turn." Tom gave Jasper the truck. It was his turn to play.

Jasper pushed the truck on the floor. Vroom, vroom. He heard Miss Lily count again. "One, two, three," she sang to the block corner. Sam put down the blocks. He waited for his turn.

Then Jasper saw Miss Lily look at him. She held up her hand. She began to count. "One, two, three, four, five." Jasper stopped the truck. He rolled it back to Tom. "Your turn," said Jasper. Tom smiled and took the truck. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten," sang Miss Lily softly.

Zoe sat in the big chair at the clinic. Her mom held her hand. A friendly nurse came in with a small tray.

"Will the shot hurt?" Zoe asked.

"Just a little pinch," said the nurse. "Then we press a cotton ball on it."

The nurse opened a paper packet. She took out a little cotton ball. She wiped Zoe's arm with it. The cotton felt cold and wet.

Zoe watched the nurse's hands. The nurse tapped Zoe's arm up and down. Then the nurse gave the shot. Zoe felt one quick pinch. "Ouch!" said Zoe. But it was already done.

"Now you press," said the nurse. She put the cotton ball in Zoe's hand. Zoe pressed the cotton on her arm. She held it there and counted. "One, two, three."

Then Zoe took the cotton off. The little red spot did not bleed. "I pressed it and it stopped!" said Zoe.

"Yes, you did that yourself," said Mom. The nurse gave Zoe a shiny star sticker. Zoe put it on her shirt.

On the way out, they walked past the window. Zoe saw a garden with yellow flowers outside. "Can we look?" she asked.

Mom opened the door, and they stepped out into the sun.

Jaxson wanted to wear his bear pajamas. But they were in the wash. "Oh no," said Jaxson.

Mama said, "First we finish dinner. Then a bath. Then clean pajamas."

Jaxson ate his noodles. All gone! Then Mama ran the bath. The water was warm, not hot. Mama checked it with her hand.

Jaxson splashed and played. He washed his tummy. He washed his toes.

Then Mama pulled the plug. The water went down, down, down. "Bye-bye, water," said Jaxson.

Mama said, "Now let's check the dryer." They looked in together. The bear pajamas were warm and dry! The wash had gone round and round. Then the dryer had made them dry.

Jaxson put them on. He looked like a little bear. "Rawr!" he said.

Papa came in and laughed. "A bear in my kitchen! I will call the zoo."

"No, Papa," said Jaxson. "This bear stays here."

Mama tucked him into bed. She read one story. The little bear closed his eyes.

"Sweet dreams, tidy little bear," Mama said. Jaxson snuggled down, warm and dry.

Xavier wants to draw a big sun at school. Miss Ana gives him a tablet. It is dark and sleepy.

Xavier presses the round button. The screen lights up. He claps his hands. The picture is bright now.

He taps one more time. A drawing app opens. There is a green crayon on the screen. Xavier taps the green crayon. He draws a big green sun. "The sun is green," he says.

Ben sits next to him. Ben taps a blue crayon. "Look, blue," says Ben. Xavier taps the blue crayon too. Now his sun has blue rays.

Time to go outside. Miss Ana says, "Let's put the tablets away." Xavier presses the top button. The screen goes dark again. One press made it bright. One press made it sleepy. He puts the tablet in the basket.

"You did it all by yourself," says Miss Ana. Xavier smiles and waves to the dark screen. "Bye bye, tablet," he says.

Olivier was at Grandma's house. His little bunny was gone. "Where can bunny be?" he asked.

He looked under the big bed. No bunny. He looked in the toy box. No bunny. Then he saw the kitty cat. The kitty was pulling something with her paws. It was a string. Bunny was at the other end of the string!

"Naughty kitty," said Grandma, smiling. "She pulled bunny all the way under the chair."

Olivier gave the string a little tug. Bunny slid out across the floor. "Bunny!" Olivier called. He hugged bunny tight.

Later, Olivier pulled his toy train by its string. The train followed him all the way to the door. Pull the string, and the toy comes along. What else could he pull next?

Zoe sat in the waiting room with her mom. Today she would get a shot. Zoe did not want a shot. She held her teddy tight.

"Will it hurt a lot?" she asked.

"Just a tiny pinch," said Mom. "Then we can skip to the car."

A nurse named Rosa came in. She had a special bottle of bubbles. Rosa rubbed Zoe's arm with a cool, wet cotton ball. It felt cold and soft.

"Watch the bubbles," said Rosa. She blew one big bubble. Zoe watched it float up. While Zoe watched, Rosa gave the shot.

"Done!" said Rosa.

Zoe looked down. There was a small round bandage on her arm. The bubbles had floated away, and the shot was already over.

"Can we do bubbles at my class tomorrow?" Zoe asked.

Mom laughed and kissed her head. "First, let's go skip to the car."

Zoe picked up teddy. She waved to Rosa. Then she skipped out the door.

Arya went to the library with Dad. She wanted a book about trucks. But the truck book was gone from its shelf.

"Let's look for shape clues," said Dad. He pointed at the book covers. "This one is a square. It has four sides, all the same." Arya patted the square cover. It felt big and flat.

They walked past the windows. The sun made bright patches on the floor. One patch was round like a circle. Arya put her shoe in the circle. It fit! She jumped to the next patch. That one had three sides. "Triangle!" she said. Dad smiled.

Then Arya saw a long, tall book on the reading table. Its cover was a rectangle, long on two sides and short on the others. She opened it. "Trucks!" she said. It was the truck book after all. A boy had left it on the table. "Thank you, book," Arya whispered. She sat down next to Dad.

Dad read about the big wheels. "The wheels spin," he said. Arya turned the page. The truck in the picture had a sharp pointy crane. "Beep beep!" said Arya, and she hugged the book tight.

Joshua went to the park with his soft bunny. He set bunny on the grass. Then he ran to play.

Joshua wanted to show bunny the slide. He looked at the grass. Bunny was gone! "Oh no," said Joshua. "Where is bunny?"

Joshua looked under the bench. No bunny. He looked by the tree. No bunny. It was hard to find bunny in the tall green grass.

Then the wind blew. The tall grass moved. It bent down low. Joshua saw something white in the grass. It was bunny!

"There you are!" said Joshua. He hugged bunny close. "The wind helped me find you."

Joshua held bunny's paw. "Do you want to share my ball?" he asked. Bunny sat and watched the ball roll. Joshua smiled and rolled it again.

Max was at school. It was cooking day. He wanted to make bread for Mom and Dad and Baby Sam.

Teacher Mia put flour in a big bowl. Max poured in warm water. He mixed and mixed. But the dough stayed flat and stiff. "It won't puff," said Max. His tummy felt sad and hungry.

Teacher Mia laughed. "We forgot the magic dust. Yeast!" Max sprinkled it in. They mixed again. Then they waited. They waited for Mom, and Dad, and Baby Sam, and the yeast.

The dough grew big. It grew and grew. It puffed up like a cloud. "Look!" said Max. "One little pinch made it big!"

Teacher Mia put the bread in the oven. Max watched from far away. Soon the bread was brown and warm.

At home, Max gave the bread to his family. Mom tore a piece. Dad tore a piece. Baby Sam got a little piece. Max ate his piece all up.

"You made this?" asked Dad.

"I did," said Max. "One pinch of dust, and poof!"

Arthur rode the bus with his mama. He held his little red truck. Then the bus stopped fast. The truck jumped out of his hands. It rolled away on the floor.

"Oh no," said Arthur. "Where did you go?" He looked by his shoes. He looked under the seat. No truck. Then the bus turned a corner. Arthur heard a small sound. Tink, tink. Something was rolling. The truck rolled out from under the big seat in front. It came right to his feet.

Arthur picked it up. "The bus moves, and you move too!" he said. He held the truck tight in both hands. Outside the window, snow was starting to fall. It made the street look white and neat. Arthur watched the snow. The bus turned again. This time the truck stayed snug and safe. "I found you," Arthur whispered.

Edouard wants to build a big tower in his playroom. He dumps out his box of blocks. Blocks roll everywhere on the soft dirt of the rug.

"One, two," says Edouard. He stacks two red blocks. He adds more. "Three, four, five." The tower grows tall. It wobbles a little.

Edouard turns a block so it sits flat. The tower stops wobbling! He claps his hands. "Six, seven, eight," he counts. Up goes the tower, block by block.

Mama peeks in the door. "Can I play too?" she asks. Edouard nods fast. Mama hands him blocks. "Nine," says Edouard. "Ten!" The tower is done. It is so tall!

Edouard giggles. He pokes the top block. The tower tips over. Crash! All ten blocks fall down. Edouard and Mama laugh together. "Again!" shouts Edouard. "One, two, three!"

Alexander wanted a snack before lunch. Mom said he could help make toast. She put the bread in the toaster herself. Alexander stood back and waited.

Soon he heard a pop. His ears caught it first. He looked with his eyes. The toast had jumped up! Mom gave him a plate. The toast was warm under his fingers.

He sniffed with his nose. It smelled like bread and sunshine. He took a small bite. Yum! It tasted good with a little jam. "Funny," he said. "The bread went in soft. Now it is brown and crisp."

"Toast is like that," said Mom. She pointed out the window. "Look, an owl is sitting on the fence." Alexander saw its big round eyes. "Do owls like toast too?" he asked. Mom laughed. "Owls sell no jam," she joked, "so they eat mice instead." Alexander touched his warm toast again. The pop had made the bread jump up. He watched the toaster very hard. "Will it pop again?" he whispered.

Eliana wanted the red pencil. Her brother Sam had it. He was drawing a big truck.

"Can I have it?" she asked. Sam shook his head. Eliana felt mad. She wanted to grab it.

Mama sat down with them. She held out a small timer. It went tick, tick, tick. "You can each draw until it rings," she said.

Sam drew his truck. The timer rang, ding! Sam gave the red pencil to Eliana. It felt smooth and cool in her hand. She drew a round sun.

The timer rang again. Eliana looked at it. She did not wish to stop. But she gave the pencil back to Sam. Sam smiled big. Then he tore his paper in half. He gave her one half!

"Draw with me," Sam said. Eliana picked up a blue pencil. It was hard to choose just one color. So they shared that one too, back and forth, until the timer rang again.

Nathan went to the little pool by the lake. Dad came too. "Time to swim," said Dad. Nathan held the side. His feet hung down. He did not move.

A big cow stood in the lake. It walked in the shallow water. The cow moved its legs. The water went swish, swish. The cow moved forward, slow and calm.

Nathan watched. Then he kicked his feet. Kick, kick, kick. The water pushed him. He moved along the wall! "Look, Dad!" said Nathan. "The water helps me!" Dad smiled and held out his arms. Nathan kicked some more. The water felt cool on his toes. Soon he could let go and float a little. "You swim like a happy little frog," said Dad. Nathan laughed and splashed with his hand.

Ibrahim woke up in his little bed. He wanted his yellow shirt. But the yellow shirt was on the floor. It had soup on it from dinner. "Yuck," said Ibrahim. "It is dirty."

Mama picked it up. "It needs a bath too, just like you," she said. First, Mama filled the tub. The water was warm. Ibrahim got in. He washed his arms, one and two. He washed his legs, one and two. The bubbles made his skin clean.

Then Ibrahim got dressed in a blue shirt. It felt good and soft. In the kitchen, Papa was stirring soup. A little fire sat under the pot. Ibrahim stood far away with Mama. He helped by holding a napkin. He did not rip it, not even a little. "Good boy," said Papa. "Soup is coming." Ibrahim sat down and clapped. "I am clean and I am hungry!"

Oliver sat at the kitchen table. Mom put two plates down. One plate had crackers. The other plate had apple slices.

"Which plate has more?" Mom asked.

Oliver wanted the plate with more. He pointed at the crackers. Then he stopped. Was he right? He had to know.

He touched each cracker one by one. "One, two, three, four, five." Five crackers!

He counted the apple slices next. "One, two, three." Three apples. Crackers had more!

Then Oliver tried something funny. He counted the crackers from the other side. He started with the last cracker. "One, two, three, four, five." Still five! The last number stayed five!

Oliver laughed out loud. He counted them again the new way. Five again!

"Crackers win," he said. He picked up the big plate. Then he gave Mom the apples.

"Crackers for me," he said. "And a soft napkin, too."

Joshua sat in the music classroom. A big drum sat near his chair. Miss Patel smiled at him. "You can hit it," she said. Joshua did not hit it. The drum looked too big.

Then a boy in class hit a drum far away. Booming sounds filled the room. Joshua wanted his drum to make a big sound too. He raised his hand.

Joshua hit the drum. He hit it soft. The drum went tap, tap, tap. Joshua stopped and looked. Then he hit it hard. The drum went BOOM, BOOM, BOOM. The big hit made the big sound. The soft hit made the small sound. Joshua hit it hard again. BOOM, BOOM, BOOM!

"Wow," said Miss Patel. "You found it out all by yourself." Joshua laughed. Outside, a car went by. Joshua drummed a boom for it. Then he hugged the drum with both arms. "My drum," he said. Miss Patel laughed too.

Emmett sat at the kitchen table. Daddy set down the big pot. Grandma smiled at everyone.

"Time for our special words," Grandma said. "You say them with me tonight."

Emmett wanted to say them alone. But the words felt too big in his mouth. He looked down at his plate.

Grandma held his hand. "Just like this," she said. "One, two, three. Thank you for our food."

Emmett tried. "Thank... you," he said. His voice was very small.

Daddy squeezed his hand. "That was good," said Daddy. "Say it again."

"Thank you for our food," Emmett said. This time it came out strong.

Grandma clapped her hands. "Now we eat!" she said.

Emmett picked up his orange cup. He took a big drink.

"I like saying the words," he said.

"Then we will say them tomorrow too," said Grandma. She put a warm roll on his plate. Emmett took a bite and smiled.

The special words came before the food. The food came after the words. Tomorrow he would say them first again.

Zachary wanted to draw a big orange sun. The tablet sat on the rug. Its screen was dark and quiet.

"Who turned it off?" he asked. "Nobody," said Mom. "It goes to sleep." Zachary pressed the little button on the side. The screen grew bright. His sun was still there, waiting for him.

He tapped the blue square. The drawing app opened. He drew the sun, fast little lines all around it. Then he drew a cup of juice next to it, because suns get thirsty too.

He asked Mom, "Can I leave it here on the rug?" "You can forget it there," she said, "and someone might step on it." Zachary looked at the rug. He looked at the big feet that walk there.

He pressed the button again. The screen went dark, just like before. He slid the tablet into its soft case. He carried it to the shelf and set it down by the books.

Mom said, "All done?" Zachary nodded. "Sun is sleeping too."

Mila and her family went camping. They were far away from home. The tent was their house now. Mila put her teddy on the little camping desk. "You sit here," she said.

Mila stepped in the creek with her socks on. Splash, splash. Her socks got all wet. "Wet socks, wet socks," she said. Daddy hung them on a string by the tent. The sun shone on the socks all afternoon.

Mila played with pinecones. She found a smooth gray stone. She watched a bird hop by the fire pit, where Mom was cooking. Soon she looked at the string again. The socks were dry! The sun had made them dry and warm. Mila touched them with her fingers. "Warm socks, warm socks," she said.

She put the dry socks on her feet. They felt cozy. Her teddy sat on the desk and watched. Daddy gave her a thumbs up. Mila stood tall. "I dried my socks," she said. "With the sun."

Charles rode the bus with Grandma. He held his sleepy bunny in his arms. The bus went bump, bump, bump. Charles dropped his mitten on the floor. He reached down for it. But now his hands felt empty. Where did bunny go?

"Bunny is lost," said Charles. He looked under the seat. He looked by Grandma's bag. No bunny. A kind lady moved her feet so he could see. "I see a string," she said. A little pink string hung down under the seat.

Charles pulled the string. The string moved. Out came the bunny, sliding right into his lap. Charles laughed and hugged bunny tight. "The string brought him back," said Charles. Grandma smiled and gave bunny a kiss on his soft ear.

Then Charles threw his arms around Grandma. "Thank you for riding with me," he said. The bus stopped with a soft hiss. Grandma took his hand. "Home time, sleepy boy," she said. Charles waved to the kind lady. "Bye bye! Thank you!" The lady waved back all the way to the door.

Sofia went to the bank with her dad. It was cold outside. Dad wore his big coat. Sofia held her little red coat in her arms.

"I want to do it myself," Sofia said. Dad smiled and waited. Sofia pushed her arms in. First one arm, then the other. Now the coat was on! But the zipper was open. Cold air came in through the gap.

She took the zipper slider and pulled it up. It went up a little, then stopped. She pulled again. It stopped again. "Why does it stop?" she wondered. She looked down. The coat edge was not sitting straight. The slider would not go past the bumpy part.

Sofia tugged the coat hem to make it flat. Then she pulled the slider again. This time it went all the way up, zip, zip, zip! The gap was gone. No more cold air. Outside, a snowflake floated past the bank window. It began to fall from the sky. "Look, Dad! My coat is zipped, and the snow can't get me," Sofia said. She marched to the bank door.

Nova was at summer camp. She wanted to make a sun out of paper. First, one big circle. Next, two little eyes. Then three, four, five yellow rays.

"Where is the glue?" asked Nova.

The glue was all gone. Nova looked and looked. Then she saw paint. Paint was sticky too. She dabbed one dot, two dots, three dots. The paint held the eyes on tight.

"Hello, sun!" said her friend Ben. "You used paint like glue. That is funny."

Nova laughed. She tipped her brush. Sparkly glitter fell down. It snowed all over her sun!

"My sun is sparkly," said Nova. She ran to the toy shelf and found an old ribbon. She glued it on top with more paint.

"Now my sun has a hat," said Ben.

"One sun, two eyes, three, four, five rays, and one silly hat," said Nova. She hung it high on the wall.

Amira ran to the math club table. Two buckets sat there. One held red blocks. One held blue blocks. "I hope the red bucket has more," she said. But how could she know?

Teacher Sam smiled. "You can count them," he said. Amira pointed at the red blocks. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven! She was ready to try the blue blocks. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six!

Then Leo came over. "Count the red ones again," he said. "Start at the other end." Amira tilted her head. Would that change the number? She pointed at the far block first. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Still seven! She laughed. "It is seven both ways!"

"So which bucket has more?" asked Leo. Amira looked at both buckets. "Red has seven. Blue has six. Red has more!" She put the red bucket on the tall stool.

"Look," she said. "My bucket is up high, because it wins!"

Luca was at the farm with Grandpa. Grandpa had a small patch of dirt. "Can we plant seeds?" Luca asked. "Yes," said Grandpa. "We can plant a garden."

Luca held three little seeds in his hand. "One, two, three," he counted. Grandpa made a hole in the dirt. Luca dropped the seeds in. Then they covered them up. Dirt on top, seeds under, all snug.

Grandpa got water from the well. Luca helped pour it on the dirt. "Will the seeds drink it?" Luca asked. "Watch and see," said Grandpa. They watered the seeds every day. One, two, three, pour.

One morning, Luca saw something green. A tiny sprout was peeking out! "Where did you come from?" Luca asked. The sprout did not say. But it was tall and new. "You grew from my seed," Luca said. He smiled.

A naughty goat came by and tried to nibble the sprout. Grandpa shooed the goat away. "No, no," said Grandpa. "This is Luca's garden." Later, Grandma took a picture of Luca by his sprout. Then they walked to the pond and watched the fish swim round and round. "More water, sprout," said Luca. "Grow big."

Mohamed sat in his car seat. The sun came in the window. It made a warm spot on his hand. "Mama, why is my hand warm?" he asked. "The sun is making it warm," said Mama. Mohamed moved his hand away. The spot on his hand got cool again. The sun made it warm. No sun made it cool.

The car stopped at the gas station. Papa got out. Mohamed wanted to get out too. "Stay in your car seat," said Mama. "You stay close to us." Mohamed stayed. Papa came back with a cup. Steam rose up from it. "Is your drink cold, Papa?" asked Mohamed. "No, it is very hot," said Papa. He put it far from Mohamed's hands. Mohamed looked at the empty cup holder next to him. He put his own little water bottle there instead. The car started again. "The sun makes warm, and the shade makes cool," said Mohamed. "That is my big dream, to know everything," he said. Mama laughed. The warm spot came back, right on his toes.

Isabelle went to the big hall with Mama and Nana. There were lanterns on the tables. There was a long table with candles. Auntie lit each candle with a match. Isabelle stood far away and watched.

Isabelle wanted to put a lantern on the table too. She held her little paper lantern. But the table was too tall. She could not reach. She tried to reach on her toes. Still too high.

Nana brought a small chair. Isabelle stood on the chair. Nana held her hand. Now Isabelle could reach the table. She set her lantern down. The lantern sat next to the candles. It glowed warm and gold.

Then a big drum began to boom. The boom made the lantern shake. Isabelle watched her lantern wobble. The drum boomed again. The lantern shook again. Isabelle laughed. She tapped her foot with the drum. Her lantern danced too. "Look, Nana," she said. "It moves!"

Rowan ran to the swing. But a girl was on it. "Can I have a turn, please?" he asked. The girl held the chains tight. "One, two, three pushes," she said. "Then you can go." Her mama pushed her softly. One, two, three. Then the girl jumped down. "Thank you," said Rowan. He climbed on.

Rowan wanted to go high. He tried to kick his legs. But the swing did not move much. It felt stuck. A boy ran past and bumped the swing. Rowan wobbled. He felt scared for a second. "Sorry!" said the boy. "Are you okay?" "I want to go high," said Rowan. "But I cannot start it."

"Ask a grown-up for help," said the girl. Rowan looked at his papa. Papa was sitting on the bench. "Papa, can you help me, please?" Papa smiled. He stood up. He held the seat. One, two, three, push! Rowan went up. The wind felt cool on his shirt. One, two, three, kick. Up and up he went.

"Thank you, Papa!" Rowan called from the sky. He could see the whole playground. He could see the slide, the sand, and the trees. "Again, please!" he said. Papa laughed and pushed once more. "Hi, birds!" Rowan called. "Hi, clouds!"

Iris went to Dad's office. She saw a big tablet on his desk. The screen was dark and still. Iris wanted to draw a monkey on it.

Dad showed her the small round button. "Push it," he said. Iris pushed the button. The screen lit up. Iris smiled big. Her push made the light come on!

Then Dad tapped a little paint pot picture. A drawing app opened. Iris picked the color brown. She drew a round monkey with long arms. The monkey had a tiny banana, too. She drew green grass under him. Then she drew red flowers, one, two, three.

"Now we put it away," said Dad. Iris pushed the button again. The screen went dark. She set the tablet down on the soft mat, just like Dad. The tablet went to sleep next to his sharp pencil cup.

"Good night, monkey," said Iris.

Emmett went to the grocery store with Dad. "We need apples for our pie," said Dad. Emmett held the small basket. He put in three red apples. Then he saw a problem. One apple rolled out. It rolled far, far away.

Emmett walked slowly. He looked under the table of bread. He looked by the big cooler. There it was, in a puddle of water on the floor. The apple was wet. Emmett picked it up with two hands. He carried it back to Dad. "I found it," he said.

At home, Dad cut the apples with a safe knife. Emmett dropped the pieces into the bowl. He sprinkled sugar on top. Dad put the pie in the hot oven. Emmett waited by the door. He watched the timer. He waited some more. Then the pie came out, warm and smelling sweet. Emmett took a big bite. "Tasty," he said. "We built a pie together."

Wesley wanted his rubber duck. It was bath time, but the duck was lost. He looked with his eyes. He saw towels and a comb. No duck. He heard water running with his ears. He smelled soap with his nose. The soap smelled like apples. Still no duck. Mama turned off the water. It was warm, but Mama tested it first, so it was safe. Wesley touched the water with his hand. Just right. He climbed in with help. He chewed a little apple slice Mama gave him. Yum. Then his toes touched something soft. It was the duck, hiding under the towel. Wesley laughed. He set the duck in the water. The duck floated straight up. Wesley patted its back. "Found you," he said.

Weston sat at the dinner table. His tummy made a tiny growl. "That is my hungry storm," he whispered. Mama set down a hot pot. She used both hands. Steam went up like little clouds. Weston wanted the pasta so much. He reached out his fork. But the pot was too far away. His fork tapped the empty air. He could not do it alone.

He looked at Mama. "Can you help me, please?" he asked. Mama smiled big. She scooped pasta onto his plate. The noodles wiggled like tiny snakes. Weston took a bite. "Yummy!" he said. "Thank you, Mama." Mama's smile grew even bigger, like the moon.

Then Weston waved his fork too fast. A noodle flew off. It landed on Papa's sleeve. Weston felt his face go warm. "Sorry, Papa," he said. Papa picked up the noodle. He made it dance in the air. "The noodle wanted to tickle me!" said Papa. Weston laughed so hard his chair shook.

Then he asked, "More pasta, please?" Mama gave him more. The hungry storm in his tummy got quiet. Weston patted his belly. "All done," he said. He blew a kiss to his plate.

Paisley had a library book. It was about a funny red truck. The book had to go back tomorrow.

She did not want to give it back. She wanted to keep it forever.

At bedtime, she sat on her bed. She held the book. She opened the front cover. Dad said, "Books start at the front."

On the first page there was a truck. Under the truck were little black marks. "Those marks are words," said Dad. "They tell the story."

Paisley turned the pages. Front to back. The truck drove up a hill. Then it drove home.

"Dad, will someone else read it?" she asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "You take it back, and someone new reads it."

"Maybe at school," said Paisley. "After my bath tomorrow, I will play truck, then we take it back."

She closed the back cover. "Good night, truck," she said.

It began to snow outside. Big white flakes fell and fell. Kinsley wanted cocoa to drink by the window.

Mama put milk in a pot. She put the pot on the stove. The stove glowed and got hot. Kinsley reached out her hand. "Stop," said Mama. "Hot pots can hurt. You stay back here with me."

Kinsley stepped back next to Mama. She watched the milk. It got warm. Little white puffs rose up. The puffs went up, up, and away. Kinsley clapped. "The hot stove made the milk warm," she said.

Mama poured the cocoa into a cup. Kinsley put her hand near the cup. It felt warm like a hug. She put her other hand on the window. The window felt cold. Snow fell on the other side.

Kinsley sat close to Mama. She made a picture with blue paint. Mama said, "That is a true winter day." Kinsley held her warm cup with two hands and took a little sip. "Mmm," she said. "More snow, please."

Zayn put on his red shoe. Then he put on the other one. "Mama, I need my library card!" he said. Mama laughed. "It is right here in my bag." They walked to the library together.

At the desk, a kind lady gave Zayn a little card. It had his name on it. "My first card!" said Zayn. He jumped up and down. Then he found a book about a big, juicy orange. "I love this book," he said. "I will keep it forever and ever." The lady smiled. "You can take it home, Zayn. But you must bring it back, so other kids can read it too." Zayn held the book tight. He did not want to let go.

At home, Zayn hid the book under his bed. "Now it is mine," he whispered. But then he thought about his friend Sam. Sam loved oranges too. Sam would never get to see the big, juicy orange. The next day, Zayn ran to Mama with the book. "We need to go back!" he said. At the library, Zayn put the book on the desk. "Here you go," he said. "Someone else can read it now." Then he found a new book about a big red fire truck. "Can I take this one?" he asked. Mama laughed. "Yes, Zayn. And guess what? The orange book will wait for you too." Zayn grinned and hugged his new book all the way home.

David climbed the big yellow bus. It was his first day of school. The steps were tall for his legs. He held the rail and went up, up, up.

David wanted a seat by the window. He looked down the long aisle. All the seats were full of kids. Then he saw one empty seat. A girl sat next to it. She had a phone in her hand. She was showing it to a boy.

"Can I sit here?" David asked.

"Yes," said the girl. "My name is Mia."

David sat down. He pressed his face to the cool glass. The bus began to roll. Outside, the trees went by, fast and then faster. David waved at a man walking a dog. The man waved back.

"I can see everything from up here," David said. "Why is the bus so tall?"

"So we can see far away," said Mia. "Watch. You can see over the cars."

David looked. It was true. He could see over all the little cars. He could even see the school way down the road. It was big and red and getting closer.

The bus stopped. The tall door folded open with a whoosh. David took Mia's hand. They jumped down the steps together.

"Race you to the door!" said Mia.

"Go!" said David.

Miles stood in the changing room at the pool. He was going to swim today. He put on his swim shorts. He put on his goggles. "Dad, why do I need goggles?" he asked. "Put them on and see," said Dad.

At the pool, Miles slid into the water. He blinked. He opened his eyes. The water did not hurt at all! He looked down. There was a big owl painted on the bottom of the pool. "I see an owl!" said Miles. "Wow, look at that," said Dad.

Next week, Miles forgot his goggles. He opened his eyes under the water. It hurt and felt foggy. "Sorry, I forgot my goggles," said Miles. Dad said, "That is okay. Try again next time." Miles put on his goggles the week after that. He looked down. The owl was waiting for him. "Hello, owl," said Miles. He waved his hand. The owl stayed on the bottom and watched him swim.

Victoria had a cold. Her nose was all stuffy. She could not smell her toast.

It was a cloudy day. Victoria sat by the window. She looked at the big tree outside. One branch, two branches, three branches. She counted them slowly.

Mom said, "Time for soup." Mom carried the hot bowl. She set it down to cool. The soup made steam. The steam went up, up, up.

Victoria leaned over her bowl. She sniffed. One sniff, two sniffs, three. Then her nose went pop, and it was clear! She could smell the soup now.

"I hope I get all better soon," said Victoria.

"You will," said Mom. "One spoon, two spoons, three."

Victoria took the spoon and ate.

Madelyn wanted to bake cookies with Gran. But the jar of flour was up high on a big shelf. "Help, please," said Madelyn. Gran reached up and got it down. "Thank you," said Madelyn.

Gran turned on the oven. The oven was hot, so Gran did the hot part all by herself. Madelyn stirred the dough with a big spoon. It was hard work. The spoon slipped, and flour puffed all over the counter. "Sorry, Gran," said Madelyn.

"That is okay," said Gran. "We can wipe it up." Madelyn wiped the flour with a cloth. The counter was clean again. Madelyn saw that wiping made the mess go away. She felt proud.

The dog barked at the good smell. The cookies baked and baked. Then Gran took them out. Madelyn waited until they were cool. She ate one, and it was sweet and soft. After the cookies, Madelyn felt sleepy. The dog was asleep on his mat. A butterfly landed near the window. Madelyn waved and said, "Thank you, butterfly. Please come again."

Everett did not want to open his mouth. He wanted his sticker now. "First we check," said the doctor, a kind man with a big smile.

The doctor held up a little light. "Look here," he said. Everett looked with his eyes. The light was small and bright. Then the doctor put cold metal on Everett's back. Everett touched it with his hand. It was cold and wet! He jumped. "That tickled," he said. His mommy laughed. Everett laughed too.

Next the doctor put on his hearing tool. "Take a big breath," he said. Everett smelled the air with his nose. It smelled like soap. He heard a beep with his ears. He took a big breath, and the man heard it in his tool. Everett blew air, and the tool made a fuzzy sound. He blew again, and the sound got big. "More air, more sound," said the doctor.

"Now the stick," said the doctor. He put a little wet stick on Everett's tongue. Everett tasted it. It tasted like cherry. He opened his mouth wide. The doctor looked and looked. "All done! A good checkup," he said. Everett got a big gold sticker. He climbed down from the table all by himself. "I did it," he said.

Mia put on her red coat. It was windy outside. The wind whooshed her hair all around. "Hold my hand," said Mom. Mom had a big tummy. A new baby was in there!

They went to the baby store. Mia wanted to find a toy for the baby. She saw a big yellow duck. She saw tiny socks. Then she saw something up high. It was a mobile with stars.

Mia had an idea. She reached up and pushed a little button. The stars began to spin. Then soft music played. The spinning made the music go! Mia pushed the button again. Spin, spin, music!

"Look, Mom!" said Mia. She pushed the button one more time. A tiny baby in a cart turned his head. His eyes got big. He smiled at the spinning stars.

"That one," said Mia. She put the mobile in the cart. "The baby will push it too."

"Maybe," said Mom. "Maybe the baby will just look."

Mia patted Mom's tummy. "Spin, spin, music," she said. Outside the window, it began to snow. "Baby, hurry up," said Mia. "The stars are waiting at home."

Edouard stood in the music room. Miss Rosa played a song on the piano. The other kids clapped. Edouard's hands clapped too fast. Then they clapped too slow. "Why do my hands go wrong?" he asked. His friend Tom said, "Watch my hands. Clap when I clap." Tom clapped. Clap, clap, clap. Edouard watched. Then Edouard clapped too. Clap, clap, clap. His claps landed right with the song. "My hands match!" said Edouard. Tom laughed. Even Miss Rosa laughed. "Now sing with me," said Miss Rosa. She sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Edouard knew that song. His brother sang it at home, all the long way to school. Edouard sang the words from his head. He clapped and sang at the same time. Clap, clap, clap. Twinkle, twinkle, little star. Miss Rosa played louder. The whole class clapped together. Edouard sang the last word, "are," and threw his hands up high. "Again!" he said. "Again, again!"

Alexander went to the baby store with Mama. "The baby needs things," said Mama. Alexander wanted to pick a cup for the baby himself.

He found a little cup with a duck on it. The cup was slippery in his hands. He held it tight so it would not fall.

Then Alexander made the duck spin around. He gave the cup a push on the shelf. Around and around it went. The baby would like that. "Look, Mama!" he said. "It spins!"

A store lady smiled and put another cup on the shelf. She spun it too. It spun even longer. "How does yours spin so long?" Alexander asked.

"Mine is smaller," she said. Alexander found a smaller cup with a duck. He spun it. It spun and spun.

"This one," he said. "It spins the best."

Mama put the little cup in the cart. Alexander patted the box. "Hello, baby," he whispered.

Ava stood at the door of her classroom. Her tummy felt jumpy. "Will I like school?" she asked her mom. "Yes," said Mom. "And I will wait right here."

Inside, Ava saw a little boy crying. His name was Sam. Ava had a pink bunny in her bag. She pulled it out. She held the bunny up so Sam could see it. Sam stopped crying. He smiled at the bunny.

The teacher put bread and cups on the table for snack time. Ava sat next to Sam. "Bunny makes friends," said Sam. "Yes," said Ava. She learned that a toy can make a sad face turn happy. At the door, Mom waved. Ava waved back with the bunny's soft paw.

Madison put on her red jersey. It was team day at the big gym. The floor was shiny and smooth. Her shoes went squeak, squeak, squeak.

Coach Tam handed Madison the ball. "Can you make a basket?" she asked. "I think so," said Madison. She threw the ball up high. It hit the ring and bounced out. She tried again. Out again. Madison made a sad face.

Then she saw the big boy on her team. He bent his knees way down low first. Then he pushed the ball up. The ball went in! "Did you bend your knees?" Madison asked him. "Yes, I bend them every time," he said.

Madison thought about that. She bent her knees low, low, low. She pushed the ball up high. The ball went swish, right through the net. "I did it!" said Madison. Her team clapped and clapped. After the game, Dad gave her a dry towel for her hot face. "Same time next week?" he asked. Madison hugged the ball and smiled.

Josephine wanted to pour the juice at snack time. But Ben was first, and Amara was second. "When is my turn?" Josephine asked. Miss Kim said, "Let's count and see."

Miss Kim held up her hand. "One, two, three, four, five," she counted, touching each cup. Then she poured juice for five friends. Josephine watched the juice splash. It smelled like apples.

Ben got grumpy. "I want more juice!" he said. "We only get one cup each," said Miss Kim. She gave him a cracker instead. Ben munched and smiled again.

"Now Josephine," said Miss Kim. Josephine picked up the big jug. It was heavy and cold. She poured slowly. One cup, two cups, three cups, four cups. Not one drop spilled!

After snack, the class sang their counting song. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" On the playground, Josephine found a small nest in the tree. She counted the eggs out loud. "One, two, three." She ran to Miss Kim. "Guess what I found!"

Ava sat at the art table. She wanted to make a picture for Dad. But her crayons were lost. She looked and looked. No crayons anywhere.

Miss Maya came over. "Try the paint," she said. She helped Ava put on her smock. Ava looked for something to paint with. She found an old bottle cap. She took the cap and dipped it in the red paint. She pressed it on the paper. A circle! A round red circle. Ava pressed again. Another circle.

Then she found a sponge. It had three sides. She dipped it in blue paint. She pressed it down. A triangle! The shape of the sponge made the shape on the paper. Ava tried a box next. Press, press. A square. A long envelope gave her a rectangle.

Ava peeled the skin off her orange snack at break time. She looked at it. Round too! She laughed.

At home, she gave Dad the picture. "A circle, a square, a triangle, and a rectangle," said Dad. "And they are all for me."

"All for you," said Ava.

Beatrice sat on Grandma's soft rug. She held the black tablet in her lap. Grandma tapped the little button on top. The screen lit up like a morning face.

"Now you try," said Grandma.

Beatrice pressed the button with one finger. The screen went dark. "Oh no," said Beatrice. She pressed it again. The light came back. She laughed. "It sleeps and wakes up!"

Grandma smiled. "What happens if you tap the green ball?"

Beatrice tapped it. The green ball opened into a drawing app. A white page appeared. Beatrice drew a big red circle. Then she drew a yellow sun.

"Can it hold my picture?" asked Beatrice.

"It will wait for you," said Grandma.

Beatrice put the tablet face down on the rug. She picked up her real red ball and rolled it to Grandma.

Later, crumbs fell on the rug. Grandma began to sweep. Beatrice took the tablet to the shelf, just like a big girl.

"Back to sleep," she whispered to the screen.

Lucy wanted tea for her teddy bear. She set him at the little table. "Tea time, friend!" she said.

Dad made the teapot warm. "Careful, it is hot," he said. He poured the tea. Lucy touched the cup with one finger. "Ouch! Hot!" She blew on it. She blew fast. Then she blew slow.

The tea was still too hot. Lucy looked around the playroom. She found a big cup and a small cup. She poured some tea into the small cup. It went wide across her teddy's cup. She touched the small cup. Now it felt cool! The big cup was still hot.

"Teddy, your tea is ready!" said Lucy. She tipped the small cup. The tea went into his cup. Not one drop would spill. Lucy sat up tall. She clapped her hands. "Big cup, slow tea. Small cup, fast tea!"

Milan went to the store with Mum. He saw a sign on a shelf. It said MILK. Mum read it out loud. The milk was right under the sign. "The word tells us where to look," said Mum. Milan found a blue box with a picture of cereal. He tried to read the letters on it, one by one.

Near the bread, there was a rack of books. Milan found a book about dinosaurs. He opened it at the front. He turned the pages, one at a time, all the way to the back. "I want this book forever," he said. Mum looked at the price. "That is a lot of pennies," she said. "We can borrow one from the library instead."

They walked to the library next door. Milan fetched a dinosaur book from a low shelf. The librarian stamped a little card. "Bring it back on this day," she said, "so other kids can read it too." At home, Milan read the book front to back, twice. On the big day, a leaf began to fall from the tree outside. Milan put the book in his bag. He carried it all the way back to the library, and set it on the desk. "Done," he said.

Adam went to the playground with his class. He saw the big red truck in the sand. He wanted to play with it.

But Ben had the truck first. Ben filled it with sand. Then he tipped it over. The sand made a big pile.

Adam ran up fast. He grabbed the truck. Ben made a sad face. Adam held the truck tight.

Miss Mia came over. She knelt down beside them. "Ben can have a turn first," she said. "Then you, Adam."

Adam gave the truck back. He sat on the bench. He waited. He watched Ben fill the truck again.

Then Ben walked over to Adam. "Here," said Ben. "Your turn now."

Adam took the truck. He filled it up with sand. He tipped it over. The sand made a big pile, just like Ben's pile.

"Thank you, Ben," said Adam.

Ben smiled a big smile. The two boys played side by side. The playground was noisy with happy kids.

"Truck," said Ben, holding out his hand.

Adam filled it one more time. Then he tipped the sand onto Ben's pile.

Gabriel had one red crayon. His big sister Mia had one blue crayon. They sat at the kitchen table. "I want blue too," said Gabriel. He grabbed Mia's crayon. Mia grabbed it back. The crayon snapped in two. Uh oh.

Now nobody had a whole crayon. Mama came over. She held out her hand. "One at a time," she said softly. "First you, then Mia." Gabriel drew a tight little circle with his red half. Then he gave it to Mia. Mia drew a wiggly snake. She gave it back. "Your turn, Gabriel," she said. Taking turns! The crayon went back and forth, back and forth.

Gabriel laughed. "The crayon tickles my hand when it draws!" The snake grew and grew. It even wore a little hat. At school tomorrow, Gabriel would show Mia's snake to his friends. "Can we draw together?" he asked. Mia smiled and pushed the paper to the middle of the table. "You start," she said.

Charles wanted to make a picture for Grandma. He had paper and crayons on the table. He drew a big sun with his orange crayon. Then he wanted to glue on leaves.

Charles found the glue bottle. He squeezed it too hard. A big puddle of glue came out. "Oh no," said Charles. The puddle was wide and shiny. He put a leaf on top of the puddle. The leaf stuck fast to the paper.

Charles touched the glue on his finger. It felt wet and sticky. He waited and looked at his picture. He peeked at his finger again. The glue was not wet anymore. It was dry and stiff. Now his finger felt like paper.

"I need to wash my hands," said Charles. Mom helped him at the sink. Then Charles ran to show Grandma his leaf sun.

Penelope went to the store with Mama. She wanted a banana. "Where do bananas live?" she asked. "Not in the toy part," said Mama.

Penelope looked at the shelves. She saw a teddy bear. The bear did not look like food. She saw a bouncy ball. That was not food either. "Toys go here," she said. "Toys are not for eating."

Then Penelope saw a low shelf with apples. Red apples, round apples. Next to them sat the bananas. She picked one up. "Found it!" she said. Mama smiled. "Good eyes, Penelope."

At the checkout, Penelope saw dog food and cat food. "Is that for me?" she asked. "No, silly," said Mama. "That food is for animals. You are not a puppy." Penelope giggled. "I am not a puppy! I am a girl!" The cashier laughed too. At home, Mama peeled the banana. Penelope took a big bite. "Bananas are food," she said. "The bear stays at the store."

Iris sat at the dinner table. She had ten peas on her plate. She wanted to eat them all, but the big ones looked yucky.

"I will count them," said Daddy. "Then they will feel smaller." He pointed at the peas. "One, two, three." Iris giggled. "Four, five, six." She poked a pea with her spoon. "Seven, eight, nine, ten."

Then Daddy ate one pea. "Now you count," he said. Iris pointed too. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine." Her voice sang like a song. Each time she counted, a pea went into her mouth. The big ones did not look yucky anymore. They looked fun.

The clock on the wall gave a little ring. It was near Iris's chair. "Bath time soon," said Mommy. Iris ate her last pea. "One!" she said. Then she held up her spoon like a flag.

Norah wants to make pancakes for her family. She gets out eggs, milk and flour. But there is a problem. The butter is cold and hard. Norah tries to stir it. The butter will not stir. "Silly butter," says Norah. "You are too hard!"

Dad says, "Let's give the butter a warm pan." Dad turns on the stove. Norah stands back and watches. Dad drops the butter in the pan. The warm pan makes the butter go soft. Now it is shiny and runny. "It melts!" says Norah. "The warm pan did that!"

Norah stirs the eggs and milk. She stirs the flour too. Dad pours the batter into the pan. The pancakes puff up big and round. Norah gives each pancake a name. "This one is Fluffy. This one is Wobbly. This one is Baby."

The family sits down to eat. Norah passes the shiny pancakes around. "Who wants Baby?" she asks. Baby is gone in one big bite.

Elias went to the mall with Mama. They walked past the toy cars. They walked past the juicy oranges at the fruit stand. Then they came to the hair salon.

"Time for your first haircut," said Mama.

Elias sat in the big chair. It was very tall. The hairdresser, Miss Kim, put a soft cape on him.

"Will it hurt?" asked Elias.

"No," said Miss Kim. "Watch."

She picked up her scissors. Snip, snip. A little piece of hair fell down. It landed on the cape. More snips, and more hair fell, like soft rain.

"Look, Mama!" said Elias. "The scissors make the hair fall down!"

Miss Kim showed him the mirror. His hair was short and neat.

"Nice and cool," said Mama. "Now we can go home and cook dinner."

Elias touched his new hair and smiled at the boy in the mirror.

Kinsley wanted to find her red car. She looked in the toy box. She pulled out a blue truck. She pulled out a green frog. No red car.

Kinsley crawled under the little table. She heard a sound. Toot, toot! The red car was stuck way up high on the shelf. Kinsley could not reach it. She jumped. She stretched her arms up. Still no red car.

Mom came in. "Let's get a step stool," said Mom. Mom held the stool steady. Kinsley climbed up one step. She reached and reached. Her fingers touched the red car. It slid down into her hands. "My red car!" said Kinsley.
