Kinsley drove the red car on the floor. It bumped into the blue truck. It bumped into the green frog. Then Kinsley found a yellow bus. Now all her cars could play together. The red car went first. "Beep, beep!" said Kinsley.

Mohamed wanted to play house with his bear. But bear looked sad on the floor. His blanket was missing.

"Bear, are you cold?" Mohamed asked. Bear said nothing. "I will fix that."

Mohamed got a small sock. He tucked it around bear like a blanket. Then he held bear close and patted his back. "Shh, shh," he said softly. "Papa is here."

In the kitchen, Mama was making soup. The pot was hot, so Mama held the spoon. Mohamed stayed back and watched. He asked, "Can bear have soup too?" Mama smiled. "Pretend soup is best for bears."

So Mohamed made pretend soup with a cup and water that was not hot. He fed bear one tiny spoon. Bear drank it all up.

Then Mohamed saw something. When he held his cup under the lamp, a shadow grew on the wall. It looked big like a giant cup! He moved the cup. The shadow moved too. "Look, Mama! My cup makes a big shadow!"

Mama laughed. Mohamed finished feeding bear. "Night night, bear," he said. He laid bear down under the sock blanket.

Then he picked up his cup again and made the shadow dance across the wall.

Norah came home with a small box. Something inside went squeak, squeak. She put the box on the floor. Out came a tiny brown guinea pig. "His name is Bear," Norah said. Her dad helped her pour soft hay into a bowl. Bear nibbled the hay. Crunch, crunch.

Then Bear sat very still. He made a sad little sound. "Maybe he is hungry," Dad said. Norah got a small carrot. She held it out low. Bear sniffed it. Then he took a bite. His whiskers wiggled. Norah laughed.

After the carrot, Bear made a happy pop sound. He jumped up, all four feet in the air. "He popped!" Norah said. Dad smiled. "Carrots make him jump for joy." Bear curled up in the hay, warm and small. Norah patted him soft, soft, soft. "Good night, Bear," she whispered.

Yesterday Arnaud painted a robot at school. It had big arms and a loud red mouth. But the paint was wet, so it had to stay on the shelf.

Today Arnaud ran to the shelf. "Is it dry now?" he asked. He touched the paper. The paint felt smooth. His robot was done!

Miss Ola smiled. "Now we can fill a frame with it," she said. She held the paper while Arnaud pushed the pins in. He was careful with the sharp pins. Miss Ola pushed them all the way.

The robot hung on the wall. "Tomorrow I want to paint a cat," said Arnaud. "Then the cat will dry too, and later we can hang it next to my robot."

Miss Ola laughed. "A cat and a robot," she said. "That will be a fun wall."

Arnaud looked at the paint pots. He picked up a brush. "Today the cat starts," he said.

Evan sat in the backyard with his friend Mia. They had big paper and cups of paint. Evan had red paint. Mia had blue paint. "Can I use your blue?" Evan asked. "Yes," said Mia. She was polite and shared.

Evan dipped his brush in red. He painted a big apple. Then he dipped in blue. He painted the sky. Then he dipped his brush in blue again. But some yellow paint was still on the brush. Evan looked. The paint turned green on the paper! He gasped. Yellow and blue made green.

He painted green grass all along the bottom. Mia painted green leaves on her tree. Then they painted one picture together. "Red apple, blue sky, green grass," said Evan. Mia laughed and hung it on the fence to dry.

Colton had a library book about boats. He wanted to keep it forever. At bedtime he held it under his arm like a teddy bear.

Mom said, "Time for bed." Colton climbed in. The book sat on his lap. He opened the front cover. On the first page, Mom's finger touched some printed words. "This says borrow," she said. The words were black and smooth under Colton's finger too.

"That means we take it home," Mom said. "But we take it back on Saturday. Then other kids can read it too." Colton looked at the pages. He turned them one by one, front to back. The words went along like little boats floating down a river. He got to the last page. Then the book was done.

Colton's tummy felt funny. He did not want it done. "Can we read it again?" he asked. Mom smiled. "Yes. Read it again and again. Until Saturday comes." Colton turned back to the first page. He could read it many times before then. "Read it again tomorrow," he whispered to the book. Then he turned off his smile, closed his eyes, and held on tight.

Weston ran to the playground with Dad. He felt so excited. The slide was big and tall. Weston wanted to slide down it fast.

He climbed up the steps. A big dog barked loud. Weston felt scared. He held the rail tight. Dad came close and held his hand. "The dog is on a leash," said Dad. "You are safe." Weston looked at the dog. The dog wagged its tail and sat down.

Weston slid down the tall slide. Whee! He laughed and felt happy. Then a girl took the swing he wanted. Weston felt angry. His face got hot. Dad said, "Take a breath. Ask for a turn." Weston took a big breath. "Can I have a turn?" he asked. The girl said, "Yes, when I count to ten."

Then came the surprise. The girl jumped off the swing. She pulled a red balloon from her pocket. "It is for you," she said. Weston had not seen it there. He hugged the balloon and smiled big. "I think I like this park," said Weston. Dad lifted him up high. "Swing time," said Dad. Weston held the balloon tight and kicked his feet.

Sarah went to the big hall with Mama and Dadu. Tonight was Diwali, the festival of lights. There were little clay lamps everywhere. "One lamp, two lamps, three lamps," Sarah counted. So many lamps!

At the water table, Dadu made a soft paper boat. He set a tiny lamp inside it. Then he set the boat on the water. Would it float? The boat floated! The little light bobbed up and down. Sarah clapped her hands.

"Can my boat have a lamp too?" she asked. A kind aunty helped her fold a soft paper boat. Sarah waited while Dadu lit the small lamp with his match. He was the grown-up, so only he touched it. He placed the lamp in Sarah's boat. Sarah held her boat low, close to the water. Then she let go. The boat floated! But then it spun around and around. "Look, it dances!" said Sarah. The little light danced on the dark water all the way to the other side.

Zoey sat in the big waiting chair. Today she would get her first haircut. Her hair was long. It kept falling in her eyes. She pushed it away. It fell back again.

"Zoey," called a lady named Miss Kim. Zoey walked over and climbed into the tall salon chair. Miss Kim gave her a cape to wear. It was blue like the sky.

Miss Kim sprayed water on Zoey's hair. The wet hair stuck down flat. It did not fall in Zoey's eyes anymore. Then Miss Kim used her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Zoey sat very still. She watched little pieces of hair drop onto the cape.

Soon the haircut was done. Zoey looked in the mirror. She could see her whole face. No hair was in her eyes. "I did it," said Zoey. Miss Kim clapped. Mommy said, "You were so brave." After that, they went home to get dinner. Zoey made a sour face at the green beans, but she smiled at her new short hair in the window.

Evan wanted to paint a picture at daycare. He looked for his favorite color. It was red. The red paint pot was empty.

"Can I help?" asked Miss Kim. She squeezed the tube. A little red paint came out. It was not enough. Evan had an idea. He put yellow paint on his brush. Then he added red on top. The colors mixed on the paper.

"Look!" said Evan. The paint turned orange. Miss Kim smiled. "That is neat," she said. Evan hurried to try more. Blue and yellow made green. His friend Sam came to look.

"Wow," said Sam. "Can I try too?" Evan gave Sam the yellow brush. Sam added blue. Green filled the page.

Miss Kim hung both pictures by the window. The orange sun and the green grass shone in the light.

"I made sun colors," said Evan.

Aubrey wanted to make her own breakfast. Daddy put warm toast on her plate. The butter sat in a little dish beside it.

"Can I do it?" Aubrey asked. Daddy gave her a dull, safe spreader. She pushed the butter. It made a big lump in one spot. She tried again. The lump slid around and around. Then she held the spreader flat and moved it slow. The lump turned into a smooth, shiny coat. "Look! It went all smooth!" she said.

Next came the milk. Aubrey held the cup with both hands. She poured too fast, and milk ran over the rim. She stopped. How slow is slow? She tipped the jug a tiny bit. The milk went in drop by drop. The cup stayed dry. She poured the second cup for Daddy the same way. Not one drop spilled.

Aubrey took a big bite of her toast. "I can do it myself," she said. Daddy held up his cup. "To my big helper!"

Oliver went to the big hall with Mama and Grandpa. Today was the lantern festival. Lanterns hung from the ceiling like pretty orange moons. Oliver wanted to find the red one with a dragon on it. Grandpa had helped him buy it at the little shop last week.

But the red dragon lantern was not lit. All the other lanterns glowed. His stayed dark. Oliver held Grandpa's hand and walked closer. The lantern had a small candle inside. Grandpa bent down. He used a long match to light it. A grown-up helper watched and nodded.

Then the candle made a warm glow. The dragon's wings turned bright gold. Oliver could feel little heat on his fingers when he leaned close. Grandpa pulled him back a step, just to be safe.

A girl next to them looked sad. Her paper fan had a tear in it. Oliver showed her his glowing dragon. She smiled big. She whispered, "That one is my secret favorite." Oliver grinned and said, "Mine too." The lanterns swayed above them, all shining together.

Violet ran to the window at daycare. Yesterday the class had planted seeds in little pots. Teacher Sam had poured the dirt for them. Violet had pushed one seed down with her finger.

Now the pots sat on the sunny sill. The dirt looked plain and brown. "Where is my plant?" Violet asked.

"It is not now," said Teacher Sam. "It grows later. First we water it today."

Violet held her small cup. She poured the cold water slowly onto her pot. The dirt turned dark. A tiny drip ran down the side of the pot. Her friend Milo watered his pot too.

Then it was playtime. Then it was snack time. Then Daddy came. Violet looked back at the sill. The dirt was still plain and brown.

"Come back tomorrow," said Teacher Sam. "The seed wakes up after it drinks."

The next day Violet ran to the window first thing. There, in her pot, was a small green loop. It had pushed up through the dirt.

"Look!" said Violet. "It came!"

"Because you watered it yesterday," said Teacher Sam.

Violet touched the tiny leaf with one careful finger.

Juliette sat at the art table. She wanted to make a picture for her mama. But her paper was empty. She waited and looked at the tray.

The teacher held a big brown potato. "This is a root," she said. "It grows under the ground." The teacher cut it with a knife. Juliette watched from her seat. Now the potato had a flat top. The teacher cut one into a circle. She cut one into a square. She cut one into a triangle. She cut one into a rectangle.

Juliette dipped the circle in red paint. She pressed it on the paper. She lifted it up. A red circle stayed there! She pressed hard again. Another circle appeared.

She stamped the square in blue. Four flat sides. She stamped the triangle in yellow. Three pointy corners. She stamped the rectangle in green. Long and flat.

Then she licked a bit of paint on her finger. "Yuck," said Juliette. "Paint does not taste good."

She made a house with the square. She made a roof with the triangle. She made a sun with the circle. She made a door with the rectangle.

The picture was full of shapes. Juliette held it up to the window. The sun shone through the paper. "Look," she said. "A house for you, Mama."

Grandma drove Ruby to her house for lunch. Ruby was hungry. She saw the soup and reached for her spoon.

"Not yet," said Grandma. "First we say our words." Grandma folded her hands. "Thank you for our food," she said. Grandpa said it too. Then they picked up their spoons.

Ruby tried. "Thank you for our soup," she said. Grandma clapped. Grandpa clapped. Then everyone ate.

After lunch, Ruby had a nap on the fuzzy blanket. When she woke up, Grandpa put out bread and butter.

"Wait," said Ruby. She folded her hands. "Thank you for our bread." Grandpa laughed and picked up his knife. Grandma picked up hers.

"More bread, please," said Ruby, and she took a big piece.

Felix stood on his stool at the big kitchen table. The toast was warm and golden. Miss Amy put a small pat of butter on top. "Now you," she said.

Felix picked up the soft butter knife. He spread one way. Then he spread the other way. The butter melted a little and went smooth. One, two, three, slow. The toast shined all over. "I did it!" said Felix.

Next came the milk. Felix poured fast. Milk splashed onto the table. Miss Amy wiped it with a cloth. "Try again," she said. Felix tipped the cup just a tiny bit. One, two, three, slow. The milk went in and did not spill.

After snack time, they would buy apples for tomorrow. Miss Amy said the market was by the beach. Felix's sock felt itchy, so she helped him pull it straight. Then he lifted his cup with two hands and took a big, careful sip.

Mason stood by the bus door. He held his mama's hand tight. The bus was big and yellow.

Mason wanted to sit by the window. But he did not know where to go. A big kid sat down fast. The seat by the window was full.

Mason walked down the aisle. He found a seat with room. He sat by the window after all. "Hi," said a girl next to him. Her name was Nia.

Mason looked out the window. He saw his mama wave. Mason waved back. Then he pressed his hand on the glass. The glass was cold and smooth. Nia saw him and pressed her hand too. Two hands, one on each side of a little mark.

The bus door closed with a whoosh. The driver turned a handle to lock it. The bus began to roll. Mama got smaller and smaller. Mason made a happy face at her. Then he looked at Nia. "Want to see my truck?" he asked. Nia nodded. Mason opened his backpack and pulled it out.

Felix stood by the wooden fence at school. He did not know anyone yet. He held his red ball very tight.

A boy ran past. The boy had a big truck. Felix wanted to play. But he did not know how to start.

Then his ball slipped out of his hands. It rolled down the hill. It rolled fast, fast, fast. Felix ran after it. The ball rolled right to the boy with the truck. It stopped next to the truck. The sand caught it. The boy picked it up. He rolled it back. Felix rolled it to him again. The sand caught it again.

"You can play with us," said the boy. Felix smiled big. He gave the boy a picture he had drawn. It was a picture of a red ball.

At home, Felix would remember this day. But now it was time to play. The ball rolled again.

Amelia stood at the paint table in the art room. She wanted to paint a purple grape. But there was no purple paint. Not one drop.

She looked at the pots. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. There was blue paint. "Red, yellow, blue," she said, pointing at each pot. Those were the three big colours.

Her teacher, Miss Jo, smiled. "Try putting two colours together," said Miss Jo. "See what your brush can do."

Amelia dipped her brush in the blue. Then she dipped it in the red. She swirled them on her paper. The red and blue began to mix. Round and round went her brush. The paint turned purple!

"My grape!" said Amelia. She painted one big purple grape. Then she painted five more.

Tom peeked over from the next table. "I want purple too," he said.

"You need red and blue," said Amelia. She held up her brush like a magic wand. "Ta-da!"

Tom mixed his colours. His paint turned purple too. "We match!" he said.

Amelia looked at the yellow pot. She wondered about yellow and blue. She tried it. Green! Like grass! Like a frog!

"Next time I will paint a frog," said Amelia. She put her purple painting in her favorite spot on the drying rack.

Ryan sat at the little desk in the library. He wanted to write his name. But the pencil kept slipping. His R looked like a wiggly worm.

Miss Jo, the library lady, put a small pencil in his hand. "Try a pinch," she said softly. "Pinch it like this." She showed him. Ryan pinched the pencil with two fingers.

The pencil stopped wiggling. Ryan made a line. The line was straight! He made a big R. It looked like a real R.

Ryan made a sour face at the crooked y. Then he pinched again. The y came out neat too.

"Can I do the a?" Ryan asked. He thought about his pinch. He wrote a, then n. The pencil went where he told it to go.

Miss Jo put his paper on the wall. Ryan pointed at it. "That one is mine!"

Grayson woke up and looked out the window. The world was white. "Snow!" he said. No school today. It was a snow day at home.

Grayson wanted to build a snow hill. He scooped snow into his bowl. He carried it to his room. He patted it into a big pile on his tray. Then he flew his toy plane over the top. "Up, up!" he said. The plane went over the bumpy hill. But then Grayson saw something. The hill was getting small. Little drops sat on the tray. The room was warm, and the snow was turning to water.

Grayson ran to Mom. "My hill is going away!" he said. Mom smiled. "Fill your bowl again," she said. "We can build it outside." Grayson put on his boots and coat. Mom helped with his zipper. Outside, they patted the snow into one big hill. Grayson flew his plane up and down. He clapped his mittens together. "The hill stays big out here!" he said. Mom laughed and patted more snow for him.

Zachary stood in the school computer lab. He wanted to draw a big blue pond. But the tablet was dark. "I can't see anything," he said.

Miss Ruiz sat next to him. "Just press the round button," she said. "Be careful and press it soft." Zachary pressed the button. The screen lit up. He smiled. The light made the dark go away. Then he tapped the little paint pot picture. The drawing app opened. He drew a blue pond with green frogs. Then he tapped a duck and gave it a yellow beak.

"Now I want a new one," he said. "First we put it away," said Miss Ruiz. She helped him tap the home square. The screen went calm. "Can we sell my duck picture at the art show?" he asked. Miss Ruiz laughed. "Let's print it first," she said, and Zachary clapped his hands.

Isabella went to Miss Dot's music room. Miss Dot had a big drum and a shiny silver bell. "Today we will clap," said Miss Dot. Isabella wanted to clap very fast. She clapped clap-clap-clap-clap like rain!

But the drum went slow. Boom... boom... boom. Isabella's claps ran ahead. Then her claps got all mixed up. "My hands are silly," said Isabella. Miss Dot laughed. "Make your hands wait," she said. "Listen first."

So Isabella watched the drum. Boom. Her hands went boom too. Clap. Boom. Clap. Boom. It was the same! When the drum went slow, she clapped slow. When Miss Dot tapped faster, Isabella clapped faster too. "One, two, one, two," said Miss Dot, and Isabella's hands followed all by themselves.

Then they sang "Twinkle, Twinkle." Miss Dot pointed to a toy cat on the piano. "Sing it to him," she said. Isabella sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." The cat's tail stuck straight up. "He likes it," said Miss Dot. Isabella sang louder. "How I wonder what you are!" Miss Dot hit the shiny bell one time. Ding! The cat jumped, and Isabella fell down laughing. "Again," she said. "Again, again, again!"

Grandma was coming to stay for a whole week. Elizabeth had a job to do. She had to make the guest bed ready.

Elizabeth put a soft blanket on the bed. She put a pillow at the top. "One blanket, one pillow, one cozy bed," she said. But the bed still did not look right. It looked flat and sad.

Then Elizabeth had an idea. She grabbed the blanket and fluffed it up. She puffed the pillow with both hands. The bed got soft and puffy, like a big nest. "Now it looks like a nest," said Elizabeth. "A tight, warm nest."

Grandma came in with her little brown bag. She touched the puffy blanket. She sat down on the soft bed. "Oh, this is lovely," said Grandma. "The puffy blanket makes the bed warm. I love it."

"One blanket, one pillow, one happy Grandma," said Elizabeth. She gave Grandma a hug.

Grandma patted the bed. "Come sit with me." Elizabeth climbed up next to her. They sat in the nest together, snug and still.

Jasmine went to the park with her dad. The sun was out. It was sunny. She wore her shiny red hat. The wind began to blow. It was windy. The wind took her hat right off her head!

"Can I get my hat?" she asked. Dad said, "Yes, let's chase it together."

The hat rolled and rolled. Then dark clouds came. Rain fell. It was rainy. The rain made the hat wet and heavy. The hat stopped rolling. Jasmine picked it up.

"Why did it stop?" she asked. "The rain made it wet," said Dad.

Then something soft and white fell from the sky. It was snow. Jasmine laughed. Snow landed on her neck. Dad put her warm coat on her. The coat was cozy.

Jasmine put the wet hat in the bag. She held Dad's hand. "Snowy parks are cold," she said, "but warm coats are just right." Dad smiled and said, "Home for hot cocoa."

Wyatt waits at the bus stop with Grandma. He wants to see the bus come. But no bus comes yet. The sun is out. It is sunny. Wyatt takes off his hat. "Too hot," he says.

Then the wind blows. It is windy now. The wind takes Wyatt's hat and rolls it down the street. "Come back, hat!" says Wyatt. Grandma laughs. They run and get the hat. Grandma puts it back on his head. She zips his coat up to his chin. "The wind is sharp today," she says.

Then the sky turns gray. Rain drops fall. It is rainy now. Grandma opens a big umbrella. Pop! The rain goes plip, plip on top. Wyatt holds Grandma's hand under the umbrella. "Bus!" he shouts. The big yellow bus rolls up. "Bus, bus, bus!"

Grandma put two plates on the table. One plate had strawberries. One plate had apple slices. "Which plate has more?" Grandma asked.

Sarah looked and looked. She could not tell. "I will count," she said.

She touched a strawberry. "One, two, three, four, five." Then she counted the apples. "One, two, three." "The strawberries have more," said Sarah. "Five is more than three."

She counted the strawberries again. This time she started at the other end. "One, two, three, four, five." Still five! She laughed. "Same number, Grandma!"

The cat jumped up. His paws were dirty. "Down, cat," said Grandma. She poured him a bowl of water.

"Can we count again?" Sarah asked. Grandma smiled. "You count," she said. "I will eat one strawberry." Sarah counted the plate. "One, two, three, four," she said. "Now the cat has more water than I have strawberries!"

Naomi wanted to make a house for Teddy. She looked at her blocks on the soft rug. First she tried the circle block. It rolled away. Thump, thump, across the floor. "Come back," said Naomi. The square block did not roll. It sat still. She stacked four squares. The walls grew tall. Naomi clapped her hands. Then she held up a triangle. It looked like a little roof. She set it on top. The house had a pointy hat now. Teddy is thirsty, Naomi thought. She found her rectangle block. It lay flat like a little table. She put a toy fork and a tiny cup on it. "Drink your water, Teddy," she said. The circle block rolled back and bumped her toe. Naomi laughed and picked it up. "You can be the moon," she told it. She held the circle up high above the house. It hung there in her hand, round and shiny, like a night light. Naomi yawned and sat down. "Time for bed, Teddy," she whispered.

Brielle got to school early. Her teacher, Miss Kim, put a pencil on her desk.

"Today you write your name," said Miss Kim.

Brielle grabbed the pencil in her whole fist. She pushed hard. The letter B came out fat and wobbly. The pencil slid away. Her name looked like a squiggle.

"My name is wrong," said Brielle.

"Try pinching it," said Miss Kim. She held her own pencil with two fingers. "Like this."

Brielle pinched the pencil too. Now her fingers could steer it. She made a B. Then an R. Then the whole line of letters.

"Brielle!" she shouted. "It says Brielle!"

Her friend Leo clapped. "Do mine next!" he said.

Brielle counted her letters. Seven letters, all hers. She drew a star under them, and the pencil did just what her fingers told it to do.

Samuel ran out to the backyard in the morning. The sun was out. "It is sunny today," he said. He put on his sun hat. Then he began to build a tower of blocks on the grass. But the wind blew. The wind blew and blew. The hat flew off his head! "Wind, why did you take my hat?" The wind did not answer. It just kept blowing. So Samuel went inside and put on his warm coat. Now the wind could not touch him.

Soon the sky turned gray. Rain fell on the blocks. Plip, plip, plip. "Rain, rain, where will you go?" The rain went down into the grass. Samuel watched from the porch. It was quiet in the rain. He clapped his hands. Then small white flakes came down too. "Mama, what is that?" Mama smiled. "That is snow." The snow made the blocks all white.

Samuel put on his mittens and his boots. He stepped into the soft snow. His boots made little marks. He picked up the snowy blocks one by one. "I will build a snow tower," he said. The snow stuck to the blocks and made them stick together. His tower stood tall and white. Samuel patted the top. "Snowy tower, hello." Mama stood by the door and waved. Samuel waved back and said, "Hello, Mama. Come see my snow tower."

Mohamed had a library book. It was about a turtle. The turtle had a green shell. Mohamed loved the turtle book so much.

"Can I keep it forever?" he asked Daddy.

"No," said Daddy. "We borrowed it. We take it back soon. Then other kids can read it too."

Mohamed held the book tight. He opened the front cover. He turned the pages one by one. He saw little black marks on the page. "What are those?" he asked.

"Those are words," said Daddy. "Words tell the story."

Daddy pointed to a word. "That says turtle." Mohamed looked. The marks did look a bit like a little turtle walking! He turned more pages. The turtle in the story found a leaf. The turtle ate the leaf. Then the turtle began to grow, bigger and bigger.

Mohamed turned the page again. Then the pages ran out. The back cover was hard and smooth. "The end," said Daddy. Mohamed patted the back cover.

The next morning, Mohamed spun in a circle. He spun and spun. Then he felt dizzy and fell down on the rug, laughing. Daddy laughed too. "Time to go," said Daddy. "The book goes back today."

At the library, Mohamed gave the book to the lady at the desk. She smiled and put it on a shelf. Another little girl picked it up right away. She sat down and opened the front cover.

Mohamed peeked at her. "That page says turtle," he whispered to Daddy.

"Do you want another book to take home?" Daddy asked.

Mohamed nodded. "One about a turtle that grows," he said. He ran to the shelf.

Charlotte went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about dogs. But where were the dog books?

She walked down a little row of shelves. A book with a cow fell out. Then a book with a duck fell out too. Hmm, were all these books about animals? She put cow, duck, and dog books together in one pile.

Next to that shelf was a shelf of food books. She found one about apples and one about bread. Then she saw a shiny red truck on the floor. It was a toy, not a book. Was this where toys went? She rolled it on the carpet. The truck had one wobbly wheel. "Silly truck," she said with a giggle.

A boy ran by and began to yell, "Where are the train books?" Charlotte knew just the spot. "The animals are here," she said. "Maybe trains are with machines." The boy looked. He found trains and cars together. Books that matched sat side by side, just like her piles at home. Dad checked out the dog book and the truck's story too.

Lennon went to the store with Mama. Yesterday, they ate all the bananas. Today, the bowl was empty. "Now we need more," said Mama.

Lennon held a little toy mouse from a shelf. She squeezed it. The mouse gave one weak squeak. Then it went quiet. "The battery is weak," said Mama. "We will fix it later, at home."

Lennon put the mouse in the cart. She whispered to it, "Sleep now, little mouse." Then she picked out three yellow bananas, one by one. Mama smiled.

At the checkout, the clerk gave Lennon a sticker. "Today is banana day," Lennon whispered to the mouse. Tomorrow, the mouse would squeak again. Tonight, Mama would bake banana bread, and Lennon would watch from her chair. "One banana for now," said Mama, and Lennon took a big happy bite.

Ayla wanted the bunny sticker on the desk. But first, the doctor had to check her.

The doctor shone a little light. "Close one eye," she said. Ayla used her eyes to look at the light. Then the doctor tapped a tiny drum. Ayla used her ears to hear the tap, tap, tap.

The doctor held a small jar. Ayla used her nose to smell it. "Orange!" she said. The doctor gave her a sweet drop. Ayla used her tongue to taste it. It was yummy.

Then the doctor touched Ayla's tummy with cold hands. Ayla felt it with her skin. She laughed and kicked her feet.

At last the doctor peeled off the bunny sticker. It had green grass under the bunny's feet. Ayla pressed it on her hand with her finger. She held her arm out so the sticker could float down like a leaf onto her sleeve.

"I'm not mad anymore," said Ayla. "Bunny stays with me."

Mateo was at Grandma's house. A new baby sister was coming home today. Mateo wanted to make her laugh. But babies cannot laugh at jokes. Mateo did not know what to do.

First he tried a funny face. He puffed his cheeks. The baby just blinked. Then he tried a loud song. The baby made a small frown. Grandma held the baby in her lap. "Try something soft," said Grandma.

Mateo looked around the kitchen. Grandma had a tall glass of water. Mateo dipped his finger and tickled the baby's tiny toes. A drop of water fell. It tickled her foot. The baby wiggled. Then she made a gurgle. Then she smiled!

"Again!" said Mateo. He tickled her toes once more. The baby kicked and gurgled again. "She likes water toes!" said Mateo. Grandma laughed too. Later, Grandma peeled a peach for Mateo. The baby touched the peach. "Ooh, slimy," said Mateo. The baby gurgled at that too. Mateo grinned and tickled her toes one more time.

Mila sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. She held her teddy bear tight. Today she was getting a shot in her arm. She did not want it. "It might hurt," she whispered to her teddy.

The nurse came in with curly hair and a smile. She wiped Mila's arm with a cool, wet cotton ball. Mila squeezed her teddy. Quick as a blink, the shot was done. Mila looked down. There was a tiny red dot on her arm.

The nurse pressed a soft white cotton ball on the dot. She held it there. "Now let's count," she said. One, two, three. Then she lifted the cotton away. The tiny red dot was gone. Pressing made it stop. Mila blinked. Then the nurse put on a pretty blue bandage with stars.

Mila slid off the chair. She did not want to hurry. She wanted to show everyone her bandage. In the waiting room, a small boy was crying. Mila held up her arm. "Look," she said. "Stars." The boy stopped crying and looked.

Leah stood in the changing room. Her wet hair dripped onto the floor. Drip, drip, drip. She watched the little dark spots grow. "Mama, look," she said. "My hair makes dots."

Leah touched her hair. It was dark now, like the wooden bench. Before the pool, her hair had been light. Now it was wet and dark.

Mama sat down on the wood bench. "Which hair is heavier?" she asked. "Wet hair or dry hair?"

Leah thought about it. She squeezed her hair. A drop ran down her arm. "Wet hair," she said. It hung down flat. Dry hair had bounced up like a puppy.

They put their towels in the bag. The room was quiet now. Leah patted her head one more time. Drip, drip went her hair on her shoulder.

"I have a little pool on me," she whispered.

Hudson stood in the big school gym. A red hoop lay on the floor. He held a small beanbag in his hand.

Hudson threw the beanbag. It landed far from the hoop. "It went the wrong way," he said. His teacher, Miss Kim, rolled the hoop closer. "Try again," she said. Hudson held his arm way up high. He dropped his arm down as he let go. The beanbag flew straight down. Plunk! It landed right in the hoop. "I did it!" said Hudson. He asked, "What made it go in?" Miss Kim smiled. "Watch me." She held her arm high and dropped it. Her beanbag went in too. Hudson saw it. High arm, beanbag goes down.

Next Miss Kim tossed him a big blue ball. Hudson reached with one hand. The ball bumped his fingers and fell. "Too big for one hand," said Hudson. He held out both hands, cupped like a bowl. Miss Kim tossed the ball again. Thump! It landed in his hands and stayed there. The gym was full of the sound of clapping. "Show us again!" called his friend Ben. Hudson held the ball up high. "Look, both hands!" he said.

Asher ran to the swings. He was so excited. "Look, Mommy! The big swing is free!"

He climbed on. Mommy pushed him gently. Asher went up. He went down. His tummy tickled. "Again!" he laughed. His face felt happy.

Then a big boy ran past. He knocked over a little girl's toy truck. The little girl began to cry. Her face was sad. The big boy looked angry. He stomped his foot and shouted.

Asher stopped swinging. He wanted to help. He walked to the girl. "Do you want my truck?" he asked. She sniffled. "Yes, please."

They rolled the truck back and forth on the ground. Asher drew a circle in the sand with his finger. The truck drove round and round the circle. Soon the girl laughed. Her sad face turned happy.

Then Asher spun himself around and around. He got dizzy and fell down in the soft sand. "Whoa!" he said. Both of them giggled.

The big boy came back. He looked at the truck. "Can I play too?" he asked in a small voice. "Yes," said Asher. He handed over the truck.

The big boy smiled. Now nobody was angry. Nobody was sad.

Asher saw the truck make everyone laugh. He clapped his hands. "Truck goes round the circle!" he shouted. "Watch it go!"

Adam had a library book. It was about a big brown bear. He held it in bed. "Read it again," he said.

Mama sat close. Adam opened the front cover. The first page had words. Adam pointed at them. "What does that say?" he asked. "It says the bear lives in a cave," said Mama. Adam looked hard. The marks on the page made the words. The words told about the bear. Adam turned the pages one by one. The story went from the front to the back.

"I want to keep this book forever," said Adam. "It is not ours," said Mama. "We borrowed it. We take it back on Friday." Adam hugged the book tight. "The book goes home to the library?" he asked. "Yes," said Mama. "So other kids can read about the bear too."

Then rain tapped on the window. A little storm was outside. It was not scary. It was soft. Adam yawned. "Will the book get wet in the rain?" he asked. "No," said Mama. "We will not forget it. We will put it in a bag."

At last they came to the last page. The bear went to sleep in his cave. Adam patted the book. "Good night, bear," he said. He closed the back cover. Mama kissed his head and turned off the light.

Ethan ran up to the bookmobile. It was a big truck full of books. A lady named Miss Jo smiled at him.

"Would you like your very own library card?" she asked.

"Yes, please!" said Ethan.

Miss Jo made the card. It had Ethan's name on it. Ethan held it with both hands. He felt very big.

He found a book about a squishy red ball. The ball went boing on every page. Ethan hugged the book. "This one is mine now," he said. "Mine forever."

"Well," said Miss Jo, "you can take it home. But you must bring it back so other kids can read it too. Then you can take another book home."

Ethan thought hard. He did like the boing book. But maybe there was a dinosaur book too.

"I will bring it back," he said. "After lunch and after bed and after lunch again."

"That sounds just right," said Miss Jo. She put the book in a bag. The bag had a bear on it.

Ethan waved to the truck. "Bye, books! I will come back!"

At home, Ethan read the boing book three times. Then he put it by the door, so it would be ready to go back.

"Boing," said Ethan, and he covered the book with his blanket to keep it safe for the night.

Isaiah sat in the school library. He wanted to find a book about dogs. But the books were mixed up on the shelf. He did not know which one to pick.

Miss Ada sat down next to him. "Let's look at the first letter," she said. She pointed to a big black book. "This one starts with D. D says duh, like dog."

Isaiah ran his finger under the letter. "D," he said. "Duh, duh, dog!" He pulled the book out. A big brown dog looked back at him from the cover.

He tried another book. "B. Buh, buh, ball!" He opened it. A red ball bounced across the first page. Isaiah laughed. The letters had shown him the way.

"Now I can find any book," he said. He hugged the dog book tight. Miss Ada smiled. The sun began to shine through the big window. Isaiah sat close to her and turned the first page.

James wanted to build a big tower. He had ten blocks on the rug. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three," he said. He patted each block as he counted.

The tower fell over. "Oh no," said James. He tried again. "One, two, three, four, five." He stacked the blocks up. The tower wobbled and fell. Mom came to sit with him. "Try again," she said. "Count slow, not quick."

James picked up the blocks. He counted each one. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." He stacked them one by one. The tower stood up tall. It did not fall.

"Mom, look! What made it stay?" he asked. Mom smiled. "You went slow and steady." James patted the top block. Then he did a quick happy dance. "Ten blocks!" he said. "Ten!"

Emmett sat at the dinner table. He wanted his ten green peas, all in a row. But his peas rolled away, one by one.

"One pea," said Mama, pointing. "Two peas. Three peas." She pushed them back with her spoon.

Emmett clapped. "Four peas! Five peas!" He pushed them too. The peas rolled again. Six peas slid under his cup. Seven peas hid by his fork.

Emmett counted louder. "Eight! Nine!" He grabbed the last pea with his fingers and set it down. "Ten peas!"

Then he looked at his cup. The six peas under it made a little green curve. "A rainbow!" said Emmett. "A pea rainbow."

Daddy laughed. "Can you teach me that song?" he asked.

Emmett sang the numbers all the way to ten. Then he ate the rainbow, one pea at a time.

Carter went to the store with Mom. He wanted to buy squishy bread for lunch. Mom held his hand at the big doors. "Stay close to me," she said.

Carter saw a pot of hot soup. Steam went up, up, up. A worker stirred it with a long spoon. Carter reached out his hand. "Hot!" said Mom. She pulled him back gently. Carter felt the air near the pot. It was warm like the sun. He stepped back one step. The warm air got small. He stepped back again. Now his face felt cool.

"Good looking, Carter," said Mom. They walked past the knives and the computer at the check-out. Carter did not touch them. He kept one hand on the cart. They found the squishy bread at last. "Can we skip home?" asked Carter. Mom laughed. "Yes, we can skip." They skipped all the way to the door.

Maya ran to the park with her bear, Blue. She wanted to play house. But the sand was wet and lumpy. Her plate would not sit straight. The leaf plate tipped over. Ping! The berry pebbles rolled off.

Then Maya saw the flat bench by the swings. It was smooth and dry. She put her leaf plate on the bench. It sat still! "Look, Blue," she said. "A table!" She laid out pebbles and a stick for a spoon.

A boy named Sam came by with his toy plane. "Can it land here?" he asked. Maya made a runway on the flat bench. The plane zoomed in. Zoom, zoom, plop! It stopped right by the leaf plate. "Time for lunch," said Maya. Sam laughed.

Then a wind blew. Whoosh! The leaf plate flew up! Maya grabbed her bear. Sam grabbed his plane. But the pebbles stayed on the flat bench. The flat bench held them tight. Maya put the leaf back down. "Wind can't take our house," she said. Sam made the plane fly again. "Dinner time for pilots!" Maya called.

Aurora waited by the school gate. Mama was late. Aurora's tummy felt empty and her eyes felt heavy. She wanted her snack and her bed.

Her teacher, Ms. Bell, stood close by. "Mama is coming soon," Ms. Bell said. Aurora held Ms. Bell's hand. It was warm.

Then Aurora heard rain tap, tap, tap. Puddles grew on the ground. One raindrop fell on her nose. It was cold. "Oh no," said Aurora. "My shoes will get wet."

Ms. Bell had an umbrella in her bag. She opened it up. It made a wide roof over their heads. The rain tapped on top, but it did not touch Aurora. Then Mama came running. "Sorry, my love!" she said. She put a thick, dry towel around Aurora's shoulders.

At home, Mama ran Aurora a warm bath. The water was cozy. After that, Aurora put on her soft pajamas. She ate apple slices and milk. Then Mama tucked her into bed.

"The rain made my shoes wet," Aurora said. "Then the bath and the towel made me dry again." Mama kissed her head. "Sleep now, little one." Aurora closed her eyes. Outside, the rain still tap, tap, tapped.

Josephine sat at the big art table. She had a fat brush in her hand. She wanted to paint a frog, but she had no green paint. She looked in her cup. Only red, blue and yellow.

She painted a red sun. It looked warm on the paper. She painted a yellow duck. The duck looked soft and sunny. Then she wanted green for the frog. She asked her friend Tom. "I have green," said Tom. "But you have blue. Can we share?"

Tom poured some yellow. Josephine poured some blue. They mixed the paint with a brush. Swish, swish, swish. The paint turned green! Josephine clapped her hands.

She painted a big green frog. It hopped on the paper, in her mind. Tom looked sad. He had no green left. Josephine pushed the cup to him. "Now we both have green," she said. Tom gave her a hug. It was not mean to take the paint. It was nice. The teacher smiled at the green frog and the yellow duck and the red sun, all drying in a row.

Bennett was at Grandma's house. Mom was coming with the new baby. Bennett waited at the window. He counted the cars. One car. Two cars. Three cars. Then Mom's car came. Inside was a tiny baby sister named Mia.

Mia made a small face. Then she began to cry. She cried and cried. Bennett felt sad. He wanted her to stop. He gave her his toy truck. She kept crying. He showed her a pencil and his drawing of a dog. She kept crying. He patted her sock. She still cried.

Then Bennett saw his blanket on the chair. It was soft and warm. He put the blanket by Mia's cheek. Mia stopped crying. She opened her eyes. She looked at Bennett. Bennett put the blanket by her cheek again. Soft and warm, soft and warm. Mia made a tiny sound. It was almost a smile.

Grandma came in with apple slices. She had used a big knife to cut the apple, and now it was safe. Grandma put one slice on Bennett's plate. "Mia likes your blanket," said Grandma. Bennett sat by the baby. He held his pencil again. "This is Mia," he said. "This is our house."

Nova went to the festival with Mama and Baba. It was a bright morning. The street was full of flags and drums. Nova held Mama's hand. She wanted to put a little clay lamp on the big shelf. All the lamps had small flames inside.

Baba knelt down by the shelf. He lit one lamp with a long match. He let it burn for a moment. Then he tipped the flame to Nova's clean, new lamp. The wick caught. A small light grew on her lamp. Nova gasped. One flame had made another flame.

"Your turn," Baba said. He lifted her up so she could reach. Nova set her lamp next to the others. It glowed beside them all. She smelled the sweet smoke and heard the drums boom. Then a paper flower fell from above. It landed right on her lamp. The flame made the paper glow warm and pink, like a little sun. Nova laughed and clapped her hands.

Violet stood by the lake pool. She held her new floaty duck. "I want to swim," she said. Mom held her hand. "Let's try," said Mom.

Violet stepped in. The water came up to her tummy. She was scared. "The water is big," she said. Mom stayed right there. "Kick your legs," said Mom. Violet kicked. Her legs made splashes. The splashes pushed her forward. She moved all by herself.

"Look, Mom! My legs push me!" Violet kicked again. Her duck floaty bobbed beside her. She bit her lip, then smiled big. The light shone on the wet water. It sparkled like stars. Violet kicked and kicked. She swam right to Mom. Mom hugged her close. "You did it," said Mom. Violet hugged her duck. "Again," said Violet. "Let's swim again."

Paisley stood in the restaurant kitchen. She had on her little apron to wear, just like the cooks. Papa worked at the big counter nearby.

"Papa, can I help?" she asked.

"Yes," said Papa. "Here is your toast. Here is the butter."

Paisley pushed the butter with her spoon. The butter stayed in one lump. It would not spread. Then Papa set the warm toast down. Paisley touched the butter again. The butter had gone soft. It slid across the toast like paint. "It spreads now!" she said.

Next came the milk. Papa put a small cup in front of her. Paisley tipped the jug fast. Milk ran out and made a puddle on the counter. Her bottom lip wobbled.

"That is okay," said Papa. "Try again. Tip it slowly, just a little."

Paisley took a breath. She tipped the jug slowly. A thin stream of milk went into the cup. Not one drop was lost on the counter. The cup filled up, and she stopped.

"I did it!" said Paisley.

"You did," said Papa. He wiped the puddle away and put a little tree-shaped cookie beside her toast.

Paisley picked up the cookie and took a big bite. "Milk and toast," she said, "my best lunch."

Hayden loved the class pet. It was a small green frog. Today the frog looked grumpy. His leaf in the tank had turned brown.

Hayden wanted to paint the frog a picture. He would paint a big green leaf. He looked at the paints. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. But no green paint. "One red, one blue, one yellow," he counted. "Where is green?"

Miss Rosa helped him drip blue paint. Then Hayden dripped yellow paint. He mixed it with his brush. The paint turned green! The yellow and the blue made green.

Hayden painted a big green leaf. It had shiny paint that seemed to shine in the sun. He held it up to the tank. The frog hopped close. He sat by the green leaf picture. He was not grumpy now.

Hayden painted one more leaf. Then one more. "Green, green, green," he said. The frog blinked at the green leaves, and Hayden smiled.

Clara ran to the water table. "Look at the ice!" she said.

There were two ice cubes. One was big. One was small. Clara pushed them both into the warm water. "Swim, ice!"

The sun was hot on the water. The little cube got smaller and smaller. Then it was gone! The big cube stayed. Clara patted the water. "Cold, cold water!"

Her teacher brought a big cup of tea. "My tea is hot," said Miss Jo. "Careful, hands off." Clara watched the steam rise up. She did not touch.

Then Clara wanted to draw. "I will draw the ocean," she said. She drew big waves and small fish. Max drew fast, zoom zoom. Clara drew slow, round and round.

"Look!" said Clara. Her little ice cube in the picture had a dot for gone. The big one she drew still there.

Clara yawned. All that drawing made her sleepy. Miss Jo put the big ice cube in the freezer. "It will get cold again," she said.

Clara waved at the freezer. "Bye bye, big ice. See you later."

Lincoln was at Grandma's house. Today his new baby sister was coming. Lincoln wanted to give her a present, but he did not have one. He looked in his little bag. He found one sock, two rocks, and three crayons. "None of these are right," he said. Then he smelled something warm from the kitchen. Grandma was baking bread. The bread smelled sweet and good. Lincoln watched Grandma take the warm loaf out. Grandma cut a soft slice and gave Lincoln a small piece to hold. The piece of bread was warm and squishy in his hand. "Can baby eat bread?" Lincoln asked. "No, she is too small," said Grandma. "But we can let her smell it." The car came up the drive. Mama carried the baby in. Lincoln held out his piece of bread near the baby's nose. The baby wiggled and made a tiny sound. "She likes it," said Lincoln. "She likes it because it smells so good."

The lights went out. The TV went dark too. Sienna sat very still on the rug.

"Mommy, I can't see," she said.

Mommy came close. "I am right here," she said. Mommy found her phone. She tapped it. The little light came on. The room was bright again, just a small bit. Sienna tapped her own toy phone. Nothing happened. "It needs power," said Mommy. "Mine is full."

Mommy lit a candle on the table. The flame made a warm circle. Sienna kept her hands far away, on her lap. "The flame makes the room glow," said Sienna.

Mommy found a plastic cup and a wet cloth. She wiped the table near the candle. Sienna watched the flame sway. Then it stood still again.

They sat together and ate bread and cheese. The candle made shadows on the wall. Sienna made a bunny with her hand. Mommy made a bird.

Soon the lights came back on. The TV hummed. Sienna blinked at the bright room. "The power came home," she said. Mommy laughed and blew out the candle.

Weston stood with his dad at the festival. Long tables had food everywhere. His tummy made a big growl. "Soon," said Dad. "First we say the blessing together."

Weston did not know the blessing. He only knew "thank you" and "please" and "more bread, please."

Everyone at the table held hands. Weston grabbed his dad's hand and a grandma's hand. The grandma smiled at him.

Then the whole table got quiet. A man said the blessing words, slow and loud. Weston listened. The words rhymed a little, like a song.

After the blessing, everyone said, "Amen!" Weston said it too, but it came out as "A-mo."

The grandma laughed a kind laugh. "A-mo works too," she said.

Then it was time to eat. Weston got rice, corn, and a salty roll. A cloud shaped like a bunny sat in the sky above their table.

"Can we say it again?" Weston asked, with rice on his chin.

"Next meal," said Dad. "It lives for every meal, every day."

Weston looked at his plate. He wanted to eat again soon. "Can we have a next meal now?"

Amelia's class had a little plant on the sill. It was small. "I want it to grow big," said Amelia. "Then it will be as tall as my teacher!"

At play time, the teacher brought out hot cocoa. The pot was big, and the cups were small. The teacher poured the cocoa. "It is too hot now," she said. "Let it get cold enough to drink." Amelia put her cup by the window, right next to the plant.

Amelia waited and waited. Was her cocoa cold yet? She touched the cup with one finger. It was warm now, not hot. She took a tiny sip. It was just right. "The hot drink got cool in the cold air!" she said.

Then Amelia saw something odd. "Why is my plant wiggling?" she asked. She looked closer. It was not the plant. It was a small gray mouse, hiding behind the pot! The mouse ran fast across the sill. Amelia jumped. The mouse ran slow, then fast, then hid again.

"Hello, little mouse," said Amelia. The teacher came to look. She smiled and helped Amelia sweep the crumbs. Now the sill was tidy, and the mouse was gone. Amelia patted the soil around her plant. "Grow big," she whispered. "I will look every day." Outside, the sun came out, warm and bright, right onto her small green leaves.

Harrison went to the library with Mama. He wanted a book about a black cat. The books were all mixed up on the big shelf.

"The books are in a muddle," said Mama. "Let's sort them." Harrison picked up a book. It had a cow on it. "Is this the cat book?" he asked. "No," said Mama. "A cow is not a cat. Cows go with animals." Harrison put it in the animal pile. Thump. It made a happy sound.

Next he found a book with a ball. "Is this a ball for animals?" he asked. "No," said Harrison himself. "A ball is a toy." He put it in the toy pile. Then he found a book with an apple. Apples are food. He made a food pile.

Harrison kept looking. A pig, no. A drum, no. Then he saw black ears and a long tail. "Cat!" said Harrison. He hugged the cat book tight.

"Reading time," said Mama. They sat down together. Harrison turned the first page. "Meow," he read.

Eloise wanted her teddy bear. She looked under the little table. No teddy. She looked behind the door. No teddy. Eloise felt sad. Her lip went down, down, down.

Then she heard a sound. "Mama!" said the teddy, from under the bed. It was Papa, squeezing the teddy and making it talk. Eloise jumped up. She felt excited! She ran to the bed. Then she stopped. It was dark under there. Eloise felt scared. "Too dark," she said.

Papa held her hand. "We can look together," he said. Eloise leaned down with him. There was teddy, all dusty and flat. Papa reached in and pulled teddy out. Eloise hugged teddy tight. She felt happy now. Then teddy bonked Papa on the head, playfully. "Hey!" laughed Papa, making a pretend angry face. Eloise giggled. She climbed into her cozy bed with teddy and Papa tucked them in. "Night night, teddy," she whispered.

Nicholas had a library book about trucks. He loved it so much. He wanted to keep it forever.

He sat on his bed and looked at the pages. There were little black marks on every page. "What are those?" he wondered. His mom read them out loud. The marks said "big red truck." The marks were words. Words told him things!

Nicholas opened the book. He started at the back cover. The story was all mixed up. The truck came at the end, not the start. "That feels wrong," he said. He turned to the front. He pointed at each word. Mom read them one by one. The truck went beep, beep, all the way to the last page.

But tomorrow the book had to go back. Nicholas held it tight. "It is due back at the library," Mom said. "Other kids want to read it too."

Nicholas had an idea. He asked Mom to read it one more time, after his bath. She did. His knee had a little hurt, so he propped the book on his pillow.

The next day, Nicholas put the book in his bag. He carried it to the library all by himself. He gave it to the lady at the desk.

Then he found a new book about dinosaurs. "Can we take this one home?" he asked.

Mom smiled and said, "Yes. And we can come back for more."

Myles sat on his big bed. He had a library book about a red truck. He wanted to keep it forever.

Myles opened the book. He turned the pages one by one. The front of the book came first. Then the middle. Then the back. He saw little marks on every page. "Those are words," said Mama. "Daddy reads them out loud."

Myles pointed at the marks. "Truck!" he said. He turned more pages, front to back, again and again. "Read it again," he said. So Mama did.

Then Mama said, "We take the book back today. It is the day it is due." Myles held the book tight. "My book!" he said. He tried to hide it under his pillow.

At the library, Myles gave the book to the lady. She smiled. "Other kids will read it now," she said. Then she gave Myles a fresh book to take home. It was about a big yellow dog who liked to chew bones.

Myles opened the new book at the front. He turned the pages, one by one, all the way to the back. "Read it again," he said.

"Again and again," said Mama. And she did.

Sofia and her family drove to a campsite. Sofia held her little bear in one hand. The tent was big and orange. "Where will I sleep?" she asked. "Right here, next to me," said Mama.

At night, the tent got dark. Sofia could not see her bear. "Bear is lost!" she cried. Papa zipped the tent open a tiny bit. The moonlight came in. Then Sofia could see bear's soft ear on her pillow.

Sofia had an idea. She put bear under her loose blanket, near the moon spot. "Now I can see you," she whispered. In the morning, the tent was light again. "Papa, why is it bright now?" she asked. "The sun came up to say hello," said Papa. Sofia clapped her hands. "Hello, sun!" she called. Then she gave bear a big pretend breakfast of leaves and tiny stones.

Iris went to the pharmacy with her dad. The pharmacy sold soap, and Iris wanted the pink soap. It had a star on the bottle. Dad said, "Yes, let's get it."

At home, Iris had to use the toilet. Then she wanted a snack right away. She reached for her apple. Dad said, "Wash your hands first." Iris looked at her hands. They looked clean. But she washed them with her new pink soap anyway.

The soap made white bubbles. Iris sang her apple song while she washed. Lots of little bubbles grew and grew. Then the water took the bubbles away, down, down the drain. Iris held up her hands. They were shiny in the sun. Dad gave her the apple. "What smart, clean hands," he said. Iris took a big, happy bite.

Anna steps up the big school bus steps. She holds the rail with both hands. The bus driver smiles at her. "First day?" he asks. "Yes," says Anna. "I am big now."

Anna walks down the aisle. She sees a boy by the window. A plane flies by, high in the sky. The boy points at it. "Look, a plane!" he says. Anna sits next to him. The seat makes a squeak. Squeak, squeak! Anna giggles. She bounces a tiny bounce. Squeak! The boy giggles too. He bounces too. Squeak, squeak!

A girl across the aisle looks sad. Her lip wobbles. Anna pats the empty seat next to her. "Sit here," says Anna. "The seat squeaks!" The girl comes over. She bounces. Squeak! Now she laughs. "You are smart," says the boy. "You made a sad face turn happy."

The bus goes beep, beep. Anna looks out the window. Mom waves from the sidewalk. Anna waves back big. "Bye, Mom! I found squeaky seats!" The bus rolls away, squeak, squeak, all the way to school.

Daniel went to the park with his grandma. He wanted to find the big ducks by the pond. He held grandma's hand the whole way. The sun made the slide very hot. Daniel put his toe near it first. The slide felt hot, so he waited. Grandma poured water on it, and the water made it cool. Then Daniel slid down, splash free and happy.

Next to the pond, Daniel saw a shiny piece of glass. He reached out his hand. Grandma stopped him fast. "We don't touch that," she said. She picked it up with a leaf and put it in the trash. Daniel watched how she did it.

The ducks came at last. They swam and splashed near Daniel's boots. He stayed close to grandma and threw small bits of bread. "The ducks like us," said Daniel. "And it is not too late for ice cream." Grandma laughed and held out her hand.

Luca stood at the bus stop with Mama. He wanted to see the big red bus come. "Where is the bus?" he asked. "Soon," said Mama.

The sun came out. It was sunny. Luca got warm, so Mama took off his hat. "Sun makes you warm," said Mama, and she held the hat.

Then the wind blew. It was windy. Luca's scarf flapped like a flag. The wind pushed a paper cup down the street. Luca held Mama's hand tight.

Then rain fell. It was rainy. Mama put up the umbrella. Drip, drip, drop. Luca put out one shoe. The rain made a wet spot on it. "My shoe is wet!" said Luca. Mama smiled and wiped it with a cloth.

The rain stopped. White flakes came down instead. "Look, snow!" said Luca. It was snowy now. The snow landed on Luca's sleeve. It sat there, small and white. Mama put his hat back on. "Snow is cold," she said. "Hat keeps you warm."

Then the big red bus came. It stopped with a big puff. The doors opened. Luca and Mama climbed up. Luca sat by the window. He saw snow on the trees. He chewed his biscuit slowly. "All ready," said Mama. The bus went beep, and off they rode.

Henry sat in his car seat. He looked out the window. A big truck went by. Then a small car went by. "That truck is big," said Henry. "That car is small."

The car went up a hill. It went slow up the hill. Then it went fast down the hill. The wind came in the window. "Windy!" said Henry. His hat blew off his head. It landed on the floor. Henry picked it up. He held it tight.

Daddy stopped the car. They were at the ice cream shop. Henry wanted cold ice cream. Daddy got a warm cup of coffee too. Daddy held the hot cup with both hands. Henry was careful and stayed away from it. He licked his cold cone. "Brrr, cold!" said Henry.

Henry ate his ice cream. The sun was warm on his arms. He watched a small bird hop by the big window. Then it was time to go. Henry climbed back into his seat. "Fast car, go!" he said. And off they went.

Jake was getting over his cold. He still had a runny nose. The tissue box sat by his bed.

Jake pulled out a tissue. He wiped his nose. Then he dropped the tissue on the floor. Soon the floor had many tissues. They looked like little white clouds.

"Jake, look at all those tissues," said Mom. She picked up the box. "Where should they go?" Jake thought about it. He pointed at the bin. Mom put the bin next to the bed.

Jake wiped his nose again. This time he dropped the tissue in the bin. It landed inside. Jake clapped his hands. "It went in!" he said.

Mom smiled. "Your room looks all fixed up now." Jake looked around. The floor was clear. Even his shy teddy bear peeked out from under the bed, as if to see the clean room too.

Jake wiped his nose one more time. The tissue went in the bin again. "Bye bye, tissue," he said.

Gabriel sat at the kitchen table. Mom gave him a big pink pencil. "Now you can write your name!" she said.

Gabriel squeezed the pencil in his whole fist. He pushed down hard. The pencil point ripped right through the paper. "Oh no!" said Gabriel. There was a big hole where the G should be.

Mom turned the paper over. "Try again," she said. She showed him how to pinch the pencil near the tip. Gabriel held it with just his fingers. He made a round, round G. Then a little a. Then a b. The letters went across the page in a wobbly line.

A woman came to the door. It was Grandma! "What is this?" she asked. Gabriel held up the paper.

"That says Gabriel," he said. "I wrote it all by myself." Grandma clapped her hands.

Bennett stood in the music room. Miss Ruiz played a song on the piano. The other kids clapped their hands. Bennett did not clap. His hands felt shy, like they wanted to hide in his pockets.

Then Miss Ruiz played "Twinkle, Twinkle." She pointed at the big yellow drum. She tapped it once. Boom. She tapped it again. Boom. Bennett watched her hand go up and down. When her hand went down, the drum made a sound. He tried clapping when her hand went down too. Clap. Clap. Clap.

Miss Ruiz poured tiny cups of milk for singing well. Bennett drank his and smiled. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star," he sang, all by himself. Miss Ruiz clapped for him. "Again," said Bennett.

Grayson found his teddy bear on the floor. "Teddy is cold," said Grayson. He wrapped teddy in a soft sock blanket. He patted teddy's tummy, pat, pat, pat. Teddy's eyes went quiet and still. "Look, Mommy! My patting made teddy sleepy."

Mommy smiled. "You have magic hands." Grayson put on his red boot, just one boot, like a daddy at work. He stomped around the room. Stomp, stomp, stomp.

Then he held up a wooden spoon like a wand. "I will do a spell," he said. He tapped the empty box three times. "Wake up, box!" The box became a baby's bed. Grayson laid teddy inside.

"Is teddy alone in there?" asked Mommy.

"No," said Grayson. "Bunny sleeps here too." He tucked bunny in next to teddy. Then he hummed a little song. Both toys lay still and cozy under the sock blanket.

"Shh," whispered Grayson. He stomped his boot away on tiptoe.

Josephine wanted warm milk for snack time. The milk was cold from the fridge. "Brrr," said Josephine. "Too cold."

Miss Ada took the small pot. She set it on the stove. A little fire clicked on under it. Josephine stood back and watched. "The fire is hot," said Miss Ada. "Only I touch the pot."

Josephine waited. She waited slowly. Then steam came up. Little bubbles went fast, fast, fast. The milk got warm. Miss Ada poured it into Josephine's big cup.

Josephine took a sip. "Warm now!" she said. She gave the cup a kiss. "Thank you, milk."

Tommy slid fast across the floor. Josephine walked slow, slow, slow, so her cup would not spill. She sat down by the big window. Outside, a big dog ran fast. A small bird sat still.

Josephine held her warm cup with both hands. "Miss Ada," she said, "the cold milk went in. The warm milk came out."

Miss Ada smiled. "Yes it did," she said.

Oliver sat at the dinner table. He had a plate of brown beans. He wanted to count them all by himself.

"One, two, three," said Oliver. He touched a bean with each word. His spoon slipped. The beans rolled away! "Oh no," said Oliver. "Where did my numbers go?"

Mama smiled. "Let's fetch a spoon that stays still." She gave him a big spoon. Oliver tried again. He tapped each bean slowly. "One, two, three, four, five." The beans stayed on the plate. Tapping made counting easy.

"Dada, count with me?" asked Oliver. Dada held up his fingers. They counted together. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten beans, all in a row.

Oliver clapped his hands. "I did it! Ten beans!" Then he picked one up and ate it. "Now nine," said Oliver, laughing.

Evan wanted a backyard picnic. But his things were all mixed up in one big box. He dumped them out on the grass.

"Let's make piles," said Mom. Evan picked up a toy car. It was his favorite toy. "Toys!" he said. He put the car, a ball and a duck that could ride on wheels into the toy pile. One, two, three toys.

Then he held up an apple. "Food!" he said. He put the apple, a banana and bread into the food pile. One, two, three foods. Then he heard a soft sound. A ladybug crawled on his shoe. "Animal," said Evan. A bird flew down too. One ladybug, one bird.

Then the dog ran by and grabbed the bread. "No, that is food for us!" said Evan. Mom gave the dog a bone instead. The dog chewed it happily.

Evan carried his toy pile to the little desk by the fence. He set his picnic on top. He ate his apple and played with the car.

Mom sat with him under the tree. The ladybug landed on the bread. Evan laughed.

"Hello, little picnic friend," he said.

Isabelle went to the farm with Grandpa. A little goat stood by the fence. "Hello, goat," said Isabelle. The goat looked at her. Isabelle looked back. "I see you with my eyes," she said. Grandpa smiled.

Next they walked to the hen house. The hens were noisy. "Cluck, cluck, cluck!" Isabelle covered her ears. "I hear the hens with my ears," she said. Then she touched a soft white feather on the ground. "I touch it with my hands," she said.

Grandpa had a gift for Isabelle. It was a shiny red apple. Isabelle held it. She sniffed it. "I smell it with my nose," she said. Then she took a big bite. "Yum! I taste it with my mouth."

Then Isabelle smelled something new. It was warm and sweet. Her nose led her to the farm kitchen. Farmer Beth was there. She was going to bake bread. "Would you like to watch?" asked Beth. Isabelle stood far back and watched. Beth put the bread in the oven.

At last the bread was ready. Beth cut a small piece for Isabelle. Isabelle sniffed it, tasted it, and hugged Beth. "My nose found it!" she said. Beth laughed and gave the goat a crust too.

Alexis sat at the table for dinner. Mom set down a basket of warm rolls. His big sister took one roll. Alexis wanted one too. He grabbed for the basket. The basket was heavy. It tipped, and a roll rolled off the table. Dad picked up the roll. "Let's try again," Dad said. Alexis waited. His sister passed the basket to him. He took one roll with his hand. The roll was soft and warm.

Mom smiled. "You waited for your turn," she said. Alexis chewed his roll. He thought about school. Ben had the red truck today. Alexis had wanted it. He had grabbed, and Ben had cried. Then Ben gave him the truck. Alexis had given it back.

After dinner, Alexis washed his hands at the sink. The water was warm. Mom held the towel for him. "Tomorrow I will wait," Alexis said. He put his teddy bear in his bag. "Ben can hold him first." Mom kissed his ear. Alexis smiled and zipped the bag shut.

Jacob stood in the bathroom. He wanted to find his red toothbrush.

He used his eyes to look. He saw a cup by the sink. No toothbrush there.

Then he used his ears. He heard a drip, drip, drip. The faucet was leaking. "Mom, the sink is talking," he said.

Mom smiled. She came in and turned the tap. The drip stopped. "There," she said. "All quiet now."

Jacob sniffed with his nose. The towel smelled like soap. He touched it with his hands. It was soft and warm from the dryer, like a furry little cat.

He looked down at a small rug. He stepped on it with his toes. The rug was fuzzy too.

Then he saw something red. It was behind the soap. "My toothbrush!" he said. He did not miss it anymore.

Mom put a dot of toothpaste on it. It tasted like strawberries. Jacob brushed his teeth.

"Nice and clean," said Mom. Jacob grinned at the mirror.

Ivy wanted to draw a cat. But the paper box at the library was empty. "Oh no," said Ivy.

The librarian, Miss Ana, held up a new tablet. "Want to try this?" she asked. "Yes, please!" said Ivy. Miss Ana pressed the little button on top. The screen woke up. It was bright, like morning.

"Now you try," said Miss Ana. Ivy pressed the button. Tap. The screen went dark. She pressed it again. Tap. The screen woke up again. Ivy laughed. "I made it sleep! I made it wake!"

She tapped the green squiggle. The drawing app opened. Ivy drew a big orange cat with three eyes. "Silly cat," she said.

Then it was time to go. Ivy pressed the button. Tap. The screen went to sleep. She put the tablet in the basket, just like Miss Ana showed her.

"I will remember this in summer," said Ivy. "My cat can wake up too!"

Ezra went to the farmers' market with Mama. A kind lady gave out warm toast. "Can I put butter on it?" Ezra asked. "Yes, you can," said the lady.

The lady gave him a small knife with a smooth, flat edge. She put a little butter on the tip. Ezra spread it slowly. The butter made the toast shine. "I did it!" he said. "Slow hands, slow hands," said Mama.

Next to the toast stood a jug of juice and a small cup. Ezra wanted milk instead. The lady found a tiny milk carton. "What if I pour too fast?" Ezra asked. "Then we wipe it up," said Mama. Ezra poured slowly. Not one drop spilled. The cup filled up. "Slow hands," whispered Ezra, and he drank his milk all gone.

Leah went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about a dog. Where could it be?

The library had big shelves. Shelf one had books with animals. Leah saw cats, birds and one big bear. She patted the bear on the cover. "Not a dog," she said.

Shelf two had books about toys. There were balls, blocks and drums. No dogs there. Shelf three had books about foods. Apples, bread and eggs smiled at her. Still no dog.

Then Leah saw a fluffy tail stick out of a bag. A real puppy! Its wet nose touched her hand. The puppy sniffed the food shelf and sat down by the animal shelf instead. "You like your own shelf!" Leah said. The librarian laughed. "Can we take him home for a visit?" Leah asked her dad. "Can we, can we?"

The big game was on TV today. Jaxon marched into the living room with his red flag. Everyone was there. Dad, Gran, and Uncle Theo. Even the neighbor, Mr. Bell.

"Where is the remote?" said Dad. It was lost. No remote, no game. Everyone looked under the couch. Gran looked behind the chair. Jaxon looked by the toy box. Then he had an idea. He pushed the big button on the TV himself. The screen lit up. The crowd on TV roared. Everyone in the room roared too.

The game began. Uncle Theo's team ran fast. Then they got slow, slow like a turtle. "Come on!" Jaxon shouted. He waved his flag high. Dad jumped up. Gran clapped. Jaxon clapped too, and Mr. Bell's little dog barked and barked.

The team kicked the ball. It went in the net. "Goal!" everyone yelled. The dog spun in a circle. Jaxon waved his flag so fast it made a whoosh sound. Uncle Theo lifted him way up high. "We win!" said Jaxon, and the room was full of happy, noisy people.

Jasper wanted to feed his toy bunny. But the bunny had no carrots. "That is a problem," said Jasper.

He looked in the toy box. He found a ball and a truck and a drum. Those were toys. A bunny could not eat toys.

He looked in the fridge with Dad. He found milk, cheese and apples. Apples were food. But bunnies like carrots best.

Then Jasper saw a big orange thing. "Guess what that is," said Dad. "A carrot!" said Jasper. Dad washed it and cut it with a safe knife.

Jasper was gentle. He set the carrot by the bunny. Then the real bunny hopped over from her cage. Nibble, nibble, nibble.

"She likes it," said Jasper. He patted her soft ears. "More carrots tomorrow," he whispered to her. The bunny's nose went wiggle, wiggle, wiggle.

Sienna sat at the craft table at camp. She wanted to make a butterfly. She had paper, glue, and sparkly paint.

Sienna poured the glue. Then she poured some more. Then some more. "Ooh, too much glue!" said her friend Milo. The glue made a big puddle. Sienna put her paper butterfly on the puddle. She pressed it down.

When she lifted it up, the butterfly stuck to her hand! "Come back, butterfly!" said Milo. They laughed. It flapped on her fingers like a real butterfly. "Silly glue," said Sienna. The teacher, Miss Jo, came to help. "Wet glue makes things stick," said Miss Jo. "We need it to dry." She gave them paper towels. Sienna wiped her dirty, sticky hands.

Then Miss Jo showed them a trick. She put the wet paintings in a bag. She hung the bag in the sun by the window. "Now we wait," she said. The children watched. Soon the glue turned clear and not sticky. Sienna peeled her butterfly off the table. It came off in one whole piece. "It can fly now," she said. She held it up and made it flap. "Look at my butterfly go!"

Sofia climbed into the car. She held her favorite toy rabbit tight. "We are going to the dentist!" said Mama. "He will look at your teeth."

Sofia was excited. Then she thought of something. "My tooth feels funny," she said. She wiggled it with her finger. It moved! "Mama, my tooth wiggles!" Mama smiled in the mirror. "That means it is getting loose," she said. "A new tooth will grow in its place."

At the dentist, the chair went up and up. The dentist looked in Sofia's mouth. "I see a loose tooth!" he said. He gave her a small mirror. Sofia looked inside. She could see all her little teeth, white as pearls. "There it is!" she said. She waved the mirror at her rabbit. "Look, one tooth is going on a trip!"

Lea sat at the big art table. She wanted to paint a green frog. But there was no green paint. "Oh no," said Lea. "My frog needs green."

Miss Mia smiled. "Look at the cups," she said. "One cup has yellow paint. One cup has blue paint." Lea counted them. "One cup, two cups," she said. She dipped her brush in the yellow. She made one dot on the paper. Then she dipped in the blue. She made one dot on top. "One dot, two dots," said Lea.

The dots touched. They mixed. The yellow and blue made green! Lea clapped her hands. "Green!" she said. Now she could paint her frog.

Next to her, a baby in a stroller watched. The baby kicked and cooed. Lea painted one green leg, two green legs, three green spots. She painted until her whole frog was full of green. Miss Mia held the paper up high to dry, near the window where the sun could warm it, like a little oven that cooks bread. "All done," said Miss Mia. Lea waved her green frog at the baby. "Ribbit!" said Lea.

Ellie sat at the big table. Grandma put down a bowl of rice. Uncle Ben put down bread. Everyone had a plate, but nobody ate.

"Wait," said Grandpa. "We say our words first."

Ellie wanted the bread now. She reached for it. Mama held her hand gently. "First the words," said Mama.

Grandpa held out his hands. Grandma took one hand. Uncle Ben took the other. Soon everyone at the table was holding hands. Ellie's hand went in Mama's hand. Then her other hand went in Grandpa's big hand. The circle went all the way around the table.

Grandpa said the blessing. His voice was slow. "Thank you for this food. Thank you for family." Everyone said, "Amen."

Ellie looked at her hands. When she held hands, the circle happened. The circle made everyone wait. Then everyone ate together.

"Now Ellie," said Grandpa. "You try."

Ellie took a big breath. "Thank you," she said. "For rice. And bread. And everybody."

"Amen," said everyone, even little Cousin Sam.

Then Grandpa picked up his fork. And Ellie finally got her bread.

Rehmat wanted to build a big tower. She found small blocks first. The small blocks made a small tower. Too small! She looked for big blocks.

She found two big blocks under the table. The big blocks made a big tower. Rehmat clapped her hands.

Then her brother ran in, fast. He bumped the tower. Down it fell. "Oh no," said Rehmat. She felt grumpy. Her face went hot and red.

Mama came in. "Slow down," Mama said to Rehmat. Rehmat breathed slowly. She pointed at the fallen blocks. "Big fall," she said. Mama smiled. "Build it again," she said.

Rehmat picked up one block. Then one more. The tower grew big again. She put a small letter block on the very top. "All done!" said Rehmat.

Weston wanted to play house in the backyard. He set his bear on a square rug by the door. "You are my baby," Weston told him. But the bear kept tipping over. He would not sit up.

Weston tried again and again. The bear flopped to the side each time. Weston felt sorry for him. "Don't worry, baby," he said. Then he had an idea. He stuffed a small blanket behind the bear. The blanket held the bear up. The bear sat tall and still. "There," said Weston. "Now you can watch me cook."

Weston stirred a pot of pretend soup. He used a stick and dry leaves. "Soup is ready," he called. Dad came over and sniffed the pot. "Yum," said Dad. "May I have some?" Weston poured the pretend soup into a cup. Dad drank it all up and smiled. Weston gave the bear a pat on his soft head.

Nova went to the big hall with her grandma. Long wooden tables stood in rows. Everyone was bringing pots and bowls. The food smelled warm and good.

Nova wanted to start eating the bread right away. Grandma held her hand. "First we say our blessing," Grandma said. "You can help this time." Grandma showed Nova how to fold her hands. Nova tried it. Her fingers slipped apart. She folded them again. This time they stayed. Grandma said the blessing, and Nova said the last word with her. When they finished, everyone smiled and picked up their forks.

Then Uncle Ben clapped his hands. "Wait!" he said. He ran to the door. A late guest stood there with a big present in her arms. "We say it again so she can hear it too," said Grandma. Nova folded her hands and said the last word loudly. The new lady heard her all the way across the wooden table.

Parker was at Grandma's house. He wanted to make blueberry pancakes for his family. Grandma said he could help. He got a big bowl and a wooden spoon.

First, Parker poured in the mix. Then he cracked an egg into a small nest of paper towels. The batter looked lumpy. "It is bumpy," said Parker. "Keep stirring," said Grandma. Parker stirred and stirred. He peeked into the bowl. The lumps were getting small. He stirred some more. Now the batter was smooth like a river. His stirring had made the lumps go away!
