Grandma put the pan on the stove. That part was for grown-ups, so Parker watched from his chair. Grandma poured the batter, and Parker dropped in blueberries. "They look like little blue boats," he said. The pancakes rose up big and round.

Soon Mom and Pop came to the table. Parker gave everyone two pancakes. He even gave Grandma the biggest one. Mom took a bite. "These are the best pancakes ever," she said. "Who made them?" Parker smiled big. "Me and Grandma. And my spoon!" After breakfast, Parker let his toy bunny ride on the empty bowl like a sled. "More pancakes tomorrow," he said.

It was Everett's birthday at Grandma's house. Everyone came in cars. They came from their own homes far away. Everett wanted to blow out his candles. But first the cake had to come out.

Grandma put the candles in the cake. Then Grandpa lit them with a match. Grandpa lit one candle. That candle lit the next candle. Then that one lit another. Soon all four candles glowed. "Look, Everett," said Grandma. "The fire walks from one to the next."

Everett watched the little flames. He waited a long time. Then everyone sang the birthday song. They sang slowly and loudly.

"Make a wish," said Grandma. Everett took a big breath. He blew and blew. All the candles went dark. Smoke curled up like a little ribbon. Everyone clapped and cheered. "Happy birthday, Everett!" they said. Everett smiled big. Then he asked, "Can we do the candles again?"

Elijah wanted to find the tiny toy horse at school. He had seen it once, under the toy shelf. He could not reach it.

Miss Ada knelt down beside him. "Let's count the blocks while we look," she said. She put ten blocks in a row. "One, two, three." Elijah touched each block with his finger. "Four, five, six," he said. The blocks made a soft tapping sound.

Then Elijah saw it. When his finger tapped block seven, the horse moved. It slid out from under the shelf. "It wiggled!" said Elijah. Miss Ada smiled. "Your tap made it move," she said.

Elijah tapped block eight, then nine. The horse slid out more. He tapped ten. The tiny horse sat right by his shoe. Elijah picked it up. It was smooth and warm. He held it to his ear. "Go, horsey," he said softly. Then he trotted it up Miss Ada's arm, all the way to her shoulder.

Peyton sat at Grandma's big table. She wanted to make a picture for Grandpa. Grandma gave her paper and glue. Peyton squeezed the glue. It made a fat, shiny line. Then she opened the glitter jar.

But the glitter jar was empty. Peyton looked all around the room. She fished in the art box for more glitter. Her hand came out with soft paper dots instead.

Peyton pushed a paper dot onto the wet glue. It stuck! The glue was still wet, so the dots stayed. She pushed on more dots. Red, blue, and yellow. The dots made a bright flower.

Grandma brought a fresh apple for a snack. Peyton kept working. Grandpa came in and saw the picture. "A flower for me?" he said.

"Yes," said Peyton. "It sticks."

Audrey went to the pharmacy with Mama. Today was a big day. Audrey would get a shot.

"I want to be brave," said Audrey. She held Mama's hand tight.

The nurse came with a little bandage. On it was a tiny cat. "You get a cat bandage after your shot," said the nurse.

Audrey looked at the cat bandage. Then she looked at the nurse. "If I get the shot, I get the cat?" she asked.

"Yes," said the nurse. "First the shot, then the cat."

Audrey sat very still. The nurse cleaned her arm with a cool, wet cotton ball. Then came the shot. It was quick, like a tiny pinch.

"Done!" said the nurse. She pressed the cotton ball down. Then she peeled open the bandage. She stuck the little cat on Audrey's arm.

Audrey looked down. The cat sat on her arm. She had gotten the shot, and now she had the cat.

"Look, Mama!" said Audrey. She waved her arm in the air.

At the desk, the pharmacist poured a cup of water for Mama. Audrey drank a deep, happy sip too.

On the way home, Audrey showed everyone her arm. "I got a shot," she said. "And the shot gave me a cat."

Bennett was at Grandma's house. He wanted to help cook lunch for the whole family. Grandma said, "You can make the butter." Bennett blinked. Butter came from the store, in a box. How could a kid make butter?

Grandma poured cold cream into a jar. She screwed the lid on tight. "Shake it," she said. "Shake it hard." Bennett shook the jar. He shook it up high. He shook it down low. He shook it so fast his arms felt dizzy and tired.

Then something changed inside the jar. The sloshy sound went away. There was no more swish, swish. Bennett looked in. A soft yellow lump sat in the jar. Little white liquid floated around it. The cream had turned into butter! It happened because he shook it and shook it.

Grandma washed the yellow lump in cold water. She spread it on warm bread. Bennett carried the plate to the table, one slow step at a time. Mom took a bite. Dad took a bite. Even the baby waved her hands.

"This is the best butter ever," said Dad. Bennett sat up tall and looked at his empty jar. "Tomorrow," he said, "I will shake two jars."

Jaxson sat at the dinner table. He banged his spoon on his cup. "Supper smells good!" he said. He felt excited.

Then Daddy set down a big bowl of pasta. Jaxson smiled a big smile. "Yum!" he said. He was happy.

But then his fork slipped. Splat! His pasta fell on the floor. Jaxson's face went sad. His chin wobbled. "My pasta," he said.

Molly the dog ran in fast. She gobbled the pasta up. Jaxson felt angry. He made a grumpy face. "Bad dog!" he said.

Then Molly licked his toe under the table. It tickled! Jaxson laughed. Hmm, he thought. First I was sad. Then I was mad. Now I laugh?

Thunder boomed outside. Boom! Jaxson jumped. He felt scared. He held Mama's hand tight.

Mama put new pasta on his plate. "Eat up," she said. Jaxson ate it all. His sister made her doll dance on the table. Jaxson giggled and clapped.

Molly wagged her tail. Jaxson waved his spoon and sang, "Happy again, happy again!"

Audrey stood by the letter wall in the school library. She wanted to find the letter for her own name. There were so many letters. She did not know where to start.

Mrs. Bell pointed at a big red letter. "This one is A," she said. "It says a, a, a." Audrey looked at the A. Then she looked at the apple picture below it. She said, "A, a, apple!" Mrs. Bell smiled and nodded.

Audrey ran her arm along the wall. She stopped at B. "B says b, b," she said. The picture below was a bee. It went bzz, bzz, bzz. Audrey laughed. She found A again. She put it and B together on the little table. "A, B," she read out loud. "That is how my name starts!" She gave the letter A a big hug, and Mrs. Bell clapped.

Rowan went to the big hall with Mama and Papa. Today was the lantern festival. Rowan wanted to hang his lantern on the long string. But the string was too high for him.

First, the lanterns stayed dark. The hall felt dim and gray. Rowan held his lantern in his hands.

Then a grown-up lit one lantern. Warm light spilled out of it. The light made the wall glow. Rowan saw the paper turn bright.

"Papa, my lantern too?" asked Rowan.

Papa took the lantern and held it near the grown-up. A little flame woke up inside. Rowan's lantern grew bright and warm.

Now came the hanging. Papa lifted Rowan up, up, up. Rowan reached out. He hooked his lantern on the string. It swayed next to all the other lights.

Then something surprised Rowan. His lantern was shaped like a bunny. Its ears made two shadows on the wall. The shadows looked like a big soft rabbit hopping.

"Look, Mama! My bunny is dancing!"

Mama held his hand. The hall was full of glowing light. Rowan smiled at his bunny dancing on the wall.

Sadie ran to the swings with her grandma. "Stay where I can see you," said Grandma. Sadie nodded. She pumped her legs. The swing went up and down.

Then Sadie saw the big slide. It was far away. She wanted to go there all by herself. She let go of the swing. She started to run. "Sadie, wait," called Grandma. Sadie stopped. Grandma took her hand. They walked together. That was better. Grandma's hand was warm.

Near the slide, a man was cooking at a little grill. It made sizzling sounds. Smoke went up, up, up. Sadie could feel heat on her face, even from far away. "That part is hot," said Grandma. "We stay back here." Sadie touched the cold metal pole of the slide. Cold felt nice. Hot did not. She kept her hands on the cold pole only.

Sadie saw something shiny on the ground. It was a short, pointy stick of metal. She reached for it. Grandma held her hand back right away. "Not that one," said Grandma. Grandma picked it up with a napkin and put it in the trash. Then it was Sadie's turn. She climbed the steps. She sat down. Whoosh! Down she went, fast, into the soft sand. "Again!" said Sadie. Grandma laughed and held out her hand.

Aubrey sat at the little table in the computer lab. She wanted to draw a cat. But the tablet was dark. She pressed the screen. Nothing happened. She pressed it again. Nothing.

"Try the round button," said her teacher. "The one on the side."

Aubrey found the round button. She held it and counted, "One, two, three." The screen woke up. It was bright now. Her round button made the light come.

On the screen she saw little squares. She looked and looked. "That one," she said, pointing to a square with a paintbrush. She tapped it. The drawing app opened. There was a white page just for her.

She picked green. She picked pink. She mixed the two colors on her page. Now she had a new greeny-pink cat with long whiskers.

Then it was time to go. Aubrey pressed the round button again, counted, "One, two, three," and the screen went dark. She put the tablet on the shelf, all by herself.

"Look at my cat," she said to her teacher. "I made it before the light went to sleep."

Her teacher smiled. "You put it away all by yourself, too."

Josephine ran to the library shelf. She wanted the counting book with the red cover. But it was too high up!

"Let's ask the singing corner," said the librarian. "Our story time is starting." Josephine sat down fast.

The librarian sang, "One, two, three, four, five." The children clapped along. Then she sang, "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Josephine clapped ten times.

After the song, the librarian stood up. "Singing made us hungry for books. Let's pick some!" Josephine followed her to the shelf.

"Now you can reach," said the librarian. She knelt down and pointed. The red book was on the low shelf, sitting straight in a row. Josephine pulled it out. She looked at all ten ducks on the cover.

"Ten little ducks," she read. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

The librarian laughed. "You found it all by yourself."

Alexander wanted to help make lunch. The kitchen was warm and sunny. He stood next to Mama at the big counter.

Mama put a pot on the stove. Alexander saw the pot make steam. The steam went up, up, up. "Steam is hot," said Mama. She held his hand near, but not close. Alexander pulled his hand back fast. Hot meant no touch.

So Alexander helped in his own way. He put bread on a plate. He drew a picture with his pencil for the menu. It was a big red pot with steam. Mama clapped. "Our best menu ever," she said.

Then the toaster went pop. Out jumped a toast, high in the air. It landed right on Alexander's picture. Alexander laughed and laughed. "Toast wants lunch too," he said. Mama smiled and took the hot toast out with her big glove. She gave Alexander the plate. "You carry the cold plate," she said. "I carry the hot things." Alexander walked slowly, holding it with two hands. He did not drop one crumb.

Evan ran up the porch steps at Grandma's house. "Grandma, I want a cookie!" he called. Grandma was shy of her cookies before lunch. "First, let's play a letter game," she said.

Grandma held up a card with a big B. Evan did not know it. Then Benny the cat jumped on the table. His tail was like a soft feather. "Benny," said Evan. "B! Benny starts with B!"

"Now you can have your cookie," said Grandma. She put it on a plate. "C is for cookie," said Evan. He bit it, and crumbs fell down. The crumbs made little dots on the table. "Look, Grandma! Dots! D for dots!" Grandma laughed. "You see letters everywhere!" Evan held up his cookie. "C is for cookie, C is for cookie!" he sang.

Julia went to the band room with her class. Mr. Bell showed the drums. He showed the bells. Then he showed a big drum with a soft stick. "This one is for you," he said. "Its name is Boomer."

Julia tapped Boomer very softly. Boomer made a small sound. Tap. It was tiny, like a mouse.

Julia wanted Boomer to be big. She tapped harder. Boom! The sound filled the room. The paper on the wall moved. The bells on the shelf shook a little. A boy named Sam covered his ears. He looked upset.

Julia put down her stick. She went to Sam. "Sorry it was too loud," she said. She gave him a hug. Sam smiled.

Then Julia tapped again. She tapped soft, soft, medium, medium. Sam clapped to the beat. Mr. Bell clapped too.

Julia held up her stick. "Watch this," she said. "Soft mouse, big bear!" Tap, tap, BOOM.

Matthew ran up the steps of the bookmobile. It was a little bus full of books. His mom held his hand.

"I want a book about trucks," said Matthew.

The library lady smiled. "First you need a card," she said. She wrote Matthew's name on a small card. It had a loose corner that wiggled. Matthew held it tight.

He found a truck book with a big red truck on the cover. He wanted to keep it forever.

"Can I keep it?" he asked.

"You can take it home," said the library lady. "But you bring it back. Then other kids can read it too."

Matthew frowned. He hugged the book to his chest.

"How will I know when?" asked Matthew.

"I will put this paper in the book," said the library lady. "When the day comes, the book goes back."

At home, Matthew read the truck book three times. He made truck sounds. "Beep, beep!"

On the way back to the bookmobile, Matthew sang a truck song. He gave the book to the library lady.

Then she showed him a shelf. "Look," she said. "A new truck book came today."

Matthew's eyes got big. "A new one?"

He took the new book home with his card. "Beep, beep," he said, waving from the steps.

Myles sat at the big art table. The sun came in the window. It was a sunny day. Myles wanted to paint a boat. But his boat looked wrong. It was just a blue smudge.

"My boat won't look like a boat," said Myles.

His teacher put a box on the table. Inside were sponges. A round sponge. A square sponge. A triangle sponge. A long rectangle sponge.

Myles dipped the square sponge in paint. He pressed it on the paper. A square appeared. It looked like a boat's body. Then he dipped the triangle sponge. He pressed it on top of the square. A triangle sail stood up.

"It's a boat!" said Myles.

He pressed the round sponge two times. Two circles made wheels for a truck. He pressed the rectangle sponge. It made a long road under the truck.

Maya leaned over. "Make a boat for me," she said.

Myles dipped the square again. He pressed it on her paper. Then the triangle went on top. Hop, hop, hop went his hand, stamp by stamp.

"Here is your boat," said Myles.

Maya held the paper up to the sunny window. The triangle sail was red. The square boat was blue. The paint dripped a little at the bottom, and Maya laughed.

Grace sat in the big chair at the dentist. The dentist looked at her teeth. "All clean," he said. He gave her a sticker and a cookie.

Grace reached for the cookie. "Wait," said the nurse. "Where did your hands just go?"

Grace looked at her hands. They had touched the chair. They had touched her shoes. "I don't know," she said. "Germs can hide on hands," said the nurse. "Do you want to see something?"

The nurse took Grace to the sink. She put soap on Grace's hands. "Rub and count," she said. Grace rubbed and counted to twenty. Bubbles grew between her fingers.

Then the nurse held her hands under the light. "Look," she said. The hands shone. Grace dried them on a fuzzy towel and got a cup of ice water.

"Now can I have my cookie?" asked Grace. She ate it all up.

Ibrahim went to his friend Nadia's house. She had a tablet on the table. Ibrahim wanted to draw a cat on it. "It sleeps," said Nadia. "Watch this."

Nadia pushed the little round button. The screen woke up. It went from black to bright. Ibrahim clapped. "Again, again!" he said. Nadia let him push the button. Tap. The screen was black. Tap. The screen was bright. "I can do it too!" said Ibrahim.

Then Nadia showed him a blue square. "Tap this one," she said. Ibrahim tapped it. The drawing app opened. There was a green shape on the screen. Ibrahim drew a cat with one ear and five legs. Nadia laughed. "That is a silly cat," she said. "He is sorry about his legs," said Ibrahim.

When they finished, Nadia put the tablet in a basket. "It sleeps there," she said. Ibrahim tapped the button first. The screen went dark. Then he laid the tablet down, soft as a sleeping cat.

Henry ran to the block corner. It was his first day of school. He wanted to build a big, big tower.

"Can I touch the tall part?" he asked his teacher.

"Build it first," she said with a smile.

Henry stacked one block. Then two. Then ten! The tower grew taller than his head.

Then he found a fat red block. It was very heavy. He put it on the very top.

The tower wobbled. The tower leaned. Down it came! Blocks went crash, boom, plunk all over the rug.

"Oh no," said Henry. "Why did it fall down?"

He looked at the fat red block. It was heavy at the top. He had an idea.

He put the heavy block at the bottom this time. Then he stacked the little blocks on top. The tower stood tall. It did not fall.

"Look, teacher! It stays up!"

A girl named Mia ran over. "Is that a tower or a doctor house?"

"It is a doctor tower," said Henry. "You can be the doctor."

Mia picked up a toy stethoscope. She touched the tower gently. "Beep beep," she said. "Your tower is healthy!"

Henry laughed and added one more small block on top.

Joshua went to Mia's house. Mia had a big toy kitchen. Joshua wanted to make soup like a grown-up.

Mia gave him a pot and a spoon. Joshua put in a red block. He put in a blue cup. He began to stir. Round and round went the spoon. "Look, my soup is moving!" he said.

Then Baby Bear fell on the floor. Baby Bear began to cry. Well, Mia made him cry. "Oh no," said Mia. "Baby Bear is hungry." Joshua held out his pot. Would soup help a bear? He tipped the spoon near Baby Bear's mouth. Mia made slurping sounds. Then she stopped crying the bear. "He feels better," she said. The soup had made the crying stop. Joshua's eyes got big.

After that, Baby Bear got tired. Joshua wrapped him in a small towel. He patted the bear's back, softly, softly. Soon the bear went to sleep.

At home time, Mia gave Joshua the spoon to keep. He held it all the way to the car. "More soup tomorrow," he said.

Charlotte went to her friend Mia's house. Mia had a tablet. Charlotte wanted to draw on it. "Can I try?" she asked.

Mia's mom said, "Yes. First you press the little button." Charlotte pressed it. The screen lit up. She pressed it again. The screen went dark. "Oops," said Charlotte. She pressed it one more time. The screen came back. Charlotte laughed.

Mia showed her the drawing app. Charlotte tapped it. Colors filled the screen. She drew a big green hill. She drew a yellow sun on top. She drew a red bird. Then she was done. "Now we put it away," said Mia's mom. Charlotte pressed the button. The screen went dark. She laid the tablet on the table. "I did it all by myself," said Charlotte. "Same time tomorrow?" asked Mia. "Yes," said Charlotte. "I want to draw a cat."

Jayden wanted to give his mama a present. He looked in his toy box. He found a small blue car. It was just right.

Jayden carried the car to the kitchen. Mama was there. Steam rose up from a big pot. Jayden reached out his hand. "Not the pot, love," Mama said. She picked him up. "The pot is hot. It can hurt you."

Jayden looked at the pot from Mama's arms. A little ice cube sat on the counter. It was melting. It got smaller and smaller. Then it was just a wet spot. "Ice is cold," said Jayden. "Hot pot, cold ice." Mama smiled. "Yes, my smart boy."

Jayden slid down and held Mama's leg with one hand. He kept the car safe in the other hand. He stayed right there, close to Mama. The pot went bubble, bubble. Jayden did not touch it. He watched the steam go up.

When the cooking was done, Jayden held out the car. "Present for you, Mama!" Mama knelt down and took it. "Thank you, Jayden." She gave him a big, warm hug.

Max sat at the kitchen table. His mom put a pencil in his hand. "Let's write your name," she said.

Max squeezed the pencil in his fist. He pushed it down hard. The tip snapped off. The little piece rolled across the table and dropped to the floor.

"Oops," said Max. His big brother Tom came to look. Tom picked up the broken tip. He showed Max his own hand. Tom held the pencil light, like a little bird sitting on his fingers.

Max tried it. He held the pencil the same way. He did not push hard. Now the pencil made a line. The line did not break. He made a big M. Then an A. Then an X.

The letters sat on the paper, side by side. "That's my name!" said Max. He looked at the pencil. Was it magic? No, it was just his hand, holding soft and slow. He wrote his name again.

Nicholas was at Grandma's house. He found a big cardboard box under the table. He peeked inside. There was a blanket, a small cup, and a teddy bear. "Whose box is this?" he asked. Grandma smiled. "It was Mommy's box. She played house with it."

Nicholas wanted to play too. He set the teddy bear on the blanket. He held the cup to the bear's mouth. The bear tipped over and fell. The bear looked grumpy lying there. "Are you hungry?" Nicholas asked. "Yes," he said in a bear voice. He pretended to feed the bear a pretend snack. The bear sat up tall.

Then Nicholas wrapped the bear in the blanket. He rocked the bear side to side. He counted, "One, two, three," softly. The bear's eyes began to close. Nicholas patted the bear's back. "Shh," he whispered. Grandma peeked in and smiled. "Goodnight, baby bear," said Nicholas.

Sarah ran into the library. She held Mama's hand tight. "Books!" said Sarah. "So many books!"

A big rug sat in the corner. Sarah saw bins on the rug. Each bin had toys in it. One bin had little animals. One bin had trucks and balls. One bin had play food. Sarah wanted them all.

She picked up a little cat. She put it in the animal bin. Then she found a banana. It did not look right next to the cat. She moved the banana to the food bin. The banana sat with the apples and the bread. Sarah clapped. "Mama, look! Bananas go with food!"

A boy dropped his teddy bear. It fell near the food bin. Sarah picked it up. The bear was soft, not rough like the carpet. "Bear goes with toys," said Sarah. She put it in the toy bin. The boy smiled.

Then Sarah found a picture book. She opened it. There was a dog in the picture. There was a cake, too. "Dog is an animal. Cake is food," said Sarah. Mama laughed. Sarah turned the page, quick and excited.

Gianna was at Milo's birthday party. A big red truck sat on the grass. It had a shovel that could dig deep holes. Gianna wanted it so much.

Ben grabbed the truck first. "My turn," he said. Gianna reached out her hand. Then she stopped. She put her hands in her lap instead. Ben dug a thin little hole in the dirt. Seeds went in the hole for a party game. Then Ben held out the truck. "Your turn now," he said.

Gianna took the truck. She dug a big hole. It was deep and round. "Look, Ben!" she said. Ben clapped his hands. "Now my turn again?" he asked. "Yes," said Gianna. "Then my turn." The truck went back and forth, back and forth. "Best diggers ever," said Ben.

Willow ran to the play corner at school. She wanted to play house with her bear. But Ben had the toy stove, and Mia had the little bed. Willow's bear had nowhere to sleep and nothing to cook. She sat down on her knee and thought.

Then she had an idea. She took an empty box and tipped it over. Now the bear had a bed! She patted the box and laid the bear down. "Sleep tight, baby bear," she said. The bear closed his eyes, as if he could not stay awake. Ben saw the box and clapped. "A bed from a box!" he said. Mia put her pot on the box's edge. "Now we can cook soup next to the bear."

The teacher came to look. "What a fine house," she said. "Can I visit?" Willow nodded fast. "Wipe your feet first," she said. The teacher wiped her shoes on the mat, very slowly. Then she sat on a tiny chair, and it looked too small for her. Everybody laughed. "More soup, please," said the teacher, holding out her cup.

Maverick went to Grandma's house. His toy pig was in his bag. The pig was cold from the car ride. Maverick wanted to warm it up.

He wrapped the pig in a small blanket. He patted the pig, pat, pat. Grandma watched from her chair. "Is piggy sleepy?" she asked. Maverick nodded. He rocked the pig in his arms. Then the pig made him feel like rocking too. When he rocked slow, the pig looked calm. When he rocked fast, the pig bounced and looked silly.

Maverick made a pretend bed from a soft towel. He tucked the pig in. "Night night, pig," he said in a polite little voice. He pushed the towel bed on the floor. The bed did a gentle swing from side to side. The pig slid off. Maverick laughed and picked the pig up. "More blanket," he said. He added another fold. This time the pig stayed snug.

Grandma hummed a quiet song. Maverick yawned. He lay down next to the pig on the rug. "Shh," he whispered. "Piggy is sleeping." Grandma covered them both with her warm, soft shawl. It smelled like sugar and lemons. Maverick closed his eyes.

Ivy went to the cemetery with Mama and Pop. They carried a picnic basket. They were going to eat lunch near Grandpa Ben's stone. The stone felt dry and warm in the sun.

Mama set out the food on a red blanket. There were bread, cheese, and sweet grapes. Ivy wanted to grab a grape right away. "First we say our greeting," said Pop. He held out his hand. Ivy did not know the words yet.

Pop held Mama's hand. Mama held Ivy's hand. Then they all held hands in a circle. "One, two, three," said Pop. They said the greeting together. Ivy said the words too. Then Pop smiled. Then Mama smiled. Then everyone picked up bread at the same time.

The next Sunday they came back. Ivy brought a small cup of juice. She set it down on the blanket. "First we say it," said Ivy. She held out her hands. Pop took one hand. Mama took the other.

"One, two, three," said Ivy. They said the greeting together. Then everyone ate. The grapes tasted sweet. A bird hopped close to the blanket. "Hello, bird," said Ivy. "You get bread after."

Anna wanted to find her robot toy. She could not find it. Where did it go?

Anna looked with her eyes. She saw her blocks. She saw her bear. No robot there. Then Anna heard a little sound with her ears. Beep, beep! "Was that my robot?" she asked. "Yes, it was!"

The beeps came from under the blanket. Anna touched the blanket with her hands. It was soft and warm. She pulled the blanket back. There was her robot!

Anna was so happy. She was not sad anymore. Mom came in with warm cookies. Anna smelled them with her nose. Yum! She tasted a cookie with her tongue. Sweet!

Anna hugged her robot. "I found you," she said. Beep, beep, said the robot.

Olivia went to the garden center with Dad. The sun felt warm on her nose. The store was loud with carts and voices. Olivia wanted to grow her own carrots.

She picked a small bag of seeds. Dad got a big pot and soft brown dirt. At home, they sat on the step. Olivia patted the dirt down flat. Then she dropped three tiny seeds on top. She covered them with a little more dirt. Dad poured water from a small cup.

Every morning Olivia ran outside. She saw nothing. She saw dirt. She pouted. "Where are my carrots?" she asked. Dad said, "Look again tomorrow."

The weather turned hot. The sun burned Olivia's bare toes on the step, so Dad got her little sandals. After that, the pot showed something green. One small leaf, then two. Olivia gasped and touched it gently.

The leaves grew tall and feathery. Dad held the pot steady. Together they pulled up one fat orange carrot. It was cold and crunchy and smelled like dirt and rain. Olivia washed it under the tap and took a big bite.

"My seed made this," said Olivia. Dad smiled. "Let's plant some more tomorrow."

Emma wants to make breakfast for her family. "Daddy, can I help cook?" she asks. Daddy says yes. They stand by the camp stove together. Daddy keeps Emma far from the hot pan. He holds the spoon. Emma cracks an egg into a bowl. Some shell falls in. Emma frowns. Her egg looks messy.

"Try again," says Daddy. Emma cracks another egg. This time the shell stays out. The egg looks smooth and yellow. Daddy pours it into the pan. The runny egg turns firm and white. Emma taps Daddy's arm. "Look! It got fat!" she says. Daddy smiles and flips the egg.

The egg goes on a plate with bread. Mommy takes a taste. "Yummy," she says. Baby brother claps. Near the tent, a green frog hops by. Emma waves at it. Then she sits close to Mommy and eats her egg all up.

Austin ran to the big slide at the playground. Mommy came too. The big slide was tall. The small slide was short. Austin wanted to go fast, but the slide was hot from the sun. "Ouch," said Mommy. "We must wait. Hot things can hurt you." Austin touched the small slide. It was in the shade. The small slide felt cool. "This one is cold," said Austin. So Austin sat on the small slide. He went down slow. He went down slow, slow, slow. Then he tried again. He wiggled his feet. Now he went fast, fast, fast! He laughed loud. A big dog ran by. Then a small horse clip-clopped past the fence. The big dog ran fast. The small horse walked slow. "Big and small, fast and slow," said Austin. Mommy held his hand. They sat in the cool shade. Austin drank cold water from his cup. "Not alone," said Mommy. "I sit with you." Austin leaned on her arm and watched the small horse walk away.

Jake wanted to play house in his playroom. He set his gray robot on a little chair. He gave his teddy bear a spot on the rug. But teddy kept falling over. He would not sit up at all.

Jake tried to prop teddy against the wall. Teddy slid down again. Then Jake saw his soft blue blanket in the toy box. He had an idea. He spread the blanket on the rug. He laid teddy down on top of it. Teddy lay very still. He looked like he was sleeping.

Jake made his voice small and soft. "Shh," he said. "The baby is sleeping." He tucked the blanket around teddy. The blanket stayed put. Teddy did not fall over anymore.

Jake picked up his gray robot. "You are the big brother," he whispered. "We must be quiet." The robot sat by the chair. Jake patted teddy's head. He tried to make a lunch for everyone, too. He filled a toy pot with pretend soup.

Then teddy's eyes seemed to open. "Time to wake up," said Jake. He lifted teddy into a hug. "You slept so well. Now we can eat." The robot got a pretend bowl, too. Jake smiled and stirred the soup round and round. "More soup, anyone?"

Nova got to Rosa's house early. Rosa's mom had not set out the toys yet.

"I want to play house," said Nova.

"Let's make a house," said Rosa.

They turned a big box over. Now it was a house with a door. Nova crawled in through the door. Rosa crawled in too.

But the baby dolls were sad on the shelf. Nova wanted to be the mom. She reached for the baby. The baby was too far up.

"Use the step stool," said Rosa.

Nova climbed the stool. She held the baby tight. It worked!

Nova wrapped the baby in a soft sock. She patted its back. The baby closed its eyes.

"Time for the bus," said Rosa. She pushed a chair to the box.

Nova held her baby and sat down. Vroom, vroom! The bus drove to the store.

Then the baby peeked out of the sock. It was wearing Rosa's tiny hat!

"How did that get there?" Nova asked.

Rosa just smiled and said, "Next stop, home!"

At daycare, Liam found a big cardboard box. "A boat!" he said. He was so excited. His hands jumped up and down.

Mia wanted the box too. She grabbed one side. Liam grabbed the other side. "Mine!" he shouted. His face got hot and red. He was angry now.

Then Mia began to cry. Big tears ran down her cheeks. Liam saw her sad face. He let go of the box. "You can go first," he said. Mia smiled a happy smile. The teacher patted Liam's head. "Kind hands," she said softly.

Suddenly the room got noisy. A loud truck went by the window. Liam felt scared. He held the teacher's hand. She gave him a gentle pat. "The truck is going away," she said. The sound got smaller and smaller. Liam climbed into the box. Mia pushed him slowly. "Boat ride!" she said. Liam laughed and laughed.

Sebastian stood in the backyard. He held a red beanbag in his hand. A hoop lay on the grass like a big circle. He wanted the beanbag to land inside it.

Sebastian threw the beanbag. It flew past the hoop. It landed in the flowers. He ran and picked it up. He stood close to the hoop this time. He tossed the beanbag down. It went right into the circle. Sebastian clapped his hands.

Then Dad brought a big yellow ball. "Catch it with both hands," said Dad. Dad rolled the ball slowly. Sebastian held out one hand. The ball bounced off and rolled away. He ran after it across the busy yard.

Sebastian tried again. This time he covered the ball with two hands. Both hands held it tight. The ball stopped. It did not roll away. "I caught it!" said Sebastian. Dad smiled and rolled the ball again. Sebastian held out both arms and waited.

Emile ran to the art table. He wanted to paint a house for his toy dog. Miss Rosa gave him a big brush. "Paint something you like," she said.

Emile painted a square. It had four flat sides. He looked at it. A square made a good house! Then he painted a triangle on top. The triangle had three sides. It sat on the square like a roof. "A roof!" said Emile.

He painted little squares for windows. He painted a rectangle door. The rectangle was long, not tall like the door. Wait. His door looked wrong. Miss Rosa turned the rectangle the other way. Now it was tall. Now it looked like a door.

Emile painted a yellow circle at the top. The circle had no sides at all. It glowed like a sun over the house. He held up his painting. "My dog has a home!" he said. Miss Rosa clapped. Emile put his toy dog on the table, right under the circle sun.

Eva went to the playground with Grandma. "Stay where I can see you," said Grandma. Eva nodded. She wanted to find the best spot to play.

Eva counted as she walked. One bench, two swings, three slides. The metal slide sat in the sun. Eva put her hand near it. The slide was hot, very hot. Grandma held Eva's hand. They walked to the shady slide instead. Eva touched it. This one was cool. Down she went, whee!

Then Eva saw something shiny in the grass. It was a bit of broken glass. She reached out. "Stop," said Grandma. "We don't touch sharp things." Grandma picked it up with a glove and put it far away. Eva watched the whole time.

"I found a cool slide," said Eva. "And a hot one too." Grandma smiled. Eva counted again. One bench, two swings, two slides. Then she ran back to the swings, right where Grandma could see her.

Zoe wanted to paint a big orange leaf for the fall wall. But the paint pots had no orange. There was red, yellow, and blue. Zoe looked and looked. No orange anywhere.

Zoe held up the red pot. "This is red," she said. She held up the yellow. "This is yellow." She pointed at the last one. "And that is blue." Her teacher smiled and gave her a big white tray.

Zoe put a dot of red on the tray. Then she put a dot of yellow next to it. She mixed them with her brush, round and round. The dots turned orange, bright as a pumpkin. Zoe gasped. Two paints had made a new paint!

She painted her leaf with the orange. It looked like fire from a dragon, she thought. Her polite friend Ben came over and asked, "Can I try?" Zoe put more red and more yellow on the tray. She gave him the brush.

"You go round and round," she said. "Watch what happens."

It was a hot summer day. Ivy wanted to go down the big slide. But the slide was busy. Lots of kids were waiting.

Ivy stood in line. A big kid began to count. "One, two, three," he said. Each time he said a number, one kid went down. Whoosh! The line got shorter.

Ivy listened. "Four, five, six." Three more kids slid down, fast. The sun was warm on her head. Her water bottle almost fell. She was careful and held it tight so it would not spill.

The big kid said, "Seven, eight, nine." Now only one kid was left. Then it was Ivy's turn. "Ten!" said the big kid. Ivy climbed up and sat down. She held on tight.

Whoosh! Down she went, fast and smiling.

"My turn to count," said Ivy. She stood by the slide and began, "One, two..."

Olivier held a tiny seed in his hand. It was small and brown. "Will this really make a carrot?" he asked. Grandma smiled. "Put it in the dirt and see."

Olivier made a little hole. He dropped the seed in. He patted the dirt on top, soft and flat. "Sleep well, little seed," he said.

Every day Olivier came to the garden. He looked and looked. One morning, a green leaf popped up! "Grandma, come quick!" he called. The leaf was small and wet from the rain. More rain fell. The leaf grew taller. Then more leaves came.

But one plant was droopy. It looked sad and flat. "Why is it bendy?" Olivier wondered. Grandma let him fill a small watering can. Olivier poured water on the dirt. The next day, the plant stood up tall.

Olivier picked a pink flower growing near the carrots. He put it by the plant as a gift. Then Grandma handed him a cookie for a snack. He munched and watched his garden. "Hello, little leaf," he said. "Grow big like me."

Isaac sat in the waiting room with his father. He hugged his favorite teddy bear. Today Isaac would get a shot. He did not want a shot.

"Shots feel like a quick pinch," said his father. "You can squeeze teddy tight."

Isaac squeezed teddy tight. The nurse came in. She wiped Isaac's arm with a cold, wet wipe. Then came the quick pinch.

"Ow," said Isaac. He squeezed teddy even tighter. Then the pinch stopped. The nurse put a round bandage on his arm.

"Done," said the nurse. "You were so brave."

Isaac looked at the bandage. His father held up a sticker. It had a red fire truck on it.

Isaac took the sticker. He pressed it right onto teddy's paw. "Teddy got a bandage too," he said.

His father laughed. "Let's go home, big boy."

Jasper looked in the sandbox. "One, no truck," he said. His special blue truck was lost.

Miss Rosa came to help. "Let's look together," she said. They looked by the slide. "Two, no truck." They looked under the bench. "Three, no truck."

The wind blew. A big leaf flew past Jasper's foot. The wind pushed the leaf along the ground. Jasper watched it slide under the little gate. "The wind pushes things," he thought.

Jasper ran to the gate. He peeked under it. There was his truck! The wind had pushed it there too. Miss Rosa opened the gate. "My truck!" said Jasper. He hugged it tight.

"Let's fix a safe pocket for it," said Miss Rosa. She put the truck in Jasper's coat pocket. Jasper patted the pocket. "One truck, all safe," he said.

Elena woke up and saw white outside. Snow! Lots and lots of snow. No school today!

She pulled on her boots. She pulled on her red coat. "Mom, can I build a snowman?" Mom said yes. Out they went into the cold.

The snow was deep and soft. Elena patted a big ball. She patted and patted. But the snow would not stick. It kept falling off. The snowman had no head. Elena felt grumpy. She stomped her boot. "Why won't it stay on?"

Then she saw Dad shoveling. The shovel made a loud sound, like a hammer hitting the ground. The snow on his pile looked shiny and packed down tight.

Elena picked up some snow. She squeezed it in her mittens. It clumped into a hard ball. She squeezed some more, and it stuck!

She packed the head tight. Up it went, and it stayed! "My snowman has a head! My snowman has a head!" Elena put a carrot nose on him. "Now let's make him a friend," she said, grabbing more snow.

William wanted the big red truck. His sister Mia had it first. William grabbed the truck. Mia cried loud. The truck fell on the rug.

Mummy knelt down. "We take turns," she said. "William, you can have the truck after Mia." William sat on the rug. He waited. He stacked two soft blocks. He stacked three. Then four.

Mia pushed the truck fast across the floor. It bumped the blocks. The blocks fell down. Mia laughed. Then she held out the truck. "Your turn," she said.

William took the truck. He pushed it fast, too. Mia waited, just like William had done. Then it was her turn again.

Soon it was dinner time. William put the truck on the shelf. He shut the toy box lid. "Truck sleeps now," he said. Mia patted the box. "Night night, truck."

Eliana was at Grandma's house. She found a purple book on the big chair. "That is my library book," said Grandma. Eliana wanted to keep it forever. It had a bear who could crawl into tiny caves. Grandma opened the book. She began at the front. The bear crawled on page one. Then page two. Then page three. "The bear goes this way," said Eliana, pointing. She turned the pages herself. She touched the little marks under the bear. "What are these?" she asked. "Those are words," said Grandma. "They say what the bear does." Eliana looked closely. The words made the bear crawl. But then Grandma said, "We must take the book back on Friday. Then other kids can read it." Eliana hugged the book tight. She read it all week. On Friday, Grandma helped her put it in a bag. At the library, Eliana set the book on the desk. The librarian smiled. She handed Eliana a shiny stamp card. "Want to pick a new one?" she asked. Eliana ran to the shelves. "I want a book with a map in it," she said.

Matteo woke up in his dark room. Today was his first day of school. He wanted to pack his own backpack. He put in his crayons. He put in his bear. But the zipper would not close.

"Let me try again," said Matteo. He pulled one side. It did not move. He pulled the other side. It did not move. He sat down and looked at the zipper. The two sides were apart. He pushed the two sides together. He heard a little click.

Now he pulled the zipper. It moved all the way up. The backpack was closed! His crayons were inside. His bear was inside too. Matteo put the backpack on his back. His shoes sat by the door. He pushed his foot into each one.

Mama smiled. "Ready for school?" she asked. Matteo ran to the door. "Yes! I did it all by myself!"

Florence wanted to play a guessing game. Grandma said, "I will guess things. You tell me how you know."

Grandma hid a pink flower behind her back. "Sniff, sniff," she said. Florence shouted, "Nose! You smell it with your nose!"

Then Grandma rang a little bell. Florence covered her ears. "Ears! We hear with ears!"

Grandma held up the flower. "Now look." Florence giggled. "Eyes! Eyes see the pink!"

Grandma let Florence touch the grass. "Toes feel tickly grass," Florence said. "Skin feels it!"

One thing was left. Grandma pointed to her tongue. "Taste! But do not lick the flower," Grandma said. She got a tiny cookie from her pocket. Florence took a small bite. "Mmm! Tongue tastes cookies!"

Grandma counted on her fingers. "Nose, ears, eyes, skin, tongue. Five!" Florence counted too. "Nose, ears, eyes, skin, tongue!"

Then Florence ran to the swing and shouted, "My skin feels the wind!"

Connor ran to the big slide at the playground. But a girl was already at the top. She sat down and slid. A boy climbed up next. Then it was Connor's turn. He slid down fast. Whee!

Connor wanted to go again. He ran to the ladder. But two kids were already waiting in line. Connor stopped and stood behind them. "Why do we wait?" he asked. "So everyone gets a turn," said the girl in front. One kid went down. Then the next kid went down. Then it was Connor again.

Near the sandbox, a boy was digging. His shovel was hard at work. Connor wanted a shovel too. There was only one. "Can I have a turn?" Connor asked. "Yes, when I am done," said the boy. He dug three more scoops. Then he held out the shovel. "Here you come," he said, and smiled. Connor dug a big hole.

A teacher clapped her hands. "Snack time," she called. "Wash hands first." Connor got in line at the water fountain. He waited. He washed. Then he sat on the bench with his present from home, a little bag of crackers. The girl sat next to him with no snack. Connor held out the bag. "Want some?" he asked. She took one cracker and said, "Thank you."

Hannah stood in the big school gym. She held a small red beanbag. She wanted to throw it into the hoop on the floor. She threw it. It hit the edge and fell out. "Why did it fall?" she asked. Teacher Mia smiled. "Try standing closer," she said.

Hannah took two steps closer. She threw the beanbag again. It went up, then down. Plunk! It landed inside the hoop. "It went in!" said Hannah. She jumped up and down.

Next, Mia rolled her a big ball. It was too big for one hand. It bumped Hannah's tummy and fell. "Why can't I hold it?" asked Hannah. She looked at her hands. She put out both hands this time. Mia rolled the ball again. Hannah caught it with both arms. The ball stayed. "I did it!" she said. Mia clapped, and the ball flew up in the air between them.

Sophie put on her red team shirt. It was her first day of soccer at the park. Grandpa held her hand on the gray sidewalk. "Where is my team?" Sophie asked. Grandpa pointed to the kids by the goal.

Coach Nina gave Sophie a ball. Sophie tapped it with her toe. The ball rolled a tiny bit and stopped. She tapped it again, soft. It rolled a tiny bit again. Then Sophie pulled her leg back and kicked the ball hard. The ball rolled far, far away, all the way past the cones.

Sophie ran after it. "Grandpa, did you see?" she called. "I kicked it and it went far!" Grandpa smiled and waved. A boy named Tom began to cry because the ball bumped his foot. Coach Nina knelt down and gave him a soft pat.

"Try again," Coach Nina said to Sophie. Sophie looked at the goal. She kicked the ball hard with her whole foot. The ball rolled and rolled, right into the net. "Goal!" the team shouted. Sophie jumped up and down. Then she lined up the ball one more time.

Asher went to the library. There was a craft table with paper and crayons. Asher wanted to make a rainbow picture.

The librarian gave him a black crayon. "Color your whole paper black," she said. Asher pressed hard. He covered all the colors. Now his paper was all black. Where did the rainbow go?

Then the librarian gave him a little stick. "Try a scratch," she said. Asher dragged the stick across the paper. A red line appeared! He scratched again. A green line popped out! The rainbow was hiding under the black. Asher scratched and scratched. A sun came out. A fish came out. A big rainbow came out too.

A girl sat down next to Asher. She looked sad. "My paper is all black," she said. Asher handed her his stick. "Scratch it," he said. She scratched a yellow star. She smiled big. "Let's make more," Asher said, and handed her another stick.

William sat in his car seat. He looked out the window. "I want my snack," he said.

Mom reached into the bag. "Let's find it," she said. "We have a banana. We have crackers. We have cheese." William pointed. "The banana!" The banana was a food. He loved it best.

William peeled it a little. The peel opened like a big yellow jacket. He held on tight. The car went bump. The banana slipped. It began to fall! "Oh no!" said William. Mom caught it in her hand. "Safe," she said. William took a big bite. The banana made him happy.

After the snack, they played a game. "Tell me what you see," said Mom. William saw a cow. The cow was an animal. "Moo!" said William. He saw a dog in a truck. The dog was an animal too. "Woof!" said William. Mom laughed.

Then William dropped his toy truck. It slid under the seat. "My truck!" he said. Mom stopped at a red light. She reached down. She found the truck and a soft ball. The truck and the ball were toys. William hugged them. "My truck, my ball," he said. "One animal, one food, one toy," said Mom. The light turned green. "Moo!" said William, and off they went.

Zayn stood on the ferry with his dad. The big boat was taking them on a trip. Zayn held his bag of crackers. He was hungry, so he ate one. He dropped some crumbs on the deck. Then a big white bird flew down. The bird picked up the crumbs with its beak. Zayn was surprised. One cracker had made a bird come!

Zayn wanted the bird to come again. He broke off a little piece of cracker. He dropped it on the deck. The bird swooped down and took it. Then more birds came. They all wanted crumbs. Dad laughed softly. "Slow down," he said. "Save some for later." Zayn held his bag tight. He dropped just one more piece, and one more bird came.

Then the wind blew. It blew Zayn's little paper hat right off his head. The hat rolled along the deck. A kind lady picked it up. She smiled and gave it back. "Thank you," said Zayn.

Later, they went inside the ferry. It was warm there. Dad stirred sugar into his tea. Dad let Zayn watch from his safe seat. Zayn had a seed and nut mix in his pocket. He munched it slowly. The ferry smelled a bit stinky, like the sea. Zayn looked out the big window. He saw the waves go up and down. The boat went up and down too. Zayn waved at the water. "Bye bye, waves," he said. "See you on our trip home."

Olivier sat in the waiting room with his mama. They were late, so they hurried in. Olivier wanted the turtle sticker at the front desk. But first he had to wait for his turn.

Then he heard a plane. It went over the roof. Rrrrrrumble. Olivier put his hands over his ears. The sound got small. He took his hands off. The rumble came back, big and loud. He did it again. Hands on, hands off. "Mama, my ears make it quiet!"

A nurse called his name. In the small room, the doctor came in. She looked in Olivier's eyes. "Your eyes see me," she said. Olivier saw her shiny blue pen light blink.

She looked in his nose. "Sniff this little tube," she said. Olivier sniffed with his nose. It smelled like soap. Then the doctor put a tiny stick near his mouth. "Say ahh." Olivier tasted something sweet, like a berry.

The doctor pressed softly on his tummy. "Your skin can feel my hands," she said. Olivier felt the warm press. He touched the paper on the bed. It was crinkly and smooth.

At the front desk, Olivier picked his turtle sticker. He pressed it with his finger. It stuck tight to his shirt. Outside, another plane went by. Olivier kept his ears open all the way home.

Evelyn went to the park with her blue bunny. She carried bunny in her arms all morning. Then it was time for a snack. Evelyn put bunny down on the grass.

After the snack, bunny was gone. "Where did bunny go?" she asked. "Let's look," said Dad.

They looked by the swing. No bunny. They looked under the bench. No bunny. "One swing, one bench," said Evelyn. "No bunny."

Then the wind blew. The wind made the big leaves move. Evelyn saw the leaves flip up and down. Something blue was under the leaves! She ran over and pushed the leaves apart. There was bunny, smiling up at her.

"The wind showed me!" said Evelyn. She hugged bunny tight. Then she carried bunny to the sandbox. "You sit here," she said. "Right next to me."

Dad sat down too. Evelyn made a little cake from sand. She put a small rock on top. "One cake, one rock, one bunny," she said. "All here."

Noah went to soccer practice. Coach Maya had one big red ball. All the kids wanted it.

Noah grabbed the ball first. He held it tight. Ben reached for it too. Then Ben got mad. His face turned red. He sat down on the grass and would not look at Noah.

Coach Maya knelt beside them. "We can write our turn list on my clipboard," she said. She wrote NOAH first. Then she wrote BEN under it. Noah looked at the list. His name was on top. He kicked the ball to Ben, and Ben kicked it back. When Noah waited, he got his turn again.

Then Noah sat down next to Ben. "Your turn now," Noah said. He pointed at the list. Ben smiled and stood up fast. He ran with the ball all the way to the net. Noah clapped his hands.

After practice, Coach Maya gave out juice. Ben drew a picture in the dirt with a stick. It was a big blue ocean with a soccer ball floating on a wave. "That is for you," Ben said. Noah sat close to his coach and held his juice. "Same time tomorrow," said Coach Maya. Noah waved to Ben all the way to the car.

Rehmat woke up and ran to the window. "Snow!" she said. "No school today!" Her tummy felt hungry, so she ran to the kitchen. Mama was there in her big warm sweater.

"I want to help," said Rehmat. Mama smiled. "You can watch the butter," she said. Mama put a little butter in a pan. Then Mama turned on the stove herself. Rehmat stood back and watched. The butter was hard and cold. Then it got soft. Then it turned to a shiny puddle. "It melted!" said Rehmat. "The heat did that."

Mama poured the melted butter into a bowl. "Now one egg, one splash of milk, one scoop of flour," said Mama. Rehmat counted each thing. "One, two, three!" She stirred slow, then slower, then slow again. It takes time to make pancakes.

The pancakes sizzled. Flips were Mama's job. Then, surprise, Mama made one pancake shaped like a snowman. "For my snow day kid," said Mama. Rehmat clapped. After breakfast, they looked out the window. The sun had come out. The snowman in the yard was getting small and drippy. "Look, Mama," said Rehmat. "He is melting like the butter!"

David woke up and saw white. The sky was full of soft snow. No school today! Dad said, "Snow day!" David wanted to sled down the big hill.

David pulled his sled up, up, up. He sat down. He pushed off. The sled did not move. It just sat in the snow. "Hmm," said David.

Dad sat on the sled too. Now it was heavy. The sled began to slide. Down, down they went. Whee! "Again," said David. He climbed the hill again.

They went down and down. Then David was cold. His mittens were wet. Mom had hot cocoa waiting. She was careful with the hot cup. David blew and blew on his cocoa. He sipped it slow. Outside, the snow fell on the hill, ready for tomorrow. "More sledding tomorrow," said David. Dad smiled and said, "Yes, tomorrow."

Raphael wanted to play house at daycare. But the baby doll was missing. Where could it be?

He looked under the table. He looked in the toy box. Then he heard a small sound. It came from the big sock pile! Raphael pulled out a thick wool sock. Something was inside it. He peeked in.

It was the baby doll, all cozy and warm. Maya had put it there for a nap. "The baby needs a blanket," Maya said. Raphael nodded. A sock could be a blanket!

He set the doll in a little basket. He patted its back, so soft. Then he made a bottle from a toy cup. He held it to the doll's mouth. Maya covered the doll with the thick sock again. The baby looked so snug.

"Time for dinner," said Raphael. He stirred a pot of toy carrots. Their teacher, Miss Jo, came to help. She held the pretend pot with two hands. "This soup smells so good," she said. Raphael smiled big.

He fed the doll one more bite. Then he wrapped the sock around it like a hug. "Sleep well, baby," he whispered.

Elizabeth went to the park with her dad. She saw a big round swing. A boy was on it. "I want a turn," she said. Dad said, "We can ask." Elizabeth waited by the fence. She counted the flowers while she waited. Soon the boy jumped off. "Your turn," he said. Elizabeth sat on the swing. Dad pushed her high. She laughed and laughed.

Next they went to the sand pit. Two kids were there. They had one red shovel. Elizabeth had a small blue bucket. "I can share my bucket," she said. The girl gave her the shovel. They dug a round hole together. It was big enough for both hands.

Then a teacher blew a whistle. All the kids ran to the benches. Elizabeth ran too. Everyone sat in a line. A grown-up handed out little cakes from a basket. Each child got one cake. Elizabeth took hers. "We all got the same," she said. She bit into her cake. It was sweet.

Dad sat close by on the bench. Elizabeth leaned on his arm. "One more swing," she said, "and then we go home." Dad smiled and held her hand.

Ayla ran into the school cafeteria. It was her first day of school! She looked for a seat. She wanted a friend to sit with.

One girl sat alone. She had a smelly tuna sandwich. Ayla saw the girl take a big bite. Then the girl's tummy made a loud rumble. "My tummy talks when I eat!" the girl said. Ayla laughed and sat down.

Ayla opened her lunch. "I have a apple, a banana, and crackers," she said. "One, two, three!" She took a big bite of her apple. Her tummy made a rumble too! The girl laughed this time. "I know that sound," said Ayla. "Winter is coming and my tummy is hungry!" The two girls counted their snacks together. Then they shared one cracker each. "Same seat tomorrow?" asked the girl. "Yes!" said Ayla, and she clapped her hands.

Charles sat at the dinner table. His tummy made a little growl. "Now I am hungry," he said. "Is dinner now or later?" Mom smiled. "Later. The pot is still cooking." Dad stirred the pot on the stove. Charles stayed in his chair and watched. Steam went up, up, up. "Yesterday we had noodles," said Mom. "Today we have soup. Tomorrow we can have noodles again." Charles picked up his spoon. He tapped it on the table, one, two, three. "Can I taste now?" he asked. "Not yet," said Dad. "Hot soup must cool down." Charles wiggled one toe inside his shoe. Waiting felt long. Then Dad set the bowl on the table. A tiny curl of steam rose from it. Charles blew on the soup. Whoosh, whoosh. The steam got smaller. He took one sip. "It's not too hot now!" he said. "Yummy soup today." Mom laughed and poured milk. Charles ate his soup all up. "Tomorrow can we have it again?" he asked. "Maybe," said Dad. "But first, one bite of bread." Charles took a big, happy bite.

Emily sat in her car seat. She was hungry. "Mom, do you have a snack?"

Mom reached into the bag. "Let's look. I see an apple. The apple is a food."

Emily took a bite. Crunch! Then she looked out the window.

A cow stood by the fence. "Look, a cow! The cow is an animal," said Emily.

Next came a big truck. It was full of soft teddy bears. "Toys!" said Emily. "So many toys!"

Then the truck hit a bump. A teddy bear fell out. It bounced on the road. Dad stopped the car, very slow and safe.

Dad picked up the teddy bear. He knocked on the truck window. The driver looked back. He saw his teddy bear. He laughed and waved.

"You saved my teddy bear!" he said.

A little spider sat on the teddy bear's ear. It waved too, or maybe that was just the wind.

Emily giggled. "Mom, can we get a teddy bear too?"

Mom smiled. "Maybe at the next stop."

Emily hugged her apple and waited for the next window surprise.

Maeve sat on the bus with her dad. She looked in her bag. "Bunny is gone!" she said. "Oh no," said Dad. "Let's look for bunny."

Maeve looked under the seat. She saw a crayon. But no bunny. She looked by her feet. The bus went around a corner. Her crayon rolled away! The crayon rolled straight under the big seat ahead. Maeve leaned down and peeked.

"Mommy, look!" said a small boy. He was holding a soft white bunny. It had been sitting under his seat. "That is my bunny," said Maeve. "Thank you for catching him," said Dad. The boy smiled and gave bunny back. Maeve hugged bunny tight. "I found you," she whispered. Bunny's ears tickled her chin, and she giggled all the way home.

Sarah wanted to make a flower picture. She sat at the big table. Mom put down paper and glue.

Sarah found some paper petals. She put glue on a petal. She pressed it down. She lifted her finger. The petal came up too! It was stuck to her skin. "Oh no," said Sarah. "My petal will not stay."

Mom sat close by her. "Try pressing it longer," said Mom. Sarah pressed the petal again. She counted to three in her head. She lifted her finger slowly. This time the petal stayed on the paper. Sarah clapped her hands.

She glued more petals, one by one. She pressed each one and waited. Each petal stayed. Then she glued a yellow circle for the middle. Her flower was done.

Sarah held up her paper. "A flower for you!" she said. Mom smiled and put it on the fridge. Sarah looked at her sticky fingers. They felt yucky and stiff. "Wash time," said Mom. They washed their hands with warm, soapy water. The water ran bubbly and soft over Sarah's fingers.

Then Mom took Sarah's hand. They walked out to see the real flowers in the garden. A big red one nodded in the wind. "It looks like my picture," said Sarah.

Billie waited at the bus stop with her mother. The sun was out. It was sunny and hot. Billie took off her hat. "Where should I put it?" she asked. Her mother put the hat in the bag. The bus was coming soon.

Then the wind blew. It was windy! The wind pushed Billie's dress. It made the leaves dance. The wind pushed a paper cup along the ground. Billie laughed and chased the cup. The wind pushed it again. Billie saw that the wind moved things.

Then big drops fell. It was rainy! "Where is the rain going?" Billie asked. "On my head," said her mother. Her mother opened a thick umbrella. The rain went plip, plop on top. Billie stayed dry under it. Billie's puppy drank rain from a little puddle.

Then white flakes came down. It was snowy! Billie stuck out her tongue. A flake landed on it. The bus came at last. Billie and her mother climbed on. Billie waved at the snow through the big window. "Look, puppy, snow!" said Billie.

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Bennett wanted to make him feel happy at home. "What does Grandpa like?" Mom asked. "Tea!" said Bennett. So they went to the market. Bennett found a big red apple. He found a loaf of fresh bread. Then he saw a little tin of tea. "Grandpa can try this," he said.

At home, Mom put water in the kettle. She made it hot, and Bennett stood back. Mom dropped the tea bag in the cup. Bennett watched. The water began to turn brown. First it was light brown. Then it was dark brown. "It changed!" said Bennett. Mom poured in a little milk. The tea turned creamy.

Grandpa took a sip. "Mmm," he said. "You picked my favorite." Bennett grinned. Tomorrow he would try the red apple trick too.

Gabriel wanted to build a house for his teddy bear. He looked for shapes all over the house. He found a round plate. "A circle!" he said. He found a book with four sides the same. "A square!" He found a slice of bread with two long sides. "A rectangle!"

But he had no roof. Teddy's head was cold. Gabriel looked and looked. Then he saw Daddy folding a napkin. Daddy folded it corner to corner. The napkin made a triangle, with three pointy sides. "A triangle roof!" Gabriel said.

Gabriel put the circle under teddy for a rug. He made square walls from blocks. The rectangle was teddy's little bed. The triangle went on top. Teddy sat inside. Gabriel clapped his hands. The clap was loud. Teddy fell over, and Gabriel caught him with one arm. "Got you," Gabriel said. "No falling out of your new house."

Snow was falling outside the daycare window. The sky was gray and soft. Ryan pressed his nose to the cold glass.

Miss Pam rang the little bell. "Snack time," she said. "Ryan, can you bring cups? We need ten."

Ryan went to the shelf. He took one cup. "One," he said. He took another. "Two." He put them on his arm. He kept taking cups. "Three, four, five." Miss Pam began to hum a counting song. The other kids sang too. "Six, seven, eight." Ryan hummed along. He took more cups. "Nine, ten!"

He carried the cups to the table. But then the stack wobbled. The cups tipped over and rolled. Ryan picked them up one at a time. "One, two, three," he said, setting them down. Each cup got a number name. "Four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Every chair had a cup by it. Nothing rolled away this time.

Miss Pam smiled. "Ten cups for ten friends." Ryan sat down. He wore his snack bib with the red truck on it. He munched his crackers and looked at the snow.

"Ten crackers left," said his friend Ben, counting his plate. Ryan laughed and counted his too.

Lily put her cold milk cup on the table. "One cup, two carrots, three crackers," she said. She touched the cup. It was cold. She wanted it warm.

Ms. Rosa took the cup. She put it in a big machine. Lily watched from her little chair. The machine made a hum. It was fast. The cup went round and round.

Lily held a letter block. It was the letter L, for Lily. Her friend Sam held a small block. Hers was big. His was small. They stacked them up, big one first, then small one on top.

The machine stopped. Ms. Rosa brought the cup back. "Careful now," she said. "It is warm." Lily touched the side. It was warm, not cold anymore. The big machine made it warm, and the fast hum told her when it was done.

At the art table, Sam dipped his brush. He painted a red line, slow and slow. Lily painted a fast line, quick quick quick. The paint felt slimy on her fingers. She laughed.

"Snack time," Ms. Rosa called. Lily did not shout. She walked. She picked up her warm cup. One sip, two sips. "Warm milk," she said. Sam smiled at her over his big cracker.

Charlotte wanted to paint with her big brother, Sam. Sam had one red brush. Charlotte had one blue brush. But Sam had all the yellow paint.

"I want some yellow," said Charlotte. Sam looked at his cup. He poured some yellow into her cup. Charlotte painted a big sun. Sam painted a bee on the sun. The bee looked happy.

Then Charlotte grabbed Sam's paper. She wanted to paint on it too. Sam said, "Give it back. That one is mine." Charlotte gave it back slowly. Mom brought a new sheet. "Here is one for you," said Mom. Charlotte painted a fat, sleepy cat. The cat looked asleep under the sun. Sam laughed. "Nice cat," he said. "Now we can hang them side by side." Charlotte held up her painting next to his.

Zoey wanted to make a special picture for Gran. She needed stickers. She had only one star sticker. One was not enough.

Mom brought a big sheet. "Let's count the stars," said Mom. Zoey pointed. "One, two, three." Mom pointed too. "Four, five, six." Zoey touched each star. "Seven, eight, nine." One star was left in the corner. "Ten!" said Zoey. She smiled.

Zoey peeled the stars slowly. Some stars stuck to her finger. She tried again. Stick, press, smooth. The stars went on the paper one by one. At last the picture was done. Zoey held it up high. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten stars for Gran!"

Madison went to the library with her dad. The floor was shiny and a little slippery. She walked carefully.

She wanted the duck book. It was about ducks at the park. But the book sat on a high shelf. "How can I reach it?" she asked. Dad brought a little stool. "Try this," he said. Madison stepped up. The stool made her taller. Now her hand could touch the book. She pulled it down all by herself.

Then story time began. The librarian sang a song. "One, two, three, four, five," she sang. The children clapped. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Madison clapped too. She counted ducks on her lap. "One, two, three," she said. She tapped each duck as she said a number. Each tap matched one duck.

"How many ducks are there?" she asked Dad. They counted together. "Ten ducks," said Dad. Madison thought about that. Ten was a big number for such a small book.

At the desk, Dad helped her check the book out. The librarian stamped it. "Ten days," she said. Madison hugged the book tight and waved goodbye to the ducks.

Emilia woke up in her sunny bed. She wanted to help in the kitchen today. First she needed to get dressed. She pulled her red shirt on all by herself. It was backwards, but Mama smiled and helped her fix it.

In the kitchen, Mama made warm oatmeal. Emilia helped stir. She stirred and stirred, and the oatmeal got thick. Then she ate it all up. "Yum," she said. After eating, Emilia dropped some oatmeal on the floor. Papa got the broom. Emilia held the dustpan. Papa helped her sweep the crumbs into it. The floor was clean again.

Then Emilia heard the bath water run. It splashed and bubbled. Mama felt the water with her hand. "Just right," said Mama. Emilia washed her toes and her tummy. After the bath, she put on her soft pajamas. She yawned a big yawn. Papa read her one story. Emilia hugged her bear and fell fast asleep.

Sarah wanted to wash her hands all by herself. Dad stood in the doorway. "Can I turn the water?" she asked. "I will help," Dad said.

Sarah reached for the tap. Dad put his hand on top. "Let me turn the hot side," he said. Dad turned it a little. Steam came up. Sarah put her hand near it. "Ooh, it is warm like soup," she said. Dad turned the cold side. The steam went away. Sarah touched the water. It felt nice and cool now.

Then Sarah saw Dad's razor on the sink. It was shiny. She reached out. "Not that one," Dad said quickly. He moved it far away. "That is for grown-ups only." Sarah pulled her hand back. She looked at Dad. "Okay," she said.

Sarah washed her hands with soap. She made bubbles. She counted them, one, two, three. "I did it!" she said. Dad clapped. "Good job, Sarah." Sarah dried her hands on the old blue towel. "Can we wash again tomorrow?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. "We can wash every day." Sarah smiled and hung the towel on its hook.

Elijah sat in the big salon chair. It was his first haircut ever. The chair was too tall, so Mommy held his hand. Elijah wanted to see what the lady would do.

The lady picked up her comb. She combed his hair up, up, up. Then she snipped with her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. They landed on the cape like dark snow.

"Look," said Elijah. "My hair came off!"

The lady laughed. "The comb lifts it. Then the scissors cut it. That is how my work goes."

She combed again. Snip, snip. More dark bits fell. Elijah patted the cape. The bits slid off his hand. He giggled.

Then the lady turned the chair to the mirror. Elijah looked. His hair was short now!

"My head looks small," he said.

"Your head looks just right," said Mommy.

The lady brushed his neck with a soft brush. It tickled. Elijah wiggled like a worm.

She held up the mirror in back. Elijah saw the back of his own head. He waved at it. The boy in the mirror waved back.

"That works," said Elijah. "Two of me!"

Grace held her mama's hand in the school hallway. The hall was long. Grace could not see her classroom door.

"Where is my room?" said Grace.

"Look at the doors," said Mama. "Each door has a picture."

Grace saw a door with a cat. She saw a door with a sun. Then she saw a door with a red balloon, just like the red balloon on her bag.

Grace let go of the balloon. It floated up and bumped the door with the cat. That was not her door. Grace pulled it back down. "Silly balloon," she said.

She walked on. The balloon bumped the door with a sun. Not that door either. Grace pulled it back again. "Silly, silly balloon," said Mama, laughing.

Then the balloon floated up to the red balloon door. It bumped the picture. A teacher opened the door. "Hello, Grace," she said. "We have been waiting for you."

Grace stepped in and found a little chair with her name on it. She sat down and waved. "Bye, Mama! This is my last stop!"

Milan went to the park with his toy elephant. He put it down by the bench. Then he ran to the slide. When he came back, the elephant was gone.

"Where did it go?" said Milan. He looked with his eyes. He saw grass, rocks and a red ball. He listened with his ears. He heard birds and a dog barking. He sniffed with his nose. He smelled popcorn near the swings. He touched the grass with his hands. It was soft and a little wet.

His mom said, "Follow your nose." Milan walked toward the popcorn smell. He saw his elephant under the snack cart. A girl was holding it. "Is this yours?" she asked. "Yes! I know that elephant anywhere," said Milan. He hugged it. "You are a lucky elephant," he said. "And I found you with my eyes, my ears, my nose and my hands."

The girl laughed. "Want one thing more?" she said. She held out a small cup. Her dad had bought warm popcorn for everyone. Milan ate one piece with his mouth. It was salty and good. He munched and smiled. "Best park day ever," he said.

Ivy sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. She was a little scared of the check-up. Her tummy felt jumpy.

The doctor came in with a smile. "Ivy, can you be my helper today?" she asked. "We are a team." Ivy nodded. First the doctor held up a small picture. "Tell me what you see." Ivy looked with her eyes. "A duck!" she said. Next the doctor tapped a little bell. Ivy heard it with her ears. "It rings!" Then the doctor held something soft. Ivy touched it with her fingers. "It feels like my teddy," she said. The doctor had a sticker that smelled like strawberries. Ivy sniffed with her nose. "It smells sweet!" Last, the doctor gave her a safe taste strip. Ivy put it on her tongue. "It tastes like nothing," she said, and she laughed.

"Good helper," said the doctor. "Now pick a bandaid." Ivy chose a shiny one with stars. She pressed it on with her finger. "My eyes saw this one," she said proudly. The doctor gave her a high five.

Maria sat on the small bench at Miss Penny's music studio. She wanted to make music like Miss Penny did. But the big drum would not make a sound for her.

"Tap it," said Miss Penny. "Soft hands first."

Maria tapped soft. The drum made a tiny sound. Tap, tap, tap. It was small like a mouse.

"Now tap hard," said Miss Penny.

Maria lifted her hand and tapped hard. BOOM! The drum made a big sound. It was big like a lion!

Maria tapped soft. Tiny sound. She tapped hard. BOOM!

"My hands make it loud!" said Maria. She tapped soft, then hard, soft, then hard.

Miss Penny laughed. "Yes. Your hands are in charge."

Maria wanted one more big boom. She tapped hard with both hands. BOOM! BOOM!

The window shook a little. The room felt warm, like the sun had come in. Maria thought the drum might feel hot from so much noise.

"Drums can build a big song," said Miss Penny. "Tap with me."

They tapped together. Soft, soft, BOOM! Soft, soft, BOOM!

Maria tapped her knees. Then she clapped her hands. Then she reached up for the drum one more time.

"BOOM!" she said, and tapped again.

Abigail looked out the window. Snow was everywhere! School was closed today. "Snow day!" said Mom.

Abigail put on her boots. Her coat was red. Her mittens were wide and puffy. She and Mom walked to the park. The snow went crunch, crunch under her boots.

Abigail wanted to make a snowball. She scooped up snow. She pressed it with her mittens. But the snow would not stick. It fell apart in a pile. "Oh no," said Abigail.

"Try the sticky snow by the slide," said Mom. "The sun sat on it. It got warm and squishy."

Abigail scooped snow by the slide. She pressed it. It stuck! She made a big round snowball. Then she made a little one on top. "A snow frog!" said Abigail. She clapped her mittens.

The snow frog sat on the slide. Abigail smiled wide. "More snow!" she said.

Isaac wanted to make pancakes for his family. He found a bowl and a spoon. His dad said, "I will pour the milk. You can stir."

Isaac stirred and stirred. Then he dropped in a few blueberries. One blueberry sat on top. It would not sink.

"Why won't it go down?" Isaac asked.

Dad smiled. "Stir harder and see."

Isaac stirred fast. The blueberry popped under the batter. Now it was hiding inside. Isaac laughed. "I made it hide!"

Dad poured circles onto the hot pan. Isaac watched from his stool. The pancakes got little bubbles on top. "Look, Dad! Bubbles!"

"That means they are ready to flip," said Dad.

He flipped one high in the air. It landed with a plop. Isaac clapped his hands.

The pancakes went onto a red plate. Mom and the baby came out to the backyard table. Everyone ate and ate.

"The best pancakes ever," said Mom.

Isaac grinned. "I hid the blueberries!"

Luke ran into the storytime room. He was going to get his very own library card! The librarian smiled at him. "Say your name," she said. "Luke!" he said, loud and round like a drum. She typed his name. Then she gave him a card with a red bird on it. Luke held it with both hands.

"Can I pick a book?" Luke asked. "Yes," said Mom. "You can take it home." Luke found a book about a seed that grows into a big sunflower. "I want to keep it forever!" he said.

The librarian shook her head. "You have to bring it back," she said. "Other kids want to read it too." Luke hugged the book tight. Then he saw a girl looking at the sunflower book. She wanted it too. Luke handed the book to the librarian. "I'll bring it back soon," he said. The girl waved at him. Luke waved back, holding his new card up high.

Kayden ran to the big sports field. Papa held his hand. "The game starts soon!" said Papa.

Kayden sat on the grass with Mama and Nia. Lots of people came to watch. The players ran and kicked the ball. The crowd clapped and cheered.

But then the wind blew hard. The wind pushed a big paper flag. The flag fell down, flop! Kayden stood up. "The wind did that!" he said.

Kayden picked up the flag. He held it up high. The wind blew again. The flag went flap, flap, flap. When the wind stopped, the flag hung still.

Papa laughed. "Hold it tight, Kayden." Kayden held it tight. He waved it when the wind came. The crowd saw the flag flapping. They cheered even louder.

The weather was not bad at all now. The sun came out. The players kicked the ball into the net. "Goal!" everyone shouted.

Kayden waved his flag. It was the best game ever. "Again! Again!" he said. Papa said, "Next week we come back." Kayden smiled big. The flag went flap, flap, flap one more time.

Violet was on the swim team. Today was the big pool day. She put on her little red swimsuit. "Kick, kick, kick," said Coach Amy.

Violet sat on the edge. She wanted to splash the farthest. She kicked her legs in the water. Splash! It was a small splash. The water felt cool on her toes.

Then Violet watched Ben. Ben was bigger. He moved his whole legs up and down. His splash went way out. It even hit the wall!

Violet wondered about that. She tried a big kick with her whole leg. Up and down, up and down. Splash! The water flew far. "Look at me!" she called. Coach Amy clapped. "Nice big kick, Violet!"

Ben gave her a thumbs up. Violet kicked again. Up and down, up and down. The water splashed all the way to Ben. He laughed and splashed her back. "Got you!" said Violet.

Everly went to the big library with her dad. She held his hand in the reading room. Today she would get her very own library card.

"Can I keep the book forever?" Everly asked.

"Let's ask the library lady," said Dad.

The library lady smiled. "You can take it home," she said. "Then you bring it back on this day." She pointed to a stamp inside the book.

Everly picked a book about a cow who could blow big bubbles. She carried it to the desk. The lady scanned her new card. Beep!

At home, Everly read the book four times. She read it to her teddy bear. The cow blew a bubble as big as a room.

Then the day on the stamp came. Everly gave the book back to Dad. They took it to the library together.

"Someone else can read about my cow now," Everly said. "And I can get a new book!"

She skipped to the shelf, and the library lady said, "Back already? You are quick!"

Emily had a library book about a bunny. The bunny had soft, curly fur on the cover. Emily wanted to keep the book forever.
