At bedtime, Dad said, "Tomorrow we take the book back. It is due. Other kids want to read about the bunny too." Emily held the book tight. "Can we read it one more time?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad.

Dad opened the front cover. "See the words?" he said. "They say the bunny's name." Emily looked. The marks on the page meant something. Dad turned the pages one by one, front to back. The bunny found a carrot at the end.

The next day, Emily gave the book back. Then the library lady smiled. "Look," she said. "The bunny has a new book, and you can borrow it too." Emily hugged the new book. "I will remember to bring it back," she said. On the way home, the cool air tickled her face. She held the new book all the way.

Rowan was hungry. He looked in his toy basket. "No snack here," he said. "Just my ball and my truck." Dad was grilling lunch in the yard. Rowan wanted to help find the food.

A bird hopped by the fence. Then a squirrel came too. The squirrel found a nut on the ground. It held the nut and ate it. Rowan watched. The squirrel looked in one place and found food. So Rowan could look too.

He ran to the little cooler by the table. He opened the lid. There were apples and cheese inside. "Dad! I found the foods!" he called. Dad smiled and handed him a cold apple from the frozen ice pack spot. Rowan took a big bite. The squirrel ran up the tree with its nut.

Zayn ran out to the baseball diamond. He wanted to hit the ball far. His coach tossed the ball. Zayn swung the bat. He slipped in the dirt and fell on his bottom. "Ouch," said Zayn. His teammate Ben laughed, but not in a mean way. "The dirt is loose here," said Ben. "Watch me." Ben dug his shoes into the dirt. He made two deep little holes for his feet. Then Ben swung. He did not slip. The ball went far, far away. Zayn stood up. "Can I try that too?" he asked. "Sure," said Ben. Zayn dug his shoes in. He made his own deep holes. He swung the bat. No slip! The ball rolled all the way to the fence. "Again!" said Zayn, and dug his feet in one more time.

Beatrice woke up and looked out the window. The world was white! No school today. "Snow day!" said Mama.

Beatrice wanted to sled down the big hill. But her sled would not go. It just sat there. Papa pushed her sled. It still did not move. "Too much snow is soft," said Papa with a smile.

Then Beatrice saw Papa stomp on the snow. His boots made the snow flat. The flat part was shiny and hard. "Stomp, stomp, stomp!" said Beatrice. She stomped her little boots too. They made a path all the way down the hill.

Beatrice sat on her sled. Papa gave one push. Zoom! The sled went fast on the flat, shiny path. "Faster!" laughed Beatrice. "Wheee!"

After sledding, they went home. Mama made cocoa. A snow worm poked out of a pile by the door. "Hello, different little friend," said Beatrice. She pretended to feed the snow worm a pretend cookie. Then she took a big sip. "Warm tummy," said Beatrice. "More sledding tomorrow!"

Everly sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. She wanted a sticker, but first she had to wait. "Can I have a sticker now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mom. "First the doctor will look at you."

The nurse came in. She held a small light. "Can you follow the light with your eyes?" she asked. Everly's eyes watched the light go up and down. The nurse smiled. Then the nurse tapped Everly's knee. Everly's leg jumped all by itself. "Why did my leg do that?" Everly asked. "It jumps when you tap it," said the nurse. Everly tapped her own knee. The leg jumped again. She laughed.

Next the doctor came. He looked in Everly's ears. He looked in her nose. He looked in her mouth. "Say ahh," he said. Everly said, "Ahh." Then he gave her a little stick to press with her finger. It felt soft and bumpy.

Then the nurse gave Everly a cookie. Everly smelled it first. It smelled sweet. She took a bite. It tasted good. "You used your nose and your tongue," said the nurse. "Where is my sticker?" Everly asked. The nurse put a shiny star sticker on her hand. Everly touched it with one finger. It was smooth. "Star!" she said.

Anna was afraid of the big drum. It sat in the band room. It was as tall as her tummy.

"I want to bang it," said Anna. "But it looks too big."

Mr. Pip held out a small drum. "Try this one," he said. "Tap it soft."

Anna tapped one finger. The drum made a tiny sound. Tappity.

Anna tapped harder. The drum made a big sound. BOOM!

Anna jumped. Then she laughed. "My hand did that!"

She tapped soft again. Tappity. She tapped big again. BOOM!

"Now you know your drum," said Mr. Pip. "Soft hands, small sound. Big hands, big sound."

Anna played a song. Tappity, BOOM, BOOM, tappity.

Tommy covered his ears. "Too loud!"

Anna tapped soft for Tommy. Tappity, tappity.

"Better," said Tommy.

After band, the teacher gave out cookies. Anna held her cookie up like a drumstick.

"Don't you dare," said Mr. Pip.

BOOM went the crumbs on the table. Anna laughed and ate her drumstick cookie all up.

Mackenzie put on her red birthday shoe. One shoe was red and one was blue. "Silly shoes!" said Daddy. Everyone laughed.

It was Mackenzie's birthday party at the bowling alley. Grandma, Grandpa, and her friend Nora came too. Mackenzie wanted to knock down the pins. All ten pins!

She picked a little blue ball. She pushed it with both hands. The ball went slow. Then the ball went into the gutter. No pins fell down. "Oh no," said Mackenzie.

"Try again," said Nora. Nora rolled her ball. Her ball went straight. It hit the pins. Crash! The pins fell down. Mackenzie watched. The ball hit one pin. That pin fell over. Then it bumped the next pin. That pin fell too. One pin made another pin fall!

Mackenzie took her turn again. She pushed her ball hard. It rolled down the middle. It hit the big pin. That pin tipped. It knocked three more pins. "Strike!" shouted Grandpa. "One pin helped the ball!" said Mackenzie.

After bowling, they ate pizza. The popcorn was salty and yummy. Then Daddy carried out the cake. He lit the candles, all safe. Mackenzie blew and blew. Out went every candle. "Happy birthday, dear Mackenzie!" everyone sang.

Then Grandma brought out one more box. It had a bow on top. "For the birthday girl," said Grandma. Mackenzie opened it. Inside was her very own little bowling pin.

Livia could not find her bunny. Bunny had one floppy ear and a pink bow. She looked under the table. No bunny. She looked in the dress-up box. No bunny.

Miss Anna sat down next to her. "Tell me where you played today," she said. Livia began to speak. "I played at the sand table. Then I read books on the big rug." Miss Anna smiled. "Let's look there."

Livia shook the rug. The rug made a soft whoosh. Something small rolled out from under it. It was a toy coin from the money tin! Then Livia spotted a pink ear sticking out too.

"Bunny!" she cried. She picked bunny up and hugged her tight.

"How did bunny get there?" Livia asked. Miss Anna laughed. "The rug was hiding her."

Livia put the coin back in the tin. She held bunny's paw all the way to snack time.

Peyton ran to the park with Dad. She wanted to find her red ball. It was lost somewhere in the grass.

Peyton used her eyes to see. She saw swings. She saw a black dog. "No ball," she said. She used her ears to listen. She heard a squeak, squeak, squeak. The swings went up and down. Still no ball.

Then Peyton used her nose. She sniffed the air. She smelled popcorn! Dad said, "Let's look near the popcorn cart." Peyton used her hands to touch the grass. It felt soft and tickly. Her fingers found something round. "My ball!" she shouted. She hugged it. Dad gave her cold popcorn to taste. Mmm, it was salty. Peyton laughed. "Eyes, ears, nose, hands, tongue. I found it all!" The black dog wagged its tail.

It was Jayden's birthday at the park. His mom put four candles on the cake. Grandpa lit them with a match. Jayden watched from his spot.

"Make a wish," said Mom. "Then blow."

Jayden blew. The little flames bent. But they came back up. He blew again, harder. The flames went out, all four.

"How did they go out?" Jayden asked.

"My wind did it," said his sister, Nia. "Watch." She puffed, and her one candle went dark too.

Then the wind in the trees blew. The napkins lifted off the table. But the candles stayed out. No flames came back.

"One candle, two candles, three candles, four," said Grandma. "All done."

Jayden laughed. "The wind outside is strong like my wind!"

He cut the air with his hand, whoosh, whoosh. Nia clapped. Then everyone sang the birthday song, and Jayden blew one more time, at nothing at all, just for fun.

Jaxon ran to the red slide at the park. A girl was already at the top. "My turn next," she called down. Jaxon stopped and waited. He watched her zoom down, fast. Could waiting be worth it? He thought maybe it could. "Your turn now," the girl said. "You waited, so you go." Jaxon climbed up the ladder. He slid down, and the wind rushed past his ears. Whee!

Next Jaxon found the sandbox. A boy had all the trucks. Three trucks, and only one boy. Jaxon wanted a truck so much. "Can I have one?" Jaxon asked. The boy looked at his trucks. Then he pushed a blue truck across the sand. "Here," the boy said. "You take this one." They made a big sand hill together. Two trucks made a bigger hill than one truck. Jaxon noticed that.

Then Jaxon saw a small pond. A turtle sat on a rock in the sun. A sign stood by the water. Jaxon's dad read it out loud. "The sign says we stay out of the pond." Jaxon nodded. Then a dog ran by and jumped in. Splash! The turtle slipped off the rock. The turtle swam away under the water. "Bye bye, turtle," Jaxon said. He waved at the rock.

On the way home, Jaxon held his dad's strong hand. He looked back at the slide. Kids were going down, one by one. One by one, like a line of little ants. "Can we come back tomorrow?" Jaxon asked. "Yes," said Dad. "We can come back tomorrow."

Athena had a little bunny toy. She brought it to daycare. But now bunny was gone.

Athena looked in the toy box. No bunny. She looked under the table. No bunny. Her friend Mia helped her look too.

It was winter, so snack was inside today. The teacher cut apples into slices. They were crunchy and good. Athena ate her snack. Then she looked some more.

Mia pulled a big rug back to sweep. The rug moved. And there was bunny! The rug had been hiding bunny all along. Athena picked bunny up and hugged him tight.

"Thank you, Mia," said Athena.

"Let's put bunny in your cubby next time," said Mia.

Athena smiled. She put bunny in her pocket, where he could not hide. Then she and Mia went to build a big tower of blocks together.

Isaiah held Mama's hand at the store. "Let's find your juice," said Mama. Isaiah loved juice. He wanted it fast!

First they passed the toy aisle. Isaiah saw a red ball and a little drum. He tapped the drum. Boom! It made a big sound. He laughed.

Next they passed the pet aisle. A puppy barked. Woof, woof! A fish swam in a small tank. Isaiah waved at the fish. The fish swam away fast.

Then Mama turned down a new aisle. It was full of food. Apples, bread, and milk! And there, on a long shelf, was the juice. Isaiah grabbed a box. It was apple juice, his favorite!

But wait. The cart had a toy duck in it. Isaiah did not put it there. He quacked, and Mama laughed. "Silly duck wants juice too," she said.

At home, Mama poured juice into Isaiah's cup. He drank it all up. "More juice, Mama! Please!"

Leah sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, bump. Her teddy bear slipped off her lap. It fell down by her feet, too deep for her little arms to reach.

"Mom, can you help me, please?" Leah asked. Mom reached back with one hand. She got the teddy bear. "Thank you, Mom," Leah said. Mom smiled at her in the mirror.

Then Leah sang a song. "One bear, one girl, one long car ride," she sang. Dad laughed at her joke. At a stop, Dad handed Leah a juice box. "Thank you," she said. She took a big sip. Oops. A drop fell on the seat. "Sorry, Dad," Leah said. "That is okay," said Dad. He wiped it with a napkin. The car went on. Leah hugged her bear and watched the trees swing by the window. "Home soon," said Mom.

Maeva went to the store with Mama. Near the apples there was a little red box. It was full of books. "One, two, three books," said Maeva, tapping each one. The top book had a fish on it. Blue fish. They could swim in deep, deep water. Maeva wanted that book. She wanted to keep it forever.

Mama pointed at the front of the book. There were little marks there. Words. "Those marks say the name," said Mama. Maeva traced them with her finger. Then she opened the book at the front, where the story begins. Page one. Page two. Page three. The fish swam and swam.

"You can take it home," said Mama. "But we bring it back soon. Then someone else can read it too." Maeva hugged the book to her chest. She sniffed the pages. They smelled like paper and apples. At home, she turned every page, one by one, all the way to the back. The very last page had a big fish. It looked right at her. "Hello, fish," said Maeva.

Owen wanted the red truck. But Max had the red truck. Max was playing with it by the blocks.

Owen grabbed at the truck. The truck fell. It hit Max's foot. Max began to cry.

"Sorry, Max," said Owen. Miss Ali came over. "You can ask for help," she said. Owen took a big breath. "Can I have a turn, please?" he asked.

Max sniffed. He held out the truck. "Okay. Your turn."

"Thank you," said Owen. He pushed the truck across the carpet. Vroom! It went far under the windy-day picture on the wall.

Then Max whispered, "It is my birthday on Friday." Owen smiled. "Then you go first with the truck," he said.

Max clapped. The two boys sat side by side. The red truck went back and forth, back and forth, all morning long.

Ryan ran into the music studio. "I want to play the drum!" he said. Miss Kim smiled. She put a big drum in front of him. Ryan hit it with the drumstick. Nothing happened. The drum made no sound at all.

"Why is it quiet?" Ryan asked. Miss Kim said, "Look at the drum top." Ryan looked. The drum top was soft and loose. It looked like a saggy blanket. "Can we fix it?" he asked. Miss Kim turned a little knob on the side. She passed the drumstick back to Ryan.

Ryan hit the drum again. BOOM! The drum top was tight now. Tight drum, big sound. Ryan hit it fast. Boom, boom, boom! His tummy jumped with the beat. Miss Kim clapped. Ryan felt very proud. "Again!" he shouted. Boom! Boom! Boom!

Mya stood at the school gate. The gate was huge and red. Mya did not want to let go of Papa's hand.

A big yellow bus stopped by the gate. The door opened with a hiss. Out came a girl with two braids. The girl waved at the bus. The bus door waved back, kind of, and then the bus drove away.

"Where did the bus go?" Mya asked.

"Home," said the girl with braids. "It comes back. We just have to wait."

Mya held the gate with one hand. She waited. She counted the cars that passed. One car. Two cars. Three cars. Then the bell rang, and the gate opened by itself.

"Look, Papa! I held the gate, and now it moves!"

"That's the magic of school," said Papa. "Every morning, the gate opens."

Inside, Mya saw a picture of a horse on the wall. A teacher smiled and said, "Hello, Mya. Come see our class horse. His name is Sam."

Mya looked back at the gate. Papa waved. Mya waved too, and then she ran to the horse. "Does Sam like to wait?" she asked.

"He waits for you every day," said the teacher.

Zayn was a small boy on a big trip. He was in a hotel room with Mama and Baba. His toy bunny was missing. "Where is Bunny?" he asked.

Zayn looked under the bed. No Bunny. He looked near the chair. No Bunny. " Bunny likes to hide," said Mama with a smile. "Bunny is silly," said Zayn.

Then Zayn saw the curtains. They went all the way to the floor. He slid the curtain to one side. Bunny was there! "I found you!" said Zayn. The curtain had made a hiding spot. Now Zayn knew a trick. He slid the other curtain too. No bunny there, just his shoe. "My shoe was hiding too!" said Zayn. Mama laughed and laughed. Baba put Bunny on the pillow. "Sleep tight, Bunny," said Zayn. Bunny slid down the pillow, soft and slow.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Amira showed her the backyard. "This is my swing," said Amira. "This is my sand box. And these are my flowers."

The flowers were droopy. Their heads hung down low. "Oh dear," said Grandma. "They look sad." Amira wondered why. Had they lost their sun? Were they too hot?

Grandma filled the watering can at the tap. Amira helped hold the handle. They poured water on the dirt, one flower, two flowers, three flowers, four. The water sank down into the soil. It went slip, slip, slip.

The next morning, Amira ran outside. She stopped and stared. The flowers were standing up tall! Their heads were high, not low. "Grandma, come see!" she called.

Grandma came out with her warm sweater on. She sat in the sun and smiled. "The water helped them," said Grandma. "They drank it all up."

Amira patted the dirt around the roots. "I will keep you watered," she told the flowers. She counted them again. One, two, three, four. All tall.

Then she ran to the porch. She picked up her woolly toy sheep and held it out. "Grandma, my sheep is thirsty too," she said. "Can sheep drink from a cup?"

Beatrice sat in a big chair at the mall. It was her first haircut. The chair was too tall, so Mama lifted her up.

The hairdresser wore a shiny key on her belt. Beatrice liked to watch it swing. The hairdresser put a cape on Beatrice. The cape was not bad at all. It felt soft.

Then the hairdresser picked up her scissors. Snip, snip. A little piece of hair fell down. It landed on the cape. It stuck there, like a small brown line.

Beatrice pointed. "It stays!" she said.

"It sticks to the cape," said the hairdresser. "Want to see more fall?"

Beatrice nodded. Snip, snip. More hair fell. More little lines stuck to her lap. She counted them with one finger.

"Pretty," said Beatrice.

Then the hairdresser brushed the cape. All the little lines slid off, one by one. Beatrice watched every one fall to the floor.

"My turn is done," said the hairdresser. "Look in the mirror."

Beatrice looked. Her hair was short and smooth. She smiled at the girl in the glass, and the girl smiled back.

Yesterday, Evelyn found a big puddle at the park. She splashed in it with her red boots. The water went splash, splash, splash.

Today the puddle was little. "Oh no," said Evelyn. "My puddle is small." Mama sat on the wide bench nearby. "The sun is out now," Mama said. "The sun makes wet things dry."

Evelyn watched the sun shine on the puddle. She sat down. She waited. She looked at a bird. She looked at the sky.

Later, the puddle was just a dark spot on the ground. Evelyn stomped her boot. It did not splash. It went tap.

"Come back tomorrow," Evelyn said to the spot. "Maybe it will rain again."

Mama laughed softly. "Maybe it will," she said. "And you can bring your boots."

Evelyn held her boots in her hands. She gave the empty spot a big pat, like a present for tomorrow.

"Bye bye, puddle," she said.

Leah wanted to find the letter S in class. It was hiding from her. She looked on the big chart. She looked on the door. No S anywhere.

Teacher Mia held up a card. "What sound does this one make?" The card had a curvy letter on it. "S goes sssss," said Teacher Mia, like a snake.

Then Leah heard it. Sun. Sun began with ssss! She whispered, "Ssss, sun." Her friend Ben laughed. "You sound like a leaky tire," he said. Leah laughed too. "Ssss, snake. Ssss, sock. Ssss, Ben!" Ben put his hands on his ears. "Not me! I start with B!"

The hard part was the curvy shape. Leah drew an S on her paper. It slipped and looked like a wiggly worm. Ben said, "That is a sleepy S." Leah tried again. Slow and curvy. There it was.

She ran to the rug and picked up her sun toy. "This starts with S," she said. "Ssss, sun." Teacher Mia gave her a star sticker. Leah stuck it on her paper, right next to the wiggly worm.

Jules ran to the community garden with a little shovel. He wanted to grow big carrots. His grandma helped him dig the soil. Jules dropped the tiny seeds into the dark dirt. Then he patted them down, pat, pat, pat.

Every day Jules came back to look. Nothing grew. Nothing at all! Jules felt worried. "Where are my carrots?" he asked. Grandma pointed at the sky. "No rain," she said. "Seeds need water to grow." Jules got his small watering can. He poured water on the dirt. Splash, splash, splash.

The next day, something green peeked out! Tiny leaves! "It grew!" Jules shouted. He watered the leaves every day. Soon the leaves grew tall and bushy. Then Jules saw a surprise. A green frog sat under the leaves! The frog hopped away, hop, hop, hop.

At last, grandma pulled up the carrots. They were big and red! Jules held one up high. "Look what water made grow!" he said. Grandma laughed and clapped her hands. "Carrots for dinner," she said. Jules hugged his red carrot tight.

Abigail was at Grandma's house. She wanted to paint a big green hill. But Grandma had no green paint.

Grandma set out the paints. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. No green anywhere.

"Where did the green go?" Abigail wondered.

She dipped her brush in blue. She made a blue hill. Then she dipped in yellow. She painted yellow on top of the blue hill.

The hill turned green!

"Look, Grandma!" said Abigail. "Blue and yellow made green!"

Grandna smiled. "Try red and yellow too," she said.

Abigail mixed red and yellow. It made orange, like a pumpkin.

After all that painting, Abigail gave a big yawn. The friendly old cat curled up beside her. Together they watched the sun go down over the green hill.

"Blue and yellow," Abigail whispered. "Green."

Elena was at Grandma's house. She wanted to feed the fish in the pond. The fish were big and orange. They liked to swim near the little bridge.

Elena could not find the fish food. The jar was too high on a shelf. She tried to reach it. Grandma said, "Stop, that is not safe. Ask me for help." Elena said, "Please, Grandma, can you help me?" Grandma smiled. She got the jar down with a long grabber tool. "Thank you," said Elena.

Elena ran to the pond. She was so happy, the jar slipped. It fell in the wet grass. Some food spilled out. "Sorry, Grandma," said Elena. "That is okay," said Grandma. "The grass likes it too."

Then they sprinkled the food together. The fish came fast. Their tails splashed. Elena felt the cool air on her face. "It is getting late," said Grandma. "One more handful, then we go in." Elena threw the food. The fish gobbled it up. Grandma held her hand as they walked to the door.

Arnaud put on his pajamas. He was happy because tonight he had his favorite toy, a soft brown cow. He hugged the cow tight.

Dad turned on the little night light. It made a warm yellow glow. Then Dad said, "Look at the wall." A big dark shape sat there. It had long ears. Arnaud did not know what it was. His tummy felt tight. He was scared. He pulled his blanket up to his chin.

"That is my hand," said Dad. Dad held his hand near the light. The shape on the wall moved its ears. It was only a shadow! Arnaud laughed out loud. Dad helped Arnaud put his hand near the light too. A small shadow grew on the wall. Arnaud opened and closed his fingers. The shadow wiggled. He felt so excited. He made a dog shadow. Then he made a bird shadow with two hands.

Then Arnaud made a sad face. He wanted a cow shadow, but his hands would not make one. "Too hard," he said. His mouth turned down. Dad sat on the bed. "Make a point with your fingers," said Dad. Arnaud tried. He made two little horns on top. "Moo!" he shouted. Now it was a cow shadow.

Dad turned the big light off. The yellow glow stayed on. Arnaud held his cow close to his chest. His eyes got heavy. He yawned one big yawn. Dad kissed his head and said, "Time to sleep." Arnaud closed his eyes. The little shadow hand on the wall waved good night.

Elijah went to the store with his mom. In the corner was a little library shelf. Elijah found a book about a cute puppy. The cover had words on it. "That says puppy," said Mom. Elijah pointed at the words. Then he opened the book. He turned the pages one by one. First page, then the next, all the way to the end. "It goes front to back," he said.

Elijah held the book tight. "I want to keep it forever," he said. Mom shook her head. "We borrow it," she said. "We take it home. Then we bring it back on the due day." A lady at the desk stamped a paper. Elijah looked at the stamp. "So other kids can read it too," said Mom.

At home, Elijah read the puppy book two times. He skip-skipped to his room with it. That night he dreamed about the puppy. In the morning he said, "We take it back on the big day." Mom smiled. "Yes," she said. "And then we can borrow one more."

Layla woke up at Grandma's house. It was a sunny morning. She wanted to help Grandma make bread. Grandma said, "First we use our hands." Layla patted the soft dough. "Hands feel!" said Layla. "That is touch," said Grandma. "One."

Then Grandma put the bread in the oven. Grandma did that part, because the oven was hot. Layla watched from her chair. Soon the kitchen smelled warm and sweet. Layla sniffed with her nose. "Nose smells!" said Layla. "That is smell," said Grandma. "Two."

The bread came out. Grandma cut one slice. Layla took a bite. "My tongue tastes it!" said Layla. "Yum. That is taste. Three." Grandma rang a little bell. Layla's ears heard it. "Ears hear! Four," she said. Then Layla looked at her favorite slice, still warm. "My eyes see it! Five!" Grandma laughed. "All five," said Grandma. Layla counted on her fingers, one by one. "Hands, nose, tongue, ears, eyes." Then she took another big bite.

Henry was at Grandma's house. He had a cold. His nose was stuffy. He wanted to play outside. But the sky was cloudy. Grandma said, "Rest today."

Henry sat at the table. He felt grumpy. Grandma made him warm soup. She stirred the big pot. The pot made steam. Little white puffs floated up.

Henry leaned over his bowl. The warm steam touched his face. He sniffed. His nose felt better. He sniffed again. It opened up. "I can smell it!" he said.

He ate the soup slowly. More steam rose. More sniffs came. His nose was all clear now. Grandma smiled. "You want more?" she asked. Henry nodded. She ladled a second bowl from the pot.

"Tomorrow we can go to the store," Grandma said. "When your nose is all better." Henry blew on his spoon. The steam curled up. He watched it go. "More steam, please," he said.

Arthur sat on the big couch. He had a cold. His nose was red and his sock feet were warm under a blanket.

Mom brought him a cup of warm water with honey. Steam rose up from the cup. "Look at the steam, Arthur," said Mom. "What does it do?" The little cloud floated up. Then it went away. Arthur breathed in. The warm air felt soft in his nose. His nose opened up! He could smell Mom's soup in the kitchen.

Arthur took another breath. Where did the steam go now? It went up to the ceiling. It did not come back down. The cup got cooler in his hands. When the steam went away, the water was not hot anymore.

Arthur sniffed the air. "Soup!" he said. "I can smell it again." His tummy made a little growl. Mom smiled. "More warm water first," she said. Arthur held the cup. New steam curled up, up, up. He watched it all the way to the ceiling.

Jules had a runny nose today. He had to stay home. Mama said his body needed rest.

Jules wanted to see out the window. But the window was all white. He could not see the birds.

In the kitchen, Mama filled a big pot. She put it on the stove. Mama kept Jules far from the hot stove. He stood by the table.

The pot went plop, plop, plop. Steam rose up. The steam floated high. It went all the way to the window.

Jules looked at the window. The white got wet. Then his finger made a line in it. He drew a big heart. He drew a sun too.

The window opened a little bit. Cool air came in. Slowly, the heart went away. The sun went away too.

Jules waited. More steam came up. The window turned white again. He drew the heart one more time.

Papa came in with soup. "Is that my heart on the window?" he asked.

"That one is for you," said Jules. He drew a little heart next to it.

Harper ran to the fence. The sheep were waiting there.

"I want to learn my senses today," she said. Grandma smiled. "Then let's go!"

First Harper peeked at a sheep. "I see it with my eyes!" she said. The sheep was white and fluffy.

Next she heard a loud "Baa!" She covered her ears. "My ears heard that!"

Harper touched the sheep's soft wool. "My hands feel it," she said. "So soft!"

Grandma picked an apple. Harper smelled it. "My nose smells it. Yum!"

Then Grandma cut the apple with her knife. She gave Harper a small piece. Harper tasted it. "My mouth tastes it! Sweet!"

Harper jumped up and down. "Eyes, ears, hands, nose, mouth!" she said. "I know all five!"

The sheep went "Baa!" again, loud and long.

"Even you know that was right," Harper said.

Matthew wanted to play house at daycare. But the baby doll was already taken. Mia held the doll and rocked it in her arms.

Matthew felt sad. He looked around the room. Then he saw a teddy bear on the shelf. It was tall and soft. He picked it up. He wrapped it in a small blanket. "You are my baby bear," he said.

Mia watched him. She put a toy bottle to her doll's mouth. The doll made a little drinking sound. Matthew listened. He found a toy bottle too. He held it to the bear's mouth. "Drink, baby bear," he said. Mia smiled at him.

Then Miss Anne came over. "Time to cook dinner," she said. She pretended to stir a pot. Matthew gave his bear a hug. He put the bear in a little chair. "Sit here while I cook," he said. Matthew remembered the shiny coin in his pocket. He took it out. "Here is money for the food," he said. Mia laughed and took the coin. "Thank you," she said. "Come again!"

Kinsley sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump over the road. She was going to Grandma's house. Yesterday, Kinsley picked peaches with Grandma. The peaches were big and juicy. One fell off the tree when she pulled it. Now the peaches sat in a basket on the seat.

"Are we there now?" Kinsley asked. "Not yet," said Mommy. "We will get there soon." Kinsley looked out the window. A big truck went by. Then a cow went by. Then the cow was gone. It was behind them now.

Kinsley held her book. She turned the pages one by one. The sun came in the window. It made a warm spot on her shoe. She moved her foot. The warm spot moved too. She put her foot back. The warm spot came back. Kinsley laughed.

The car stopped. "Here we are," said Mommy. Grandma stood by the door. She had flour on her hands. "We will bake a peach pie today," said Grandma. "And tomorrow, we will eat it." Kinsley climbed down from the car seat. She carried the basket with both hands. "I picked these yesterday," she said. Grandma smiled and opened the door wide.

Oliver was at Grandma's house. The big game was on TV. Everyone wanted snacks, but the popcorn bowl was empty.

Grandpa said he would make more. Oliver watched from his chair. Grandpa put kernels in a pot. Then he turned on the stove. "You stay back, buddy," Grandpa said. Oliver stayed back.

Soon the pot went pop, pop, pop. Each pop made a white puff jump up. The puffs filled the pot. Then the puffs filled the big blue bowl.

Oliver clapped his hands. The pops had made the bowl full again! Grandpa carried the bowl to the couch. Everyone took a handful.

Oliver ate one puff. It was warm and salty. "More pops, more popcorn," said Oliver. Grandpa laughed and pointed at the pot.

"Want to watch it pop again?"

"Yes," said Oliver. "I will not blink."

Victor was three today. Grandma and Grandpa came. So did his friend Sam.

On the table was a big cake. On the cake were three little candles. Daddy lit them with a match. Daddy held the match far from Victor.

The candles made small flames. They jumped and wiggled.

"Are the flames scary?" asked Victor.

"No," said Mommy. "They are small. And we blow them out."

Victor chose to blow. He took a big breath. He blew hard.

The flames went out. All three! Smoke curled up like little gray ribbons.

Victor laughed. "I did that!"

Then Sam wanted a turn. But the candles were already out. So Mommy put one new candle on a cupcake. Sam blew, and that flame went out too.

Everybody clapped. "Happy birthday, Victor!" they said.

Victor blew a kiss to the smoke.

Jack stood at the airport with Mama. He wanted to see Grandma first. "Look for a blue coat," Mama said. Jack watched the big doors. One, two, three people walked out. Then a blue coat came too. "Grandma!" Jack shouted. Grandma hugged him tight.

Grandma had one big bag and one small bag. Jack pulled the small bag on its wheels. The bag was heavy, so it rolled slow. Then Jack pulled it on the smooth floor, and it rolled fast. "Like an ant carrying a big leaf," Grandma said with a laugh. The young helper smiled.

At home, Grandma unpacked her things. "Here is a gift," she said. It was a soft teddy bear. Jack hugged the bear. "Will you stay a long time?" he asked. "A whole week," said Grandma. "One whole week with you."

Maya stood in the school hallway. Her mama held her hand. Maya saw a row of little hooks on the wall. Each hook held a backpack. But one hook was empty. "That one is for you," said Mama.

Maya reached up. She hung her backpack on the empty hook. She let go. The backpack stayed put. Maya smiled. The hook held her bag, just like the others.

A teacher came to the door. "Come see the sand table," she said. Maya ran to it. She pushed her hands into the cool sand. The sand ran between her fingers.

Then Mama waved. "Bye, Maya. I will be back soon." Maya did not cry. She knew the hook would keep her backpack safe. She knew Mama would come back too.

She filled a red cup with sand. Then she tipped it over. "Look, teacher!" said Maya. "I caught the sand in my hand."

Natalie was on the Bunny team. All the players had to wear red shirts. Natalie was shy at the first game. She stood still and did not kick the ball.

At practice, Coach Kim said, "Try a big kick, Natalie." Natalie kicked the ball soft. The ball rolled a little bit. Then she kicked it hard. The ball went far, all the way to the net. "Whoa," said Natalie. A big kick made the ball go far.

The next game, Natalie ran to the ball. She saw a little ant on the grass. She stepped over it. Then she took her kick. The ball flew across the field. Her friend Maya caught it and kicked it too. "Nice kick!" Maya called.

The other team got the ball. Maya felt sad. Natalie patted her back. "You can try again," Natalie said. Maya smiled.

Near the end of the game, the ball came to Natalie one more time. She looked at the net. She pulled her leg back and kicked with all her might. The ball went in! The Bunnies cheered. Natalie jumped up and down with Maya. "We did it!" said Natalie.

Wesley stood by the fish tanks at the pet store. He saw a little gold fish swimming in a circle. "I want that one," said Wesley. His mom smiled. "That one can be yours."

At home, Mom helped him set up a small tank. Wesley poured the water. The fish swam fast in its new home. Then the fish bumped the glass. It swam to the top. It bumped again. Wesley felt worried. "Is he hungry?"

Mom got the tiny food can. Wesley dropped one small pinch in. The fish swam up fast. It opened its little mouth. Gulp, gulp. The food was gone. "He was hungry," said Wesley. He clapped his hands.

Now Wesley feeds the fish each morning with Mom. He taps the tall tank gently. The fish swims over in a circle to say hello. "Good morning, little fish," says Wesley. The fish blows a tiny bubble.

Natalie sat at the paint table at daycare. She wanted to paint a big green frog. But there was no green paint. She looked in the cups. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. She asked her teacher, "Where is the green?"

"You can find out," said the teacher.

Natalie dipped her brush in the yellow paint. She made a yellow frog on her paper. Then she dipped the same brush in the blue paint. She brushed it over the yellow frog. The yellow frog turned green! Natalie clapped her hands. Her hands were messy with paint.

The sun did shine in the window. It made the green frog glow on the paper. Then Mia came over with a red knee. The doctor had given her a bandage. Natalie pointed at it. "My frog has red eyes too," she said. She dipped a clean brush in the red paint. She added two red eyes. "There," said Natalie. "Hello, green frog."

Brielle stood in the gym with her class. Miss Kay, a kind woman with a big smile, put a hoop on the floor. "Watch me," she said. She tossed a beanbag. It landed in the hoop. Everyone clapped.

Now it was Brielle's turn. She held the beanbag in her hand. She threw it. The beanbag flew far. It landed past the hoop. "Oh no," said Brielle. Leo threw his next. His beanbag missed too. Leo made an angry face and stamped his foot. Miss Kay knelt down. "Try again," she said softly. "Just a little throw." She moved close and held out her hand near the hoop.

Brielle looked at Miss Kay's hand. She tossed the beanbag soft and low. It went in! "I did it!" said Brielle. Leo tried a little throw too. His beanbag went in. "Good throw, Leo!" said Brielle. Leo smiled big.

Then Miss Kay rolled a big ball to Brielle. The ball hit her chest and fell down. It rolled away. "Hold out both arms," said Miss Kay. Brielle held out both arms like a big hug. Miss Kay rolled the ball again. Brielle squeezed it with both hands. She caught it!

"Again!" said Brielle. Miss Kay rolled the ball. Brielle caught it and hugged it tight. Leo clapped for her. Then Brielle rolled the ball gently to Leo.

Mateo sat on a soft red rug at the library. He wanted to find a book about turtles. But he could not read the letters yet.

A girl sat next to him. She had a thick book full of letters. "This is M," she said. "It says mmm, like milk." Mateo patted the letter. "Mmm," he said. "M is for Mateo."

Then he looked at the shelves. He found a sign with M on it. "Mmm, mmm," he said. The sign said MICE. He pulled out a book. The cover had a little mouse on it. He opened it. It was a mouse book, not a turtle book.

"Almost," said the girl. "Try T. T says tuh, like top." Mateo walked slowly along the shelf. He waited. He looked at each sign. Then he saw it. A big red T. "Tuh," he said. "T is for turtle!" He pulled the book out. A green turtle smiled at him from the cover.

Mateo sat back on the rug. He put his hand on the cover. "Tuh, tuh, turtle," he said softly. The girl clapped. "You found it," she said.

Wesley came to school early. He saw his teacher, Miss Kim, at the play table. She had a big box. "What is in the box?" Wesley asked. "Open it and see," said Miss Kim.

Wesley used his hands to open it. Inside were little cups. He picked one up. He sniffed it with his nose. It smelled like oranges. He put it near his mouth. He took a tiny taste with his tongue. It was sweet. "It is orange juice?" he asked. "Yes," said Miss Kim. "You found out with your nose and your tongue."

Then Wesley heard a shout. Miss Kim shouted, "Look out!" A tower of wood blocks fell over. It made a big sound in his ears. Wesley looked with his eyes. His friend Tom had pushed it. The blocks were all over the floor.

But there was a surprise inside the tower. A little red car was hiding there. It rolled right to Wesley's feet. Wesley touched it with his fingers. It was smooth and cool. "Vroom," said Wesley. He smiled. "Can I keep it?" Tom laughed and said, "It is yours now."

Sienna sat in the car seat. Her bunny was not in her lap. "Where is Bunny?" she asked. Mom looked in the mirror. "Let us look together," said Mom.

Sienna looked down by her feet. She saw a shoe. She saw a cracker. No bunny. She looked under her coat. No bunny. Her tummy felt tight. "I want Bunny," she said.

Mom stopped the car in the driveway. She turned on the lamp above Sienna's head. The warm light made the seat bright. Now Sienna could see into the dark corner. There was Bunny, wedged under the brown strap. "Bunny!" said Sienna. She pulled Bunny out and hugged him soft.

Mom helped Sienna out of the car. Sienna held Bunny close. "Thank you, Mom," she said. "The lamp helped me see." Mom smiled and kissed her head. They walked to the door, hand in hand.

Inside, Sienna put Bunny on the pillow. She patted his ears. "Bunny can rest now," she said. "You too," said Mom, and she tucked them both in.

Violet went to the library with her mom. The room smelled like paper. It was quiet. Violet heard pages turning.

She found a book with a red boat on the front. She wanted to keep it forever. "Can I take it home?" she asked.

The librarian gave her a little card. "You can borrow the boat book," she said. "Bring it back soon, so other kids can read it too."

Violet held the book tight. She did not want to share it. She tried to hide it under her coat. Mom saw her. "The book has to go back," Mom said softly. "But we can come again."

At home, Violet opened the book. She turned the pages from the front. On each page, words sat in rows. Mom pointed at the words. "These tell the story," she said. Mom read them out loud. The words made the boat sail in Violet's mind.

Soon it was time to go back. The book shelf looked empty without the red boat book. Violet gave it to the librarian. Then she found a new one. "This one," she said, holding it up high.

Thomas was at Grandma's house for the party. Everyone was singing songs for the holiday. Thomas wanted to hold a candle like the big kids.

"You are too small for fire," said Auntie May. "Here is your own special light." She gave him a little lamp with a switch.

Thomas pressed the switch. The lamp glowed. He pressed it again. The lamp went dark. "Look, Grandma! I can make night and morning!"

Grandma laughed. "You are the sun now, Thomas." Thomas made the light blink on and off. His baby cousin clapped her hands each time.

Later, they all walked down the street with their candles. It was getting late. Thomas held his lamp up high. Every time he pressed the switch, his shadow jumped on the wall.

"I have a dancing shadow!" said Thomas. "On, off, on, off!" His shadow grew tall, then small, then tall again. "Best lamp ever," he whispered to it.

Stella woke up and saw snow. Lots of snow! The sky had been stormy last night. Now school was closed. It was a snow day at home.

Stella ran to the backyard. She wanted to slide down the little hill. But her sled was in the shed. The shed door was stuck. Dad pulled and pulled. It would not open.

Then Stella saw the big snow pile by the fence. She pushed it with her mittens. The snow moved! She pushed again. A big ball rolled away. "Look, Dad! My hands make it go!"

They rolled three big balls. Stella stacked them up. Dad put on a carrot nose. "It's a snow cow!" said Dad. "Moo," said Stella. She touched its cold, lumpy back. The snow cow smiled all morning.

Theodore stood in the school yard. His teacher Miss Ann held out a hoop. "Try to toss the beanbag in," she said. Theodore squeezed his hat under one arm. He tossed the beanbag. It hit the edge and fell out. He frowned. His friend Ben's beanbag went in. Ben stood close to the hoop. Theodore saw that. He took two steps closer. He tossed again. The beanbag went up. Then it came down. It landed in the hoop. "It went in!" said Theodore. Then Miss Ann rolled him a big ball. It bumped his chest and fell. He tried one hand. It fell again. He held out both arms. Miss Ann rolled the ball. It landed soft in his hands, like a big crunchy apple. "I caught it!" he said. Miss Ann clapped.

Axel wanted to paint a rainbow. But he could not find his paints. He looked under his bed. He found only a red sock. He looked in his toy box. He found only a blue car.

Mama said, "We can make our own paint." Axel watched from his chair. Mama cut up a yellow lemon. She squeezed it into a cup. Then she cut a green apple. She squeezed that too.

Axel held his paper. Mama brushed the lemon juice on it. The paper looked plain and wet. "Wait," said Mama. They waited together. Axel watched and watched. Then the paper turned pink where the lemon had dried.

"More colors," said Axel. Mama squeezed a berry. The juice made red dots. Axel dipped his finger in the blue berry cup. He pressed it on the paper. He made a blue sun. He pressed green dots below it. Now his rainbow had red, blue, yellow and green. Axel held it up high. "I build a rainbow too," he said, pointing at his blocks.

Chloe went to the store with Dad. She wanted a toy pig. The pig sat high on a big shelf.

Chloe could not reach the pig. The shelf was too tall. She looked around the store. She saw red balloons by the door. She saw blue bins full of balls. She saw yellow signs that said "Toys" with a big arrow.

Chloe followed the yellow arrow. It pointed to a green step stool. The stool was heavy, so Dad helped her carry it. Chloe put the stool by the shelf. She climbed up one small step. She reached out her hand and grabbed the pig!

Dad laughed and hugged her. "Good looking, Chloe." On the way home, Chloe let the pig swing in the bag by her hand. The pig was pink and happy, just like her.

Nathan went to the park with his dad. He saw a little turtle by the pond. The turtle was very small. "Can we take him home?" Nathan asked. Dad said, "Yes, he can be your first pet."

At home, Nathan put the turtle in a clean tank. The turtle sat very still. He did not walk. He did not eat. Nathan was sad. Then Dad filled the tank with warm water. The turtle popped out his little head. He began to swim! He munched a leaf too.

"Water makes him happy!" Nathan said. Nathan gave the turtle fresh water every day. He held his water cup tight so it would not spill. One morning, a big surprise waited in the tank. A baby turtle sat next to his pet! Nathan clapped his hands. "Now we have two!"

Charles sat at the little blue table. It was writing time at school! Miss Patel gave him a yellow pencil and paper.

"Today we write our names," she said.

Charles grabbed the pencil in his whole fist. He pushed hard. The pencil slipped. The letter C came out wobbly and fat, like a potato. Charles frowned at it.

Then he watched his friend Maya. She held her pencil with three fingers, like a little bird sitting on a stick. Her letters came out neat and small.

Charles tried it. He put three fingers on his pencil. He made a C. It was round like a moon! He made an H. He made an A. He made R, L, E, S.

The pencil did not slip anymore. The letters lined up in a row.

Miss Patel came to look. "Charles! You wrote your name!"

Charles held up the paper like a flag. "I can write it on my shoe box too," he said. "And on my cozy blanket. And on everything!"

Elijah stood at the vet's desk. He held a small box. Inside was his new bunny, Pip.

"Pip looks grumpy," said Elijah. "Why is she grumpy?"

The vet smiled. "Maybe her tummy is empty."

Could that be it? Elijah wondered. He looked at Pip. Pip was chewing on the box corner.

"She chews because she is hungry!" said Elijah.

The vet gave Elijah a carrot. Elijah held it near the cage. Pip sniffed it. Then Pip munched and munched.

Elijah listened. The grumpy tummy sounds went quiet. "Her tummy is full now," said Elijah. "Food made the grumpy go away!"

At home, Elijah fed Pip each morning. Every morning, Pip munched. Every morning, Pip's tummy stayed quiet and happy.

"Are you hungry too, Pip?" Elijah asked.

Pip hopped to her carrot.

Austin went to the store with Mama. He wanted a big orange carrot. The carrots sat high on a shelf. Austin could not reach them. He jumped. He stood on his toes. Still too high.

"Can you help me, please?" Austin asked a store man. The man smiled. He reached up. He put a carrot in Austin's little hand. "Thank you," said Austin. The man gave him a sticker too. It was a shiny star.

Then Austin saw a tower of cans. It looked like a castle. He touched one can. The whole castle fell down. Boom, boom, boom. Cans rolled on the floor. "Sorry," said Austin, in a small voice.

The store man came back. "Let's build it again," he said. Austin handed him cans, one by one. The castle grew tall again. It was even taller now. Mama put the carrot in her bag. "Time to go home," she said.

Austin waved at the store man. "Bye-bye! Thank you!" The man waved back. Austin held Mama's hand. He looked at the carrot all the way to the car. "We will cook it," said Mama. Austin smiled big. "My carrot!"

Olivia wanted to paint a picture of a tree. She had red paint, yellow paint, and blue paint. But her tree was green, and she had no green paint. She stopped and looked at her cups. She had a big question in her head.

"Can I make green?" she asked Mama.

Mama sat down with her at the wooden table. "Try it," said Mama. "You have three colours."

Olivia dipped her brush in the blue paint. She made a blue spot on the paper. Then she dipped her brush in the yellow paint. She put yellow on top of the blue spot.

Olivia leaned close. The spot was turning green! Blue and yellow made green. She jumped up and down in her chair.

"My tree can be green now!" she said.

She painted a big green tree. She painted red apples on it. She painted a yellow sun above it.

Then she had an idea. She put red on top of the yellow sun. The red and yellow made orange! Olivia laughed and laughed.

"Mama, look! I made a new sun!"

The sun in her picture was orange, just like the one outside the window.

Tonight was Diwali at Madeline's house. Grandma was making sweet dumplings in the kitchen. Madeline wanted to make one too. But every time she touched the dough, it fell apart. "It's too dry," Grandma did say. Grandma poured in a little milk. Madeline watched. The dry crumbs stuck together. The dough turned into a soft ball. "Can I try?" Madeline asked. Grandma gave her a small piece. Madeline pressed it flat. Then she pressed in a mold. She tapped it out. A little flower shape fell onto the tray. "I made one!" she said. Outside the window the sky looked stormy, but inside the lamps glowed. Grandpa lit the candles with a match, because only grown-ups do that. Madeline set her flower sweet by the lamp. She even left one for the tooth fairy cup where her loose tooth had been. "My shape made the tray look pretty," Madeline said. Grandma smiled and pointed at the tray full of flowers.

Sophia sat at the dinner table. The lamp was on. It made a warm circle of light.

"I want apple juice now," said Sophia.

"The juice is all gone," said Mama. "We drank it yesterday."

Sophia looked at her cup. It was empty. She turned it over. One drop fell out.

"Today we can buy more," said Mama. "We can go to the shop later."

"After dinner," said Papa. "First we eat."

Sophia ate her pasta. One spoon, two spoops, three spoons. Then she was done.

"Now?" she asked.

"Now we put on shoes," said Mama.

Sophia found her shoes. One shoe, two shoes. Her laces were messy. Mama helped tie them.

At the shop, Sophia held Mama's hand. They found the juice shelf. Sophia got to shake the bottle a little. Then she put it in the basket.

"Tomorrow we will have juice again," said Mama.

"And today too," said Sophia.

At home, Mama poured the juice. Sophia drank it all down.

"More now?" she asked.

"That's all for today," said Papa. "More tomorrow."

Sophia looked at the lamp. She yawned one big yawn.

"Tomorrow is after sleep," she said.

"Yes," said Mama. "Sleep now. Juice tomorrow."

Mya wanted her red ball. It was hiding under the big block tower. She could see just a bit of red.

She began to take the blocks down. "One," she said. She put the block in the basket. "Two." Another block went in. "Three, four, five." The tower got smaller and smaller.

Her little brother Sam sat nearby. He dropped his teddy on the floor. Mya picked it up for him. Sam smiled and hugged the teddy tight.

She kept counting like the song on her toy radio. "Six, seven, eight." The tower was almost gone. "Nine." One block was left. Mya lifted it up high. "Ten!"

There was her red ball. She pushed it to Sam. Sam rolled it back. It bumped her toe. Mya laughed. "Your turn, Sam. That is your job now." Sam patted the ball with both little hands and pushed it again.

Rosalie put on her short blue dress. Today was a big family party at Grandma's house. Grandma called everyone to the table. The candles were lit, and Grandpa said the blessing. Rosalie watched from her chair. The flames were little and bright.

After the blessing, Grandma made sweet tea. Rosalie wanted to help. Grandma held the cup, and Rosalie poured in the milk. The dark tea turned light brown. "Look, Grandma! I made it change!" she said. "Pour more," said Grandma. Rosalie poured more milk. The tea got even lighter.

Then it was time to spin the dreidel. Grandpa spun it first. It spun like a little wheel, then it fell down. Rosalie clapped. She spun it too. It wobbled and fell. "Again!" she called. The dreidel spun round and round on the table.

Jake ran to the block corner at school. "I will build a big tower!" he said. He stacked the red blocks up, up, up. His tummy felt bouncy and light. He was so excited.

Then Tom bumped the tower. The blocks fell down with a clatter. Jake's face got hot. His hands made tight fists. "My tower!" he yelled. Tom looked down at the floor. His eyes were sad and wet.

Jake saw Tom's sad face. His own fists got soft again. "It was an accident," Tom said, in a tiny voice. Jake took a deep breath. "Let's build it again," he said. "Together." Tom smiled a big smile. They stacked the blocks higher than before. Jake clapped his clean hands. "Teacher, look!" he called. "We can spell T-O-W-E-R too!" The teacher laughed and said, "You built a fine one." At circle time, Jake whispered to Tom, "Same team tomorrow?" Tom nodded, and patted the very top block.

Jacob wanted to ride the big slide. But the big slide was in the sun. It felt hot on his hand.

"Ouch," said Jacob. He pulled his hand back fast.

He looked at the small slide. That one sat in the shade. He touched it. It felt cold and smooth.

"The small slide is cold," said Jacob. "Can I go fast on a cold slide?"

"Try it and see," said Mom.

Jacob climbed up. He sat down. He went slow at first. Then he went fast, fast, fast.

"Wheee!" he shouted.

A boy named Sam ran over. "You went so fast! Can the small slide do that?"

"Watch me," said Jacob. He ran back up the steps.

Jacob slid down again. Sam put his hand on the big slide. "Ow, this one is hot," said Sam. "It's a smelly old slide, too."

"Come to my slide," said Jacob. "It's cold like ice cream."

Sam climbed up behind him. They went down one by one. Then they went down again and again.

At the end, Mom called, "Time for a snack! I brought you a gift."

The gift was two juice boxes, cold from the cooler. Jacob took a big sip. Then a small sip. The big sip was better.

"See," said Sam. "Big and cold wins."

The bookmobile came to Edouard's street. It was a big van full of books. Edouard wanted a book about trucks. He wanted to keep it forever.

A lady inside gave him a card. It was his very own library card. He picked a truck book and held it tight. "This is mine now," he said.

"Not forever," the lady said kindly. "You can take it home. Then you bring it back on a certain day." She stamped a day inside the book. "Other kids want to read it too."

Edouard took the book home. He read it three times. He read it to his cat until the cat fell asleep. At bedtime he put the book by his door.

On the stamp day, he walked back to the van. He gave the book to the lady. Then she put it on the shelf. A girl picked it up right away.

Edouard watched her hug the book. His old book made a new girl happy. He smiled and picked out a book about trains.

Blake wanted to be a mommy today. Her old teddy bear would be the baby. She wrapped him in a small towel. Then teddy fell on the floor. He bumped his head. "Oh no," said Blake. She gave teddy a soft pat. She put a bandage on his fuzzy ear.

Then teddy got hungry. Blake found a toy cup. She held it to teddy's mouth. She made a little slurping sound. Teddy felt better right away. "Good job drinking," said Blake.

Next Blake gave teddy a job. He would watch the paper flowers she had made. But a breeze came in the window. The flowers danced away across the rug! Teddy sat very still. Blake laughed and chased them. She taped one flower to teddy's paw. Now teddy could plant it in a tiny pot. "You are a garden bear now," said Blake. TeddBlake wanted to be a mommy today. Her old teddy bear would be the baby. She wrapped him in a soft towel. Then teddy slid off the chair. He bumped his fluffy head. "Oh no," said Blake.

She patted teddy's head. She gave him a pretend bandage. Then teddy got hungry. Blake filled a tiny cup with pretend milk. She held it to teddy's mouth. She made a little slurp sound for him. Teddy drank it all up.

Then Mommy called from the kitchen. Blake ran to see. Mommy was planting seeds in little pots. "Can teddy have one?" asked Blake. Mommy gave her the smallest pot. Blake pressed one seed into the dirt. She set teddy beside it. "Your job is to watch the seed," said Blake. Just then, teddy tipped over and his paw patted the dirt flat. "You helped plant it," said Blake. She clapped her hands.

Sara ran to the park with her bunny toy. She wanted to show everyone. But when she sat on the swing, her hands were empty. Bunny was gone!

"Bunny, where are you?" Sara looked by the slide. No bunny. She looked by the sandbox. No bunny. She looked under the bench. No bunny. A dog began to bark, bark, bark at a tall bush. Sara peeked in. The branches were thin and wavy. The wind blew and the thin branches moved. And there, when they moved, she saw something white!

"Bunny!" The wind stopped. The branches hung down and hid Bunny again. The wind blew once more. The branches moved, and Sara saw Bunny's soft ear. She reached in fast and pulled Bunny out. She hugged him tight.

Sara sat by the dog with a cup of juice. She gave Bunny a drink too, pretend juice, from her own cup. "Wind, thank you!" she said, and waved at the tree.

Mia was thirsty. She wanted cold milk from the big fridge. "Can I help?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Get the small cup."

Mia looked at the cups. One was big. One was small. She took the small one. Dad poured the cold milk. "One cup, one splash," he said.

Mia watched Dad make tea. The kettle was fast. It huffed and puffed. Dad poured hot water. "Stay back," he said. "The tea is hot. Your milk is cold."

Mia touched her cup. Cold! She blew on Dad's mug. Would it cool down? Dad smiled. "The tea is slow to cool," he said. Mia sipped her milk. Then she held up her small cup next to Dad's big mug. "Small," she said. "Big!" Dad laughed and clinked his mug against her cup.

Scarlett wanted to find her favorite color at school. She looked at the big paint table. There were four cups of paint. One cup was red. One cup was blue. One cup was yellow. One cup was green.

"Which one is my favorite?" she asked. Her teacher smiled. "Try them and see," said Miss Ana. Scarlett dipped her brush in the red paint. She patted red dots on her paper. The red dots looked like little apples.

Next she painted a yellow sun. Then she painted a green grass hill. Last she painted a blue river. Then something surprising happened. Her blue river ran into her yellow sun. The paint mixed on the paper. The wet spot turned green!

Scarlett gasped. "The blue made green with the yellow!" she said. She tried it again. She patted blue on yellow. Green came back. "It does it every time," she said.

Miss Ana hung the painting on the wall. She put a little sign under it. The sign said "Scarlett's Colors." Tomás clapped for her. "I like your green," he said. Scarlett smiled big. Now she knew her favorite. It was green, the color she made herself.

Zoe rode in the car with Daddy. They drove down the long road to the hospital. The sky was cloudy, but Zoe felt happy inside. Mama was at the hospital. A new baby was coming today.

Zoe wanted to give the baby a present. She had a little red hat. She put it in her small bag. She held the bag on her lap all the way.

At the hospital, Zoe saw Mama in a big bed. Mama held a bundle with a small face. "This is your baby brother," said Mama. The baby was asleep. His hands were very tiny.

Zoe wanted the baby to see the red hat. She held it up. The baby did not wake up. Then the baby made a little sound. He turned his head. His eyes opened. He saw the red hat! He reached out one small hand and grabbed it. The hat fell over his nose. Zoe laughed softly.

"He likes my present," Zoe whispered. The baby held the hat tight. Zoe patted his hand, very gently. "My hat, my baby," she said. Mama smiled at both of them.

Mason sat at Grandma's big table. He wanted to write his name. Grandma gave him a fat pencil. He grabbed it in his whole fist. He pushed and pushed. The letter M came out fat and wobbly. "It looks like a sleepy cat," said Grandma. Mason laughed. "Why does it look so funny?" he asked. "Try two fingers and your thumb," said Grandma. "Like this." She showed him her hand.

Mason tried it. He held the pencil with two fingers and his thumb. Then he turned the paper a little. He wrote M, A, S, O, N. Five letters! One, two, three, four, five. "I did it!" said Mason. "That's me!" Grandma clapped. The cat jumped on the table. Mason was not afraid. He showed the cat his name. "Look, cat. M for Mason," he said. The cat sniffed the pencil. "That's mine," said Mason.

Owen got to the playground early. The grass was still wet. The slide shone in the sun. Owen felt excited. He ran to the swing.

The swing was high. Owen felt scared. He held the chains tight. His feet did not reach the ground. "What if I fall?" he asked. "Hold on tight," said Mom. Owen held on. Mom pushed him soft and slow. Up he went. Down he came. Up and down, up and down. Soon Owen was not scared. Now he felt happy. He laughed out loud.

Then a big boy ran past. He bumped the swing. Owen fell off into the soft sand. He felt angry. His face got hot. He wanted to yell. But then he saw his ice cream cone on the ground. That made him sad too. Mom helped him up. She brushed off the sand. They sat on the bench together. Mom shared her own ice cream with him. Owen clapped his hands. He licked the sweet, cold cream. "Swings are hard," said Owen. "But ice cream is easy," said Mom. Owen laughed and licked again.

Evan wanted the big red truck. Ben had the big red truck. Evan grabbed it. Ben held on tight. The truck did not move.

Then the truck slipped. It fell on the floor. A wheel came off. Now nobody could play with it.

Miss Dana picked up the wheel. She put it back on. She held up the truck. "One truck," she said. "Two friends."

Evan looked at Ben. Ben looked at Evan. Could they both play? Evan had an idea. He would dig in the sand box. Ben could have the truck first. Then they could swap.

Ben drove the truck to the sand box. He scooped sand with it. Evan found a stick. He drew a road in the sand. The truck drove on the road.

Soon Ben held out the truck. "Your turn," he said. Evan took the wheel. Beep beep! The truck went down the road fast.

Then the bell rang. Time to clean up. Evan put the truck on the shelf. The last block went in the basket too. Ben waved. "Truck again tomorrow?"

Elena sat on her bed. It was windy outside. The wind made the curtain puff out. The curtain went swish, swish. Elena felt scared. She pulled the blanket up to her chin.

Then the curtain puffed again. It knocked her teddy off the sill. Ted fell on the floor with a soft thump. Elena looked down at him. His face looked sad in the dark. She did not want him to be sad. So she leaned over and picked him up. She held Ted close. Now she felt a little brave.

Mama came in with a little lamp. She set it on the table. The warm light made the room yellow. Elena felt happy. She showed Mama the curtain. "The wind did it," she said. Mama smiled. "Yes, the wind sent Ted flying." Elena laughed. That was silly. She hugged Ted tight.

Mama sat down and opened a picture book. It had a duck on a pond. Elena clapped her hands. She felt so excited. "Duck, duck!" she said. Mama read one page. Then another. Outside the wind went whoosh. But inside, Elena was warm and sleepy. She gave Ted a kiss on his nose. "Night night, Ted," she said.

Matteo stood at the edge of the pool. The water was blue and thick with little waves. His teacher, Miss Ana, held out her hands.

"Hold my hands," she said. "We will practice kicking."

Matteo held on tight. He kicked one foot. He kicked the other foot. Small splashes popped up.

"I want to go fast like the big kids," Matteo said.

The big kids kicked their legs hard. They made big splashes. Then they moved through the water, fast fast fast. Matteo watched them. He saw their kicking. He saw their splashing. Then he saw them zoom.

Matteo kicked harder. His legs went up and down. Big splashes flew everywhere. One splash hit his own nose!

"Hey!" he shouted, and he laughed.

But then something happened. Matteo moved forward. The kicking pushed him along. He glided past Miss Ana's elbow.

"You did it!" MissAna called. "Kick, kick, kick!"

"Kick, kick, kick!" said Matteo. He kicked again. He moved again. He glided all the way to the wall.

Dad clapped from his chair. A little girl in a red hat pointed at Matteo.

"He goes fast," she said. Then she whispered to her own teacher, "I want to kick like that."

Matteo grabbed the wall. Water dripped from his chin. He turned around and shouted one more word.

"Again!"

Wyatt wanted to build a big tower at school. He found some big blocks and some small blocks. He put the big blocks on the bottom. He put the small blocks on top.

The tower grew tall. Then Wyatt bumped it with his elbow. The tower was weak at the top. The small blocks fell down. The big blocks stayed up. Wyatt gasped. He looked at the floor. He looked at his teacher. "It fell," he said.

His teacher smiled. "Try again," she said. Wyatt built the tower once more. This time he made the bottom big and strong. He was slow and careful. He did not go fast. The tower stood tall.

Then it was snack time. The teacher gave Wyatt a cup of cold milk. Wyatt touched the cup. "Cold," he said. The teacher held a pot of hot soup. "That is hot," she said. "Only I touch it." Wyatt drank his cold milk. Then he ran back, fast, to his tower. It was still standing.

Leon wanted to find his lost blue truck. He looked under his bed. He found a stuffed rabbit there instead. "Hello, rabbit," said Leon. He put the rabbit in his toy box with his blocks and his drum. Still no truck.

Leon followed a trail of crumbs across the kitchen floor. The crumbs led to the fridge. Inside, he saw fresh apples, milk and cheese. "Maybe the truck is hungry," he said. Daddy lifted the cheese. There sat the blue truck! A little mouse was sitting in the truck, holding a tiny crumb.

"The mouse was driving it," laughed Daddy. Leon made a small bed for the mouse from a sock. The mouse curled up in it. Leon tucked the truck in beside the sock. "Good night, drivers," he whispered.

Nathan held Dad's hand on the ferry. "One brother, one mama, one papa, one Nathan," he said, counting his family. The boat was big and white. The water below was deep blue and splashing against the side.

Nathan leaned on the rail. The wind pushed his hair back. Then the big horn went, "Whooo!" The sound was so loud that a black bird flew up off the water. Nathan laughed. "The horn made the bird fly away!"

His little brother Sam began to cry. The horn had scared him. Mama gave Sam his soft red blanket. Sam hugged it and stopped crying. Nathan patted Sam's foot gently.

"Boat, water, bird, blanket," Nathan said, naming things. Then he saw something in the waves. A fish jumped up, quick and shiny, and slipped back down. "Mama, look!" said Nathan. Sam looked too, and pointed his small finger at the water.

Layla woke up in her bed. She was wide awake. "I want my bear shirt today," she said. She looked in her closet. She could not find it. "Mama, can I ask you something? Where is my bear shirt?"

Mama smiled. "First bath, then shirt," said Mama. Layla made a silly face. "A bath? In the morning?" Mama filled the tub. The water was warm. Layla splashed with her hands. The soap made bubbles. The bubbles made her skin slippery. Mama scrubbed her toes. "These toes smell like cheese," said Mama. Layla laughed. "Silly Mama. Toes smell like toes!"

Mama poured water on Layla's head. The bubbles ran down. All the soap went away. Layla looked at her arms. They were shiny and clean. "The bubbles went down the drain," said Layla. She waved at them. "Bye bye, bubbles."

Mama wrapped Layla in a big towel. The towel was soft. Layla's skin was warm and pink. Then Mama opened a drawer. "Look who was hiding here," said Mama. It was the bear shirt! It was folded under her pajamas all along. Layla pulled it on by herself. Her head popped out of the top. "I did it!" she said. Her heart felt happy and bouncy. She ran to the mirror. The bear on the shirt smiled at her. Layla smiled back. "Now I need socks," she said. "Bear socks."

Rose wanted her red crayon. It was lost. The sky was cloudy, so the house looked dim.

Rose looked with her eyes. No crayon under the table. She heard a tiny sound with her ears. Tippy tap. It came from the kitchen.

Rose smelled something sweet with her nose. Apples! Mama was cooking. "Come see," said Mama. Rose touched the floor with her hands as she crawled. There it was! The red crayon was by the fridge.

"Good finding," said Mama. She gave Rose a cool apple slice. Rose tasted it with her tongue. Sweet and yummy.

Rose sat down and colored a big red apple on her paper. "Just like the real one," said Mama.

Lea rode the bus with Gran. She held Gran's hand. They were going to the big library.

"I want a book about a cat," said Lea. "A snowy white cat!"

At the desk, a kind lady gave Lea a little card. It had Lea's own name on it. Lea picked a cat book. The lady put it in a bag.

"Can I keep it forever?" Lea asked.

"You take it home," said Gran. "Then we bring it back on Thursday. Other kids want to read it too."

Lea hugged the bag. At home, she read the cat book three times. The cat in the book felt soft in the pictures.

On Thursday, they rode the bus again. Lea gave the book back. Then she saw it. A boy took her cat book off the shelf. He sat down to read it.

"He is reading my book," said Lea. She smiled at Gran.

Gran smiled back. "Now you can pick a new one."

Lea ran to the shelf. She found a book about a big snowy bear. "This one!" said Lea.

Alice wanted to make breakfast for her family. "I will make pancakes," she said. "Big ones."

First, Dad got out the bowl. Alice poured in the flour. Some flour puffed onto her nose. "You look like a snow girl," said Dad. Alice laughed and laughed.

Alice stirred the batter. She stirred and stirred. Then she poured a little circle onto the pan. Dad held the pan, because the pan was hot. But the batter did not spread out. It sat in one fat lump. "That is not a pancake," said Alice. "That is a pancake rock."

Dad tipped the bowl. The batter was thick and slow, like glue. Alice thought hard. Then she had an idea. "It needs milk," she said. She poured in some milk. She stirred again. Now the batter ran off the spoon, quick and smooth.

Dad poured the batter into the hot pan. This time it spread out wide. It made a big round pancake. "Look what the milk did," said Alice. "Runny batter makes a big pancake!"

The pancakes stacked up on a plate. Alice put two blueberries on the top one. They looked like two eyes. Mom came in and gasped. "A pancake is looking at me!" Mom said. Alice giggled and said, "Bathe it in syrup, Mom. It likes that."

Charlie ran into the backyard with a box. Inside was a little bunny. "His name is Floppy!" said Charlie.

Floppy hopped out of the box. He began to chew the green grass. Then Floppy chewed a flower. The flower fell down. Charlie gasped. Floppy was hungry!

"Mom! Floppy needs food!" Charlie called. Mom came out with her phone. She looked at it. "We can get bunny food at the store," she said.

Charlie filled a bowl with water. Floppy drank it all up. Then Floppy ate some lettuce from Mom's hand. His tummy got round.

Mom put up a little fence. "This keeps Floppy safe," she said. Floppy hopped inside his new home.

Charlie clapped his hands. "Floppy lives here now!" he said. Floppy wiggled his nose at him.

Felix went to the library with his mama. He wanted a book about trucks. "Where are the truck books?" he asked.

"Let us look on the shelf," said the librarian. Her name was Miss Jo. Miss Jo pointed to a low shelf.

Felix saw books about animals first. A black cat sat on one cover. A cow and a pig sat on the next one. "These are all animals," said Felix.

Then he saw books about toys. A ball, a drum, and a teddy bear. He tapped the teddy bear book. Miss Jo nodded her head.

Then he saw books about foods. Apples, bread, and eggs. "Can books go in groups?" asked Felix.

"Yes," said Miss Jo. "Each shelf holds one group."

So Felix looked and looked. He found a shelf with trucks, cars, and buses. "Toys that go!" he said. He pulled out a big red truck book.

"Good finding," said Miss Jo. She showed him where the soft chairs were.

Felix sat down with mama. He turned the pages slowly. "Vroom," he said. "The truck is black on this page!"

Hunter wanted to help Dad cook lunch. But the grill was outside, so they went to the backyard. Hunter stayed close to Dad, like a little duck.

Dad put meat on the hot grill. Hunter saw smoke go up, up, up. The grill was hot. Hunter did not touch it. He could smell the yummy food. He put his hands behind his back and watched.

Then Hunter saw a sharp stick on the grass. He picked it up to poke a mud block. Dad said, "Let me take that, buddy." Dad held the stick for him, and Hunter poked gently. The mud block went squish. It made a messy, funny mark.

"Hot grill, sharp stick," said Hunter.

"Yes," said Dad. "And we stay together." Hunter held Dad's hand all the way to the door.

James ran into the writing club room. He wanted to write his name all by himself. "Today I will do it!" he said.

Ms. Rosa gave him a big pencil. James grabbed it with his whole fist. He pressed hard. The letters came out wobbly. His J looked like a squiggle worm.

"Try two fingers and a thumb," said Ms. Rosa. She showed him how. James held the pencil the new way. He made a slow, careful J. It popped onto the page, round and neat. Then a, then m, then e, then s.

"Look!" said James. "My name is full of letters!" He held up the paper. "That's me! I wrote me!"

Ms. Rosa clapped. "Write it again," she said. James smiled big and picked up the pencil.

Kayden ran to the kitchen. Lunch was on the table. It was a peanut butter sandwich, cut in little squares.

"Hands first," said Mom. She lifted Kayden up to the sink. She turned on the water. It was warm, not hot. Kayden put his hands under the fall of water. "Do you feel it splash?" Mom asked.

Mom gave him the soap. Kayden rubbed his palms together. Bubbles grew. One, two, bubbles. Three, four, bubbles. They counted all the way to twenty. The bubbles caught the light. Where did the dirt go? Into the bubbles, down the fall of water, away. Kayden looked at his hands. They were dry and shiny after the towel. The sandwich tasted good. Kayden looked at his clean fingers and smiled. "My hands are so bright!"

Leo ran to the play corner at school. A big cardboard box sat there. "It's a house!" said his friend Mia.

Leo peeked inside. The box was empty. No table. No baby. No plates. "Our house needs things," said Mia.

Leo looked around the room. He saw a rug on the floor. He rolled it up and carried it in. The rug turned the box floor soft and cozy. "One rug!" he said. He found a basket and a hat. "Two things for the baby!" He put the hat on a teddy bear. Now the bear was their baby.

Mia held the bear. "The baby is hungry," she said. Leo found a cup and a spoon. He stirred air in the cup. "Soup for you," he said kindly. The baby got a pretend hug too.

Then the baby started to cry, because Mia made a sad face. "Rock the baby," said Leo. He turned the bear side to side, slowly, slowly. The pretend crying stopped. Mia clapped her hands.

"My sister rocks her baby like that," said Leo. "At home, every day."

The teacher rang the bell. Time to clean up. But first, Leo gave the bear one more hug.

"Bye-bye, baby," said Leo. "See you tomorrow."

Sienna sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. "Will the shot hurt?" she asked. Mama held her hand. "Just a quick pinch," Mama said. "Then we go for ice cream."

The nurse wiped Sienna's arm with a cool, wet cotton ball. "Now squeeze Mama's hand," the nurse said. Sienna squeezed tight. She felt one quick pinch. Then it was done! A small bandage with a flower on it went on her arm.

At the ice cream shop, Sienna peeked under the bandage. Her arm had a tiny red dot. "Look, Mama. The dot is small," she said. Mama smiled and gave her a spoon. Sienna took a big bite of pink strawberry ice cream. Outside the window, the sky looked a little stormy, but inside it was warm and sweet. Sienna licked her spoon and said, "I was brave, and now I get ice cream."

Wyatt wanted a big garden in the backyard. Dad dug the dirt with a shovel. Wyatt dropped little seeds into the holes. He patted the dirt down with his hands. "Will you grow?" Wyatt asked the seeds.

Every morning Wyatt ran outside to look. The dirt stayed flat and brown. Then one morning, Wyatt saw green. Tiny leaves were pushing up! "Dad, come see!" he called. The seeds had turned into little plants.

Wyatt watered the plants with a spoon. One spoon for each plant. Some water dripped down into the dirt. The plants drank it up and grew taller. The leaves got big and wide. "What is hiding under there?" Wyatt wondered.

Soon Dad found something. He pulled hard on a green top. Up came a fat orange carrot! Wyatt laughed. The little seed had made a whole carrot. Dad washed it at the sink and cut it into rounds. Wyatt took a bite and began to chew. "My seed did that," said Wyatt. He ran back out to look at his garden.

Amira ran to the class window. A bird was making a nest in the tree. The nest had small red leaves in it. "A baby bird will come," said her friend Leo. Amira clapped her hands. She was so excited.

Then a big wind blew. The nest tipped over. The leaves fell down, down, down. The mother bird flew round and round. She looked sad, and Amira felt sad too. Leo stamped his foot. "I feel angry at the wind," he said.

"Let us help the bird," said Amira. She and Leo picked up the red leaves. Their teacher helped them put the leaves back in the tree. The wind blew again. Amira held on tight with her mittens. She was a little scared, but she did not let go. Then the mother bird came close. She sat on the nest. "Happy bird, happy me," said Amira. Leo smiled too.

Lillian wanted to build a house for her toy snake. She looked for walls in her block box. First she tried the round blocks. They rolled away! Round blocks cannot be walls, she thought.

Then she found square blocks. She stacked them up. Four flat sides, side by side. The wall stood tall! "Look, snake, a square wall!" she said. She made a long wall with rectangle blocks, too. The rectangles were like big long squares.

Now she needed a roof. Squares were too flat. Then she saw a triangle block. It had three sides and a pointy top. She set it on the wall. It sat just right! "A triangle roof!" she shouted.
