She put her snake inside. "Welcome home, silly snake," she said. The snake peeked out the round window she had left. Then Lillian grabbed crayons to color a flag for the top. A square flag, of course.

Owen sat in the waiting room with his mom. He wanted to feel brave. But today he would get a shot. He held his stuffed bear, Brown Bear, very tight.

"Will the shot hurt?" Owen asked.

"Just a tiny pinch," said Mom. "Then it is done."

A nurse stepped in. "Hello, Owen," she said. "Do you want your bear to get a shot first?" Owen looked at Brown Bear. The nurse touched the bear's arm with a cotton ball. "All done," she said. "Brown Bear was so still."

Then it was Owen's turn. He sat on Mom's lap. She gave him a nice, big hug. The nurse cleaned his arm. Then came the tiny pinch. Owen blinked. It was over already!

"Why did the bear go first?" Owen asked.

"Because the bear showed you it was quick," said Mom.

Owen looked at his arm. There was a small bandage with a star on it. "My turn is done," he said. He held Brown Bear up high. "We are both brave."

Athena ran to the park with Dad. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Athena wore her sun hat. Then the wind came. It blew her hat right off!

"My hat flew away!" said Athena. The windy day took the hat under a tree. Dad got it back. "Hold it tight," said Dad. Athena held it tight.

Then gray clouds grew big and dark. Rain fell. Plop, plop, plop. Athena was scared of getting wet. "Don't worry," said Dad. He gave her a rain coat and rain boots. Now the rain could not get her. Athena jumped in a brown puddle. Splash! Her boots kept her feet dry.

Later it got very cold. Soft white snow began to fall. "Look, snow!" said Athena. Dad put warm mittens on her hands. She caught a snowflake in her mitten. Then she and Dad drank warm cocoa from a little glass cup. "Sunny, rainy, windy, snowy," said Athena. Dad smiled and held her hand.

Ivy went to the library with Dad. She got her very own card. It had her name on it. She picked a book about a worm in a garden. "I want to keep this book forever," she said.

Dad shook his head. "Not forever," he said. "Other kids want to read it too. We bring it back soon." Ivy held the book tight. The book smelled like paper. The pages felt dry and smooth.

At home, Ivy read the worm book three times. Then she read it again. After some days, Dad said, "Time to take the book back." Ivy was sad. But then she saw the shelf of books. So many books! She could take a new one home. Ivy put the worm book in her bag. "I will borrow another one," she said.

Ava and her family drove to the beach. Grandma came too. Ava held her small yellow bucket the whole way. "Is this Grandma's beach?" Ava asked. "Yes, it is," said Grandma.

Ava wanted to find a shell. She looked and looked. Then she saw one by the water. The waves came in. The water lifted the shell. The shell floated up and slid back to Ava's feet. She picked it up. "The water brought it to me!" she said.

Grandma held Ava's hand. They walked a short way along the sand. Ava put the shell in her bucket. The sun felt warm. "Time for a snack," said Grandma. They sat together on a big towel. Ava ate her crackers and smiled. "We can come back tomorrow," said Grandma. Ava hugged her shell tight.

Lena woke up in her bedroom. She ran to the window. "Is it store day now?" she asked. Yesterday Grandma had said, "We will go to the store in two days." But how many days had gone by?

Lena looked at her little calendar. Every night, Grandma put one sticker on it. Yesterday had a sun sticker. Yesterday was gone, like a finished bowl of cereal. Today had no sticker yet. So the store was not today. It was tomorrow.

"Can tomorrow hurry up?" Lena asked. Grandma smiled. "Tomorrow comes after we sleep," she said. "First we eat, then we play, then night comes."

Later that day, thunder made a loud boom. Rain tapped the window. Lena watched the drops. The rain came, and then puddles came. One thing made another thing happen, just like that.

That night, Grandma helped Lena pick a star sticker. Lena pressed it onto today. Now today was finished too. "Thank you, star," she whispered. She closed her eyes.

In the morning, the sun was bright. Lena jumped up. She looked at the calendar. There was one empty square left. "That square is today!" she shouted. Today was store day at last. She ran to find her shoes.

Raphael stood in the pool changing room. He held his new goggles in his hands. They looked big and round like frog eyes. "Will they stay on?" he asked. "Let's try," said Dad.

Dad helped him pull the straps tight. Raphael blinked. The world looked blue and clear. Then he put them on his head. The straps snapped back and hit his nose. "Ouch," said Raphael. But then he laughed too. He tried again, slow and careful. This time the goggles sat just right.

In the pool, Raphael put his face in the water. He could see his toes. He could see Dad's legs. He could even see a shiny coin on the bottom. "Look, Dad!" he said. Dad smiled and held his hand. "Ready to kick?" asked Dad. Raphael kicked and the water went splash.

Aubrey sat at the dinner table. She had green beans on her plate. She did not want them.

"I want to count them," said Aubrey.

Mama smiled. "Count with me."

Aubrey poked one bean. "One." She poked another. "Two, three, four." The beans rolled apart. "Five, six, seven." More rolling. "Eight, nine, ten!" Ten beans, all counted.

Dada peeked over his cup. "Ten beans! That is a lot."

Aubrey looked at her beans. Then she ate one. "Now there are nine," she said. She ate another one. "Eight!" She ate one more. "Seven, six, five."

Dada laughed. "Each bite makes the pile smaller."

Aubrey kept going. "Four, three, two." One bean left. Little brother Ben looked upset. He had no beans yet. His plate was empty.

"Here, Ben," said Aubrey. She gave him her last bean. "One bean for you."

Ben clapped his hands. He made a happy sound.

"Zero beans for me," said Aubrey. "All done!"

Mama gave her a small spoonful of rice. Aubrey peeked at it. "One spoon," she said. "Maybe I can count that too."

Dada poured milk into her cup. The milk went up and up. "Stop!" said Aubrey, laughing. "It will make a river!"

Mama stopped just in time. "No milk river tonight," she said.

Aubrey drank her milk. Then she counted her spoons of rice. "One, two, three, all gone."

Ben banged his spoon on his tray. "More!" he said.

"Ben wants to count too," said Aubrey.

Mama put three peas on Ben's tray. Ben pushed them around with his spoon. "Ba, ba, ba," he said.

"He is trying," said Aubrey. "Good job, Ben."

Charlie sat in her reading nook with her letter cards. Mama sat close by with a cup of tea. Charlie held up the card with B on it. "B says buh," she said. She looked around the nook. Her bear sat on the pillow. She put the B card next to the bear. The bear got a letter!

She held up the card with F on it. "F says fff," she said. A soft feather lay by her blanket. She put the F card on the feather. The feather got a letter too!

Then she held up S. She could not remember the sound. Her tummy felt tight. "I forgot this one," she said. Mama gave her hand a little pat. Charlie wiggled her toes. Her socks were stinky! She laughed. "S says sss, like stinky socks!" She put the S card on her sock.

Then she poured pretend tea for bear, feather, and socks. "Tea for all my letters!" said Charlie.

Sofia sat at the big table. She had her letter cards in a small bag. She pulled them out one by one.

" That is M," she said. "Mmm, mmm." Her mouth made the sound all by itself. She tried B. "Buh, buh." Her lips popped open when she said it. She tried S. "Ssss." Her mouth made a long thin sound, like a snake.

Then Sofia tried P. "Puh." A little bit of air came out. She held her hand in front of her lips. She said "Puh" again. She felt the air puff on her fingers! She stopped and stared at her hand.

"Mmm," she said. No air puff. "Buh." A tiny puff. "Puh." A big puff. She tried each card again. Some letters pushed air at her hand. Some letters did not.

Sofia ran to find her big brother, Marco. He was so young when he learned these cards, Mom said. "Marco, put your hand here," Sofia said. She held up the P card. "Puh!"

Marco felt the puff. "Do it again," he said. Sofia smiled and said, "Puh, puh, puh."

Liam looked out the big window. The sun was bright. "It is sunny today," said Mom. Liam put on his little cap. Off went the cap, because the sun made him too warm.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain fell, tap tap tap. Liam heard it on the roof. He looked for his rain boots. Mom helped him put them on. Liam and Mom stepped outside. The rain made little puddles on the stones. Liam jumped in one. Splash! His boots kept his feet dry.

The wind came next. It blew the tree back and forth. Liam's scarf flapped like a wing. "Where is the wind going?" Liam asked. Mom said, "The wind goes where it wants to." Then soft white snow began to fall. Liam held out his mitten. A snowflake sat on it. Mom zipped his coat up straight. "Warm now," said Liam. He caught one more snowflake on his tongue.

Sara found a big orange scarf on the bench. She picked it up. She held it over two chairs. It made a roof. Now she had a little house!

"I need a baby," said Sara. She put her teddy bear in the house. The wind blew. The roof fell down. The teddy fell over too. "Oh no," said Sara.

She looked around. She found a stick. She pushed the stick under the scarf. The stick held the roof up. The wind blew again. This time the roof stayed!

"One chair, two chairs, one stick, one teddy," said Sara. "My house is strong now."

She gave teddy a pretend bottle. He drank it all up. Then teddy got a hug.

Sara heard her mom call, "Time to go home!" Sara waved at the little house. "See you later, house!" she said. She took teddy's paw and walked to the gate.

Emilia wants a book about sleepy bears. She and Mama go to the library. There are so many books!

Emilia finds a red book. She opens it. The pages have little marks on them. "Those are words," Mama says. "The words tell the story." Emilia turns the pages. First this page, then that page, all the way to the end.

"Can I keep it forever?" Emilia asks.

"We take it home," says the librarian. "Then we bring it back on library day. Other kids want to read it too."

Emilia hugs the book. At home, Mama reads it to her. Emilia kicks her feet on the floor. One story, two stories, three stories, again!

On library day, Emilia holds the red book. She gives it back to the librarian.

"Good returning," says the librarian. "Now it is someone else's turn."

Emilia picks out a new book. It is blue. She opens it and looks at the words. "Read this one too, Mama," she says.

Amelia ran to the play corner at daycare. She wanted to play house with her friend Ben. But Ben already had the baby doll. He hugged it tight.

Amelia peeked in the little toy crib. It was empty. Then she saw the teddy bear under the chair. "You can be my baby," she told the teddy. She wrapped it in a small blanket. She held it in her arm and rocked it side to side.

The teddy's eyes fell shut? No, but Amelia made a soft snore sound. "Shh, baby is sleeping," she said. Ben put his doll down too. He ran to get a toy pot. "I will cook soup," he said. Their teacher, Miss Kim, stirred the pretend pot with a big wooden spoon. "Almost ready," said Miss Kim.

Amelia's teddy woke up with a wide yawn. She held it close. "Time to eat, baby," she said. She tapped the teddy's mouth with a toy spoon. "Yum, yum!" said Ben, and he clapped his hands.

Aaron went to the pool with his dad. He was learning to swim. Aaron was scared of the huge pool. "Will the water hold me up?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "You will wear your water wings."

Aaron held Dad's hand. He stepped in. He kicked his legs. He blew bubbles. Dad held him the whole time.

Then it was time to get out. They went to the changing room. Aaron was shaking. His teeth went click, click. "Why am I cold?" he asked. "Your skin is all wet," said Dad. Dad wrapped Aaron in a big towel.

Aaron sat still. His skin got warm. His teeth stopped clicking. "The towel made me warm," said Aaron.

Then something fell on the floor. It was Aaron's goggles. They left a drip of water. The drip made a little blue spot, like paint. Aaron laughed. "My goggles are painting the floor," he said.

Dad laughed too. He helped Aaron get dressed. Aaron put on his warm socks. "Next time I will blow more bubbles," said Aaron. Dad gave him a hug.

Aurora is going to the dentist. It is her first time. She holds Mama's hand tight.

The chair is big. It has a wheel on one side. The dentist turns the wheel. The chair goes up, up, up! Aurora laughs. "Can it go down too?" she asks. "Yes," says the dentist. He turns the wheel back. The chair goes down, down, down.

Aurora opens her mouth wide. The dentist counts her teeth. "Ten little teeth," he says. "Open like a hippo!" Aurora opens bigger. The dentist giggles. Then he gives her a small mirror. Aurora looks inside. "I see my teeth!" she says. She turns the mirror a little. Now she sees her own eye. "Silly mirror," she says, and everyone laughs.

Lucy wanted to paint a picture for her doll. But she could not find the paint cups. "Where did they go?" she asked. She looked under the table. She looked in the toy box. Then she looked in the deep toy basket. There they were!

Lucy set out four cups. Red, blue, yellow, green. "One, two, three, four," she said. She tapped her brush. She put red paint on the paper. Then she put yellow paint right on top. Something funny happened. The red and yellow spot turned orange!

"Ooh," said Lucy. "Red and yellow make orange!" She tried blue and yellow next. That spot turned green like grass. Then she dipped red into blue. That spot turned purple like grapes.

Her doll sat on the chair and watched. "Which color do you like best?" Lucy asked her. The doll did not say. Lucy laughed. "I think you like all of them."

Mama came to look. "What a pretty picture," said Mama. Lucy held it up high. "Look, doll! Red, blue, yellow, green, and orange, green, purple too!"

Logan had a little drum. He wanted to play a song for Mom. He hit the drum with his hand. It made a big boom. Logan hit it soft. It made a tiny tap.

"What a small sound," said Mom.

Logan wanted a big song. He hit hard, but not too hard. The drum went boom, boom, boom. Then Logan stopped. He wanted the drum to be quiet. He held his hand still on top. The drum stopped right away.

"You made it quiet all by yourself," said Mom.

The cat ran into the room. Logan tapped soft, soft, soft. The cat sat down to listen. It did not run away. Logan tapped a little louder. The cat's ears went up.

"A song for the cat," said Logan.

Mom clapped her hands. Logan read the drum like a book, his hands telling it what to say. He played boom, tap, boom. The cat purred on the rug, and Mom sang along.

Clara wants to help at school. Teacher Max is making warm soup for snack time. He stirs the big pot. Clara has a small cup of cold water. She puts her fingers near the pot. "Hot," says Teacher Max. "Stay back, please." Clara steps away.

Clara wants to help fast. She runs to get a spoon. The spoon falls on the floor. "Slow down," says Teacher Max with a smile. Clara walks back, slow and careful. She picks up the spoon. Now she can stir the little bowl of fruit. She stirs slow, slow, slow.

Then Clara sees something. Her cold cup sits in the sun by the window. She touches it. The cup feels warm now! The sun made cold water turn warm. "Teacher Max, come look!" He puts his hand on the cup. "You found it," he says. "That is a good trick."

Sam from the rug calls, "Was it a joke? Did you hide the warmth?" Clara laughs. "No, the sun is a little naughty. It took my cold away." Sam laughs too. Teacher Max gives Clara a broom. Clara helps sweep the crumbs under the table, big sweeps and small sweeps. She sweeps up one crumb that hides by the chair leg. "I see you," she tells it, and sweeps it into the dustpan.

Isabella ran to the window at school. Yesterday, her class planted little seeds in pots. Today, the pots sat in the sun. But nothing was growing yet. "Where is my plant?" she asked. Miss Kim smiled. "Not now. Water it now, and look again later." Isabella got the small watering can. She tipped it over her pot. The dirt turned dark and wet. She waited. She looked and looked. Still nothing. Miss Kim said, "Come back tomorrow." Tomorrow felt far away. Isabella watered her seed again after dinner time, when the class had a snack. Then she went home to eat dinner with her family. The next day, she ran to the window. A tiny green sprout stood there, high as her finger tip. "You grew!" said Isabella. Miss Kim clapped. "Water it today, and tomorrow it will grow even more." Isabella held her can up high. "I will water you now!"

Leon was at Grandma's house. It was a snowy day. Leon wanted to bake bread for his family.

"Can we make bread?" Leon asked.

"Yes," said Grandma. "We can make a small loaf."

Grandma let Leon pour the flour. Leon mixed it with a spoon. Then Grandma added warm water. She put in the yeast. Grandma always touched the hot stove, never Leon.

The dough sat in a big bowl. Leon looked at it. The dough was small and flat.

"Why is it so little?" Leon asked.

"Wait and see," said Grandma.

They waited. They washed the bowls. Then Leon looked again. The dough was big and puffy! It had grown and grown.

"It got big!" said Leon.

"The warm water made it rise," said Grandma. She smiled.

Grandma shaped the dough. She put it in the oven. Soon a yummy smell filled the kitchen. The oven made a soft noise.

The bread came out golden. Grandma cut it. Leon carried the plates to the table. Mom and Dad clapped for Leon.

"Try it!" said Leon.

His dad took a big bite. "This is the best bread," he said.

Leon took a bite too. It was warm and good. Outside the snow fell. Inside, Leon felt cozy and happy.

Gabriel went to the park with his dad. The duck pond was quiet. A little fish jumped up and went splash. Gabriel laughed at the silly splash.

Dad brought a hoop and a beanbag. "Throw it in," said Dad. Gabriel threw the beanbag. It went up. Then it came down. It landed on the grass, not in the hoop. Gabriel tried again. He threw it high. The beanbag went up, and then it went down into the hoop. It stayed there. Gabriel clapped his hands. "It fell right in!"

Then Dad rolled a big ball to him. The ball was too big for one hand. It bumped his arm and rolled away. Gabriel held out both hands. Dad rolled the ball again. Gabriel caught it with two hands. The ball sat still in his arms like a warm, round pumpkin.

They sat on the bench by the café window. Gabriel looked at the fish pond through the glass. The little fish jumped again. Splash. "Did you see that?" said Gabriel. Dad smiled and rolled the big ball one more time. Gabriel caught it with both hands.

Wyatt wanted to help set the table. Mom said, "We need ten crackers." Wyatt started to count them out. "One, two, three," he said. The crackers made a crunchy sound in the bowl.

He put a small cracker on his sister's plate. She smiled and clapped. "Four, five, six," he counted. Then a tiny crumb fell on the floor. A small bug came out to look at it. Wyatt laughed. "Hello, bug," he said. Mom swept the crumb away. The bug went home too.

"Seven, eight, nine," said Wyatt. He looked in the bowl. Only one cracker was left. "Ten!" he said. He put it on the last plate. The table was ready. Wyatt sang his counting song. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Dad came in and said, "Perfect. Now we can eat."

Alexander sat on the small red chair. In front of him was a big drum. His teacher, Miss Rao, handed him two soft sticks.

"Tap the drum," she said. "See what happens."

Alexander lifted a stick. He tapped once. The drum made a deep sound. The skin on top went wobble, wobble. A toy pig sat on the table near the drum. When Alexander tapped hard, the pig bounced a little. When he tapped soft, the pig sat still.

"I can make it jump," said Alexander.

"Try tapping fast," said Miss Rao.

Alexander tapped fast. The pig wiggled and slid toward the edge. Miss Rao caught it with her hand. Alexander laughed and tapped slow this time. The pig did not move at all.

"My sweater feels itchy," said Alexander. He pulled his sleeves down over his hands. Then he tapped the drum with his covered fingers. The sound came out soft, like a whisper.

Miss Rao smiled. "That was a quiet tap," she said.

Alexander tapped soft, then loud, then soft again. The pig sat still, then hopped, then sat still. Alexander tapped his very best slow beat, and the pig stayed calm as a sleeping cat.

Elizabeth wanted to feed her toy animals. But all her things were mixed up. The toys were with the bananas. The animals were with the crackers. "Oh no," said Elizabeth.

Mama came to help. "Let's make piles," said Mama. Elizabeth put the dog and the cat in one pile. They were animals. She put the ball and the blocks in another pile. They were toys. She put the apple and the bread in the last pile. They were foods.

Then Elizabeth had a big idea. "The animals want food too," she said. She took a toy carrot from the food pile. She gave it to the toy bunny. The bunny got the carrot. Elizabeth clapped her hands. It worked!

Then Elizabeth heard a soft sound outside. She looked out at the street. A real cat sat there. It looked gentle and small. Elizabeth gave the window a kiss. "Bye bye, cat," she said. She waved and waved. The cat stretched in the sun.

"Now my toys are all in piles," said Elizabeth. She hugged the toy bunny tight.

Jake stood by the back door. He wanted to play the senses game, but he forgot the words. "Can you help me, Mama?" he asked. "Yes," said Mama. "We can find each one."

Mama picked a red flower. Jake put his nose close. He sniffed. "I smell it with my nose!" he said. "That is one," said Mama. Then they heard a bird sing. Jake pointed to his ears. "I hear it with my ears!" Mama touched the warm dirt. Jake touched it too. "I feel it with my hands!"

The sun felt nice on Jake's face. He closed his eyes. "I feel the sun with my skin!" he said. Then he licked his lips after a sweet berry snack. "I taste with my tongue!" One sense was left. Jake looked all around. He saw a big yellow butterfly. "I see it with my eyes!" he said. "Five senses, all found!" Jake clapped. "I did it!"

Matthew went to the store with Mama. He wanted apples for a snack. But how many apples should they get?

Mama held up one finger. "Can you count them?" she asked. Matthew put one apple in the bag. "One," he said. He put in another. "Two." He kept going. "Three, four, five."

A lady nearby was counting oranges. "One, two, three, four," she said. Matthew listened. Counting words were everywhere! "Mama, do other people count too?" he asked. "Yes," said Mama. "We count to know how many."

Matthew saw a lamp on a shelf. He touched the shade. It was not hot. It was just warm. "Does the lamp make light?" he asked. Mama nodded. "Press the little button." Matthew pressed it. The lamp made light. He pressed it again. The light went off. "It works!" said Matthew.

At the bread shelf, they counted together. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten," said Matthew. Ten rolls went in the bag. At home, he would eat one apple. Nine would be left. Matthew patted the full bag. "One, two, three," he said, all the way to the door.

Aurora sat on the big clean rug. Family and friends filled the room. Grandma stirred a bowl of dip. Dad opened a bag of chips. On the TV, the big game was starting.

The red team ran with the ball. Aurora picked up her red scarf. She waved it high. Everyone saw her scarf. They waved their arms too. The room filled with cheering.

Then the blue team got the ball. Aurora put her scarf down. She picked up her blue hat. She waved the hat instead. Uncle Ben laughed and waved his blue cup. Everyone cheered for blue now.

The blue team kicked the ball into the net. The whole room jumped up. Aurora jumped too. Grandma handed her a chip with dip. Aurora ate it and waved her hat again. "More blue!" she shouted.

Ellie went to the library with Dad. She wanted to find a book about animals. But she did not know where the animal books were.

The library was big. Ellie saw many shelves. "Let's look," said Dad. Ellie looked at a shelf. She saw trucks and balls and teddy bears. "Toys, toys, toys," said Ellie. Those were toy books, not animal books.

They walked to a new shelf. Ellie saw apples and bread and milk. "Foods, foods, foods," said Ellie. Still no animals. Ellie got a little sad. Dad said, "Try one more shelf."

Ellie tried the next shelf. She saw cats and dogs and ducks. "Animals, animals, animals!" said Ellie. She found the animal books! Ellie picked a big cat book. Then she found a soft pillow in the reading corner. She sat on it with Dad.

Ellie read the cat book. The cat in the book was sleepy. It curled up and went to sleep. Ellie yawned too. "Sleepy girl," said Dad with a smile. He helped Ellie close the book. "Good night, cat," said Ellie.

Ella sat on her bed with her library book. It was a book about a little red cat. She wanted to keep it forever.

She opened the front cover. The first page said "1". The last page said "20". She turned the pages one by one. The words on each page told about the cat. Ella could not read them yet. But her mom could. Mom read them out loud, and the cat story came alive.

"Can the cat be mine?" Ella asked.

"No, it is a library book," said Mom. "We take it back on Thursday. Then another kid can read it too."

Eella held the book tight. She brushed her hand over the smooth cover. Then she looked out at the cloudy sky and thought.

"Can we read it again first?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "We can read it many times before Thursday."

So they read it two more times. Ella turned each page, front to back, all the way to the end. The little red cat went home to his mom. Then Ella put the book on her shelf, next to her paint set.

"Good night, cat," she said. "I will take you back on Thursday."

Maeva went to the lantern festival with Mama and Papa. The street was full of people. Paper lanterns hung on long strings above them. Maeva wanted to let one go up into the sky, like the big kids did.

Papa held a small lantern for her. "How does it go up?" Maeva asked. "The warm air inside lifts it," Papa said. "It rises slow, like a balloon." Mama lit the candle with a match. Maeva watched from far away, holding Papa's hand.

Then Maeva saw it. The candle made the lantern grow round and fat. The paper puffed out. The lantern pulled up, up, up. "It wants to fly!" she said. Papa let go of the string. The lantern slipped out of his fingers and floated over the rooftops. Maeva waved until it was just a tiny dot. "Goodbye, lantern," she called. "Fly slow."

Elijah wanted to spell his name. He had a big plate of letters. Each letter was a magnet. They lived on the fridge door.

He picked up a letter. "B," said Mama. "B says buh." Elijah put it down. His name did not start with buh. He picked up a wiggly letter. "M," said Mama. "M says mmm." That was not his sound either. Elijah looked and looked. His fingers were sticky from the honey on his toast. One magnet stuck to his thumb. It tickled a little when he pulled it off.

The sticky magnet was E. "E says eh," said Mama. "Eh, eh, Elijah!" Elijah clapped his hands. He put the E on the fridge. Then he found an L. "L says lll," said Mama. Lll was in his name too. Elijah found an I and a J and an A and an H. He lined them all up in a row.

Mama traced the letters with one finger. "E L I J A H," she read. Elijah tapped each letter too. "Eh, lll, ih, juh, ah, huh," he said. The letters made his name. They made sounds when he tapped them. His name was right there on the fridge, made of letters.

Papa came in with his tool box. He had been fixing the gate. Elijah pulled him to the fridge. "Look, Papa! My letters! Tap them!" Papa tapped the E. "Eh," said Elijah. Papa tapped the L. "Lll," said Elijah. Papa tapped every letter, and Elijah said every sound, all the way to the end of his name.

Athena went to the park with her dad. She wanted to feed the ducks. She had a bag of bread in her hand. "The ducks will like this," she said.

Athena tore off a small piece. She dropped it in the pond. It did not sink. The bread could float! A duck swam over fast. The duck ate the bread. Then more ducks came. They ate the bread too.

But a squirrel ran up. It grabbed the whole bag! Athena said, "Oh no!" The squirrel ran to a big tree. The bag had a hole in it. Apples fell out of the bag. They were round. They rolled down the grass.

The apples rolled near a bench. A boy sat there with a toy truck. He stopped the apples with his truck. "Here you go," he said. Athena picked up her apples. She shared one with the boy. The ducks got more bread. "Thank you," Athena said. The boy pushed his truck again. Vroom!

Luka ran to the park with his dad. He wanted to play the sense game. His big sister had shown him. Now he wanted to try it all by himself.

Luka closed his eyes. "I hear a bird," he said. "My ears hear it!" Then he touched the slide. "The slide is cold. My hands feel it!" A dog barked. Luka giggled. His ears heard that too.

Then Luka saw something tiny in the grass. It was a shiny red ladybug. Luka got close. "My eyes see it!" he said. His dad handed him an apple. Luka took a bite. He chewed slowly. "My mouth tastes it. Sweet!" Then he sniffed the air. Flowers were growing near the fence. "My nose smells them. They smell like rain!"

Luka stood up tall. "Ears, hands, eyes, mouth, nose," he said. "That is all five!" His dad clapped. "You did it, Luka." Luka spun around fast. "Daddy, watch me!" he shouted. The ladybug flew up. Luka's eyes followed it all the way to the rainbow flowers by the gate.

Abigail sat at the little red table. There was a tablet in front of her. It was dark and still. She wanted to draw a big round sun on it.

"Press the round button," said Miss Kim. Abigail pressed it. The screen lit up. She had made the dark screen turn bright. Miss Kim smiled and helped her tap the drawing app. It had a picture of a paint brush. Abigail tapped it, and the white page appeared. She drew a round sun. Then she drew a bird. She made the bird fly across the page with one long line.

Tommy came to the table next. He wanted a turn too. Abigail saw him waiting. She pressed the top button, and the screen went dark again. She put the tablet in the basket, just like Miss Kim showed. The tablet lay soft and quiet on top of a book.

"Your turn, Tommy," said Abigail. "Press the round button. Watch it light up." Tommy pressed it. The bright screen came back. "It works!" he said. Abigail went to the toy corner and picked up a round ball.

It was Charlie's first day of school. She stood by the fence. Her tummy felt funny. She wanted a friend, but she did not know how.

A boy sat in the sandbox. He had a red truck. He poured sand into the truck. The sand made a little hill. Charlie watched and watched. She walked over slowly. She picked up a small cup. She scooped sand and poured it in too. Now the hill was bigger. The boy smiled at her.

Then they dug a long line in the sand. "Look, a worm road," said the boy. A real worm wiggled into the hole. It made the sand move. "Silly worm," said Charlie, and she laughed. The teacher rang the bell. Charlie and her new friend ran to the line, hand in hand.

Penelope wanted to wear her boots at daycare. But when she reached for her bag, one boot was gone.

"Where is my boot?" she asked. Her friend Tom looked under the table. "Not here," he said.

After snack time, they washed their hands. The water was warm. Penelope watched the bubbles slide down her fingers. Then she saw something stuck in the drying rack. It was her boot, full of soapy water!

"Yuck!" said Tom, and he laughed. "Your boot took a bath!"

Miss Anna poured the water out. She helped Penelope dry the boot with a towel. Penelope wiggled her toes inside. The boot was warm and damp.

At nap time, Penelope put the boot beside her mat. "Sleep now," she whispered.

When she woke up, the boot was dry. She pushed her foot in. It fit just right. Penelope stomped around the room. Stomp, stomp, stomp!

"My boots match again!" she said. Tom clapped, and they went to color a picture of two happy boots.

Felix wanted to paint a picture for Grandma. He hoped she would love it. At school, there were paint cups on the table. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. There was green paint.

Felix picked the red brush first. He made a big red sun. Then he dipped his brush in the blue cup. But the brush was still red. The blue cup turned purple!

"Oh no," said Felix. "My blue is gone!" He felt a little scared. Grandma loved blue. He wanted blue flowers in the picture.

Miss Mia came over. "Try a clean brush," she said. She gave him a fresh one. Felix dipped it in the blue cup. The blue stayed blue! He made five blue flowers.

Then he painted a green frog. He painted a yellow moon. He painted red spots on the frog, with a clean brush each time.

"Grandma will say wow," said Felix. He held the picture up high. The red sun smiled down on the blue flowers.

Ava sat in her car seat. She was hungry. "Mom, I want a snack," she said. "We will stop soon," said Mom. The car went past a big farm. Ava saw a cow. Then she saw a sheep. Then she saw a horse. "Animals!" said Ava. She waved at them.

The car stopped at a small shop. Mom held Ava's hand. They went inside. Ava saw apples, bread, and milk. "Those are foods," said Mom. Ava picked a red apple. Then she saw a bin of small cars. "Can I look at the toys?" she asked. "Just look," said Mom. Ava found a tiny blue car. It had kind eyes painted on it.

At the counter, Mom gave the man money. The man put the apple and the little car in a bag. "The car too?" asked Ava. Mom smiled. "The car too." In the car, Ava ate her apple. She held her new toy. The cow in the field watched them go by. Ava blinked, and the cow blinked back. "It saw me!" she said.

Elizabeth got her blue coat from the hook. The zipper was open all the way down. She pulled the pull, but it did not move.

Teacher Sam smiled. "Try the bottom first," he said.

Elizabeth looked at the bottom of her coat. There was a little tooth on one side and a slot on the other side. She pushed the tooth into the slot. Click.

She held the slot with one hand. She pulled the pull with her other hand. Zip! The zipper went up, up, up. The coat closed all by itself.

Elizabeth laughed. She pulled the zipper down fast. Then she did it again. Tooth in, slot held, pull up. Zip!

Teacher Sam clapped. "Your coat is on, Elizabeth."

Elizabeth patted her zipped coat. "All by me," she said.

Gianna waited at the airport. She held a big paper sign. The sign said Grandma.

People came and went. One bag. Two bags. Three bags. Where was Grandma?

Then Gianna saw a red hat. "Grandma!" she yelled. Grandma hugged her tight. Grandma had one big suitcase. Gianna tried to pull it. It did not move. It was too heavy.

Grandma pushed the handle down. Then she pulled it up. The suitcase stood on little wheels. Now it rolled! "Can I fish for more wheels?" Gianna asked, looking around. She looked at a stroller. It had wheels too. Then a cart. Wheels again!

"Wheels make heavy things roll," Gianna said. Grandma laughed. "You are a smart girl. But one question first. Was that a mean old suitcase?" "No!" said Gianna. "It just needed wheels!"

Gianna rolled the suitcase all the way to the car. Wheel, wheel, wheel, it went.

Madelyn woke up in her warm bed. The sun was on her window. "Time to get dressed," said Mom. Madelyn picked her own socks. One sock was red. One sock was wild with spots. She pulled them on all by herself.

Then Madelyn smelled something good. Mom was cooking eggs at the stove. Mom did the hot part. Madelyn carried the spoons to the table. She ate her eggs and a big apple. Crunch, crunch. When she ate the apple, her tummy felt happy.

After breakfast, Madelyn ran outside. She got mud on her feet. Now her feet were brown! "Bath time," said Mom. Mom filled the tub. Madelyn splashed and washed the mud away. The water turned brown, and then Madelyn turned clean. She rubbed her eyes and yawned. "Sleepy?" Mom asked. Madelyn found her bear. She snuggled into bed. "I wish the mud would come back tomorrow," she whispered.

Mateo sat at the little red table. He wanted to paint a picture of his baby sister. But he did not know how to start.

Miss Ana handed him a cup of purple paint. "Try shapes," she said. Mateo dipped his brush. He made a circle. Round and round it went. "That is her head," he said.

Then he painted a square below the circle. It had four flat sides. "That is her body!" He laughed. He painted two small circles for hands. He poured a little more purple paint into his cup. The paint made a soft plop sound.

Next he wanted to make her hat. He tried a rectangle, but it looked wrong. The top was too pointy. Miss Ana leaned over. "Look," she said. "It has three sides."

"A triangle!" said Mateo. The pointy hat sat on the circle head. Just right.

A boy next to him dropped his brush on the floor. Mateo picked it up and gave it back. "Thank you," said the boy.

Miss Ana hung the purple baby picture on the wall. "My turn to look," said Mateo, and he stood back to see.

Henri ran up the steps to Grandpa's house. Today the new baby was coming! Henri wanted to make the baby laugh. He had a plan.

The baby arrived in a soft blue blanket. His name was Sam. Sam looked tiny. Then Sam began to cry. Henri froze. His plan felt gone.

Henri grabbed his fuzzy bear. He made the bear dance. Sam kept crying. Henri found a shiny rattle. He shook it fast. Sam stopped! Sam looked at the rattle. Then Sam made a small gurgle. It almost sounded like a laugh.

"Again!" said Henri. He shook the rattle. Sam gurgled again. Henri clapped his hands.

Grandpa laughed too. "Sam likes your rattle," he said.

Henri followed Grandpa to the porch. "Can I hold Sam now?" he asked.

Grandpa sat down and put Sam in Henri's arms. Sam grabbed Henri's finger and held on tight.

"Hello, Sam," said Henri. "I am your big brother."

Outside, a little worm wiggled on the step. Sam's eyes followed it all the way.

Paisley's baby doll was crying. It was only a pretend cry, but it sounded very sad. "Waa, waa," said her friend Mia, making the doll's voice. Paisley wanted to help the baby feel better.

She looked around the pretend house corner. There was a small pot. There was a soft blanket. There was a toy spoon. First Paisley wrapped the baby in the blanket. The crying kept going. Then she patted the baby's back, gently, gently. The crying got smaller. Then she rocked the baby in her arms. "Shh, shh," said Paisley. The baby went to sleep.

"Let's make the baby soup," said Mia. They dug in the sandbox for pretend carrots. They drove a toy truck down a pretend road to bring them home. The soup smelled stinky, so they stirred in pretend flowers too. The baby woke up and smiled. "More soup!" said Paisley, holding out the little pot.

Harrison stood at the bus stop with Mama. He held his yellow hat on his head. The sun came out first. The sun made his nose feel warm. "Mama, why do I squint?" he asked. "The sun is bright," said Mama. She put sunglasses on him.

Then the wind blew. The wind took his hat right off! The hat flew up, up, up. "Come back, hat!" said Harrison. Mama reached out her hand. She caught the hat in the air. She put it back on his head. "Wind likes to blow hats," she said.

Next, rain began to fall. Pit, pat, pit, pat. A drop landed on Harrison's toe. "Mama, my toe is wet!" he said. Mama opened a big umbrella. The rain tapped on top of it. The drops could not reach his toe now.

At last the rain stopped. Little white flakes came down instead. "What is that?" asked Harrison. "Snow," said Mama. She zipped his coat up to his chin. Snow landed on his mittens. It did not land on his hands. Harrison looked at his sweet mittens and smiled. The bus came, and they climbed on together.

Leah was three today. She wore her yellow party dress. The backyard had balloons on the fence. Grandma put a big cake on the table.

Leah wanted to blow out the candles. But she was too far away. "Come near, Leah," said Daddy. Leah hopped close on one foot. Then she stood by the cake.

Daddy lit the candles with a match. The flames went up. Leah took a big breath. She blew hard. The candles went out. The smoke curled up into the air. "I did it!" said Leah. Everyone clapped. Grandma cut the cake. Leah got the first big piece, with pink frosting on top.

Wren sat at the dinner table. She wanted more peas. She reached across the big bowl. The bowl began to tip. "Careful," said Dad. The peas rolled onto the table.

"Sorry, Daddy," said Wren. Dad smiled. He wiped up the peas. Wren looked at her empty plate. She could not reach the bowl. "Daddy, can you help me, please?" she asked. Dad scooped peas onto her plate. "Thank you," said Wren.

Then Grandma came in. She wore a soft winter hat. "My head was cold," she said. "The hat works so well." Wren giggled. Grandma sat down and helped herself. Wren passed her the bread. Grandma said, "Thank you, Wren." Wren grinned and put a pea on her fork. "You're not lazy at supper," said Grandma. "You are a big helper." Wren ate her pea and smiled.

Beatrice went to the store with her dad. She wanted a warm bun for breakfast. The store was big. Beatrice was small.

She pushed the cart. First it went fast. Then it went slow. "Why does it go slow?" she asked. Dad pointed at the floor. A bump made the cart slow down. Beatrice pushed again. Smooth floor made it go fast.

Next they came to the cold fridge. Beatrice touched the glass. Brrr! Cold glass made her fingers hurt a little. Dad opened the bakery case. Warm air came out. The buns were hot, so Dad used a big paper bag to hold one. Beatrice watched. Would the bag get hot too? Yes! The warm bun made the bag warm.

Dad put the little bun in the cart. "One warm bun," he said. Beatrice smiled. "That is my answer," she said. "A silly bump, a cold fridge, and a hot bun!" She carried the bag all the way home, very slowly.

Henri sat in the big waiting chair. He held his doll tight. Today he would get his first haircut. He did not want snippy scissors near his doll.

The hairdresser waved him over. "Bring your doll," she said. "She can sit on the lap of the chair."

Henri sat down slowly. He put the doll on his knees. The hairdresser put a soft cape on Henri. Then she sprayed water on his hair.

"Look," she said. She sprayed a tiny bit of water on the doll's hair too. The doll's hair went dark and flat.

"Now she looks silly," said Henri. He laughed a small laugh. The wet hair stuck to her head like little stripes.

The hairdresser cut Henri's hair bit by bit. Henri did not move. He watched the bits fall. They landed on the cape like tiny snow.

At last she took the cape off. She shook it, and all the hair bits spilled to the floor.

Henri picked up his doll. Her hair was dry now. It was soft and fluffy again. Henri patted it smooth. "You look pretty," he whispered to the doll.

He jumped off the chair and ran to Mama with the doll held up high.

Sofia wanted to play the senses game at school. But she could not remember them all. "Maybe I can practice at home," she said.

Mama was baking bread in the kitchen. Sofia stood next to her. "Close your eyes," said Mama. "What do you smell?" Sofia sniffed with her nose. "Bread! My nose knows smell!" Then Mama said, "Now look at the oven." Sofia used her eyes to see. "That is seeing!" she said.

Next, Mama tapped the pan. Tink, tink. "My ears hear that," said Sofia. The bread came out. Mama cut one slice. The knife was sharp, so Mama did the cutting. Sofia touched her slice. "Warm and soft. That is my hands touching!" Then she took a bite. "Yum! My tongue tastes it!"

"Four senses," said Sofia. "One more to go." After dinner, Papa took her to the window. The moon was up. "Look how fast the clouds move," said Papa. Sofia looked with her eyes. Then she counted on her fingers. Nose, eyes, ears, hands, tongue. "Five! I did it!"

Papa laughed and gave her a hug. "All five," he said.

Grayson ran to the window at daycare. "Look, look!" he said. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. "Sunny days mean no coats," said his friend Mia. She hung her coat on the hook.

Miss Patel held up a paper sun. "We will make a weather sign," she said. Grayson got the glue. He glued the yellow sun on the poster. It looked bright and warm.

Then the sky changed. The wind blew hard. It was windy now. Papers flew off the table. "Hold them tight!" said Miss Patel. Grayson grabbed the paper hat. He glued it down too. The wind had made the papers fly.

Next came rain. Tap, tap, tap on the window. Grayson glued a paper umbrella on the sign. "Rainy days need boots," said Mia. She showed her red boots. Grayson laughed and clapped.

A shy boy named Sam peeked at the poster. He had never glued before. "You can help," said Grayson. Sam glued on a mitten. "Snowy days need mittens," said Grayson. Sam smiled big. Their weather sign was done. It had sun, wind, rain, and snow. "Let's show everyone!" said Grayson.

Emilia sat at the big table. Mama put warm toast in front of her. Mama put a little dish of soft butter there too. Emilia wanted to spread the butter all by herself.

Emilia pressed the butter with her spoon. The butter slid off the toast. It fell on the plate. Emilia looked at the spoon. She tried again, slowly. This time she used the flat side of the spoon. She moved it gentle and slow. The butter went smooth across the toast. "Look, Mama," said Emilia. "It is smooth now."

Then Emilia wanted milk in her cup. Papa held the big jug low, near the cup. Emilia poured slowly. The milk went up, up the side. Papa said, "Stop now." Emilia stopped. The milk was at the top, but it did not spill. Emilia looked at her toast and her cup. She took a big bite. An ant walked across the table, far from her plate. "Hello, ant," said Emilia. "I did it myself."

Livia could not find her bunny. Bunny had soft white fur and a pink nose. Livia looked under her pillow. No bunny there. "Where are you, Bunny?" she said.

She looked in her toy box. She looked behind the chair. She peeked under her bed. Bunny was not far away. Livia could feel it. But the room was big, and Bunny was small.

Then Livia saw something move. It was her cat, Milo. Milo tapped a little bell with his paw. The bell rolled across the floor. It went fast, and then it stopped under the blanket. The blanket moved up in a small bump. Livia peeked at the bump. There was her bunny, all cozy and warm!

"Milo, you found Bunny!" said Livia. She hugged Bunny tight. Milo purred and rubbed her leg. "Where are you, Bunny?" Livia said again. But this time she laughed. Bunny was right there, safe in her arms.

Mama came to the door. "Time for milk," she said. Livia carried Bunny to the table. She set out a little cup for herself. She set a small bowl of water on the floor for Milo. Milo drank, and Livia patted his head.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. On Saturday, Sienna held her hand at the market. "Grandma looks sad," Sienna whispered to Mama. Grandma lived far away, and her cat had stayed home.

The market smelled like bread and flowers. Sienna saw a man with paper and brushes. "Can I paint?" she asked. Mama paid the man, and Sienna sat down. She painted Grandma's cat, black with white paws. "I remember him," Sienna said. She painted his long tail and his little pink nose.

The big clock at the market chimed. It was time to go home. Sienna carried her painting with two hands. At home, she gave it to Grandma. Grandma looked and looked. "My cat," Grandma said. "You made him here with me." She hung the painting by her bed.

All week, Grandma smiled at the painting. When she packed her bag, she folded her clothes around it. "This comes with me," she said. "Then you are with me, even far away." Sienna grinned and waved at the door.

Anthony rode the big bus with Mama. He held his little red dinosaur. Then the bus went bump. The dinosaur jumped out of his hands.

"Oh no," said Anthony. "Where did it go?" He looked down. He looked under his seat. He saw a shoe and a paper. No dinosaur.

The bus went bump again. A paper ball rolled out from under the seat. It rolled right to Anthony's feet. Did the bump make it roll?

Anthony peeked into the hole under the seat. There was his dinosaur! The bump had made it roll there too. It looked like a little nest of lost things.

"Is this your true home?" Anthony asked the dinosaur. "No, you come with me."

He pulled it out. It was dusty. Mama helped him clean it with a tissue. Anthony held it tight all the way home.

Florence held Mama's hand on the bus. They were going to the dentist for the first time.

"Will it hurt?" Florence asked.

"First we look at your teeth," said Mama. "The dentist counts them."

A man sat near them. He had a bag with fish and chips. "Do you want to taste one?" he asked his little boy. The boy tasted a chip. Then he smiled.

The bus went round and round. Florence wanted it to stop. She was scared of the dentist.

"Watch," said Mama. She pushed the red button. Ding! The bell rang.

"Did the button make the bell?" asked Florence.

"Push it and see," said Mama.

Florence waited. The man's little boy pushed the button too. Ding! The bus stopped at the next street.

"The button stops the bus," said Florence.

"That's right," said Mama.

They got off near the dentist's door. Inside, a kind lady said, "Open wide." Florence counted her teeth, one by one.

"Ten!" said the lady. "All clean."

Florence picked a sticker. It had a fish on it, shiny and blue.

Leah ran to the swings at the playground. She wanted to swing high like the big kids. But every swing was full.

Leah stood by the fence and watched. Then she heard something. A boy on the bench was singing a counting song. "One, two, three, four, five," he sang. Leah listened. Then she sang too. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

A girl on a swing turned her head. She looked at Leah and smiled. "I like that song," she said. "Want my swing next?" The girl jumped off and held the swing for Leah.

Leah sat down and pushed with her legs. The swing went up. She sang her counting song as she flew. "One, two, three," she called to the sky. The girl sat on the bench and clapped.

Arthur was at Grandpa's house. Grandpa had a big dirt patch. "We can plant seeds here," said Grandpa. Arthur jumped up and down.

Arthur made little holes in the dirt. He dropped a seed in each one. Then he covered them up. "Now what?" he asked. "Seeds need water," said Grandpa. Arthur held the watering can. He poured water on the dirt. Splash, splash, splash.

The next morning, Arthur ran outside. The dirt looked the same. "Nothing grew!" he said. "Watch and wait," said Grandpa.

Arthur watched. Days went by. Then one morning, Arthur saw green leaves in the middle of the dirt! "Grandpa, come quick!" he shouted.

The little leaves grew tall. A small yellow flower opened up. Then the flower fell off. Under it was a tiny green bean! Arthur picked it and held it high. "Grandpa! The seed made a bean!"

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Juliette was so excited. She wanted to give him a surprise. A big red apple would be perfect!

Mommy took Juliette to the market. They walked past the bread stand. They walked past the flower stand. At last they found the fruit stand. But oh no! No red apples. Only green ones.

"Sorry," said the fruit man. "The red apples are gone." Juliette felt sad. Then she saw Grandpa's big straw hat. He was wearing it at the market too! The green apples were hiding under his hat brim. No, wait. They were just sitting in a pile. Juliette had an idea.

"Grandpa loves green apples!" she said. "He eats one every day." Mommy smiled. They bought three green apples. One for Grandpa. One for Mommy. One for Juliette.

At home, Grandpa waved his arms. "My favorite!" he said. He took a big bite. Crunch! Juliette gave him his apple in her own little bowl. Grandpa said it was the best surprise ever.

The next morning, Grandpa wore his hat to breakfast. "Can we go to the market again?" he asked. Juliette jumped up and down. "Yes! Yes! Yes!"

Owen ran to the park with his dad. He was so excited. The big slide looked fun today.

Then Owen saw a small dog. The dog was sad. It sat by a tree all alone. "Where is your friend?" Owen wondered.

A loud truck went by. The dog got scared and hid. Owen sat down near the tree. He patted his knees softly. The dog came closer. It sniffed his shoe. Owen laughed. The dog licked his hand. Now the dog looked happy!

Then a big boy ran by and took the dog's ball. The dog got angry. It barked and barked. "Give it back, please," said Owen's dad. The big boy gave the ball back. He threw it far. The dog jumped high to catch it. The ball did not bite the dog's nose. It was soft!

A lady called out, "Buddy! Time to go home!" That was the dog's name. Buddy ran to her, wagging his tail. He was not smelly or sad anymore. He was a happy dog with his ball and his friend.

Owen waved. "Bye, Buddy!" he said. Then he ran to the big slide.

Yesterday, Penelope planted a seed at school. She put it in a little pot. Today she walked over to see it. The pot sat on a low shelf by the window. The top of the soil was still flat and brown. "Nothing yet," said her teacher. "The seed is sleeping. Later it will wake up."

Penelope watered the soil with a small cup. She put the pot back on the low shelf. Then she painted a picture of a green shoot. She gave the picture a tall stem and a round top.

"Now we wait," said her teacher. "Tomorrow we will look again."

All day, Penelope looked at the pot. After story time, she looked again. After snack, once more.

At home time, she walked past the shelf slowly. The soil was still flat. But tomorrow was coming.

Penelope put on her coat. "See you tomorrow, little seed," she whispered.

Jasmine had a library book about a rainbow. She loved the rainbow pictures. At bedtime she wanted to keep the book forever. "Can it stay mine?" she asked. "We borrowed it," said Mama. "We take it back so other kids can read it."

Jasmine held the book close. She opened the front cover first. The words made a story. Mama read them out loud. Jasmine pointed at a page. "What does that say?" she asked. "It says the rainbow is red and blue," said Mama. The words meant something. Jasmine turned page by page, all the way to the back.

Then she got an idea. She would draw her own rainbow book. She drew a red page, then a blue page. "Mine can stay forever," she said. "It's true!" The next day, she gave the library book back. Then she picked a new one to take home.

Henry sat at the paint table at school. He had red paint, yellow paint and blue paint. His teacher, Miss Jo, held up a card. "Red," said Henry. "Yellow," said Henry. "Blue," said Henry. "One, two, three colours," said Miss Jo.

Henry wanted to paint a sun. But the orange paint pot was empty. No orange in it at all. Henry looked and looked. He wanted orange so much. His tummy felt tight like a squeezed pillow.

Then Mia dipped her brush in yellow. She put yellow on the paper. Henry dipped his brush in red. He tapped red on top of the yellow spot. He moved his brush round and round. The spot turned orange! Henry gasped. "Look, look!" he said.

He painted a big orange sun. Mia wanted one too. Henry helped her. Red on yellow, round and round. "Orange sun," said Mia. "Two suns," said Henry. They counted them. "One, two." Miss Jo smiled and put a white paper cloud next to the suns. Henry laughed and gave the cloud a tickle of yellow. The cloud turned sunny too.

Max saw a big red truck at school. Sam was holding it. Max wanted the truck so much.

Max grabbed for the truck. The truck slipped. It rolled under the pillow corner. Now nobody had the truck.

The teacher, Miss Joy, picked it up. "Sam first," she said. "Then Max." Max sat on a pillow and waited. His sock felt itchy. He wiggled his foot. He kept waiting.

Sam pushed the truck up a ramp. The truck went fast. Sam laughed. Max laughed too.

Then Sam put the truck in Max's hands. "Your turn," said Sam. Max pushed the truck down the ramp. It zoomed right into the block tower. The blocks fell down with a big crash.

Sam clapped. "Again!" he said. Max put out the truck. "You first," said Max.

Riley sat at the little blue table. Teacher Mia put out letter cards. Riley wanted to find the first letter of her name.

She picked up a card. It was M. "M says mmm," said Teacher Mia. Riley put M down. That was not her letter.

Riley picked up another card. It was R. She looked at it for a long time. "R," she said slowly. Then she tried the sound. "Rrr," she said. The card had two little legs and one arm.

Teacher Mia smiled. "Try it again," she said. Riley waited. She looked at the R. "Rrr," she said again. "R is for Riley!"

Then Teacher Mia held up a picture card. It was a rabbit. "Rrr," said Riley. "Rabbit goes rrr!" She laughed and clapped her hands.

Riley put the R card next to the M card. "Mmm," she said. "M is for Mia!" Teacher Mia laughed too.

At dinner that night, Riley looked at her cup. She saw a letter on it. "Rrr," she said. "R is for Riley and for my cup!" Mommy smiled. "Say it one more time," said Mommy. Riley took a big breath. "Rrr," she said, nice and slow.

David waited by the gate. His tummy made a little rumble. He wanted his snack, and he wanted it now.

Mama came with his bag. She opened it up. Out came his green cup. David drank some water. His tummy felt better. "Snack time at home," said Mama.

At home, David sat at the table. Mama used a safe knife to cut his apple. The apple fell into little white pieces. One cut, and the big apple was small pieces. David ate them all up.

Then Mama ran the bath. The water was warm. Mama checked it with her hand. David took off his socks. He got in the tub. He washed his toes and his nose.

David put on his soft pajamas. He brushed his teeth with Mama. He picked his hat for the morning, his blue one with the star. He put it on the chair.

"Night night, hat," said David. He climbed into bed and closed his eyes.

Sadie sat at the dinner table. She wanted the red jello. But the jello was not ready yet.

"When can I have it?" she asked.

"Later," said Dad. "It has to sit in the fridge. It was wiggly yesterday. It is firm today."

Sadie poked her peas with her spoon. She watched Dad open the fridge. The jello sat there, shiny and red. Now it was just sitting. Later it would be on her plate.

"How long is later?" she asked.

"Later is after dinner," said Mom. "First peas, then carrots, then jello."

Sadie ate one pea. Then two. Then three. She named each bite. "Pea, pea, pea." The peas went down. The carrots went down too.

"Now can we look?" she asked.

Dad opened the fridge again. The jello jiggled just a little. He tipped the bowl. The whole red shape slid out onto a plate. It held its shape!

"Tomorrow," said Mom, "we can make blue jello. Then it will sit in the fridge too."

Sadie clapped her hands. First red, then blue! She ate her jello one happy spoonful at a time.

"What color comes after blue?" she asked.

Mom laughed. "We can talk about it tomorrow."

Jayden was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to build a tower in the yard. He could not find his red blocks.

"Let's look," said Grandpa.

They looked by the blue door. No blocks there. They looked by the yellow chair. No blocks there. "One, two, three places," said Grandpa.

Then Jayden saw something green. The grass by the steps was bumpy. He pushed the green grass aside. There were the red blocks, hiding!

"Bad grass," said Jayden, laughing. "You hid my blocks."

Grandpa smiled. They sat on the porch. Jayden stacked the blocks up high. He put a small blue block on top. Then a small yellow block. The tower stood tall.

Grandpa brought out a plate of apple slices. Jayden ate one, red and shiny. "My tower is the best," he said. He counted it out loud. "One, two, three, four, five!"

Charlie sat down at the little red table. Today he would write his name! His teacher, Miss Kim, gave him a fat pencil.

"Pinch it like this," said Miss Kim. She showed him. "Then rest your hand on the paper."

Charlie squeezed the pencil very hard. He wrote a C. It looked wobbly. It wiggled all over like a road with bumps.

"Yucky C," said Charlie.

Miss Kim smiled. "Try a soft pinch."

Charlie lifted his fingers. He pinched soft. He wrote a C again. This C sat straight and neat on the line!

"I did it!" said Charlie.

He wrote the next letter. Then the next. "C, H, A," he said out loud.

Miss Kim clapped. "Keep going!"

Charlie gripped soft, and every letter came out clean. Seven letters, all in a row. He held the paper up high.

"That's my name!" said Charlie.

Camille ran onto the ice rink floor. Her dad held a red hoop and a beanbag. "Can I try?" Camille asked. "Yes, you can!" said Dad.

Camille threw the beanbag. It hit the edge. It fell down. "Oh no," said Camille. Dad put the hoop lower. "Try again," he said. Camille threw the beanbag up. The beanbag went in. It sank to the bottom of the hoop. "I did it!" she shouted.

Then Dad brought out a big blue ball. "Catch!" he said. The ball bounced off her hands. It rolled away. "That ball is too big," said Camille. "What do I do?" "Hold out both arms," said Dad. Camille held out both arms. She made a big circle. Dad rolled the ball slowly. The ball came right into her arms. She hugged it like a blanket. "I caught it!" she yelled.

Camille threw the beanbag again. In it went. She caught the ball again. "Watch me, Dad!" she said. Her arms went out wide, and the big blue ball came rolling in.

Amira wanted to sing the counting song. Her big brother Sam knew all the words. Amira knew the first part only. "One, two, three," she sang. Then she stopped. She scratched her head. The rest of the words were hiding from her.

Sam was setting the table for lunch. "Can you bring the cups?" he asked. Amira carried one cup. Then two cups. Then three. "Four, five," said Sam, counting with her. At lunch, Mama put grapes on Amira's plate. "Six, seven, eight," said Mama, counting them out loud. Amira ate one grape. It tasted sweet and new.

After lunch, Papa called from the porch. "Amira, come see!" Ten little ants walked in a line. Papa pointed at each one. "Nine, ten," he said. Amira looked at the ants. The whole little world of them marched on.

That night, Sam began the song. "One, two, three," he sang. Amira took a big breath. "Four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Sam clapped his hands. "You did it!" Amira sang it again, all by herself.

Aurora was grumpy. Her tummy was empty. Dinner was not ready yet.

Mom put a big pot on the stove. Aurora watched from her chair. Mom stirred and stirred. The soup turned red like paint. Soon steam went up, up, up. Aurora sniffed with her nose. Mmm, it smelled like tomatoes.

"It is ready," said Mom. She poured soup into a bowl. The bowl sat in the middle of the table. It was too hot. "Blow on it," said Mom. Aurora puffed with her mouth. She blew and blew. The steam danced away.

Would the soup be cooler now? She touched the bowl with one finger. Warm, not hot! She took a little taste with her tongue. Yum. Then she listened. Slurp, slurp, slurp.

"My mouth heard that!" she said. Mom laughed and poured her some more.

Jasmine wanted to make the big teddy bear move. She pulled him on the floor. He went slow. Then she pushed the small car. It went fast! "Zoom!" said Jasmine.

Mama came in with warm cocoa. "Careful, it is hot," said Mama. Jasmine touched her own cup of cold water instead. It felt nice. She took a sip. It was a little sour from the lemon. She made a funny face, and Mama laughed.

Jasmine found a string. She tied it to the small car. Now she could pull the car fast. She tied the string to the big teddy bear too. She pulled and pulled. The bear slid across the floor, slow but moving! "You did it," said Mama. Jasmine gave the bear a pat and licked the cocoa foam off her spoon.

Quinn went to the pet store with Dad. She held his hand. There were fish and birds and a bunny. "I want that one," said Quinn. She pointed at the bunny.

The shop lady put the bunny in a box. The box had holes for air. Quinn peeked in. The bunny was very still. "Is it sad?" Quinn asked. "It is scared," said Dad. "It is in a new box."

At home, Quinn put the box on the floor. She opened the top. The bunny did not come out. Quinn reached in her pocket. She pulled out a little carrot. She put it near the hole. Then she sat back and waited.

The bunny sniffed the carrot. Out came one ear. Then out came the whole bunny. It nibbled the carrot in her hand. Dad put water in a bowl. Quinn filled a dish with food. The bunny hopped to the bowl and drank. "You like your new home," Quinn whispered. The bunny's nose went twitch, twitch.

Hayden went to the library with his dad. He wanted a book about a cat. He looked on the shelf. One book, two books, three books. No cat book there.

A big book fell off the shelf. It landed on the floor with a thump. "Sorry, book," Hayden said. He picked it up. He could not reach the high shelf to put it back. So he asked the lady at the desk for help. "Can you help me, please?" he said.

She smiled and put the book back. "Thank you," said Hayden. Then she pointed to a small shelf by the window. There sat the cat book, with a cloudy blue cover. Hayden hugged it tight. One book, two books, three books, and one was just right. His dad read it to him by the big window. "The cat says thank you too," said Hayden.

Felix sat in his car seat. The road was bumpy. Bump, bump, bump went the wheels.

"I am hungry," said Felix.

Mom reached into the bag. "Look what I brought," she said. It was an apple. Apples are food. Felix took a big bite. Crunch!

Felix looked out the window. He saw a cow. He saw a sheep. He saw a duck. "Animals!" said Felix. The cow said moo. The sheep said baa. Felix laughed.

Then the car stopped. Dad pointed. "Look, a surprise!" A dog was running by the road. It had a red ball in its mouth. Balls are toys. The dog dropped the ball. It rolled and rolled.

The dog ran after it. The ball went far. The dog went far too. "The ball makes the dog run," said Felix.

"Doggy, come back!" Felix waved. The dog picked up the ball. It came back to the fence. Then it sat.

"Bye bye, doggy," said Felix. He blew a kiss. The dog wagged its tail.

Mom gave Felix a cracker. Crackers are food too. Felix ate it all up.

The car went on. Bump, bump, bump. Felix yawned. He held his apple tight. "Nap time soon," said Dad.

"Night night, animals," said Felix. He closed his eyes.

Alice wants to play on the big swing. But all the swings are full. "How many swings are there?" she asks. Her grandma counts with her. "One, two, three, four." Four swings, and four kids swinging.

Alice waits and counts too. "One, two, three." She counts the clouds going by. Then she hears a boy on the slide. He is counting as he climbs the steps. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" he calls out. Then he slides down, fast, with a little bump at the bottom.

Alice sees the boy leave the swings. Now one swing is free! She runs over and climbs on. Grandma gives her a soft push. "One, two, three," says Alice, pumping her legs. She feels like she is flying, just like in her dream last night. "Higher, Grandma, higher!"

Louis stood at the little table. The toast sat on his plate. The butter was soft in its dish.

Louis picked up his knife. He touched the butter. The butter stuck to the knife. Then he touched the toast. The butter stayed on the toast! "Look, Teacher Maya," said Louis. "The butter moved!"

"Spread it slow," said Teacher Maya. Louis spread it slow. The butter went far across the toast. Now the toast was all yellow.

Next came the milk. Louis held the cup with one hand. He poured with the other. A drop chased a drop down the side. "Oops," said Louis.

"Tip the cup less," said Teacher Maya. Louis tipped the cup less. The milk went into the cup. Not one drop fell. "I did it!" said Louis. His heart felt big. He drank his milk and ate his toast. "More toast, please," said Louis.

Brooks had a runny nose. He was getting better, but his cough came back at night.

"Mama, my cough is loud," said Brooks.

"We need more cough syrup," said Mama. "Let's go to the pharmacy."

At the pharmacy, Brooks sat in the cart. He saw shelves and shelves of bottles. A man in a white coat waved at him.

Brooks coughed one big cough. The man in the white coat heard it. He walked over and showed Mama a small brown bottle.

"This one helps little coughs," said the man.

Mama put the bottle in the cart. Brooks held his stuffed bear tight.

At home, Mama poured a small spoon of syrup. It tasted like cherry. Brooks swallowed it.

That night, Brooks lay in his bed. He waited for the big cough. It did not come. He coughed one tiny cough, and then no more.

"Mama, listen," said Brooks. "My cough is all sleepy."

Mama smiled in the dark. Brooks hugged his bear and closed his eyes.

Connor wanted to build a tall tower. His tower fell down. It fell fast. Connor sat on the floor and began to wonder. Why did it fall?

"Try a big block at the bottom," said Mom.

Connor put a big block at the bottom. He put small blocks on top. The tower stood up. It did not fall. Big blocks made the tower strong. Small blocks made it tall.

Mom brought hot cocoa. "Careful, it is hot," she said. She held the cup for him. Connor blew on it. The cocoa got cool. He took one slow sip. "It was hot. Now it is cold," he said.

Then his hands were dirty from the blocks. Mom gave him a small towel, a good tool for messy hands. He wiped them clean.

"Can I make another tower?" Connor asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Make it big." Connor stacked the blocks high.

Asher ran to the park with Mama. He wanted to find the big red slide. "Stay close to me," said Mama. Asher held her hand.

They walked past a grill. The grill made sizzling sounds. Asher saw steam rise up. "That is hot," said Mama. She put her hand out. Asher stopped. The grill was for the man with the hot dogs. Only the man touched it. Asher watched from far away. Then he saw it. The man touched the grill, and the hot dogs got warm. Hot things made other things hot.

Asher found a shiny bottle on the grass. He reached down. "Not that," said Mama softly. "We do not touch bottles we find." She picked it up and put it in the bin. Asher clapped. He loved helping.

Then came the surprise. The man from the grill walked over. He gave Asher a warm hot dog in a bun. Asher took it to the picnic table. Mama brought his cup of juice. Asher sat close to her and took a big bite. "Happy!" said Asher, with juice in his hand and Mama by his side.

Isiah sat in his car seat. His tummy felt funny. "I want my milk," he said.

"It is at home," said Mama. "It is cold there."

A big truck went by. Vroom! It was fast. Their car was slow. Isaiah clapped. "The truck wins, Mama!"

Then they stopped. A little red car pulled up. It was small. Their car was big. Isaiah laughed. "We are big!"

Sun came in the window. It made Isaiah's arm warm. "Hot," he said. He moved his arm away. Then he touched the cold window glass with one finger. "Brrr!"

They got home. Mama took the milk from the big fridge. She gave Isaiah the cup. He drank it all down.

"Cold milk," said Isaiah. He gave Mama a big hug. "More tomorrow?"

"Yes," said Mama. "More tomorrow."

Raphael sat in the big chair at the dentist. He was waiting for his turn. His tummy felt hungry. Mama had brought apple slices for after.

"First we wash hands," said the friendly nurse. She took Raphael to the little sink. She gave him soap. Raphael rubbed the soap on his hands. Bubbles grew and grew. He rubbed and rubbed. The nurse sang a song while he rubbed. The song had two parts.

Raphael looked at his hands. The sticky jam from breakfast was gone. The bubbles had carried it away down the sink. He held his hands up to the light. They were clean and shiny.

Then Raphael got his apple slices. He ate them in the middle of the waiting room. No jam, no dirt, just apple. He licked his fingers. They still smelled like soap.

After his checkup, Raphael went to the toilet. Then he ran back to the sink. "Soap please!" he said. He rubbed the bubbles all over again. A small boy watched him from the door.

"Look," said Raphael. He showed his clean hands. "Now you try." The boy got soap too. They sang the song together. Then the boy skipped back to his mama, holding his clean hands up high.

Arlo sat at the big table. He wanted to make a garden picture. He had paper, glue, and little paper flowers.

Arlo put glue on a flower. He pushed it onto the paper. It stuck! "It stays," he said.

He put glue on another flower. Then more glue. Then more. Now the paper was very slippery. The flower slid down, down, down. It landed at the bottom. "Oh no," said Arlo. "My flower slid away!"

Would a little glue work better? He could guess and try. Arlo put on a small dot of glue. He pressed one flower. It stayed. He pressed another flower. It stayed too.

"One flower, two flowers, three flowers," said Arlo. His garden picture grew and grew. All the flowers stayed in place.

Mama came to look. Arlo held it up high. "Look at my garden!"

Avery sat at the little red table. She wanted to paint a picture of her pet cat. The cat was yellow with white paws.

She found the yellow paint first. She made a round yellow body on the paper. "Good," said her teacher, Miss Kim. "Now you need green eyes."

Avery looked for green. She could not find it. Then she saw Ben using the green pot. She waited, but Ben tipped the pot over. Green paint spilled across the table.

"Be careful," said Miss Kim. She wiped up the green spill with a cloth. Then she scooped some green paint into a small cup for Avery.

Avery painted two green eyes. Then she painted a red ball next to the cat. The cat in the picture looked just like her pet at home.

"Meow," said Avery, and she held the paper up high.

Beau sat in his car seat. He wanted his blue toy truck. It was not in the bag.

"Let's look for it," said Mom. The car went down the road. Beau looked out the window.

"I see a cow!" said Beau. The cow stood by a fence. Then he saw a sheep. Then a dog. "Animals, animals!" said Beau.

"Look in your lunch bag," said Mom. Beau found his banana. He found his crackers. He found his juice. "Food!" said Beau. Still no truck.

The wind blew on the window. It was windy outside. A leaf flew up, up, up. Beau laughed.

Then the car bumped. Something slid out from under the seat. It was the blue truck!

"Truck!" Beau shouted. He hugged it tight. "You were hiding under the seat."

Mom laughed too. "Truck, you found us," she said.

Elizabeth stood by the classroom door. Her coat was zipped up to her chin. Her tummy felt jumpy. She wanted to see her mama, but mama was gone.

A boy sat on the rug. He was crying. His shoe was stuck in a puddle of glue. Elizabeth looked at the glue. Then she looked at her shoe. She stepped on the sticky spot too. Her shoe stuck, just like his.

She pulled hard. Her shoe came off. She sat down and looked at it. The glue was slimy on the bottom. She rubbed her shoe on the rug. The glue came off, little by little. She picked up the boy's shoe too. She rubbed it on the rug the same way.

The boy stopped crying. He put his shoe back on. "Thank you," he said. Elizabeth smiled. Then she unzipped her coat all by herself. She hung it on a little hook with her name on it. The teacher gave them each a red crayon. Elizabeth drew a big sun. The boy drew a sun right next to hers.

Eva stands with her dad. The big yellow bus comes around the corner. It stops with a soft hiss. The doors fold open.

Eva climbs up. One step, two steps, three steps. She finds a seat by the window. The glass is cold on her nose.

A car stops next to the bus. A little dog sits inside it. The dog has a pink nose. Eva taps the window. The dog wags its tail. She taps again. The dog barks. She laughs and taps one more time. The dog's ears go up.

The glass is foggy now. Eva writes on it with her finger. She makes a wobbly letter E. Then the bus starts to move, and the dog slides out of sight, tail still wagging.

Nora was at her friend Mia's house. Mia had a tablet. It was dark and still. "Watch this," said Mia. Mia pushed the little round button. The screen lit up! It showed colors and little pictures.

"Can I try?" asked Nora. Mia's mom said yes. Nora pushed the button too. Tap. The light came on again. She tapped the green square with a crayon on it. A white page opened, big and empty. Nora drew a purple cat. Then she drew a messy orange sun. She tapped blue, and the line turned blue. One tap, one new color. How did it know?

Then it was time for a snack. Mia's mom said to put the tablet away. Nora tapped the button and held it. The screen went dark again. She slid it into its cover, like a book going to bed on the shelf.

But wait. The cover had a little flap. Nora lifted it, and there was the tablet's name written inside. "It has a name!" said Nora. "Mine is called Pickle," said Mia. Nora smiled and patted the cover gently. "Night night, Pickle," she said.

Lennon went to the cultural center with Mama and Papa. There was a big table of paper lanterns. Each lantern had a little candle inside. Lennon wanted to send her lantern down the little water path, like the other kids.

Papa lit her candle with a long match. Then the wind came in the door. Whoosh. The little flame went out. The room felt dark on her side. Lennon frowned. Her lantern looked wrong with no light.

Mama held her hands around the flame. Papa lit it again. The flame stood up straight. "Your hands stop the wind," said Mama. So Lennon put her hands around it too. She cupped them like a tiny house. The flame did not go out this time.

Lennon walked to the water. She set her lantern down. It floated away, warm and bright. She watched it go. "Bye bye, lantern," she said. She waved and waved.

Lucy went to the park with Gran. The sun was out. It was sunny. Lucy wore her sun hat. "My hat keeps my head cool," she said.

Then the wind came. The wind blew Lucy's hat off! It rolled on the grass. Gran ran and got it. "It is windy now," said Gran. "Put on your coat." Lucy put on her coat. The wind could not get in.

Then dark clouds came. Rain fell. It was rainy. Gran opened a big umbrella. Lucy stood under it with Gran. "I keep dry here," said Lucy.

Then the rain turned white and soft. It was snowy! Lucy held out her hand. The snow felt cold. Gran put warm mittens on Lucy's hands. "What kind of snow is this?" Lucy asked. "Soft snow," said Gran.

Lucy looked at her hat, her coat, her mittens. All her clothes helped her stay and play. "Same park," said Lucy. "New sky!" Gran laughed and held her hand.

Hailey sat in the cafe with her dad. A kind waiter brought paper and a pencil. "Can you write your name?" Dad asked. Hailey wanted to sign her own picture. She squeezed the pencil in her whole fist. She made marks. The marks looked ugly and wobbly. "H" looked like a squiggle worm.

Dad drew a little crab on a napkin. The crab held a stick with its small claw. Hailey looked at her own hand. She pinched the pencil with two fingers, like a crab claw. She pressed down and made an H. Then an A. The letters stood up straight! She wrote H-A-I-L-E-Y all by herself.
