She held up the paper. "I painted my name!" The waiter clapped. Dad gave her hand a soft kiss. "Write it again," he said. Hailey pinched the pencil and wrote it again.

Paisley ran down the sidewalk. The bookmobile was here! The big blue truck had shelves and shelves of books inside.

"Today you get your very own library card," said Mama. "Your very first one."

Paisley jumped up and down. She picked out a book about a red fire truck. The cover felt rough on her fingers. The librarian typed Paisley's name into her computer. Then she handed Paisley a little white card. Paisley held it with both hands. It was hers, all hers!

"Now the book is yours to take home," said the librarian. "But you must bring it back. Another girl wants the fire truck book too."

"No," said Paisley. "I want to keep it forever and ever."

"Let's walk home and read it first," said Mama.

Paisley read the fire truck book at breakfast. She read it in her tent. She read it to her teddy bear. Then on Saturday, they saw the girl from the bookmobile at the park. The girl was holding a book about fire trucks. It was not the same one. It was a different one, and she looked sad.

"The bookmobile book," the girl said. "You have the fire truck one. I am next."

Paisley ran all the way home. "Mama! Mama! We have to walk back to the bookmobile!"

They found the big blue truck. Paisley gave the book to the librarian. The librarian gave it to the girl. The girl hugged the fire truck book tight.

"Thank you," she said. "Now I get my turn!"

"And next week," said the librarian, "you can pick a new book, Paisley. A green dinosaur book came in today."

Paisley grinned. "Next week," she said. "Next week, next week!"

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. On Monday, Myles took him to the park. "Look, Grandpa! Ducks!" said Myles. Grandpa sat down on a bench. He put his hat over his face. Soon his eyes were closed. He was asleep.

Myles wanted the ducks to come close. He clapped his hands. The ducks flew away. Myles clapped again. The ducks went even farther. "Oh no," said Myles.

Then Myles had an idea. He sat still like a rock. He sat still like a rock on the grass. One duck looked at him. It came back. Then two ducks came back. Then five ducks waddled right up to his shoes!

Grandpa woke up. "Look at all those ducks!" he said. "Shh," whispered Myles. "I am a rock." Grandpa sat still like a rock too. The biggest duck looked at them both. Then it nibbled the grass next to Grandpa's big toe.

Ibrahim sat in his big seat in the car. They were going to Grandpa's house early in the morning. Ibrahim saw a river out of the window. "The river is so wide," he said. He wanted his water bottle. It had slid far away on the seat.

"Can you help me, please?" Ibrahim asked. Mama reached back and picked up the bottle. "Here you go," she said. "Thank you," said Ibrahim. He took a little drink.

Then the car went over a bump. The bottle jumped and spilled on Mama's coat. "Oh no," said Ibrahim. "Sorry, Mama." Mama smiled at him in the mirror. "That is okay," she said. "It was only a bump."

Ibrahim held the bottle tight with both hands. The car went over another bump. This time nothing spilled. He had held it, so it stayed dry. "Mama, look!" said Ibrahim. He showed her the dry bottle. Mama laughed softly. "You held it so well," she said. Grandpa's door was coming up ahead, and Ibrahim waved through the window.

Lily wants to draw a cat on the big tablet. The screen is dark and still. She waits. It stays dark.

Lily taps the screen one time. Nothing happens. She taps it two times. Nothing happens. Then her teacher, Miss Kim, comes over. "Try the little stick," says Miss Kim. She points to the side.

Lily finds the small stick button. She pushes it and holds it. She counts slowly, "One, two, three." The screen lights up. Lily claps her hands.

The tablet has little pictures on it. Lily looks for the drawing one. She taps the crayon picture. The drawing app opens. Now the screen is white and empty. Lily moves her finger on it. A red line goes straight across the screen. She moves her finger again. A round circle appears. That will be the cat's tummy. She adds two ears and a tail.

Then the bell rings. Time to go. Lily taps the crayon picture the way Miss Kim showed her. The app closes. She pushes the little stick and counts, "One, two, three." The screen goes dark. She sets the tablet on the shelf, all neat and straight. "Bye, cat," says Lily. "I will draw you again tomorrow."

Sarah went to the store with Mama. She wanted red apples for a snack. "How many apples do we need?" Mama asked. "Let's guess," said Sarah. "Maybe four!" Mama held the bag. Sarah picked one apple. Then two apples. Then three apples. Then four apples. "Can I count them?" asked Sarah. "Yes," said Mama. "One, two, three, four." Sarah put one apple back. "Now I have three," she said.

At the bread shelf, Sarah saw a song card. It had ten little ducks on it. A boy was singing near it. "One, two, three, four, five," he sang. Sarah listened. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" she sang too. The boy smiled at her.

Sarah saw Mama put coins in a machine. The machine rolled the coins. It made a round shape, like a triangle but round. Then it gave back paper money. "Can I hear it again?" asked Sarah. "Yes," said Mama. She put in more coins. Click, click, click. Sarah laughed. "That is a cute little sound," she said. They walked to the car. Sarah held the apple bag all the way home.

Lydia stood at the baseball diamond. She held a purple beanbag in her hands. A hoop sat on the grass in front of her. She wanted the beanbag to go in the hoop.

"Throw it low," said Dad.

Lydia threw it high. The beanbag flew over the hoop. It landed in the grass. Dad went to bring it back to her.

"Try again," said Dad. "Nice and easy."

Lydia looked at the hoop. She looked at her hand. She threw the beanbag low and slow. It went in the hoop. It stayed there.

"It went in!" said Lydia. She clapped her hands.

Then Dad brought a big ball. He rolled it to her on the ground. Lydia reached out with one hand. The ball bounced off her fingers. It rolled away.

"Use both hands," said Dad.

Dad rolled the ball again. Lydia held out both hands. The ball bumped right into them. Her two hands closed around it. She held it tight.

"I caught it!" said Lydia.

"Yes, you did," said Dad. "One more time."

Lydia threw the beanbag into the hoop. Then she caught the big ball with both hands. She did it again and again, and the sun went down slowly over the baseball diamond.

James wanted to paint a picture at school. He wanted to paint a green frog. But the paint pots had no green paint.

James looked at the pots. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. James tried the yellow pot first. He made a yellow frog on his paper. The frog did not look right.

Then James had an idea. He let some blue paint drip onto his brush. He mixed the blue with the yellow. He stirred it slowly. The paint turned green! James painted his frog green. He painted a red flower too.

Teacher Mia wrote his name on the paper. Then she hung it up to dry. "My green frog has a name," James said. "His name is Hop."

Charlie could not find her bear. "Where can he be?" she asked.

Mama smiled. "Look in the bathtub."

Charlie ran to the tub. No bear there. But there was a wet sock. "The bath made you wet!" she told the sock. She hung the sock on the rail. It dripped, dripped, dripped.

Next she looked under her bed. No bear. But there was her plate from snack time. "Oh no," said Charlie. "You still have cheese on you." She carried the plate to the kitchen. Papa washed it. "You are a smart helper," he said.

Then Charlie pulled her pajama shirt over her head. Something soft was inside it. It was bear! "You were in my shirt!" Charlie laughed. "Did you want to sleep in it?" Bear said nothing. Bears are quiet like that.

Mama tucked them both in tight. "Night night, sleepy bear," said Charlie. She closed her eyes and gave him one more hug.

Addison went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about a mean dragon. Dad said, "Let's look for shapes first. Then we find the dragon."

Addison found a rug with a red circle. She put her foot on the circle. The circle was as big as her foot and her hand together. She jumped to a blue square next to it. The square had four sides, like a window.

Then she heard a scratch, scratch, scratch. A toy box was rubbing on the floor. The box was a rectangle, long like a loaf of bread. Addison pushed the box away from the wall. The scratch stopped. She pushed it back. The scratch came back. She laughed. "The box makes that sound!"

A librarian walked by with books stacked high. "That stack looks like a triangle," said Dad. The bottom row was wide. The top had just one book. Addison held up her hands like a triangle too. Her fingers touched at the top.

At last they found the dragon book. The dragon on the cover had a round tummy. "Look," said Addison. "The mean dragon is full of circles!" Dad laughed. They sat down to read. Addison turned the first page.

Beatrice ran to the play corner at school. She wanted to play house with her baby doll, Rose. But Rose was gone! The basket was empty.

Beatrice looked under the table. No Rose. She looked in the toy oven. No Rose. Then she heard a sound. "Ba ba ba." It came from the dress-up box.

Beatrice opened the lid. There was Rose! Tommy had tucked Rose inside a hat. "She is sleeping in her bed," Tommy said. "One hat, one blanket, one baby."

"Rose is hungry," said Beatrice. She held Rose on her lap. She bent a small spoon towards Rose's mouth. She made a pretend pot of soup. "One spoon, two spoops, three spoons," she counted. Rose drank it all up.

Then Rose got a bump. Beatrice kissed the bump. She wrapped Rose in a scarf. "One scarf, one hug, all better," she said.

Tommy put a tiny cup beside Rose. "Tea for baby," he said.

Beatrice smiled a happy smile. The play corner had become a whole house. She rocked Rose to sleep.

Athena wanted pancakes, big ones. Mama poured a big circle of batter. It spread out wide, wide, wide. Then Mama poured a small circle. "That one is for you," Mama said. Athena clapped. The small pancake was just her size.

The big pancake sat on the hot pan. Athena stood far away and watched. It went sizzle, sizzle, sizzle. Bubbles grew on top. When Mama flipped it, it flew up fast, like a flying carpet. Athena gasped. "It's a magic pancake!" she said. "It flies!" Mama smiled and flipped the small one too. It flew up slowly, gently, like a little bird learning to fly.

Mama put the pancakes on plates. They were too hot to touch. "We will wait," said Mama. Athena waited. She wiggled her curly hair with her fingers. Then she touched her cold glass of milk with both hands. The milk was cold like snow. The pancakes slowly stopped steaming.

At last Athena took a tiny bite. It was just right. She ate the small pancake all up. "I helped wait," she said proudly. Her family laughed and ate together. Athena looked at her empty plate and held it up high. "More magic pancakes, please!"

Lillian had a cold. She caught it from her brother last week. Now she was home, and her nose was all stuffed up.

Lillian wanted to smell her toast. She sniffed and sniffed. She could not smell a thing. That made her sad.

Mama made warm soup on the stove. Steam rose up from the pot. Lillian watched from her chair. Mama set the bowl in front of her. The steam curled under her nose. Lillian breathed it in. Slowly, her nose began to open. Then she smelled the soup. It smelled so good. "I can smell it!" she said.

Lillian slurped the warm soup. Her nose ran a little, so Mama gave her a fresh tissue. Lillian blew, soft and gentle. Then she looked out the window. A plane flew high in the sky. It made a little white line behind it. Lillian sniffed the air again. "Mama, I can smell the toast too," she said. Mama smiled and pushed the plate closer.

James put his arms in his coat. One arm went in easy. The other arm went in easy too. Now for the zipper.

James pulled the zipper up. Nothing happened. He pulled again. Still nothing. The zipper stayed open and his tummy felt the cold air.

Mom was busy at the bank desk. James wanted to zip it all by himself. He looked down at his coat. What was wrong?

Then James saw it. The little zipper parts were not together at the bottom. One side was up high. One side was down low. Could he fix that?

James sat on the bank bench. He put the pointy zipper tab into the slot at the very bottom. He heard a small click. He touched the tab to make sure.

James pulled the tab up. Zip! The coat closed all the way to his chin. No more cold air on his tummy.

Mom came back. She saw his coat. "Did you do that yourself?" she asked.

James smiled big. "Zip!" he said, and pulled it down, then up again.

Rosalie and her family went to the beach. It was far from home. They packed a big bag. Rosalie packed her tiny yellow duck. "Where will we sleep?" she asked. Mom smiled. "We will call Grandma when we get there."

At the beach, the sand was warm. The water went swish, swish up the rocks. Rosalie made a sandcastle. She patted the sand. Pat, pat, pat. Then a wave came. Swish! The wave took her castle away. Rosalie gasped. Where did it go?

She made a new castle. A wave came again. Swish! It was gone again. "The water takes the sand," said Rosalie. She watched the wave pull back. Could she see it pull the sand? She looked close. Yes! Tiny bits of sand moved with the water.

Dad called, "Time to call Grandma!" Rosalie ran to him. She held the phone. "Grandma, the water takes my castle!" she said. Grandma laughed. Rosalie waved at the sea. "Bye bye, water," she said.

Yesterday Milo put a bean seed in a cup of dirt. His teacher, Miss Ada, helped him pat the dirt down. She had a loose tooth that wiggled when she smiled.

Today Milo ran to the window shelf. He looked at his cup. There was only dirt. No bean. No green. He wanted to see his plant now. "Not now," said Miss Ada. "Plants come later. Water it and wait." Milo gave the cup a little drink of water. The dirt turned dark. It went from dry to wet. A woman from the lunch room came by with a tray of cups. "Pay attention to that bean," she said. "My class grew beans when I was small. I watered mine every day." She set a straw by Milo's cup so he could drip the water slow.

Tomorrow morning, Milo came back to school. He looked at his cup. A small green tip was poking up. It was bent like a tiny hook. He had watered the dirt, and now the bean was coming. "Look," he said to Miss Ada. "It came up." She wiggled her loose tooth and clapped her hands. "Let's give it more water," she said.

Jake went to the library with his mom. He wanted the big dinosaur book. It had shiny teeth on the cover.

A girl named Mia grabbed the book first. Jake grabbed the other side. The book went "boing" between them. The librarian put her finger to her lips. Everyone froze like statues. Jake let go of the book. Then Mia held it out to him. "You first," she said. Jake sat down and turned the pages. The dinosaur looked like it winked at him.

When Jake finished, he slid the book across the rug to Mia. "Your turn," he said. Mia smiled. Then a little bee flew past the window, buzzing like a tiny truck. Jake and Mia watched it together, side by side, sharing the last page of the dinosaur book.

Kai sat on Grandma's big red rug. Grandma played her old piano. The song had a steady beat. One, two, one, two.

Kai wanted to clap along. He clapped fast, fast, fast. "Too fast," said Grandma. She stopped the song.

Grandma clapped slow claps. One, two, one, two. She clapped and waited. Kai watched her hands. Then he clapped, too. One, two, one, two. His claps matched the piano. When the song went steady, his claps went steady. When the song stopped, his claps stopped.

"Now sing with me," said Grandma. She sang "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star." Kai hummed. He tried again. He hummed the tune. Then came the words. He sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." He did not stop there. "How I wonder what you are." He sang it all by himself.

"Kai, that was like a little gift," said Grandma. "And your claps were not naughty one bit. They were just right." Kai laughed. He patted the piano keys. "Again," he said. Grandma's fingers wiggled like fish that swim in water. "Again," she said. One, two, one, two.

Mohamed went to the farmers' market with his mama. He held a loose coin in his little hand. A bird tried to fly away with his bread roll. "Silly bird," laughed Mohamed. "That is my bread!"

Mohamed wanted to bake an apple cake for his family. He picked three red apples from a big crate. "These smell sweet," he said. He sniffed one apple, twice.

At home, Mama peeled the apples with a sharp knife. Mohamed stayed far from the knife. He helped mash the apples in a bowl. He pushed the spoon down. The big apple chunks turned soft and squishy. "Look, Mama," he said. "I push, and they go smush!"

Then Mohamed pressed the dough with his palms. The dough got flat and wide. He patted it like a drum. Papa laughed and said, "Are you fixing a cake or using a hammer?" Mohamed giggled and patted some more.

Mama put the cake in the hot oven. Mohamed watched from his chair. Soon the kitchen smelled like sweet apples. Papa sniffed the air. "Mmm," he said. "Is it ready yet?"

At last the cake came out, golden and warm. Mohamed took a big bite. "I made this," he said. "With apples and smushing and patting." Papa gave him a thumbs up and said, "Best cake ever, little baker."

Jaxon woke up at Grandpa's house. The sun was warm on his blanket. He wanted his teddy bear, Brown Bear. But Brown Bear had a big oatmeal spot on his tummy from breakfast. "Oh dear," said Grandma. "Let's wash him."

Grandma filled the sink with warm, soapy water. Jaxon dipped Brown Bear in. He rubbed the spot with his small hands. The bubbles smelled like flowers. The spot grew lighter and lighter. Then it was gone. "Clean!" said Jaxon.

Grandma carried the wet bear outside. She hung him on the clothes line with two wooden pins. Brown Bear swung in the soft breeze. Jaxon waited on the steps. He knocked on the door to call Grandpa. "Come see!" he said. Grandpa came out, and they waited together.

The sun shone and the wind blew. Soon the fur looked fluffy. Jaxon touched it. Dry! He hugged Brown Bear close. The bear felt warm from the sun. A shy little ladybug sat on the clothes pin. It opened its wings, then flew away. "Bye bye," whispered Jaxon, waving his hand.

Mason lost his monkey. The monkey had soft arms and a spotted tummy. "Where can he be?" said Mason. He looked under the bed. No monkey. He looked in the toy box. No monkey. Where can he be?

Mason went to Grandma's big chair. A blanket was on the chair. The blanket made a lump. Was the lump the monkey? Mason pulled the blanket. The lump was only a pillow. But the pillow was on top of something. The blanket had been hiding it! There sat the monkey. "You were under the pillow!" said Mason. He gave the monkey a big hug.

Grandma laughed. "Shall we build a tower now?" she asked. Mason sat on the rug. He stacked one block, two blocks, three blocks. The monkey watched from his lap.

Ava sat at the dinner table. Her tummy made a little rumble. "I want my milk," she said. Mama poured the white milk into her cup. Ava drank it all up. "Look, my cup is empty now," she said.

After dinner, Mama ran the bath. Ava heard the water splash. She touched the bubbles with her toe. "So soft!" she said. The water washed the peas and the milk away. Now she was clean.

Mama put on her soft pajamas with cows on them. "The cow says moo," said Ava. Outside, the sky was dark and stormy. Rain tapped on the window. Ava yawned a big yawn. "Is it time for bed?" she asked. Mama kissed her head. "Yes, little one. Sleep now." Ava closed her eyes.

Emile loved the truck book. It had a thick red cover and a flag on the first page. Miss Ada put the book in his hands. "You can take it home," she said. "Bring it back on Friday."

Emile looked at the pages. The letters sat under the pictures. Daddy ran his finger along them. "Truck," Daddy read. The word meant truck. Emile turned one page, then the next. The book went front to back, like a little road.

At school, Emile held the book tight. "Can I keep it forever?" he asked. Miss Ada shook her head. "Someone else wants a turn." Emile gave her the book. Ben smiled and took it. Emile found the shelf where the truck book lived. He put a small paper flag there. "That means my book," he said. Ben waved from the reading corner. "I will bring it back on Friday too."

Blake went to Mia's house. Mia had a music box. It played a song. "Let's clap!" said Mia.

Blake tried to clap. Her claps were too fast. Then her claps were too slow. She could not find the clapping. "I lose the song," said Blake.

Mia's mom put soap on her hands. She clapped the soap bubbles away. "Look," said Mia. Her claps went clap, clap, clap. They were steady, like walking feet.

Blake watched Mia's hands. She clapped when Mia clapped. Clap, clap, clap. Now her claps fit the song! "I did it!" said Blake. "It is easy now!"

Then they sang too. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Blake knew all the words. She sang the whole song all by herself.

The music box stopped. But Blake kept clapping and singing. "Again! Again!" she said.

Mia's mom wound the little key. The song began once more. "Our song!" said Blake.

Felix was at Grandma's house. He found a big red book on her shelf. "What does it say?" he asked. Grandma opened the front cover. The words said DOG. "Look, the letters spell dog," she said. Felix turned the pages one by one, front to back. At the end, the dog found his bone. But the book had to go back. Grandma had borrowed it from the library. It was due today. "I want to keep it forever," said Felix. Grandma shook her head. "Other people want to read it too. But we can borrow it again." So they walked to the noisy library. Felix put the red book on the desk. The librarian smiled and stamped a little card. Then she handed Felix a new book. It was blue. On the cover, the letters spelled CAT. Felix hugged it tight. "This one comes home with us," he said.

Florence went to the library with her dad. She found a book about a little mouse. The cover had words on it. "Those words say The Tiny Mouse," said Dad. Florence opened the book. She turned the pages one by one. The story came in order, from the front to the back. At the end, the mouse found her home.

"I want to keep this book forever," said Florence.

"You can take it home," said Dad. "But we must bring it back. Other kids want to read it too."

Florence hugged the book. At home, she read it three times. The words stayed the same each time. On the last page, the mouse waved.

Then Florence put the book in her bag. "Time to go back," she said. She held Dad's hand all the way to the library, and set the book on the desk, ready for the next reader.

Brooklyn went to the library with her mom. She wanted to find a book about ducks. On the shelf was a big rug with letters. Brooklyn sat down on the rug.

She put her hand on a letter. "B," her mom read. "B says buh." Brooklyn made the sound too. "Buh, buh, buh." Then she saw something. Her own name started with B. "B is for Brooklyn!" she said.

She looked for more B words around her. She saw a book. "Buh, book!" she said. She pointed at the rug. "Buh, bath rug! Ducks take baths." Her mom laughed a soft laugh. "Yes, they do," she said.

Brooklyn found the letter D next. "D," said Mom. "D says duh." Brooklyn looked around. "Duh, duck!" she said. There was a picture of a duck on the wall. The sun came in the window. It made the shiny duck picture shine.

Brooklyn picked out a duck book. At the desk, the librarian stamped it. "Bad weather is coming," the librarian said, looking at the gray sky. "Read fast." Brooklyn hugged her book. "Buh, book," she whispered. "Duh, duck." She held her mom's hand and they walked out the door together.

Isla went to the pharmacy with Dad. There was a little sink by the counter. A nurse stood there. She had a bottle of soap with a fox on it.

Isla wanted to open the soap. It was hard to open. The nurse helped her. Then Isla pumped the soap. Bubbles came out on her hands. "Now we sing," said the nurse. They sang a little song about a fox. Isla rubbed and rubbed. The bubbles got big and white. They smelled like flowers.

Then the water washed the bubbles away. Isla's hands were shiny and clean. The nurse clapped. Dad held out a cracker for Isla. Isla looked at her clean hands. She looked at the cracker. Then she took a big bite. Dad smiled. "Yum," said Isla. The fox on the bottle seemed to smile too.

Hudson sat at the kitchen table. He wanted to paint a big brown bear. But there was no brown paint. He looked and looked. He only had red paint and yellow paint.

Hudson dipped his brush in the red. He made a spot on his paper. Then he dipped his brush in the yellow. He painted right on top of the red spot. The spot turned orange! Hudson's eyes got wide. He stirred the spot some more. It looked warm and brownish, just right for a sleepy bear.

He painted a big bear body. He painted soft round ears. Then Mom sprinkled salty salt over the wet paint. The salt made tiny sparkles, like stars on the bear. Hudson held his painting up to the light. "My bear can sleep under sparkly stars now," he said, and he laid the painting flat on the table to dry.

Eleanor woke up on her birthday morning. "Today is my day!" she said. Mama was in the kitchen. Grandpa was blowing up balloons. Eleanor watched a balloon get big and round. Then Grandpa let go of the string. The balloon flew up and bumped the ceiling!

Eleanor wanted to make one fly too. She tried to blow a balloon. Puff, puff, puff. It stayed small and flat. "It is too hard," she said. Grandpa smiled. "Watch me take a big, big breath," he said. He puffed and puffed. The balloon grew fat and strong. Then he gave it a tap. Up it went to the ceiling!

"Again!" said Eleanor. Grandpa blew one more. This one had a wheel drawn on it. Eleanor gave it a push. It zoomed up and bounced down. The friends came to the party. They all tapped the balloons up high. Dad lit the cake candles, one by one. Eleanor made a wish and blew them out. The candles went dark. Her breath did that! She grinned and blew at the balloons too. "You cannot blow those down," laughed Grandpa. Eleanor laughed too. "I will pretend I can!" she said, and tapped one way up high.

Leah held her doll and walked into the big store with Mama. "Look how big it is!" said Leah. Her doll was small in her arms. The store doors slid open fast. Then they slid shut slow.

Leah wanted cold milk from the freezer. She touched the glass. "So cold!" she said. "It feels like winter." Then they passed the bakery. Mama pointed. "The oven is hot," she said. "Dad will carry the warm bread." The bread smelled yummy.

At the checkout, a cart went fast. Beep, beep, went the scanner. Then it was their turn. The scanner went slow for their milk. Leah whispered to her doll, "We did it!" Dad put the bread in the bag. Leah took Mama's hand, and they walked out the sliding doors together.

Eli had a library book in his bedroom. It was a book about a big red pot. He wanted to keep it forever.

Eli opened the book. He looked at the first page. He saw little black marks. "Those are words," he said. He pointed at them. He turned the pages one by one, front to back, all the way to the pot picture at the end.

Mama came in. "It is time to take the book back," she said. "It is due today. Other kids want to read it too." Eli held the book tight. "But it is mine," he said. He put it under his pillow. He waited. He waited some more.

Then he heard a frog outside. It went jump, jump, jump. Eli peeked out the window. He saw the frog hop on a leaf.

Eli got the book out from under his pillow. He gave it to Mama. She put it in her bag. "We can borrow it again soon," she said. Eli waved at the book. "Bye, pot," he said.

Miles sat at the art table. He wanted to paint a big green frog. But there was no green paint.

He had red paint. He had blue paint. He had yellow paint. No green. "Where is green?" he asked.

His teacher said, "Try mixing two colors."

Miles dipped his brush in blue. He added some yellow. He stirred. Outside, a dog began to bark. Miles looked at his paper. The paint was green!

"Green!" said Miles. "I made green!"

He painted the frog. It was a big green frog. Then he put yellow on top of blue again. More green. He made the frog a green hat, too.

A dot of paint got on his nose. He spun around to show his teacher and felt a little dizzy. She laughed and wiped his nose.

"My frog is green," said Miles. "I made green all by myself."

Kinsley went to her friend Mia's house. Mia had a big doll named Rosie. Rosie had no blanket. "Rosie is cold," Mia said.

Kinsley wanted to help. She looked around the room. She saw a small red sock on the floor. She put the sock over Rosie's toes. Now Rosie had warm feet. Mia smiled. Then Mia covered Rosie with a play blanket too. "Now Rosie is cozy," said Mia.

The girls played house next. Kinsley set the table with tiny cups. Mia gave each bear a cup. One bear tipped over. Its cup fell on the rug. Kinsley got a cloth. She helped clean the spill. Soon the top of the table was dry and shiny again.

Then the bears got hungry. Mia held a pretend bowl. Kinsley stirred with a pretend spoon. "Time to eat," she said in a big voice. The bears sat very still. After the meal, the bears went to sleep. Kinsley patted them softly, one by one.

"Shh," whispered Mia. "The babies are sleeping." Kinsley tiptoed to the door.

Xavier went to the grocery store with Mama. He held his soft bunny in his arms. "Stay close," said Mama.

Then Xavier saw the apples. He picked one up. It was big and red. He put bunny down on a low shelf. He put the apple in the cart.

"Where is bunny?" asked Xavier. Bunny was gone! He looked by the bread. No bunny. He looked by the milk. No bunny.

Mama spoke to a store man. The store man moved a big box of cereal. "Look," he said. "The box was tipped. Bunny slid down, down, down."

There was bunny, under the box! Xavier hugged him. "Bunny, you slid like a slide!"

At lunch time, they shared a snack. Bunny sat right next to Xavier. "No more sliding," said Xavier. Bunny's ears went flop.

Julia stood in the kitchen next to Grandma. She wanted warm milk, but the milk was cold. "Brrr," said Julia. "My tummy likes it warm."

Grandma poured the milk into a big pot. Julia had a small cup waiting. The pot was big. The cup was small. Grandma put the pot on the stove. "Stay back," said Grandma. "The stove is hot." Julia stood on her step, far away. She watched.

The milk was cold. Then steam came up. Then the milk was warm. Julia saw that hot things made cold things warm. She clapped her hands.

Grandma poured fast, and milk splashed. "Oops," said Grandma. She poured again, slow and careful. The milk went right into the cup. A gray cat ran in. It was fast. It bumped Julia's leg. Julia laughed.

Julia held her warm cup with two hands. It felt good. The cat sat by her feet. "Warm milk for me," said Julia. "And a soft pat for you."

Nova sat at the big art table. She had red paint and yellow paint. She wanted to paint a green cow for her dream last night. But there was no green paint pot.

Nova looked in the tray. She found blue paint. She looked again. Still no green. Her friend Sam had green, but his pot was almost empty. "You can have a little," Sam said. He poured a tiny drop into her tray. It was not enough.

Nova dipped her brush in yellow. She dipped it in blue. She moved the brush on the paper. The paint turned green! "Look, Sam!" she said. Sam leaned over to see.

Nova painted her green cow under a high blue sky. She painted a big yellow sun. Sam smiled and clapped. Nova made one more green dot and gave it to him.

Raphael ran into the doctor's office. He wanted a truck sticker. But first, the doctor had to check him.

"Look at my light," said the doctor. Raphael looked with his eyes. The light was small and bright. He blinked, and the room went dark for a second.

"Now listen," said the doctor. She tapped his knee. Raphael heard the tap with his ears. Then his leg kicked up all by itself! He laughed. "It jumped!" he said.

He smelled the soap on the doctor's hands. He tasted the sweet juice Mom gave him. He touched the soft bed with his fingers.

"You are all done," said the doctor. She held out two stickers. Raphael took the truck one.

"My leg kicked for a sticker too!" he said.

Charles sat on the big rug at book club. He had a card with the letter B on it. He wanted to find B in his book.

"Is this B?" he asked, pointing to a crooked letter. "No, that is R," said his friend Mia. Charles laughed. R looked like B with one bump missing.

Then his mom said, "B says buh, like bear." Charles looked at his book. He found a big brown animal. "Bear! B!" he said. Mia found a bee. "Bee! B!" she said. They counted the B words. Bear, bee, ball. Three B words!

Charles itched his itchy sweater. His hands were dry from the windy walk. He rubbed them on his knees. Then he pointed at the bear page again.

"Bear starts with B," he said. "One bump, two bumps, B!"

Mia held up a D. "D says duh, like dog," she said. Charles clapped. "I want D next!"

He turned the page to find a dog.

Kai was in the garage with Dad. Dad turned on the radio. A song came on, bouncy and loud.

"I want to clap," said Kai. He clapped fast, like he was chasing a fly. His claps ran ahead of the song. Then his claps fell behind. His hands got all mixed up.

"Try this," said Dad. Dad patted his knee. Pat, pat, pat. It went the same speed as the song. Kai watched Dad's knee. Then Kai patted his own knee too. Pat, pat, pat. His hands and the song walked together, step by step. "It matches!" said Kai. Dad laughed. "Now try claps." Clap, clap, clap. The claps landed right on the song. Not too fast. Not too slow. Just right.

"Now the words," said Dad. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Kai knew some words, but not all. He froze like a statue when the middle part came. Dad sang it slow. Then Dad sang it again. Kai tried once more. "How I wonder what you are!" The words came out, all by themselves, from inside his head.

Kai stood up tall. He clapped and sang at the same time. The radio played. His hands went clap, clap, clap. His voice went up and down. Dad clapped too, silly and big, on purpose too slow just to tease. "Dad, you're too slow!" said Kai. Dad scooped him up in a hug and spun him around. The song kept playing, and Kai kept singing from the middle of the hug. "Like a diamond in the sky!"

Amelia woke up and looked out the window. The backyard was white. Snow had come in the night. No school today. It was a snow day at home.

Amelia wanted to make a snowman. She put on her boots and her red coat. Then she went outside. The snow was deep and soft. Her boots sank in. Every step made a hole. Amelia stomped her foot. The snow packed down flat. She stomped again. Now the ground was hard and firm. She could stand right there to build.

Amelia rolled a big ball. It grew bigger and bigger. Then she rolled a small ball for the head. The snowman had a stick arm and a leaf for a hat. "He is so pretty," said Amelia.

Then Amelia saw the bird feeder. It was empty. The birds were cold and hungry. "Wait, birds," she said. Dad came out with a cup of seed. Amelia held out her hand and helped him pour. The birds flew down to eat. Nearby, a small train of ants had gone quiet under the snow, but the birds were here now, and they were happy.

Dad called, "Cocoa time!" Amelia waved to the snowman. "Bye bye. I live here, so I will come back soon." She ran inside, and her boots left little white footprints on the mat.

Mateo was going to the store with Mama. But his little blue dinosaur was gone! "Not my dino," said Mateo. "He rides with me!"

Mateo looked under his seat. No dinosaur. He looked by the door. No dinosaur. "Dino, where are you?" he called.

Mama said, "Look in the back." Mateo turned around. The sun was shining in the window. The sun made his seat shine too. Then something small and shiny rolled out from under the blanket. The sun made it gleam!

"My dino!" shouted Mateo. "The sun made him sparkle! That is how I saw him!" He grabbed his dinosaur and hugged him tight. "You were not alone, dino. The sun was with you."

At the store, Mama said, "They sell toy dinosaurs here too. Do you want a friend for dino?" Mateo held up his dinosaur. "No thank you. This one is my best one."

In the car again, Mateo buckled up. He set the dinosaur on his lap, right in the sun. "See, dino? Now you shine!" The dinosaur gleamed all the way home.

Harper held her mom's hand at the dentist's door. She wanted to be brave. But her tooth felt funny, and she did not know what the dentist would do.

A kind woman in a gray coat said hello. "My name is Doctor Lee," she said. "Let's count your teeth." Harper sat in a big chair. It went up, up, up. Doctor Lee counted out loud. "One tooth, two teeth, three teeth," she said. Harper counted too. She got all the way to twenty.

Then Doctor Lee showed Harper a little tool. "Watch what it does," she said. The tool made water. The water went on a toy tooth. The toy tooth had spots on it. The water washed the spots away. Now the tooth was clean and shiny.

"Will you clean my teeth too?" Harper asked. "Yes," said Doctor Lee. "The water will help." Harper opened her mouth wide, like a little mouse nibbling a cracker. The water tickled a bit. Then it was done. Harper ran to show her mom her clean smile. "Look at my shiny teeth!" she said.

Levi ran to the art table at school. He wanted to build a house for his toy animal. Miss Maya gave him paper shapes. There was a round circle. There was a boxy square. There were three more shapes too.

Levi tried the circle for the roof. It rolled right off! He laughed and chased it. The circle would not stay on top. Then he tried a triangle. It had three pointy sides. It sat still on the square. The roof stayed up!

Levi picked two rectangles. He pressed them on for walls. The square became the floor. His toy animal went inside. "A house!" Levi shouted. Miss Maya clapped. Levi put the circle on top of the roof, like a moon. "Look at my new house!" he said.

Matteo wanted his red ball. It rolled away at the park. "I will find it," he said.

He used his eyes to look. He saw green grass and a big tree. He used his ears to listen. He heard a bird sing. Then he saw a bucket by the sand. "Maybe my ball is in the bucket," he said.

He used his nose to smell. He smelled flowers, not his ball. He walked on. "Use your eyes, use your ears," said Mama. She held his hand. "Be careful near the water."

Then Matteo touched the bucket with his fingers. The sand felt warm and soft. His ball was not there. Then Mama opened her bag. She took out a snack. Matteo tasted an apple. It was sweet.

A boy came by. "Is this red ball yours?" he asked. "Yes! Thank you!" said Matteo. He gave the boy a big hug.

Ava sat at the big table at writing club. She had a yellow pencil and some paper. She wanted to write her name all by herself.

Ava held the pencil in her whole fist. She pushed hard. The line went bump, bump, bump. It did not look like an A at all. "My letters are wiggly," said Ava. "Like a bee flew over my paper!" said Leo, laughing.

The teacher, Miss Pam, showed Ava how to pinch the pencil near the tip. "Try it like this," she said. Ava pinched the pencil with two fingers. She made a slow line down. Then another line. Then a line across. It was an A! A real A, just sitting there on the paper.

Ava made a V next. Then another A. Ava looked at her letters. Pinch the pencil, and the letters came out neat. Squeeze the pencil, and they wiggled away. She held up her paper. "Look!" she said. "A, V, A! That's me!" Leo clapped. Miss Pam drew a little yellow star next to the A. Ava pinched her pencil again and made one more star of her own.

Luke went to the mall with his dad. They walked past the toy shop. Luke stopped at a low table. On it was a big red magnet. He picked up the magnet and touched it to some paper clips. The clips jumped up and stuck. "Why do they stick?" he asked. "The magnet picks them up," said Dad.

Then Dad said, "Time for your first haircut." Luke sat in a big chair at the salon. The barber put a cape on him. It felt soft and cool. Then the barber picked up the scissors. Snip, snip. Luke watched the mirror. A piece of his hair fell down. Snip, snip. More hair fell. It slid down the cape and landed on the floor.

"Can the magnet pick up my hair?" Luke asked. The barber smiled and tried. The magnet did not pick up the hair. The hair just lay there. So Luke leaned down and picked up one little piece with his fingers. It was soft and brown. "I will bring this home to show my teddy," he said. The barber put it in a tiny bag and tied it shut. Luke held the bag all the way to the car.

Elizabeth went to the park with her dad. She saw the big slide. She wanted to slide down fast.

Elizabeth put her hand on the slide. The slide was very hot. She pulled her hand back quick. "Ouch," she said. The sun had made the slide hot. Her dad felt it too. "Let's find a shady slide," he said.

They found a little slide under a tree. Elizabeth touched it. This one was cool. She climbed up and slid down. Slip, slip, slip. She laughed and did it again.

Then she saw the grill by the picnic table. Smoke came out of it. It looked big and warm. Was it hot like the slide? Elizabeth began to walk over. Her dad took her gentle hand. "The grill is very hot," he said. "Daddy touches it. Not you." Elizabeth stayed with her dad and watched from far away.

The hot dog was ready. Her dad gave her a cool one on a plate. Elizabeth held her dad's hand all the way to the bench. "I sit close to you," she said. Her dad smiled. "Yes, you do."

Thomas put his arms in his coat. He pulled the zipper up, up, up. But the zipper stopped. It would not move.

The store was cold by the freezer. Thomas shivered. He wanted his coat zipped all the way. He tugged again. The zipper still stuck.

Daddy knelt down. "Look at the bottom," he said. Thomas looked. The two sides were apart. He pushed them together. The little metal part clicked into place. Then Thomas pulled the zipper up. It went all the way to his chin! "Neat!" said Thomas. He put his hand on his chest. The coat was snug.

They walked to the fruit. There was a long line at the apples. Thomas got to put four apples in the bag. Then he wanted to try again. He unzipped his coat all by himself. He lined up the bottom. Click. Up went the zipper.

On the walk to the car, Thomas zipped and unzipped. "I did it," he said. "All by me."

Avery went to the store with Dad. She wanted a red apple. But when they got to the fruit bin, there was one apple left. A boy was already standing there. He reached for the apple too.

"You go first," said the boy. He held out the apple. "Then I can pick a pear." Avery took the apple. "Thank you," she said. The boy smiled and took a green pear.

At the bread counter, there was a long line. Avery asked Dad, "Why do we stand in line?" Dad said, "So everyone gets bread in turn." Avery watched. One lady went, then a man, then a girl. Each person got bread, one by one. Soon it was Dad's turn, and he got a warm loaf.

The checkout lady's phone rang. She answered it, then put it down. "Now I can help you," she said. Avery put the apple on the belt. The scanner beeped, and the numbers danced on the screen. Dad paid with coins. He gave Avery one small coin to hold.

Outside, Dad cut the apple with a sharp knife, safely at the picnic table. He gave half to Avery and half to the boy, who was sitting there too. "Half and half," said Dad. Avery bit her piece. It was sweet and crunchy. "We both got some," she said. The boy raised his pear like a toast. "To apples and pears," he said.

Nora looked out the big window. "It is sunny today!" she said. The sun made bright spots on the floor. Nora put on her orange hat. Off she went to paint a picture of her toy turtle in the sun.

Then the sky got dark. Drip, drop, drip. "Oh no, it is rainy!" said Nora. The rain wet her picture. Mommy gave her boots and a rain coat. Splash, splash went the puddles.

Then the wind began to whoosh. "It is windy!" said Nora. The wind blew her orange hat away. Daddy ran fast and caught it. "My hat!" said Nora. She hugged it tight.

Then white flakes fell down. "It is snowy!" said Nora. Mommy helped her put on mittens and a warm coat. Nora made a little snow turtle. It was sunny again. Nora clapped her hands and said, "Look, look, look what I made!"

Isaiah sat on the rug in the living room. The big game was on TV. Grandma sat beside him. Uncle Max and Cousin Mia were there too. Everyone was shouting and clapping.

Isaiah wanted to see better. The big chair was in his way. He tried to peek around it. He could only see half the TV. "I can't see the game," he said.

Then Isaiah saw Grandma wave a big fan. The fan made air move. The air made the curtain spin and puff out wide. When the curtain puffed, the TV showed through the gap! Isaiah tugged Grandma's sleeve. He pointed at the curtain. Grandma smiled and held the fan steady. The curtain stayed wide open. Isaiah saw the whole game.

The team scored. Everyone jumped up. Isaiah clapped so hard his tooth pinged, the loose one. "We won!" he shouted. Grandma pulled him onto her lap for a big hug.

Jacob sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted a sticker, but first the doctor had to check him. "Open your eyes wide," said Dr. Ana. Jacob saw a little light. "Good. Your eyes see the light," she said.

Then she took out a tiny hammer. Tap, tap, it went on his knee. His leg jumped up all by itself. Jacob laughed. "My leg moved!" he said.

"Yes, your knee sent a message," said Dr. Ana. She tapped again. Tap. Up went his leg again.

Next she held a cup near his nose. Jacob sniffed it with his nose. "Orange!" he said. She gave him a sweet candy for his tongue. Then she whispered, "Can you hear me?" Jacob's ears heard the soft words.

There was a fish tank in the corner. The blue water looked like a little river. "I remember that tank," Jacob said. Dr. Ana smiled. "Your voice was weak last time. Now it is strong."

She tapped his knee one more time. Up it went, and she handed him a shiny dinosaur sticker.

Ella wanted to play house at daycare. But Ben had the baby doll. Ella said, "Can I hold her?" Ben shook his head. Ella felt sad.

Then the baby doll fell on the floor. "Ow," said Ben. A little scratch showed on the doll's arm. "Oh no," said Ella. "Is she hurt?" Teacher Mia came over. "She needs a bandage," she said. She put glue on a paper bandage and stuck it on. "There. Now she needs a mama."

Ben looked at Ella. "You can be the mama," he said. Ella took the doll. She wrapped her in a soft blanket. The doll stopped crying right away.

"Shh," said Ella. "Sleep now." She patted the blanket. "Sorry you fell." Teacher Mia smiled and sat close by. The baby slept, and Ella rocked her, very gentle, very slow.

Aubrey sat on the red rug at daycare. Miss Jo held up a big bag. "These books are from the library," she said. "We can take them home. But we bring them back on Friday, so other kids can read them too." Max grabbed the dinosaur book. "This one is mine forever," he said. He hugged it tight.

Aubrey peeked at a book about a little duck. She opened it. "Miss Jo, what does this say?" Miss Jo pointed at the words. "Those letters say, 'Duck goes for a swim.'" Aubrey gasped. The marks on the page were words. Words that Miss Jo could say out loud. Aubrey turned one page, then the next. She started at the front and went to the back, just like Miss Jo showed.

Then Max began to cry. "I want to keep it forever," he said. Aubrey had a question. She thought hard. "Miss Jo, can Max take it home and bring it back on Friday?" Miss Jo smiled. "Yes, that is how it works. Then it comes back for Aubrey." Max wiped his eyes. "You can have it after me," he said. Aubrey clapped. "And then it comes back for you again," she said. Max held out the book so they could both peek at the very first page together.

Ivy held a small box on the walk home. Inside was her new goldfish. He was small and orange. His name was Pip.

At home, Dad put water in a bowl. "Pip needs food too," Dad said. "Just a little pinch."

Ivy opened the food can. She took a big handful with her hand. Dad shook his head. "Too much," he said. "A little pinch, like snow flakes falling."

Ivy put back most of the food. She pinched two little flakes. She dropped them in the bowl. The flakes sat on top of the water.

Then Ivy saw it. Pip swam up, up, up. He opened his tiny mouth. He ate a flake. He ate the other one too.

"Look, Dad! He likes it!" Ivy said.

The old bowl still had spots on the glass. "It looks ugly," said Ivy. Dad wiped it with a cloth. Now it was shiny and clear.

Ivy fed Pip one pinch every day. Each time, up he came, mouth open wide.

"Hello, Pip," said Ivy.

Max was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a jar of honey and a big orange. Max wanted to taste the honey. Grandma put a little honey on a spoon. Max licked it. "Yum!" he said. "My tongue did that!"

Grandma cut the orange. It smelled sweet. Max put his nose close. "My nose smells it!" he said. Then he heard a bird at the window. "My ears hear the bird!" Max tapped his toes. "My feet can hear too?"

Grandma laughed. "Try this," she said. She held up a soft, red mitten. Max touched it. "My hands feel it. It is soft." Then Grandma pointed at the mitten. "What do you see?" Max looked. "My eyes see red! I did not miss it!"

"Now close your eyes," said Grandma. Max closed them tight. He was brave in the dark. "Can you see the mitten?" she asked. "No," said Max. "My eyes are sleeping." Then the bird sang again. Max smiled. "But my ears still work!"

Grandma hugged him. "Five helpers," she said. Max counted on his fingers. Then he touched the mitten one more time, just to be sure.

Rosalie stood by the pool with her swim team. The water was blue and cool. Her coach pointed to a big red ball. It sat flat on the water, floating like a boat.

"Can you move the ball without touching it?" asked Coach Ben. Rosalie tipped her head. "How?" she wondered. Coach Ben smiled. "Try kicking your feet in the water."

Rosalie sat on the edge. She splashed her feet. Small waves went out. The red ball bobbed. She kicked faster. Bigger waves rolled across the pool. The ball began to move! It drifted all the way to the ladder.

"I did it!" Rosalie shouted. "My feet made waves. The waves pushed the ball!" The other kids clapped for her. Then they all sat down and kicked too. Soon the whole pool was full of rolling waves, and the red ball danced across the water.

Arya sat on the big red rug at the library. Miss Jo sang the counting song. "One, two, three," she sang. Arya loved that song. But the numbers ran away from her after three.

Arya wanted to sing the whole song. "Four, um, six?" she said. The boy next to her giggled. "Not quite," he said kindly.

Miss Jo had an idea. "Count my books," she said. She put a book in Arya's hands. Arya patted it. "One!" Another book came. "Two!" Miss Jo kept handing her books. Pat, say. Pat, say. "Three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

Arya looked at the tall stack. Ten books! The top book wobbled. Arya held it steady.

Then she sang the whole song all by herself. "One to ten!" she shouted.

"Shh," said the boy, giggling. He clapped very quietly.

Miss Jo gave Arya a small salty cracker. "My best counter," she said.

Elena wanted to draw a duck at the park. But the duck kept swimming away. The duck was fast. Elena could not see it well.

A big duck came near. It was very big. Then a small duck came too. It was very small. The small duck sat on the water and stayed still. Now Elena could see a duck that did not move.

The sun felt hot on her head. Mommy gave her a cold drink. "Ahh," said Elena. The cold drink felt good. She took a big sip and picked up her crayon.

The small duck stayed slow and still. Elena drew it, slow and careful. She drew its small head. She drew its small tail. Then she wrote her name on the paper.

"My new drawing!" said Elena. Mommy clapped. Elena held it up to the pond. The small duck swam by, slow as can be. "Look, duck," said Elena. "That is you."

Ali stood in the backyard. Mama sat in the big chair with a bundle in her arms. "This is your baby sister," Mama said. Ali looked at the tiny face. "She is so small," he said.

The baby began to cry. Ali felt sad. "She is crying," he said. Then he saw his red ball on the grass. He rolled it gently to the baby's feet. The baby stopped crying. She watched the ball. Ali rolled it again. She made a small sound, like a laugh.

"You did not lose your spot, Ali," said Papa. "You are still our big boy." Ali picked up his last toy from the sandbox. He put it by the baby's blanket. "This is for you," he said. The baby grabbed his finger and held on tight.

Anthony sat in the car with Mom. They were going to meet a hair cutter. "Will she use scissors?" Anthony asked. "Yes, the small kind," said Mom. Anthony touched his long hair. He liked his hair.

At the salon, a lady put a cape on Anthony. It was blue and shiny. Then she picked up her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Anthony watched in the big mirror. Each time the scissors closed, a piece of hair fell down. Snip, then a piece fell. Snip, and another piece fell. Soon little hairs lay all over the floor, like soft brown snow.

Then came the surprise. Anthony looked in the mirror. His hair was short now. His ears were showing. Back in the car, Mom flipped down the sun visor. Anthony looked in the little mirror there too. "That's me!" he said. He turned his head one way, then the other. The boy in the mirror turned too. Anthony smiled at him. The boy smiled back.

Riley went to the vet with her dad. There were pets in little rooms. A dog barked. A rabbit ate a leaf. One tank held a long, quiet snake. Riley looked and looked. Then she saw a small orange fish. Its water was cloudy. The fish sat very still. "I want this one," said Riley. The vet smiled. "Then we must help him feel better." Dad poured out the cloudy water. He poured in clean water. Riley watched and waited. The water turned clear. Then the fish swam all around. It wiggled its little tail. At home, Riley sorted her new things. The food went in one cup. The shells went in a row. Each morning she dropped one tiny bit of food in the tank. The fish swam up fast and ate it. "Hello, little fish," said Riley. The fish blew a bubble.

Jasmine ran to the sandbox with her bear. She set bear on a big rock. "You sit here, baby," she said. But bear kept tipping over. He fell into the sand again.

Jasmine wanted bear to sit like a grown-up. She looked around. Then she dug a small hole in the sand. She pushed bear's bottom into the hole. The sand held him up. Bear sat tall and still!

"Time to cook," said Jasmine. She found two cups and a spoon. She put sand in one cup. She put sand in the other. She mixed them with the spoon. "Soup for my baby," she sang.

A boy named Sam came by. "Can I play?" he asked. "Yes," said Jasmine. "You can be the dad." Sam picked up a leaf. "I will cook a leaf pie," he said.

Then bear tipped forward. His nose went right into the soup cup. "Oh no, baby is hungry!" Jasmine laughed. She lifted him up and patted his back. She held the warm cup to his snout. Sam waved a friendly hand at bear.

"More soup," said Sam. "Coming right up."

Declan wanted to wash his hands all by himself. He stood by the sink and looked at the shiny tap. "Can I do it?" he asked. Mama smiled and stood close behind him.

Mama turned the red tap a tiny bit. The water came out. Declan put one finger near it. "Ooh, warm," he said. He pulled his hand back fast. Warm water could feel too hot. So Mama turned the blue tap instead. Now the water ran cool and soft. Declan let it run over his fingers. "Cold feels nice," he said. He rubbed the soap into white bubbles. The bubbles smelled like paint, fresh and clean. He blew one bubble off his thumb. It popped in the air.

Next to the sink sat a little pink bottle. Declan reached for it. Mama's hand came down quick and soft. "That one is for grown-ups," she said. Declan put his hand back in the water. The tap turned off. The water stopped. Declan turned it on again. The water ran. He turned it off. The water stopped. His tap, his water, his trick.

"You did the whole wash," said Mama. Declan looked at his hands. They were shiny and clean. Then he saw something small in the mirror. A shy little smile, and it was his own.

Emile had a small toy bear at daycare. He wanted to build the bear a house. "A house needs a door," said Emile.

He found a round block. He put it by the wall. The round block rolled away. "Come back, circle," said Emile.

He tried a block with three sides. It stood still, but it was too small for the door. The bear could not fit through.

Then Emile found a block with four flat sides. Two sides were long, and two sides were short. It stood like a door. "Hello, rectangle," said Emile.

He set the rectangle in the wall. The bear went in. The bear came out. "You can go in and out," said Emile.

Outside, his shoe tapped the floor. He looked at the window and saw cold rain. That was fine. The bear was dry inside.

Emile put a triangle on top. "Now it has a roof," he said. "I wish I could fit in there too."

Billie ran to the playground with her grandma. The sun made the slide very hot. Billie put her hand near it. The slide felt hot like her soup at lunch. She pulled her hand back.

Grandma poured cool water on the slide. Billie watched the water run down. She touched the slide again. Now it was cool. The water had made it cool. Billie went down the slide. "Whee!" she said.

Then Billie saw something shiny in the sand. It was a broken bottle. She wanted to pick it up. "Stop," said grandma. "That can cut you." Grandma picked it up with a bag. She put it in the bin. Billie threw away some paper she found. They sorted the trash together.

A big dog ran by. Billie held grandma's hand. The dog sniffed them and trotted off. Billie and grandma sat on the bench. "The sun makes things hot," said Billie. Grandma smiled. Billie pointed at the shady tree. "That spot is not hot." They sat in the shade and ate their crackers.

Matteo was in the car seat. He wanted to see ten trucks before the farm. "Look, one truck!" said Mama. "One!" said Matteo. The truck went past the window. Then two cars went by. "Two cars!" said Matteo. He clapped his hands. Mama honked the horn. A big old bus beeped back. "Beep, beep!" laughed Matteo. Three cows stood by the fence. Then four birds flew over the road. "This is the best car ride," said Matteo. Five, six, seven cars went by in a line. "I count them!" he said. Eight bikes rang their bells. Then came a big red truck. "Nine!" said Mama. Matteo leaned forward. One more truck came around the bend. "Ten!" he shouted. "I did it! I saw ten!" Matteo could not wait to tell his teacher all about it.

Wyatt put on his coat all by himself. But the coat looked wrong. One arm went in the hood! He pulled it out and laughed.

Mommy waited by the cart. "Ready for the store?" she asked. "Not yet!" said Wyatt. He shook the coat like a big feather. It fell flat and smooth. Now he could see the two arm holes.

He pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. It worked! He pulled the zipper tab down, up, down, up. Then he zipped it all the way to his chin. "I did it!" he said.

At the store, Wyatt bounced down the aisle. His coat was warm and zipped tight. He picked out a big red apple. "My coat did this," he told the apple.

Eloise went to the big stadium with Mama and Papa. It was her favorite place. The field was green and wide. The seats were red and clean.

The game began. The crowd stood up and cheered. "Hooray! Hooray!" Eloise sat in her seat. All she could see was a big blue coat. The game was hiding behind it.

Then the people sat down. Eloise saw the players again. One player kicked the ball. The crowd jumped up. The blue coat came back. The game hid again.

Eloise tried something. When the people stood, she stood too. One, two, three, up! She could see the whole field. When they sat, she sat. One, two, three, down!

The people cheered and cheered. Eloise cheered too. She clapped her hands. That night, she dreamed of the green field and the happy crowd.

"One more cheer," she said in her sleep, "one, two, three!"

It was Miles's birthday at the park. There was a big table with cake and juice. Mom put down a little glass of apple juice just for him.

Dad brought out the cake. It had four candles on top. Dad lit them with a match, far from Miles's hands. The flames were small and orange. They wiggled in the breeze. "Make a wish," said Mom. "Then blow," said Grandma.

Miles took a big breath. He blew at the candles. The flames bent over. But they came right back up. Miles tried again, a soft little puff. The flames just danced. His eyes got wet. "I can't do it," he said.

"You can," said Dad. "Try one big, long blow." Miles filled his cheeks. He blew as hard as he could. Whoosh. All four flames went out at once. Smoke curled up in thin gray ribbons. Everyone clapped and cheered. Grandpa laughed a happy laugh.

Miles begged to do it again. "Maybe next year," said Dad, "with five candles." They ate cake in the warm sun. The juice was cold and sweet. Miles looked at the candles, all dark and quiet now. "My breath did that," he said.

Charlotte went to the store with Dad. She wanted apples for snack time. "Let's try to find red ones," said Dad.

The store was big and bright. Charlotte saw yellow bananas first. Then she saw green grapes. "Not apples," she said.

She heard a cart wheel squeak. She heard a man call, "Blueberries here!" Charlotte walked with Dad down the fruit aisle. She touched a big round apple. It was red and smooth.

"Dad, this one!" she said. Dad put six red apples in the bag. Then they saw Mom's favorite things. "Mom likes blueberries," said Charlotte. "Can we get some?"

"Yes, good idea," said Dad. He put blueberries in the cart too.

At home, Dad baked pizza for lunch. The oven was hot, so Charlotte sat far away at her little table. She waited. Soon Dad brought out the pizza. He blew on her slice so it would not be hot for her.

Charlotte ate her pizza with red apple slices beside it. She held up a yellow cup. "Cheers, Dad," she said.
"Cheers, Charlotte," said Dad, and tapped her cup with his.

Madelyn went to the library in the morning. Her mom held her hand. Madelyn wanted ten books about ducks, but she could only find one. One duck book sat on the shelf. The rest did not want to be found. "They like to hide," said the librarian, Miss Polly. "Let's hunt together." Madelyn was not alone. Miss Polly tapped the shelf. A second book slid out. Thump! Madelyn tapped too. A third book slid out. Thump! She tapped again and again. Four, five, six. Thump, thump, thump! The books smelled like paper and old rain. Seven books now sat in her arms. Eight was under a chair. Madelyn reached down and grabbed it. Nine was behind the puppet box. Miss Polly lifted it out with a smile. "One more," said Miss Polly. Madelyn looked up. The tenth book was on top of the shelf. It was too high for her little hands. "May I?" asked Miss Polly. She reached up and took it down. Madelyn counted them all. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Ten duck books, warm in her arms. Mom found a soft rug. They sat down side by side. "Read the big one first," said Madelyn.

Michael ran to the table. Lunch was ready. His favorite sandwich sat on his plate.

"Hands first," said Mom. "Wash with soap."

Michael sighed. He wet his hands. He rubbed the soap. The bubbles felt smooth and slippery. Then he rinsed fast and ran back.

"Michael, look," said Mom. She held his finger under the light. A smudge of dirt was still there.

Michael looked at his sandwich. He looked at his finger. He ran back to the sink.

This time he rubbed and rubbed. He sang his song while he scrubbed. The bubbles covered both hands. He rinsed until his hands felt squeaky.

He held his hands up. Every finger was clean now. The dirt was gone.

He sat down and picked up his sandwich. His clean hands felt warm on the bread. He took a big bite.

"Good washing," said Mom. She gave him a thumbs up.

Michael smiled. Later, after the toilet, he ran to the sink all by himself. He rubbed the soap until more smooth bubbles grew. He sang his song again.

The soap bottle sat by the sink. Michael gave it a little pat, like planting a tiny high five on its side. Then he ran off to play, hands clean and smelling like flowers.

Maeve sat on the grass at the big field. Mama sat next to her. Uncle Dan was way out there, playing in the game. He was just a small dot from here.

Maeve wanted Uncle Dan to see her. She clapped her hands. She called, "Dan! Dan!" He did not look. The game was loud. People were cheering all around her. Her tummy felt funny. She wanted him to wave back.

Then Maeve found her red scarf in the picnic bag. She held it up high. She waved it and waved it. The scarf was big and red like an apple. It moved in the wind, way up over the crowd. Uncle Dan looked up. He saw the red scarf. He smiled and waved right at her. Mama said, "He sees you!"

Maeve skipped in a little circle on the grass. The scarf was still up high in her hand. She waved it one more time. Uncle Dan blew her a kiss.

Sadie sat in her car seat. She wanted her red puzzle book. It was on the floor, far from her toes.

"Help, please, Mama," said Sadie. Mama reached back and got it. "Thank you," said Sadie. She smiled.

Sadie looked at the puzzle book. She tried to read the words. The words were too big. She turned the pages slowly, one by one.

Then her cup fell. It bumped Mama's arm. "Sorry, Mama," said Sadie. "That's okay," said Mama. They waited at a red light. It was long.

Sadie asked again, "Please, more water, Mama?" They stopped the car. Mama filled the cup. The water was cool. Sadie drank it all.

Then Mama pointed out the window. "Look, Sadie. Cows!" The cows stood by the fence. Sadie waved at them.

"Thank you for the water," said Sadie. She held her cup up high. "More cows, please!"

Lea packed her little red bag. In went her hat, her shell, and her duck. "We go far away today," said Mama. "The beach is not near our house."

The car ride was long. Long, long, long. Lea looked out the window. "Everything looks different here," she said. "The trees are different. The houses are different."

At last they reached the beach. Lea took off her shoes. The sand was warm. She ran to the water with her duck. She set the duck on a little wave. The duck sat on top. The duck did not sink. The water lifted it up and up.

"It floats!" said Lea. "Duck, you float!" She pushed the duck again and again. Each wave came in, and each wave took the duck back to her. Papa laughed. "The waves bring your duck home, just like our car brings us home." Lea hugged the wet duck. "You had a trip too," she whispered. "A big, wet trip." The next wave came in, and Lea jumped over it with a splash.

At school, Ruby sat at the little red table. On the table was a string of shiny beads. Her teacher, Miss Pam, had put them there. Ruby wanted to know how many beads she had. She wanted to tell her friend Leo, who had a string too.

Ruby began to count. She lifted the string with both hands. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." She stopped. Was seven right? She was not sure. She turned the string around. She counted from the other end. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven again! "Did I get the same number?" Ruby asked herself. "Yes," she said. "Seven. It is seven both ways."

Then Leo held up his string. "Which one has more?" he asked. Ruby counted Leo's beads. "One, two, three, four, five." She looked at her own string. "Mine has more," she said. "Seven is more than five." Leo nodded and smiled.

Ruby counted her beads once more, just to see. "Seven," she said softly. The shiny beads clicked together on the string. Outside, a bird sang at the window. Ruby put her string down next to Leo's. His looked short. Hers looked long. "Mine is longer, too," said Ruby.

Nolan ran to the community garden with a little shovel. "Today we plant seeds!" he said. Grandma had three carrot seeds in her hand. The soil was brown and soft. Nolan poked a hole. He dropped a seed in. He patted it down smooth.

"Will it grow today?" Nolan asked. Grandma said, "No, it needs rain and sun first." Just then, drip, drip, drop! Rain fell on the garden. Nolan felt wet dots on his nose. He laughed. The rain made little ponds in the dirt.

The next day, the sun came out. Nolan looked at his pot. A tiny green leaf was poking up! "Look, look!" he shouted. He had made a hole, put in a seed, and now a plant was growing. Nolan ran to the water pump. "Grow, little carrot, grow!"

Lucy woke up and looked out her window. Everything was white. "Snow!" said Lucy. "No school today," said Mama. "It is a snow day."

Lucy put on her warm red coat. She put on her boots and her mittens. Then Lucy, Mama, and Daddy walked to the big sledding hill. Lucy saw a little brown leaf on the snow. It looked so funny on all that white.

Lucy sat on her sled on the flat snow. She pushed and pushed. The sled did not go. Then Daddy said, "Let's try the hill." Lucy sat on the sled at the top. Daddy gave one little push. The sled went zoom, all the way down.

Lucy laughed and laughed. She ran back up the hill. She sat down again, and zoom, down she went. "The hill makes my sled go fast!" said Lucy. Then she went down one more time, with her arms out like wings.

Layla saw the big red truck. Ben had it first. He pushed it across the carpet.

Layla wanted the truck. She reached out and grabbed the back. The truck stopped. It would not go. Ben held on, and Layla held on, and the wheels did not turn at all.

Layla let go. She sat down and put her hands in her lap. Ben pushed the truck again. Now it rolled fast, all the way to the wall. Layla watched the wheels spin.

"The truck goes far when I share it," Ben said. He rolled it to her. Layla caught it with two hands.

"You can have a long turn," she said. "I need to wrap a present at the art table first." Layla carried her present back and showed it to Ben. Then he rolled the truck to her again.

Athena sat by the piano at Miss Rosa's studio. She wanted to play a whole song. But her little fingers pressed two keys at once. The sound was big and jumbled. "That is not my song," said Athena. "Why does it sound muddled?" Miss Rosa smiled. "Try one finger at a time," she said. "Then you will hear."

Athena looked out the window. The sky was stormy and gray. Rain tapped on the glass, tap, tap, tap. Athena listened to the rain. Then she pressed one key. One finger made one clear note. She pressed another key. Another clear note came out. "One finger makes one sound!" said Athena. She laughed and did it again.

Then came a surprise. Athena played her notes slowly, one by one, and the taps of the rain seemed to play along with her. Miss Rosa clapped her hands. "That was lovely," she said. "You played a real song." Athena pointed at the big picture on the wall. It showed a piano with rain around it. "Rain and piano," said Athena.

At home time, Athena gave Miss Rosa a hug. "Thank you," said Athena. "Can we play more next time?" "Yes," said Miss Rosa. Athena waved and called out, "Bye, piano! Bye, rain!" The rain kept tapping on the window all the way to the car.

Maverick sat at the little table. He had a big white paper and two paint pots. One pot was yellow. One pot was blue.

"I want green paint," said Maverick. "Where can green come from?"

Miss Rosa smiled. "Try mixing and see."

Maverick dipped his brush in yellow. He made a yellow cat with a long tail. Then he dipped the same brush in blue. He made a blue ball for the cat.

The yellow brush touched the blue paint. The blue pot turned green where the brush went in! Maverick opened his eyes wide. Yellow and blue had made green.

He counted his new paint. "One green, two green, three green spots."

Then he painted a big green grass. The yellow cat could sit on the green grass with his blue ball.

His friend Poppy had no paint left. Maverick gave her his green brush. "Here, you can use it."

"Thank you," said Poppy. "That is very kind."

Miss Rosa hung both pictures on the wall. The yellow cat smiled from the green grass.

Claare wanted to play outside. She stood at the front door and looked out.

The sun was shining. "It is sunny today!" said Claire. She put on her sun hat.

Then the wind blew. It blew her hat right off her head. The hat rolled on the grass. "Oh no!" said Claire. Her dad ran and caught the hat. "It is windy too," he said.

Then gray clouds came. Rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drop. "It is rainy now," said Claire. Puddles grew by the step. Claire put a leaf in the puddle. The leaf floated like a little boat.

The rain stopped. The sun came back. Claire saw something white on the ground. It was a small pile of old snow. The sun shone on it. The snow got smaller and smaller. Then it began to melt. Soon there was only a wet spot.

Claire put on her boots and her coat. Dad held her hand. They stepped outside together.

"Sun, wind, rain, and snow," said Claire. "All in one day!"

"Yes," said Dad, and he spun her hat onto her head.

Brielle ran into the sunny backyard. A red hoop sat on the grass. A big blue ball sat by her feet. Papa held a little beanbag.

"Try it," said Papa. "One, two, throw!"

Brielle threw the beanbag. It went up, up, and over the hoop. It landed in the grass behind it.

"Again," said Brielle.

"One, two, throw!"

This time she held the beanbag low. It went up and dropped right into the hoop. The hoop wobbled and the beanbag stayed in.

"I did it! I did it!" said Brielle.

"Now the ball," said Papa. "Hold out both hands."

Papa blew a whistle. The sound was loud and bright. He rolled the big ball to her.

Brielle held out one hand. The ball bounced off her fingers and rolled away.

"Both hands," said Papa. "One, two, catch!"

Brielle held out both hands. The ball rolled right in. Her two hands squeezed it and it stopped. It did not roll away.

"One, two, catch!" said Brielle. She caught it again. And again. And again.

"Big catch!" said Papa. He clapped his hands.

Brielle hugged the big blue ball and laughed.

"One, two, throw!" she said, and tossed it back to Papa.

Theodore went to the farmers' market with Dad. "Apples for our pie!" said Dad. Theodore picked a big red one. He put it in the basket. The basket was getting heavy.

At home, Theodore had a job. He would help bake the pie. Dad cut the apples with a sharp knife. Theodore stayed back and watched. He was safe.

Then Theodore stirred the apple pieces in a big bowl. He added sugar and cinnamon. Stir, stir, stir! The apples got all covered in brown sugar.

Dad rolled the dough flat. Theodore pressed it into the pan. "Now the apples," said Dad. Theodore poured them in. They made a mountain of apples.

Then Dad put the pie in the hot oven. Theodore watched from his chair. He could not wait.

Soon the kitchen smelled like sweet apples. "Sniff, sniff!" said Theodore. Dad tapped the pie crust. "Knock, knock," it went. "It is ready!" said Dad.

The pie came out golden and warm. Theodore took a big bite. The apples were soft and sweet now. They had been hard before. Baking had changed them! Theodore roared like a happy lion and jumped up tall.

"Frozen ice cream for pie!" said Dad. Theodore clapped his hands. "Yes! Ice cream on my warm pie!"

Ibrahim went to the park with his mama. He had his red truck in his hand. But when he ran to the swings, his hands were empty. "My truck is lost," he said.

Ibrahim began to search. He looked under the bench. He only found a wet leaf there. He looked by the big tree. He found a smooth brown nut. No truck. The grass felt cold on his knees. His nose felt cold too, like winter was near.

Then Ibrahim saw the wind blow. The wind made a pile of dry leaves tumble over. The leaves rolled and skipped across the grass. Something red peeked out under the last leaf. It was his truck!

He tried to grab it, but the wind pushed one more leaf on top. Ibrahim laughed. He picked up the leaf first, then the truck. He held it up high. "Mama, the wind helped me find it!" he said. The wind blew again and ruffled his hair, soft and cool.

Isabelle went to the big hall with Mama and Papa. It was a rainy day, so they hurried inside. There were lanterns and flowers everywhere. Today was a special celebration.

Isabelle saw a little clay pot with water in it. Grandma dipped a flower in the water. Then Grandma touched the flower to Isabelle's head. The water felt cool and soft. "Can I do that too?" Isabelle asked. "Yes, you can try," said Grandma. Isabelle dipped the flower in the water. The flower came out wet. She touched it to Mama's head. Mama smiled.

Then Grandma lit a little lamp with a match. Papa kept Isabelle back, safe. The lamp made the whole corner glow. Isabelle held Mama's hand and watched the light dance. "The lamp makes it bright," said Isabelle. Grandma hugged her close.

Theo went to the community center with his dad. There was a music room there. On the wall hung little drums, bells, and a big drum.

A teacher named Ms. Rosa said, "You can pick one." Theo picked a little drum. He wanted to make it go boom. He sat on the floor and looked at it. He patted the drum very softly. The drum made a tiny sound. Tap, tap.

Theo wanted a big sound. He looked at the drumsticks. He took one in each hand. He lifted his arms up high. Then he brought them down fast. Boom! The drum made a big sound. Theo sat very still. He tapped soft again. Tap. He hit hard again. Boom!

He tried it on the bells, too. A soft touch made a little ring. A big swing made a loud ding. Theo smiled at his dad. "I can make it loud," he said. He tapped his favorite drum one more time. Boom, boom, boom. Outside the window, a duck waddled by on the grass.

Leah sat on the big rug in the living room. She wanted to draw a cat. Her paper and crayons were all gone. But the tablet was on the table.

Mom picked up the tablet. She held it and pressed the little round button. The screen lit up with colors.

"Can I do it?" Leah asked.

"You can try," said Mom.

Leah pressed the round button too. The screen lit up again! Her finger made that happen.

She found the little paint pot picture. She tapped it with one finger. The drawing app opened. A big white page was there, waiting.

Leah drew a cat. She drew orange ears and a long tail. She drew tiny whiskers, one by one. The cat looked sleepy, so she drew a bed under it. She drew a yellow sun up high, because cats like warm spots that are not too hot.

"Mom, look at my cat!" said Leah.

"What a soft, sleepy cat," said Mom.

Leah was done now. She knew just what to do. She pressed the button again, and the screen went dark. She laid the tablet on the table, flat and safe.

"All put away," said Leah. She patted the tablet, just like she patted her cat.

Ali ran into the big kitchen. The tables were long and wide. Toast was waiting on a plate. Soft butter sat in a little bowl. Ali wanted to make his own toast today.
