He held the spoon. He patted the butter on the bread. He pushed too hard. The toast slid away! The cook, Ben, laughed. "Try soft hands," said Ben. Ali tapped the butter, soft like snow falling. The butter made a yellow coat on the toast. It looked so cute.

Next came the milk. Ali lifted the cup with two hands. He poured slow, slow, slow. Milk went up, up, up. Not one drop spilled! Ben gave him a thumbs up. Ali blew on the milk like it was hot cocoa, just for fun. Then he took a big bite of his toast. "More please!" said Ali.

Florence put her crayons in her little bag. She was going to the hospital to meet the baby. "I will draw the baby a picture," she said.

At the hospital, Mummy held a small bundle. A tiny face peeked out. "This is your baby brother," said Daddy. Florence drew a picture of a cat and a mouse. She held it up. The baby's eyes opened wide. He looked and looked. Then he waved his small hand. "He likes it!" said Florence. "The picture makes him look!"

Florence drew another picture. This time she drew a ball. She held it up. The baby waved again. "Again!" said Florence. Mummy laughed. "The baby is watching you," she said. Florence drew one more picture, slowly this time. It was the whole family, even the cat. The baby made a small sound, like a coo. Florence leaned close, very gently. "That is you," she whispered. "And that is me. I got that part wrong, but I fixed it." She pointed to her own smiling face, with its big round cheeks, drawn just right.

Eva went to the library with Mama. She saw a book about a little bear. The cover had shiny gold words. "Those words say bear," said a big girl next to her. Eva touched the words. Words talk to you, she thought. Like magic!

Eva opened the book. She turned the pages one by one. Front to back, front to back. The bear found honey on the very last page. "I love this book," said Eva. "I want to keep it forever and ever."

The library lady smiled. "You can take it home. But you must bring it back. Other kids want to read it too." Eva hugged the book tight. At home, she read it to her teddy. She read it to her socks. Then she read it one last time. "Come on, teddy," said Eva. "Time to take our book back to the library."

David put on his little apron. He was at school, in the cooking room. Today he would make bread for his family. Teacher Maya stood right beside him.

David mixed flour and milk in a big bowl. He made a soft ball of dough. Then he patted it flat. It looked small and sad. "Will this be enough for Mom and Dad?" he asked. Teacher Maya said, "We will give it time. Watch what happens."

They set the dough on the warm shelf by the oven. David read a book about a fox while they waited. The fox found berries that smelled sweet. David peeked at his dough. It had grown! It was big and puffy now. Teacher Maya put the pan in the oven, because ovens are hot.

Soon the bread came out, all golden. David carried it home in a box. Mom cut a slice. Dad took a bite and smiled. "This bread tastes sweet, like honey," said Dad. David patted his tummy and laughed.

Everly was at Grandma's house. A new baby sister was coming home today. Everly wanted to give the baby a present. But what could a baby use?

She looked in Grandma's kitchen. Grandma was going to cook soup. The pot was hot, so Grandma stirred it herself. Everly stood back and watched. The soup smelled warm and good.

Then Everly saw something. Grandma blew on a spoon of soup. The soup was too hot. When she blew, the soup got cool. The baby could not eat hot food. Everly knew what to make.

"Grandma, can I have a bowl?" she asked. "Yes, dear," said Grandma. Everly found a little blue bowl. She put it on the table. She blew into the bowl, whoosh, whoosh. It felt cool inside. "This bowl is for the baby," she said.

The door opened. Mama came in with the baby. Everly held up the bowl. "The baby can have cool food," she said. Mama smiled big. Grandma gave the baby a soft little spoon too.

Everly sat close and watched her sister. The baby yawned. Everly whispered, "I made that for you."

Mason wanted his red lion cup. It was up on the big shelf. He reached and reached. His fingers could not touch it.

Mason tugged the shelf. It began to shake. The cup wobbled. "Mason, stop," said Mom. She held his hand. "The shelf could tip over. Ask me for help instead."

"Help, please," said Mason. Mom smiled. She lifted the red lion cup down. "Here you go." "Thank you," said Mason. He hugged the cup to his chest.

"I am sorry I shook the shelf," he said. "That's okay," said Mom. "Asking for help is the polite way." Mason took a drink. The water was cold and good. Mom kissed the top of his head.

Mason held up the cup. "Roar," he said. Mom laughed and roared back.

Violet ran to the swing. It was her favorite swing, the red one. But when she got there, a boy was already on it. Violet felt like crying.

She took a big breath. "Can I have a turn, please?" she asked. The boy looked at her. "Okay," he said. "You can go next." He hopped off and held the rope. "Thank you," said Violet.

She swung up high. Her hat blew right off! "Help, Dad!" she called. Dad picked up the hat and put it back on her head. "Your hat is itchy," he said with a smile. He helped her zip her jacket up tight so the hat would stay.

Then Violet bumped into the boy by the slide. "Sorry," she said. The boy laughed. "It's okay! Want to slide together?" Down they went, one, two, whoosh!

Nova ran to the block corner at daycare. She wanted to build a big tower. Taller than her! She stacked one block, then two, then ten. Her tummy felt bouncy and light. She was so excited.

Then Ben grabbed the bottom block. The tower fell down with a crash. Nova's face got hot. She stomped her foot. "My tower!" she yelled. Ben's lip wobbled. He looked sad and backed away.

Nova felt bad now too. Then she heard a small sound. It came from the doll corner. Little Mia was hiding under the table. She was afraid of the loud crash. Nova crawled over. "It was just blocks," she said softly. "You can stay by me." Mia came out and held Nova's hand. Miss Amy smiled at them. "Nova, your tooth is showing," she laughed. Nova laughed too. Then all three friends built a new tower together. Mia put the top block on. It stayed tall. Nova clapped and clapped.

Leah wanted to play house at school. But the doll corner was full. The big plastic baby doll was already in Ben's arms.

Leah sat down to watch. Ben wrapped the doll in a scarf. Then he made a small crying sound. "Wah, wah," he said. "The baby is hungry."

Leah had an idea. She ran to the sand table. She filled a small bucket with pretend food. She carried it back, but the bucket was hard to hold. Rice bits fell out on the floor.

"Wait," said Ben. He put the baby in the toy cradle. Then he scooted over and held the bucket with her.

"You feed her first," said Leah. She held a wooden spoon to the doll. Ben patted the doll's back. The crying sound stopped.

"Now she is full," said Leah. "Now she can sleep." Ben tucked the scarf in tight. The baby closed her eyes, because Ben blinked them shut with his fingers.

"Tomorrow you can feed her first," said Ben. Leah smiled and picked up the empty bucket.

Weston ran into daycare. He wanted to find his toy truck. But the toy shelf was empty. "Where did the toys go?" he asked.

Miss Rosa smiled. "The toys are all mixed up. Can you help sort them?" She held up a little dog. "This is an animal. Animals go in this basket." Weston looked. He saw a cat and a bunny. He put them in the animal basket too.

Then he found a ball. Balls are toys. He put the ball with the blocks and his truck. The truck was there! He held it tight.

Next came snack time. Miss Rosa put crackers in one bowl. She put apple slices in another bowl. "Foods go here," she said. Weston ate a sticky apple slice. Then he picked up his truck again.

"Animals in this basket," he said. He put the bunny in. "Toys here too." The shelf looked neat now. Miss Rosa clapped. "Good sorting, Weston." He smiled and rolled his truck on the rug.

Aaron was staying at Grandma's house. Grandma had a library book. It was about big red trucks. It was Aaron's favorite book.

"Can I keep it forever?" Aaron asked.

Grandma shook her head. "The book has to go back. Other kids want to read it too."

Aaron held the book tight. He did not want to give it up. Then he turned the pages, one by one. The words on each page told the truck story. Grandma pointed to the first page. "We start here," she said. "Then we go to the back."

Aaron saw the words make the story. The front came first. The back came last.

Soon it was time to hurry. The book was due today. Aaron put it in his bag. He and Grandma walked to the library together.

Aaron gave the book to the library lady. "Other kids will read it now," she said.

"Can we get it again?" Aaron asked.

"Yes," said Grandma. "And we can take a new one home."

Aaron picked a book about trains. He hugged it all the way home.

Willow sat in the car with her teddy bear. They were going to the dentist. "First time," said Daddy. Willow held teddy tight. "What if it hurts?" she asked.

"Let's practice," said Daddy. "Open your mouth wide." Willow opened her mouth wide. "Now say ahh." Willow said, "Ahh." Daddy looked inside. "I see all your teeth," he said. "You opened wide, so I can see. That is smart." They practiced again. "Open wide. Say ahh." Willow did it one more time.

At the dentist, the chair was big and went up. Willow sat on it. The dentist said, "Open wide." Willow opened her mouth wide. She said, "Ahh." The dentist looked at all her teeth. Then Willow gave teddy a turn. "Open wide, teddy," she said. "Say ahh."

Joshua sat at the big table at camp. He had glue and paper and bits of yarn. He wanted to make a hat for his teddy bear. But the yarn would not stick. The pieces slid off the paper and fell to the floor.

Then Joshua put lots of glue on one bit of yarn. He pressed it down with his whole hand. He counted to ten in his head. He lifted his hand, and the yarn stayed put. "Look, Miss Amy!" he said. "It stayed!" Miss Amy smiled. "That is a good strong hat," she said.

Joshua added a red feather on top. The feather stuck too, because the glue was still wet. He put the hat on his teddy bear. Then he held the bear up high. "Now you can sing at camp!" Joshua said. The bear wore his hat all afternoon.

Sienna sat by the train window with her mama. They were going to Grandma's house for a family trip. Sienna held her teddy bear in her lap. In her other hand she held a chocolate from Grandma's gift box.

"Look out the window," said Mama. So Sienna looked. One cow. Two sheep. Three little houses. "One cow. Two sheep. Three houses," said Sienna. The train went clickety-clack, clickety-clack.

The sun came in through the window. It made a warm patch on Sienna's knee. The warm patch sat right on her chocolate. Sienna squeezed the chocolate. It was soft and squishy now. "Oh," said Sienna. "The sun made my chocolate melt." It went gooey between her fingers like warm honey.

Mama laughed softly and wiped Sienna's hand with a fresh, clean napkin. Then Mama reached into her bag. "Look what else I have," she said. It was a small cool box. Inside was a cold yogurt drink. Sienna touched it. It was not warm at all, because it had stayed in the shade of the bag.

Sienna looked at the window, then at her empty wrapper. The sun made things melt. The shade kept things cool. She put the wrapper under her teddy bear, safe and tucked in. Then she counted again out the window. "One cow. Two sheep. Three houses. Four trees!" Then she saw something new by the fence. "Mama, look! A little goat is waving at me!"

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Eleanor wanted to give her a present on the very first day. But what could she give? She looked around the backyard. She saw a tiny yellow flower. She picked it and put it in a cup of water. Then she put the cup on the table in the middle of the yard.

The sun came out. It shone on the cup all day. Eleanor skipped over to look. The flower had opened wide, like a little sun itself. "Grandma, come see!" she called.

Grandma looked at the flower. "It opened for the sun," Eleanor said. She turned the cup so the flower faced Grandma's chair. "Now it can look at you." Grandma smiled and sat down in the sun too.

Gabriella went to Mia's house. Mia had a big doll named Rosie. Rosie was crying, Mia said. "She needs a mama."

Gabriella picked Rosie up. She patted Rosie's back. Rosie kept crying. Then Gabriella wrapped Rosie in a soft blanket. The crying stopped. Mia clapped. "You made her sleepy!"

Then the dolls wanted to swim. Mia filled a small tub with cool water. The dolls dipped in. "Their skin gets wet and shiny," Gabriella said. She dried each doll with a tiny towel.

Next they played bakery. Gabriella spotted a spotted cat under the table. "A customer!" she said. She gave the cat a pretend cake. The cat licked its lips and purred.

Mia's mom brought real crackers. "Snack time for mamas too," she said. Gabriella rocked Rosie one more time, and Rosie's eyes closed tight.

Cooper sat at the little table. He wanted to paint a big sun. He got a brush and some yellow paint.

Then the bell rang. It was noisy. Cooper jumped, and his brush fell. It landed right in his cup of water.

Cooper pulled out the brush. He touched it to his paper. But the paint had washed off! The brush made only clear, wet marks. No sun. Cooper felt sad.

His teacher came over. "Let's fix that," she said softly. She gave him a fresh cup of paint. Cooper dipped his brush in. Now the yellow came back! He made a big round sun.

Then he dipped the brush in the glass of water. He touched it to the paper. A soft yellow puddle spread out. Cooper laughed. "It's a sun with rain!"

Eliana sat on the soft rug. The living room was full of people. Grandpa sat in his big chair. Aunt Meg sat on the couch with a bowl of popcorn.

The big game was on TV. Everyone was shouting at the screen. Eliana could not see the TV at all. Uncle Ben's back was in her way.

She wanted to see the game. She pulled her little stool over. The stool made a soft scraping sound. She stood on the stool, holding Grandpa's arm.

Now she could see the whole screen. The players ran fast. Everyone clapped when a goal was scored. Eliana clapped too, and the popcorn bowl wobbled.

Grandpa smiled at her. "Best seat in the house," he said.

Nolan was at Grandpa's house. His hair had grown very long. It fell over his eyes. "Time for your first haircut," said Grandpa. "Hooray!" said Nolan.

They walked to the salon down the street. Nolan sat in a big chair. Grandpa stood right next to him. The hairdresser picked up her scissors. Click, click, click went the scissors.

Snip! A little piece of hair fell down. It landed on the cape. Snip! Another piece fell. The scissors cut, and the hair dropped. Nolan watched each piece fall. "More hair is falling!" he said. "It works!" said the hairdresser. "Every snip makes a piece fall."

Soon the cape was covered with hair. It looked soft and curly. The hairdresser brushed it all away. Now the cape was clean again. Nolan looked in the mirror. He could see his whole face! "I can see my eyes!" he said. Grandpa laughed. "You look so big," he said.

On the way home, Nolan found a piece of hair on his shirt. He held it up. "Look, Grandpa! One more snip fell!" Grandpa smiled. "We will show Grandma," he said. They hurried home fast. Nolan could not wait.

Raphael sat by the big window at the community centre. Miss Ada put two bowls of crackers on the table. "Which bowl has more?" she asked.

Raphael counted the first bowl. "One, two, three, four, five." Then he counted from the other end. "One, two, three, four, five." The last number was the same! He counted the second bowl. Six crackers there.

"This bowl has more," said Raphael. "Six is more than five." Miss Ada smiled and gave him a cracker.

His friend Sam dropped his cup. Ice fell out and sat on the table. Soon the ice began to melt into a little puddle. Raphael shared his crackers with Sam. One of Sam's crackers was broken in half, but it still tasted just fine.

"Can you count my crackers too?" Sam asked.

"Yes," said Raphael. "One, two, three."

Emile was at Grandma's house. It was time for dinner. Everyone sat at the big table. Grandma held up one hand. "We say our blessing first," she said.

Emile wanted to eat his noodles right now. But then he saw Grandma's hand. It was open, like a little hat. Papa put his hand on top. Mama put her hand on top too. The hands made a tall tower. Grandma smiled at Emile. "Your turn," she said.

Emile put his small hand on the tower. His hand was warm on top. "Thank you for our food," everyone said together. Emile said it too, in his small voice. Then Grandma poured juice into his cup. The tower of hands fell down with a plop. "All gone," said Emile. "Like magic," said Papa. Emile giggled and picked up his spoon.

Kai sat at the art table. He wanted to paint a big frog. He had red, blue, and yellow paint. But a frog is green. He had no green paint.

"Where is the green?" Kai asked his teacher.

"Look in your cups and see," she said.

Kai dipped his brush in blue. He made a blue dot on his paper. Then he dipped his brush in yellow. He painted right on top of the blue dot. He rubbed the brush back and forth. The dot turned green!

Kai leaned close. "It changed!" he said. He sniffed the paint. It smelled like summer watermelons.

He made more dots. Red and yellow made orange. Red and blue made purple. The bad part was that his brush got mixed up. He washed it in the water cup. Then it was clean again.

Kai painted his frog all green. It had big eyes and a wide mouth. "Ribbit," said Kai.

His teacher smiled. "That is a fine green frog."

Kai zipped his brush back and forth one more time. The frog got greener and greener.

Gabriella sat at the art table. She wanted to paint a rabbit. She had white paper and clean brushes. But she did not know how to start.

She looked around the table. Ben had a stamp shaped like a circle. He pressed it down. It made a round dot. "That looks like a tail," Gabriella said. Ben gave her the circle stamp. She pressed it on her paper. Now her rabbit had a tail.

Next she found a square sponge. She dipped it in white paint. She stamped it down. The square made the rabbit's body. Then she found a triangle stamp. One triangle made an ear. She stamped another triangle too. Now there were two pointy ears.

A long rectangle made the rabbit's feet. A small circle made the eye. The teacher helped her add a tiny triangle for the nose. Gabriella stepped back and looked. Her rabbit had shapes all over it. "I made a rabbit from shapes," she said. Then she picked up a crayon and drew a big orange carrot beside it.

Asher went to the store with Mama. In the corner stood a little book shelf. "One book, two books, three books," said Asher. He counted them all.

He picked a soft book about a red truck. The cover had words on it. "T-R-U-C-K," said Asher. Mama read the words out loud. "It says truck!" Asher smiled big.

Asher sat on the floor. He opened the book at the front. He turned page one, page two, page three. Front to back. Front to back. "Not the back first," he said. "Front first!" That made Mama laugh.

The lady at the desk stamped the book. "Look," said Mama. "A day is on the stamp." Asher touched the stamp. The book had to go home with them for now. But it could not hide under his bed forever. It had to come back on the stamp day, so other kids could read it too.

Asher hugged the red truck book. "You visit me," he said. "Then you visit a friend." On the stamp day, Asher put the book in his bag. He carried it back all by himself. A small girl took it next. She opened it at the front. "Truck!" she said.

Asher sits in a big chair at the barbershop. The chair is too big, so Daddy lifts him up. Asher wants to look like Daddy. Daddy has short hair. Asher's hair is long and curly.

The barber picks up his scissors. Snip, snip, snip! Little curls drop down. They fall on the floor. They fall on Asher's hand. Asher picks one up. The curl is small and soft now.

The barber holds up a mirror. Asher looks. His hair is short, just like Daddy's! "I look like Daddy!" he says. Asher is so happy. He does not want to miss one look. He keeps looking in the mirror. The barber sweeps up the curls with a broom. Swish, swish, swish! Asher waves the little curl in his hand. "Bye bye, curls!" he says.

Beatrice wanted to play with the big red truck. Tom had the truck. He was pushing it across the rug.

"Can I have a turn?" Beatrice asked. Tom held the truck tight. "It's mine," he said. Beatrice sat down and waited. She counted the blocks near her feet.

Soon Tom rolled the truck to her. "Here," he said. "You can have a turn." Beatrice pushed the truck fast. She made a loud beep-beep sound like a robot. "That is a nice beep," said Tom.

Then it was Tom's turn again. Beatrice gave him the truck. They took turns, one after one. The teacher walked by and gave them a wave.

At tidy-up time, the teacher rang the little bell. All the children put the toys in the basket. Beatrice put the truck in first. Tom put the blocks in next. The room looked clean and nice.

"Same time tomorrow?" said Tom. "Yes," said Beatrice. "Truck friends."

Sienna ran to the table. "Snack time!" she shouted. Mama put apple slices on a plate.

"Wash your hands first," said Mama. Sienna looked at her hands. They had dirt on them. Real dirt from the garden.

Mama turned on the water. Not too hot. Just warm. Sienna put her hands under it. Then came the soap. Bubbles! So many bubbles!

"Now we count," said Mama. "One, two, three." Sienna counted too. "Four, five, six!" She rubbed her hands together. The bubbles got bigger. "Seven, eight, nine, ten!" They counted all the way to twenty.

Sienna looked at the bubbles. The dirt was gone! The bubbles had lifted the dirt away. Now her hands were clean and shiny.

"Look, Mama! The dirt went far away!"

Then Sienna showed her teddy bear. "Teddy needs soap too!" she said. She rubbed teddy's paws with bubbles. Teddy's paws got wet. Teddy got soapy all over!

"Teddy will dry on your bed," laughed Mama.

Sienna ate her apple slices. They tasted so good. Clean hands, sweet apples, and a soapy teddy waiting on the bed.

"Again tomorrow?" asked Sienna.

"Yes," said Mama. "Every single day."

Benjamin was excited. Today he could ride the big red slide. He held his papa's hand and walked fast. The sun was warm. The sand was soft under his shoes. Near the swings, a boy was crying. His ice cream had fallen in the sand. The boy felt sad. Benjamin watched him. He had a banana in his pocket. He gave it to the boy. The boy stopped crying and smiled. Now he felt happy. Then a big dog ran by, barking loud. The dog looked scary. Benjamin held papa's leg. He felt scared. But the dog only wanted to chase a ball. It ran to its owner and sat down. Benjamin laughed. Then it was his turn. He climbed the steps. He slid down, fast and smooth. "Again!" he shouted. "Again, again!"

Grandpa came to stay at Harrison's house. He brought a big bag and his big shoes. Grandpa put the shoes by the door.

In the morning, Harrison could not find Grandpa. "Where is he?" Harrison asked Mom. Then Harrison heard a sound. Tappity tap. Tappity tap. It came from the hall. Harrison put one foot out of his room. The sound got louder. Grandpa was walking in his big shoes!

"There you are," said Harrison. He laughed and clapped his hands. "Your shoes go tap tap tap!"

"That they do," said Grandpa. He held out his hand. It was warm and soft.

All week, Harrison listened for the tap tap tap. When he heard it, he ran to Grandpa. One day Grandpa wore quiet socks. No tap came. Harrison looked and looked. Then he saw Grandpa's big feet under the kitchen table.

"Found you!" said Harrison. Grandpa lifted him up for a hug.

Mia was ready for bed. But her horse was missing. She looked under the bed. No horse. Mia felt sad. She wanted to hug her horse.

Daddy helped her look. Mia looked in the toy box. Only blocks. She started to feel angry. She put her hands on her hips. "Horse, where are you?" she asked. Then she listened. She heard a small sound. It came from the laundry basket.

Mia peeked in. There was her horse. She felt so happy. She hugged him tight.

Outside the window, soft snow was falling. Mia felt excited. "Daddy, will the snow cover the grass?" she asked. "Yes, by morning," he said. Mia felt scared of the dark for one little minute. Daddy held her hand. She felt calm again.

Mia tucked the horse under the blanket. "Night night, horse," she said. Her eyes closed, and she fell asleep.

Avery went to the store with Mama. She saw a big red apple. Avery wanted the apple. Mama said, "One apple for you, one apple for Ben." Avery put the apples in the bag. One for her, one for Ben. Same size, same color. Fair.

At the bread table, there was one bright yellow bread roll left. A boy was there too. Avery reached out her hand. The boy reached too. They stopped and looked at each other. The baker said, "We have more in the back." He came back with a whole tray of rolls. Now there was one for Avery and one for the boy. The boy smiled. Avery smiled too.

Avery waited in the line with Mama. She held the bag with both hands. When it was their turn, the shopkeeper said, "Hello, Avery." Avery gave him the bag. He put the apples on the scale. Then he put them back in the bag.

At home, Avery gave Ben his apple. Ben took a big bite. Avery took a big bite too. Avery said, "We both got one." Ben said, "Thank you, Avery."

Sarah sat at the restaurant with her family. The big game was on the big screen. But a tall man sat right in front of her. Sarah could not see the screen at all. She stood up. Still she could not see. "Sorry, little one," said the tall man. He did not know he was blocking her.

A waiter saw Sarah's face. He went to the desk and got a tall stool. He set it down next to Papa. Sarah climbed up on the stool. Papa held her arm so she was safe. Now she was higher than the tall man. She could see the whole big screen!

The team scored a goal. Everyone clapped. Sarah clapped too. The waiter waved at her from across the room. "We should buy him a big cookie," Sarah said. Papa smiled. "Good idea."

Paint day at daycare! Everett ran to the art table. He wanted to paint a frog. A frog is green.

He looked for green paint. No green! There was red. There was blue. There was yellow. No green at all. Everett frowned at his paper.

Then he had an idea. He put his brush in the blue paint. He painted a big blue blob. Then he put his brush in the yellow paint. He painted right on top of the blue blob. The blob turned green! Green! Real frog green!

Everett painted a cute green frog with big eyes. Then he tried more. Red on yellow made orange! He painted an orange fish too.

Outside the window, white snow covered the ground. Everett held up his paper and shouted, "Look what my colors can do!" The teacher clapped, and everyone came to see the green frog.

Brielle sat in her reading nook with a big pile of letter cards. She wanted to find the letter B, the one that started her own name. She picked up a card. It was M. She put it aside. She picked up another. It was S, like the start of sock.

Then she saw it. The card with two bumps, one on top of the other. "B!" she said. She made the B sound too, buh, buh, Brielle. Then she looked down at her sock. The sock started with S. She said the S sound, sss, and then sock. The sounds fit together like puzzle pieces.

Her brother came in and knocked the pile over. Brielle got mad for a minute. Then she laughed and started to clean up the cards. She put B in her pocket. At bedtime, she tapped the card and said, "B is for Brielle."

Henry went to the hospital with Dad. Mom was in a bed. She had a new baby. The baby was a girl. She was very small.

"I want her to hold my hand," said Henry.

Dad lifted Henry up. Henry put one finger near the baby's hand. The baby did nothing. Henry waited. He put his finger closer. The baby's tiny hand opened. Then it closed. She held his finger tight!

"She is holding me!" said Henry.

"She likes you," said Mom.

Henry leaned in slow. He gave the baby a soft kiss on her head. She let go of his finger. Then she grabbed it again.

"Good girl," said Henry. "I will show you my sand box at home."

Kayden wanted to bake cookies with Grandma. Yesterday, the cookie jar was empty. Today, Grandma said, "We can bake now." Kayden jumped up and down.

First they had to mix the dough. Kayden poured in the sugar. He cracked one egg into the bowl. A little shell fell in, but Grandma fished it out. "You can try again later," she said. The second egg came out clean. Kayden smiled.

The dough had to sit in the fridge. "Now we wait," said Grandma. Waiting felt long. Kayden looked out the window. He saw a plane fly by. He waved at it. The plane was high and small, like a shy bird far away. "Is it cookie time now?" he asked. "Not yet," said Grandma. "Later, when the bell rings."

The bell rang at last. Grandma put the tray in the hot oven. Kayden stood back and watched. Soon the cookies were warm and golden. Grandma let one cool on a plate just for him. Kayden took a big bite. "We can bake more tomorrow," said Grandma. Kayden nodded, with crumbs on his chin.

Ryan was at summer camp. It was time for lunch. He ran to the picnic table and grabbed his sandwich.

A man at camp put a hand on his shoulder. "Wash first," the man said. He was kind and polite. Ryan went to the sink.

He got his hands wet. He made soap bubbles. The bubbles felt slippery and light. Ryan rubbed and rubbed. He sang the ABC song while he washed.

Then he rinsed. The bubbles went down the drain. His hands were clean and shiny now.

Ryan sat down and ate his sandwich. It tasted good.

After lunch, a little girl dropped her cup. Ryan picked it up for her. "Thank you," she said. She looked at his clean hands and smiled.

Ryan went back to the sink. He made more bubbles. He sang the whole song again.

Bennett ran to the park with his dad. He wanted to ride the big red fire truck toy. But when he got there, another child was on it.

Bennett watched. The child pedaled fast. Then the child pedaled slow. Then the truck stopped. The child got off and waved. "Your turn," the child said.

Bennett climbed on. He pushed the pedals, but the truck did not go. Dad showed him how. The big wheels went round and round. Now Bennett went fast down the little hill. Then he went slow up the big hill. He held the wheel straight and smiled.

Dad called, "Come get a snack." Bennett touched the truck seat. It was hot from sitting in the sun. He pulled his hand back. Dad held a cold juice box. "This will help," Dad said.

Bennett drank the cold juice. He looked at his hand. The juice made the hot feeling go away. "Again!" said Bennett, and he ran back to the little red truck.

Elizabeth was on the farm with Grandpa. She wanted to win the farm game called Five Senses. To win, she had to name each sense and the body part that goes with it.

Grandpa held up a red apple. Elizabeth closed her eyes. She could not see it. "My eyes see," she said. Then she sniffed the apple. "My nose smells apple pie!"

Grandpa touched her hand to a soft black sheep. "My hands feel soft wool," she said. Grandpa rang a big bell. "My ears hear it!" she laughed.

One sense was left. Grandpa gave her a sweet apple slice. Elizabeth took a bite. "My mouth tastes it! I win the game!"

Grandpa laughed. "And the sheep wants a taste too." The black sheep nibbled her empty plate.

Lucas sat at the kitchen table. Mama put a big pencil in front of him. It was yellow and long and smelled like new wood. "Today you write your name," said Mama. Lucas clapped his hands.

Lucas grabbed the pencil in his whole fist. He pressed down hard. The pencil slipped. The letter L came out wiggly and dark. "It runs away!" said Lucas. Mama showed him how to pinch the pencil near the tip, with two fingers and a thumb. Lucas pinched it too. One finger, two fingers, thumb. He pressed soft and slow this time. The line came out thin and neat. "Look, Mama, look!" he shouted.

Lucas wrote L, then U, then C, then A, one letter at a time. Four letters, all by himself. "That is the most beautiful word I ever made," said Lucas. He held the paper up high. "My name can live on the fridge now!" Mama laughed and got the tape.

Sadie sat at the camp table. Lunch was coming. It was peanut butter sandwiches and apple slices.

Sadie had used the toilet. Then she had run to the table without washing. A small crumb of dirt was still on her thumb. She saw it. It sat right there on her skin.

Sadie walked back to the wash stand. She pumped the soap. It was white and slippery. She rubbed her hands. The camp teacher sang a little song. Sadie sang too. The soap made bubbles between her fingers. When the song was done, Sadie rinsed. The bubbles went down the drain. She looked at her thumb. The dirt crumb was gone. Her hands were clean and shiny.

Sadie carried her plate to the table. She held her sandwich in her clean hands. The apple slice was sweet. Later, her friend Max washed his hands too. They sang the song together, loud and happy. Then Max said, "My hands are clean like yours."

Jackson sat at the kitchen table. Mom put a pencil in his hand. "Let's write your name," she said.

Jackson squeezed the pencil in his fist. He made a big line. It went off the paper. "I miss the J," he said. The line hit the table instead.

Mom turned the pencil around. "Pinch it like this," she said. Jackson pinched it with two fingers. Now his hand felt lighter.

He tried again. The pencil made a small curve. "A J!" said Jackson. He made a round O. He made more letters. J, A, C, K, S, O, N.

"I did it!" he said. Mom clapped her hands.

Then Dad came in the door. "Whose name is that?" he asked.

"Mine!" said Jackson. He held up the wet paper. One letter had a little smudge. Jackson laughed and pointed at it.

Sophie sat at the dinner table. She wanted a cookie for after dinner. "Can I have one now?" she asked. "Not now," said Mom. "You can have one later, after your peas."

Sophie ate one pea. She looked at the cookie jar. It sat on the high shelf. She could not reach it. "Is it later yet?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mom.

Sophie ate more peas, one by one. Dad told her about the day. "Yesterday we picked apples," he said. "Today we eat dinner. Tomorrow we can bake a pie." Sophie liked that. She looked at the flower in the middle of the table. It was open wide.

At last her bowl was empty. "Now it is later," said Mom. Mom reached up and took down the jar. The cookie was warm and soft. "Tomorrow," said Sophie, "can I help with the pie?" "Yes," said Dad. Sophie smiled and took another little bite.

Addison sat at Grandma's big table. Grandma put out three cookies. Addison grabbed two cookies fast. Then she saw her cousin Sam had none. Sam's bottom lip went down.

Addison looked at her two cookies. She pushed one across the table. Sam smiled and took it. Grandma clapped her hands. "One for Addison, one for Sam," said Grandma. "That is fair."

After cookies, they played a game. It had a big red button. Addison wanted to press it first. But Sam held the spinner. He spun, then he sent the spinner to Addison. She pressed the button and the horse jumped ahead. Then she sent the spinner back to Sam. Press, pass, press, pass. The game went round and round. Grandma poured cold milk into two blue cups. The cookies were tasty. Addison took a sip, then gave Sam his cup. "Your turn," she said.

Josephine went to Mia's house. Mia had a tablet. Josephine wanted to draw on it, but the screen was dark.

"What made it dark?" Josephine asked. "Maybe a finger can wake it up," said Mia's mom. Mia's mom pressed the round button with one finger. The screen lit up. The picture came back. Josephine tapped the button too. Tap, and the light went on.

"Now I can draw," said Josephine. Mia's mom showed her the little paint pot. Josephine touched it. A big white page opened. She drew a thin line. Then she drew a cat with long, thin whiskers. She drew a red sun. "My cat will win a prize," she said, and she laughed.

Then it was time for cookies. "All done," said Mia's mom. Josephine touched the top of the screen. The page went away. She put the tablet on the shelf. "It sleeps there," said Josephine. "Just like me in my bed." Mia's mom smiled and handed her a warm cookie.

Weston wanted to paint a green tree. But where was the green paint? He looked in his box. He found red. He found blue. He found yellow. No green. "Hmm," said Weston. "Where can green be?" He put some yellow on his paper. Then he put some blue on top. He stirred with his brush. Look! The paint turned green! Weston made a big green tree. He made a red apple on it. He made a yellow sun above it. Then he made a blue sky all around. A noisy crow landed on the fence. "Caw! Caw!" it said. The crow looked at the painting. Weston held it up high. "This tree is for you," he said. The crow tipped its head. Then it flew down and sat by the green tree in the real yard, right next to his paper one.

Arlo ran to the park with Dad. Yesterday the ice cream truck came. Arlo was too slow. It drove away before he got there.

"Maybe it will come back today," said Dad. "We can wait."

They sat on the bench. The sun was warm. There was no snow now, but Arlo remembered the snowy day last winter. That day there was no ice cream truck at all.

"Now we wait," said Dad. "Waiting is slow. But slow can be okay."

Arlo watched the ducks. He heard a bell. Ding, ding! It was not the truck. It was a boy on a bike.

Arlo waited some more. Then he heard music. "Dad! I hear it!" He grabbed Dad's hand.

The truck stopped right by the bench. Arlo picked a vanilla cone. He licked it slow.

"Can we come back tomorrow?" asked Arlo.

"Yes," said Dad. "Same bench. Same time."

Arlo smiled and took one more lick.

Matteo went to the church hall with his grandma. There was a long table with white cloth. People were bringing bread and soup and cups. Matteo wanted to help, but he did not know what to do.

Grandma said, "We say a blessing together before we eat." She told Matteo he could hold the bread basket. Matteo held it with both hands. He walked very slowly. His elbow bumped a chair, but the basket stayed steady. A lady smiled at him.

Then everyone stood up. They held hands in a big circle around the table. Grandma held one of Matteo's hands. A boy on the other side held his other hand. "One, two, three," said the pastor. Then all the people said the blessing together. Their voices went around the table like a big warm hum.

After the blessing, everyone sat down. The bread basket was passed from hand to hand. Matteo watched each person take a piece. When the basket came back to him, he took one small piece for himself. "You held the bread," said Grandma. "That was a lucky job."

Matteo ate his soup and his bread. At the end, he helped stack the cups. Grandma said, "Same time next week?" Matteo nodded and picked up his crayon from his pocket. He drew a big table with many hands on the paper tablecloth.

Maverick planted tiny seeds in the dirt. He patted them down with his hands. "Now grow, little seeds," he said. Every day he came to the community garden. He looked and looked. But nothing grew. Just flat, dry dirt.

The sun made the ground hot and hard. Miss Ana pointed at the dry dirt. She poured water from a big can. Maverick watched the water sink in. The next day, the dirt was dry again. "The plants need a drink too," said Miss Ana. So Maverick got his own little can. He poured. He poured. He poured.

Soon a green sprout peeked out. Then two sprouts. Then three! One slip of water each day made more leaves come. Maverick counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four." He watered again and smiled. "Grow, little seeds, grow."

Grayson walked on the nature trail with his dad. He wanted to solve a puzzle. The puzzle was about his five senses. He had to name them all.

First he saw a purple flower. "I see it with my eyes," he said. Then he heard a bird. "My ears heard that!" A pine needle felt prickly. "My hands tell me it is sharp." He sniffed the air. "My nose smells pine."

"One more," said Dad. Grayson thought hard. Dad gave him a small cracker from his pocket. Grayson ate it. "My tongue tastes it," he said. "That is five!"

They walked to the big oak tree. Grayson put his hand on the bark. He closed his eyes. "I can still feel it," he said. "Hands work in the dark too!"

Emilia ran to the park today. Yesterday it rained, so she could not come. Today the sun was out and the sky looked beautiful.

"I want to swing," she said. But the swing was wet. Daddy touched it with his hand. "Wet now," he said. "It will dry later." Emilia stood by the swing and waited. Would it dry? She touched it too. Still wet. She touched it again. Not so wet now! The warm sun was doing it. The sun made the swing dry.

"Now it's dry!" she said. Daddy helped her onto the swing. She went up and down, up and down. "Can we come back tomorrow?" she asked. "Yes," said Daddy. "Tomorrow we will come again."

A duck walked by the pond. "Where is the duck going?" Emilia asked. "Maybe to find lunch," said Daddy. The duck walked into the water. Emilia laughed and kicked her feet high. "See you tomorrow, duck!" she called.

Hannah sat by the window on the big train. Her teddy sat on her lap. "We are going on a trip," said Mama. "We will sleep somewhere new tonight."

The train began to move. Hannah watched out the window. The station slid away. Trees went by, fast and slow. Then Hannah saw a field. A pink pig stood in the grass. Hannah tapped the glass. The pig ran. Its little legs went pitter, patter. The running pig made the mud splash up. Hannah laughed.

Mama held out a rice cake. Hannah took a small bite. Outside, another field came. The same pink pig? No, a brown cow. The train went faster. The cow got small, then it was gone. Hannah waved. "Bye, cow."

The train went into a tunnel. The window turned dark. Hannah held her teddy tight. Then the light came back. The window was bright again. Hannah saw hills and sheep. She shut her eyes, then opened them wide. The sheep were still there.

"Look, Mama," said Hannah. She pointed at the window. "Sheep!" Mama smiled and looked too. The train puffed on and on, all the way to their trip.

Sofia went to the library with Mama. She wanted a book about trucks. But she could not find one.

Then Sofia saw a circle on the rug. She stood on the circle. She clapped her hands. The clapping made a loud sound. A boy looked up from his square book. He held up a green truck book. "Is this the one?" he asked.

"Yes!" said Sofia. "Thank you."

The boy had a loose tooth. It wiggled when he smiled. "Can you wiggle it again?" Sofia asked. He did. She laughed.

They sat at the rectangle table. It had triangle flags on it. They read the truck book together. The wheels on the trucks were circles too. Then the library lady sang a song. Sofia and the boy clapped along.

Lydia stood in the reading corner. A big red chair sat there. A shelf held books about bears and frogs.

The librarian said, "Here is your first library card." Lydia held it with both hands. She picked a book about a little red fox. "This one is mine," she said. "Mine forever and ever."

"You can take it home," said the librarian. "But you bring it back next week. Then other kids can read it too."

Lydia hugged the book tight. "But I love the fox," she said.

At home, Lydia read the fox book six times. Then Mama read it to her two more times. Lydia clapped when the fox found his den.

Next week, Mama took Lydia back to the library. Lydia gave the book to the librarian. She felt a small sad spot in her tummy.

Then a boy took the fox book off the shelf. He sat in the big red chair. He laughed at a funny page.

Lydia whispered, "He likes the fox too." She picked a new book about a frog. "This one is mine for now," she said.

The librarian smiled. "For now," she said. "And there is a song at story time next."

"Can we clap at story time?" asked Lydia.

"We always clap," said the librarian.

Eliana went to the store with Mama. Eliana held Mama's hand. "Stay close," said Mama. "One, two, my hand and you."

First they went to the bread corner. The oven there was big and hot. A man opened the door. Hot air puffed out. Eliana felt it on her face from far away. The man used a big pad to pull the bread out. "The pad helps him," said Eliana. "Yes," said Mama. "He is careful with hot things."

Next they stopped at the freezer. Eliana put one finger near the cold door. Brrr! It felt like ice. She pulled her finger back. "One finger, that is enough," she said.

Then Eliana saw a shiny knife on a low shelf. She reached out. Mama caught her hand right away. "We do not touch sharp things," said Mama. "We can look with our eyes." Eliana looked and looked. The knife was silver and long.

At the checkout, a kind woman gave Eliana a sticker. It had a doctor on it. The doctor was smiling. "The doctor helps people who get hurt," said Eliana. "Yes," said Mama.

At home, Eliana helped Mama clean the table. She wiped it with a cloth. One, two, three wipes. The table was clean. Then Eliana washed her hands. The water started cold. Mama turned the tap, and warm water came. Eliana held her hands under it.

"One finger in the freezer, two hands in the warm water," said Eliana. Mama smiled and clapped.

It was sharing day at school. Weston brought his toy box to show. But when he opened it, the box was all mixed up. Cars sat with bananas. A sock sat with his teddy bear. Weston wanted to sort it all out.

His friend Mia came to help. "Let's make piles," she said. They put the toy animals in one pile. The cow went in. The pig went in. The duck went in. Soon the pile was full.

Next they made a food pile. Apples went in. Crackers went in. Then Weston saw something odd. A toy dog was in the food pile. "That does not fit," said Mia. Weston moved the toy dog to the animal pile. It fit there just right.

Then Weston heard a sound. Tap, tap, tap. He stopped to listen. A real class turtle was walking across the floor. The teacher picked it up. "Where does the turtle go?" she asked. Weston laughed. "Not in the food pile!" He pointed at the animal pile. "Right there, with the duck."

Rowan wore his red team shirt. It was game day on the big court. His sister came to watch. She sat on the long bench with Mom.

Rowan bounced the ball. It came up small. He pushed it down soft. It came up small again.

"How do I make it go high?" Rowan asked.

"Push it down hard," his sister called.

Rowan pushed down hard. Up went the ball. It went high, high, high.

"Again," said Rowan. One hard push, one high bounce. Two hard pushes, two high bounces.

Coach blew the whistle. Rowan ran with the ball. He pushed it down hard all the way. Bounce, bounce, bounce. Then he stopped and shot. The ball went up and in.

The team cheered. Rowan bounced the ball one more time, just for fun.

Alexander dug a small hole in the dirt. He dropped in a seed and patted it down. "Grow, little seed," he said.

Every day he looked at the spot. Nothing came up. Alexander felt sad. His grandpa said, "Try giving it a drink." So Alexander filled his watering can. He tipped it over the dirt. Water ran down in little streams. A bird watched from the swing and clicked its tongue on the seed in its beak.

The next morning, something green stood in the dirt. It was small and new, like a tiny hand. "Grandpa, come see!" Alexander called. He poured more water on it, and the drops hung on the leaves. The little plant seemed to stand taller in the sun.

Penelope wants to make pancakes for her family. She stands on her step stool at the counter. Papa helps her pour the flour.

She stirs the milk and eggs. The batter is lumpy and smelly at first. "That's okay," says Papa. "Keep stirring."

Penelope stirs and stirs. The lumps go away. The batter turns smooth. One thing made another thing happen.

Papa puts the pan on the stove. Penelope stays back, because the stove is hot. Papa pours a small circle of batter. It bubbles all over.

"Look at that," says Penelope. The bubbles grow big. Papa flips the pancake. Now it is golden on top.

Her little brother, a boy named Sam, hangs on the gate and watches. "More," he says.

Papa stacks the pancakes on a blue plate. Penelope carries the plate to the table. Mama and Sam sit down.

Penelope passes out the forks. Everyone takes a big bite. "Yummy," says Sam, with syrup on his chin.

Penelope smiles. "I stirred it smooth," she says. Papa gives her a thumbs up.

Kinsley held her pink pig toy tight. Today was her first haircut at the mall. Mama said, "We can't be late for the salon."

The hairdresser put a big cape on Kinsley. "Snip, snip!" went the scissors. They were very loud. Kinsley hid her pig under the cape.

The scissors cut a little piece of hair. The hair fell down, down, down. It landed on the cape with a soft tap. Snip, snip. Another piece fell. Tap, tap.

"When the scissors cut, the hair falls down!" said Kinsley.

"That's right," said the hairdresser. She snipped some more. Soon the cape looked like it had snow on it. Grey snow, brown snow, little snow.

Kinsley lifted her pig up. "Pig, look at the snow!"

Then she shook the cape. All the hair bits fell off, down to the floor. The hairdresser swept them into a little pile.

Kinsley looked in the mirror. Her hair was short and neat. "Snip, snip, tap, tap," she said, and kissed her pig on the nose.

Iris wanted to find her white cat, Snow. Snow was hiding somewhere in the house.

Iris looked in the toy box. She found a ball, a drum, and her robot. "Not Snow," she said. The robot blinked its lights, but no cat.

Next she went to the kitchen. Mom was there, wiping the table. Iris found an apple, some bread, and a banana. "Not Snow here either," she said. Her tummy made a little growl. Mom smiled. "You can eat the banana. Then keep looking."

Iris peeled the banana. It felt smooth and smelled sweet. She took a bite. Then she heard a soft sound. Pur, pur, pur.

The sound came from the laundry basket. Iris peeked in. Snow was curled up on a warm towel, fast asleep. "Found you!" Iris whispered. She petted Snow's soft fur. Snow purred even louder. Mom came over and said, "Shh, let the kitty nap." Iris sat down next to the basket and ate her banana, very quietly.

Madeline went to the park with her dad. She wanted to find colors for her picture. "One, two, three, four," she said. She needed red, blue, yellow and green.

First she looked at the big tree. The leaves were green. "Green!" said Madeline. She pointed up high. She could not reach a leaf. Then the wind blew. One green leaf fell down. Madeline picked it up. The wind gave her the green leaf.

Next she saw the swing. The seat was blue. "Blue!" said Madeline. She sat on the swing. Dad pushed her up high. She held on tight. She jumped off and landed in the soft sand. Now she wanted red and yellow too.

She looked all around. She saw red roses by the bench. She picked up one red petal from the ground. "Red!" she said. Then she saw a yellow ball rolling near the slide. A boy threw it back to his friend. The yellow ball rolled to Madeline's feet. She touched it. "Yellow!" she said.

Madeline put her green leaf, red petal and a yellow flower Dad picked on the ground. Dad folded a paper hat for her. Madeline said the colors again. "Green, red, yellow, and... blue!" She ran back to the blue swing. "I found them all," she said. "Colors, colors, everywhere."

Hunter turned four today. The party was at the big hall. There were balloons on the wall. Grandma had made a cake. It sat on the table.

But the candles were not lit yet. Hunter wanted to blow them out. That was his special job. He waited and waited. He tapped his shoes on the floor.

Dad came over with a long match. "Watch now," Dad said. Dad was careful with the match. He lit each little candle. One by one, small flames popped up. They danced and glowed.

Hunter stood close. The flames were warm. He did not touch them. Dad said, "Only my hands, Hunter. Flames can hurt." Hunter nodded and kept his hands back.

"Now blow," said Grandma. Hunter took a big breath. He blew hard. The flames all went out. Little smoke curls went up. Hunter laughed. He had done that! His breath had made the flames go away.

Mom brought a soft feather from the party bag. She touched it to Hunter's nose. It tickled. Hunter sneezed a tiny sneeze. Everyone clapped and sang the birthday song. Then Dad cut the cake with a careful hand. Hunter got the first big slice. He looked at his empty candles and smiled. "Again next year," he said.

Eleanor sat at the table. She wanted spaghetti for dinner. But Mom said, "Not today."

"Yesterday we had spaghetti," Mom said. "Today we are having soup." Eleanor looked into her bowl. It was warm and orange. She puffed out her cheeks. She wanted to be brave and try it.

"Now we fold our napkins," said Mom. Eleanor folded her napkin into a small square. Then she folded it again. It got smaller and smaller. "I folded it four times!" she said.

Eleanor took one little sip of soup. It tasted like carrots. She took another sip. Then a big sip. "Soup is good," she said. Mom smiled.

"After dinner we will wash the bowl," Mom said. "And later, it will be bedtime." Eleanor looked out the window. The sky was turning pink. "And tomorrow?" she asked. "Tomorrow," said Mom, "you can help me pick dinner."

Eleanor clapped her hands. "Spaghetti tomorrow!" she said. She picked up her spoon and took another big sip. Then she folded her napkin one more time and put it under her bowl.

Alexis ran to the park with his red ball. He was so excited. "Watch me, Mama!" he said. He kicked the ball high, high up.

Then the ball rolled under a big bush. Alexis felt sad. His lip went down, down. A little girl by the swing saw him. Her face looked sad too. "I will help," she said. She pushed a stick into the bush. Out came a squeaky toy duck!

The duck went "Squeak, squeak!" Alexis jumped back. He was a little scared. Then he laughed. "The duck talks!" he said. The girl laughed too. Her face turned happy, like sunshine.

A boy ran by and grabbed the duck. "Mine!" he yelled. His face was red. He was angry. Alexis stamped his foot. But then the boy fell down, and the duck flew out of his hands. "Ouch," said the boy. He started to cry.

Alexis picked up the duck. He held it out. "You can share it," he said. The boy wiped his eyes. They sat on the cozy warm grass and counted ducks, one, two, three duck toys in a row. "Squeak!" said the duck, one more time.

Theodore ran to the art table. He wanted to make a house for his toy mouse. The teacher put out a bucket of paper shapes.

Theodore picked a big square. He glued it down. The square made the house walls. Then he found a triangle. The triangle sat on top. It made the roof. "It looks like a real house!" said Theodore.

But the door was missing. He looked in the bucket again. He found a small rectangle. The rectangle made a good door. Then he found a tiny circle. The circle made a window. Theodore spelled the word mouse and glued letters under the house too.

The teacher hung his picture on the wall. Theodore held up his toy mouse. "Look, mouse! Here is your new home." The mouse sat right by the picture, looking in the tiny window.

William sat on the clean grass in the backyard. Grandma had a basket of seeds. "Can I help plant them?" he asked. "Yes," said Grandma. She put a seed in his hand. William looked at it. It was little and brown. "My eyes see the seed," he said. He put the seed in his ear. No, that was wrong. Ears hear sounds, not seeds. A bird sang. "My ears hear the bird!" William listened a long time. Then he dug a small hole. The dirt felt soft on his fingers. "My hands feel the dirt." He put the seed in the hole. Grandma patted the soil. A flower smelled sweet nearby. William sniffed with his nose. "One more!" he said. He kissed Grandma's cheek. "My mouth gives kisses!"

Lennon went to the library with her dad. She saw a tablet on a small table. She wanted to draw a cloud on it. But the screen was dark and still.

Her dad showed her the little button on the side. "Press here," he said. Lennon pressed it. The screen lit up. She pressed the drawing app, and it opened. Now she could draw. She drew a big white cloud. Then she drew a noisy bird next to it.

A boy came to the table. He wanted a turn too. Lennon pressed the button again, and the screen went dark. She put the tablet back in its box. She slid the box to the boy. "Your turn," she said. He smiled and pressed the little button.

Norah wanted to paint a green frog. But the paint pots had no green. There was red, blue and yellow. No green at all. Norah felt like crying. "How will I make a green frog?" she asked.

Her teacher, Miss Kim, sat down next to her. "Let's try something," she said. She helped Norah scoop some yellow paint. Then she helped Norah add some blue. Norah stirred it with her brush. The paint turned green! "It's frog green!" said Norah. She laughed and painted a big fat frog.

The room smelled a little stinky, like paint and glue. Norah did not mind. She paid close attention to her frog. Then Miss Kim hung it up with a magnet on the big board. "Look up high," she said. The green frog looked down at everyone.

Myles sat at the big art table. He wanted to paint a park. He had blue paint and yellow paint. But the grass was green. How could he make green?

He looked at his paper. He painted a blue sky first. Then he drew a red swing under a tree. He added a brown trunk. He stuck a furry pom-pom on for a dog. But the grass under the swing was still plain white.

Myles had an idea. He dipped his brush in blue. Then he dipped it in yellow too. He swirled the brush on the paper. What was that? The paint turned green! Green like real grass. He stared at the brush.

He painted and painted. Green grass went all around the swing. He pressed the furry pom-pom dog onto the green. A drop of green paint fell onto the table. "Miss Kim, look!" said Myles. "Blue and yellow made my grass!"

The teacher smiled and hung his painting up high. "Green park," said Myles. "My best one."

Athena went to the store with Dad. Yesterday she had seen pink cupcakes there. She wanted one today. "The cupcake shelf is empty," said Dad. Athena frowned. Where did the cupcakes go?

The baker came out. "We sold them all yesterday," she said. "Bread needs to rest all night. So do cupcakes." Athena looked at the big bowl. The baker showed her the dough. It was puffy and soft. "Now it rests," said the baker. "Later it becomes cupcakes."

Athena wanted to see again. Dad said, "We can take the bus home now. We can come back tomorrow." Athena held Dad's hand. The bus was big and yellow. She looked out the window all the way home.

Tomorrow came after sleep. Athena put on her shoes. "Bus time!" she said. Dad laughed. They rode to the store. The shelf was full of pink cupcakes now. Athena picked the biggest one. She took a big bite. "The dough rested," she said. "And now it is a cupcake." Dad nodded and smiled. "Let's get one for Mom, too."

Rowan sat at the dinner table. He wanted his yellow cup. But his yellow cup was not there. Where could it be?

"I want my yellow cup," said Rowan. Mom said, "Look at your hands, Rowan." Rowan looked. His hands were dirty from the sandbox. "First we wash," said Mom. She carried him to the sink. The warm water ran. Rowan patted the soap bubbles. Bubbles went pop, pop, pop. Then his hands were clean and shiny.

Back at the table, there was his yellow cup. Dad had put it out while Rowan was washing. Rowan drank his milk. It tasted good. "Washing hands makes dinner come faster," Rowan wondered out loud. Maybe. He ate his rice. He wiggled his sock foot under the table. Soon his eyes felt sleepy. Dad said, "Bath time next, then pajamas." Rowan smiled and took one more sip.

Levi marched onto the running track with Coach Amy. He carried a red beanbag and a big blue ball. Coach Amy put a hoop on the grass. "Throw the beanbag in," she said.

Levi threw the beanbag soft and low. It hit the edge and fell out. He tried again, harder. The beanbag flew over the hoop and landed far away. Then Levi looked at the hoop. It was close. What if he threw it just a little bit hard? He threw it. The beanbag went up and came down. Plink! It landed in the hoop.

"Now the ball," said Coach Amy. She rolled it to him. He held out one hand. The ball bounced off and away. "Hmm," said Levi. He held out both hands. The ball rolled right in and sat there, warm and smooth, like a real hug. "I got it!" Levi said. Coach Amy clapped.

Jake sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. He held his teddy bear on his lap. The nurse came in with a small tray.

"Will the shot hurt?" Jake asked.

"Just a tiny pinch," said the nurse. "Then it is all done."

Jake's mom sat next to him. "You can squeeze teddy tight," she said. "Squeezing helps your hands stay busy."

"Okay," said Jake. "I will try that."

The nurse cleaned his arm with a soft white ball. It felt cold and wet. Then she got the little shot ready. Jake hugged teddy very tight.

"One, two, three, squeeze," said Mom.

"One, two, three, squeeze," said Jake. He squeezed teddy with all his fingers.

The nurse gave him the shot. It was one tiny pinch. Then it was over. Jake looked at his arm. "That was fast!" he said.

The nurse put a cute bandage on his arm. It had yellow ducks on it. Jake smiled at the ducks. Then he got a sticker, too.

At home, it was lunch time. Jake sat at the table with his fork. He used the fork to feed himself little bites of pasta. He fed teddy a pretend bite, too. "Teddy was brave," said Jake. "So was I."

Mom gave him a hug. "You did it," she said. "Next time will be easy, too."

Jake looked at his duck bandage. He patted it once, very softly.

It was Diwali at Felix's house. Felix wanted to put the little lamps on the window. But the lamps were not out yet. "Where are they?" he asked. Mama pointed to a big box on the table.

Felix helped open the box. Inside were clay lamps, all stacked up. "So many!" said Felix. Mama put a wick in one lamp. Then she lit it with a match. Papa was there too, holding the match, because matches were for grown-ups. The lamp glowed. One little flame made the whole room warm and bright.

"Now you," said Mama. She gave Felix a tray. Felix put the lamp on the tray, very slowly. He carried it to the window. Then Papa lit more lamps, one by one. Each new lamp made the window brighter. Soon the whole window glowed, like stars. Grandma clapped. "Look what Felix did!" Felix yawned. He was a sleepy boy now. "Happy Diwali, Felix," said Papa, and he lifted him up to see the lights one more time.

Iris went to Grandma's house. Grandma had a card in her hand. "This card says it is your turn," Grandma said. Off they went to the hair salon.

The salon had a big chair. Iris sat in it. Her feet did not touch the floor. She kicked her feet, up and down. The lady with the scissors came over.

"Will it hurt?" Iris asked. "No, it just tickles," said the lady. Snip, snip. A little piece of hair fell down. It landed on the cape. It looked like a tiny soft string.

Another snip. More hair fell. Iris watched it fall. The scissors made the hair come off! She turned her head to see. There was a small piece on her shoulder too.

Then the lady spun the chair around. Iris saw a mirror. A girl with short hair looked back. Who was that girl? It was Iris! She smiled a big happy smile. Grandma clapped her hands.

Ayla went to the park with her teddy bear. She put teddy on the bench. "You sit here," she said. Then a big wind blew. The wind made teddy fall off the bench. Teddy fell into the mud. "Oh no," said Ayla. "Teddy is all dirty."

Ayla picked up teddy. She brushed off the mud with her hand. The mud made a brown mark on her dress too. "Now we are both dirty," she said. She giggled. "Silly teddy."

Then Ayla had an idea. She took off her scarf. She wrapped teddy up, nice and snug. "This is your cozy blanket," she said. She held teddy like a baby. "I am your grandma now," she said in a big voice. "Time for a nap, little one." She patted teddy's back, very soft. Teddy closed his eyes, pretend.

Daddy came over with a juice box. "Is the baby sleeping?" he asked. "Shh," said Ayla. Daddy tiptoed, big feet, slow slow steps. "Oops," he whispered. "Grandmas need quiet." Ayla put teddy on her lap. She rocked him side to side. "Hush, little teddy," she sang. The wind blew again. But this time teddy did not fall. The scarf held him tight. "Good blanket," said Ayla. She gave teddy one more little pat.

Luca sat in the family car. He held his blue blanket. It was soft and warm. "The baby is coming home today," said Mama. Luca wanted to give the baby a gift. But the baby was very small. What could a baby use?

Luca looked around the car. He saw his teddy bear. Too big. He saw his drum. Too loud. Then he saw his blanket. It was soft like a kitten. Maybe the baby would like it.

Daddy stopped the car. The door opened. Mama carried in a tiny bundle. "One, two," Luca counted. "Mama, Daddy, and the new baby!" The baby made a small cry. Luca put the blanket near her. The baby grabbed it with one little hand. She stopped crying. "She likes soft things," whispered Luca. The baby held on tight.

It was game day morning at Charles's house. Grandma was sweeping the floor. Daddy set out one big bowl, two small bowls, and three cups. "One team, two teams," said Grandma. "Red and blue!"

Charles sat with Mom on the big couch. Uncle Ben sat in the soft chair. Everyone shouted when the red team ran. Charles shouted too. Then the baby next door began to cry. Her cry sounded scary and loud.

Charles clapped his hands once. The baby stopped. He clapped again. She smiled at him. "She likes your claps," said Mom. So Charles clapped one, two, three times. The baby clapped her small hands too.

When the game was over, the red team won. Everyone cheered, and the baby clapped hardest of all. Charles waved to her. "Good game," he said.

The lights went out. The living room went dark. "Oh no," said Leo.

Dad came in with a candle. He lit it on the table. The flame stood up tall. The dark went away around it. Leo clapped his hands.

Then Mom brought more candles. She lit each one from the first candle. One flame touched another. That candle lit up too! "More light," said Leo. "Big light!"

Mom smiled. "We are a team tonight," she said. Leo sat on the rug. The candle flames tickled the dark with little dancing lights. His shadow jumped on the wall. He waved his hand. The shadow waved back!

"Can I light one?" asked Leo. "Not yet," said Dad. "Flames are hot. You watch, and I light." Leo watched the wick catch. Another light! The room got brighter.

"I hope the lights come back soon," said Mom. "Or not," said Dad. "This is fun." They ate crackers on the rug. Leo told a story about a candle that flew. The flames danced along. "Bedtime soon," said Mom. "No," said Leo. "Stay up with the candles!" Mom laughed. "Just a little, since it is a dark night." Leo leaned on Dad and watched the flames dance.

Asher stood at the school gate. He held his mama's hand very tight. He wanted to go in, but his feet did not move. The gate was big and his tummy felt funny.

A girl stood by the gate too. She was crying. She had dropped her water bottle. It rolled under the gate and stopped. Asher looked at it. The ground was wet and slippery from the rain. The bottle just sat there, out of reach.

Asher let go of mama's hand. He found a stick by the fence. He pushed the stick through the gate. He tapped the bottle. Tap, tap. The bottle rolled back out. The girl stopped crying. She picked it up.

The girl smiled at Asher. "My name is Nia," she said. "I have a picture of a farm on my bag." Asher looked. There were cows on the bag. Mama waved from the gate. Asher took Nia's hand. "Let's go in together," he said. His feet moved all by themselves.

Charlie wanted to play with the big red truck. Her brother Sam had it. He held it tight with both hands.

"Can I have a turn?" Charlie asked. "When I am done," said Sam. Sam pushed the truck. Vroom, vroom. Then he stopped. "Okay. Your turn now." He handed her the truck. Charlie pushed it. Vroom! It rolled under the table.

"Now your turn," Charlie said. Sam got down on his knees. He reached for the truck. He pulled it out. "Thanks, Charlie," he said.

Mama called them for lunch. "Trucks stay on the floor," she said. "We leave them for later." Charlie put the truck down by the chair. She looked at Sam. "Why do we take turns?" she asked. Sam shrugged. "It just works good." They sat down together and ate their sandwiches. The truck waited by the table, ready for more turns.

Willow could not find Bunny. Bunny was her favorite toy. She looked under the table. No Bunny. She looked in her toy bag. The bag had blocks and a yucky old sock, but no Bunny. Willow sat down on the rug. She felt sad.

Then Willow heard a little sound. Scratch, scratch. It came from the big chair. She peeked behind the chair. Kitty was there, pawing at something soft. Kitty pushed Bunny out with her paw. Bunny slid right out onto the floor. "Bunny!" said Willow. She picked Bunny up and hugged her tight. Kitty purred and rubbed on Willow's arm. "Thank you, Kitty," said Willow. She held Bunny close and gave Kitty a soft pat.

Zoey sat at the little red table. The teacher held up a card with a big letter on it. It was the letter S.

"S makes a sss sound," said the teacher. "Like a snake."

Zoey wanted to know all the letters. But some letters looked the same to her. She mixed up S and Z. She frowned.

Her friend Sam slid his chair close. "Draw a snake," he said. "A snake looks like an S."

Zoey picked up her crayon. She drew a wiggly snake on her paper. Then she drew a big S next to it. They looked the same! She said, "Ssss." The snake sound came out.

Next came the letter Z. Zoey drew a little zigzag road. The road looked like a Z. "Zzzz," she said, like a bee.

At play time, Zoey looked at her beautiful sweater. She found a Z in the zipper. "Zzzz," she said, and pulled it up and down. Sam laughed. Then he made his hands swim like fish. "F," he said. "Fff, fff, fish."

Zoey clapped. "Letters are hiding everywhere!"

Sam nodded. "Look," he said, pointing at the door. "D for door."

Zoey ran to the window. "W!" she shouted. "Wuh, wuh, window!"

The teacher smiled and gave her a gold star sticker. Zoey stuck it on her sweater, right next to the zipper.

"Zzzz," she whispered, and gave the sticker a pat.

Gabriel was at Grandpa's house. He wanted his yellow ball. It was not in the toy box. It was not under the chair.

Grandpa drew a map on paper. "Here is the green grass," he said. "Here is the blue pond." Gabriel held the map with both hands. He walked past the green grass. He walked to the blue pond. Still no yellow ball.

Then Gabriel saw Grandpa's red blanket on the swing. Maybe the ball hid there. He pulled the red blanket down. He gave it a big wave. The yellow ball rolled out and bounced on the grass. "Found it!" said Gabriel.

Grandpa clapped his hands. "Good looking," he said. They sat by the pond. Gabriel tossed the yellow ball. Grandpa shared his salty pretzels. Gabriel ate one and drank his cold milk. The red blanket was warm in the sun. Gabriel patted it, soft like a cat.

"One more throw?" asked Grandpa.

"Yes!" said Gabriel. "Watch my ball go high."

Blake marched down the school hallway with her dad. Her backpack was huge on her small back. The floor smelled like soap and crayons.

Then Blake stopped. A boy was crying by the water fountain. His name tag said Sam. "Are you lost?" Blake asked him. Sam nodded. His lip wobbled.

Blake saw her teacher open a door. The door had a dog picture on it. When the door opened, kids went in. When it shut, they stayed inside. "That is our room," Blake said. "The dog shows us where to go." She took Sam's hand. They walked to the door together.

The teacher smiled. "Welcome, friends," she said. Sam wiped his eyes. He hung his bag next to Blake's bag.

"What is your dog's name?" Sam asked.

"Spot," said Blake. "Come on. Let's find the crayons."

Wren stood by the kitchen door. Her pink coat hung on the hook. Mom was making lunch at the counter. "Put on your coat," said Mom. "We will go out soon."

Wren pushed her arm in one sleeve. Then the other arm went in. The coat hung crooked, and the zipper end hung low. She pulled and pulled. The zipper would not start. The two sides were far apart.

Wren remembered the zipper trick. She sat down on the kitchen step. She pushed the zipper end into the slot. She held both sides close together. The zipper end made a little click. Then she pulled the zipper up, up, up. It worked! The coat was warm and snug.

"That is a pretty zipper," said Mom. "Ready for lunch in the park?" Wren nodded. She pushed the zipper down, then up again, all by herself. "Zip," she said. "Zip."

Victor sat at the little table in the school library. He wanted to write his name on his paper. The teacher gave him a big red pencil. He held it in his whole fist, like a spoon. He pressed hard. The letter V came out all wobbly and fat. The i lost its dot. The dots ran away down the page.

Victor felt sad. "My name looks squished," he said. The teacher sat next to him. She showed him her hand. "Try pinchy fingers," she said. "Pinchy fingers," said Victor. He pinched the pencil near the tip, like a little crab. His fingers felt funny at first.

Then he made a V again. It was straight and tall. He made the i, and the dot stayed right on top. One letter, then the next. "Pinchy fingers," he whispered. At the end, he had a surprise. His name fit on the paper, and it looked like the name on his cubby at school. Victor washed his hands and carried his paper to show the teacher. "Look! It's me!" he said.

Addison sat with Mom and Dad at a restaurant. A big screen showed a game. Everyone at the tables was watching it too.

Addison wanted to see the game up close. But the screen was far away. A tall man in front stood up. Now she could not see the ball at all. Addison stood on her tiptoes. Still no ball. Then Dad had an idea. He lifted her onto his lap. Now she was taller than the man. She could see the whole screen.

On the screen, a player kicked the ball. It went into the net. The net moved and the crowd jumped up. Addison clapped her hands. The people around her clapped too. Her cup was empty, so she took a smooth, cold sip of Dad's root beer. It helped fill her tummy with happy bubbles.

The waiter brought a warm plate of fries. Dad put some on her plate, because they were hot. Addison waved her little flag. On the screen, the players were smiling. "We won," she said softly. Mom kissed the top of her head.

Charles went to the art studio with his grandma. He wanted to make a picture for his mom. He picked red paint and yellow paint. He also picked a big fat brush.

Charles painted a red circle. Then he painted a yellow circle. He wanted to make a red flower and a yellow flower. But the two circles touched each other. The paint began to mix. The red and yellow made orange where they touched.

Charles looked at his picture. "Oh no," he said. "My flowers are orange." He showed his grandma. She smiled and waited. Charles looked some more.

Then Charles got a new paper. He painted a red circle. He left a big white space next to it. Then he painted a yellow circle in the white space. He let the red dry first. The red stayed red. The yellow stayed yellow.

Charles looked at both papers. "Grandma, look!" he said. "This one is all orange. This one has red and yellow." Grandma helped him put a shiny sticker star on top. Charles carried his picture home very carefully with two hands. "For Mom," he said.

Ibrahim sat at the art table. He had paper and crayons. He wanted to draw a house for his bear. But the bear had no house yet.

Ibrahim looked around the table. He saw a round lid. He traced around it. He made a circle! He held his paper up. "Look, a circle!" he yelled. His teacher smiled. "Nice circle," she said. "Now draw more shapes."

Ibrahim found a square block. He traced it. He made a square. He found a ruler. He traced it. He made a long rectangle. He picked up a brown crayon. He drew a triangle on top. "One circle, one square, one rectangle, one triangle," he said.

The circle became the sun. The square became the room. The rectangle became the door. The triangle became the roof. The house was done! But the door was too small for the bear. Ibrahim made a bigger rectangle. Now the bear fit right in. "Good night, bear," said Ibrahim. He laid the bear by the paper door.

John was at Grandma's house. He wanted to go outside. The frogs by the pond were singing. They made a loud song.

"Put on your coat," said Grandma. "But the zipper is hard," said John. Grandma smiled. "Try it yourself first."

John pushed his arms in. One arm went in the wrong hole. "Silly arm," said Grandma. John laughed and took his arm out. He found the right hole this time.

Now the zipper. John pinched the little tab. He pulled it up, up, up. But the coat had a bump inside. The zipper stopped. It would not go past the bump. John pulled and pulled. Then he smoothed the bump flat with his hand. He pulled the tab again. Zip! The zipper went all the way to the top!

"I did it!" said John. "Zipper up, frog song, let's go," said Grandma. They ran out to the pond. A fat frog sat on a rock. "Ribbit," it said, very loud. "He likes your coat," said Grandma. John patted his zipper. "Good zipper," said John. The frog jumped in with a splash.

Paint day was here at school. Charlotte sat at the open table. She had red paint, yellow paint, and blue paint. Teacher Mia said, "Name your colours first." Charlotte pointed. "Red. Yellow. Blue." Then she had a want. She wanted to paint a big orange sun. But there was no orange paint on the table. "Where is the orange?" she asked. Teacher Mia smiled. "Try mixing two colours."

Charlotte put her brush in the red. She put it in the yellow. She stirred them together on her paper. The paint turned orange! Her sun was big and round and bright.

A boy named Sam ran over to look. "How did you do that?" he asked. Charlotte held up her brush. "Red and yellow made orange," she said. Then she dipped into blue and yellow too. Green swirls grew on her paper. Outside, a dog barked once, soft and happy. Charlotte painted on and on.

Lena wants to draw a yellow sun. But the tablet is dark and still. She taps it. Nothing happens.

Her teacher, Mia, comes over. "Press the round button," says Mia. Lena presses the round button. The screen lights up. Lena smiles big.

She sees little pictures on the screen. One picture looks like crayons. Lena taps it. The crayon picture opens. Now she has colors to draw with. She picks yellow. She draws a big round sun. Then she draws a yellow flower too.

Mia reads a story to the other children. Lena wants to hear it too. She puts the tablet down on the shelf. The tablet goes to sleep, all dark again. Lena runs to sit with her friend Bo.

"Lena drew a sun!" says Bo. He saw her picture on the shelf. Lena nods and points at it. "It is yellow like my mom's phone case," she says.

Mia opens the book. Lena leans on Bo's arm. "Read the dog part," she whispers.

Jasper wanted his blue sock. It was lost somewhere. Yesterday he wore it. Today he could not find it.

Jasper looked under the bed. "No sock," he said. He looked in the toy box. "No sock." He looked behind the bear. "No sock."

"Keep looking," said Mom. "Now check the basket." Jasper looked in the basket. One sock, two socks, three socks. The third one was blue!

"I found it," said Jasper. He was sorry the sock had made him wait. "Tomorrow I can wear it," he said.

"Not tomorrow," said Mom. "Later today, after your nap." Jasper put the sock on his shelf. He patted it gently. "Wait here," he whispered. "I will come back soon."

Natalie sat in her playroom. She wanted to paint a frog. But frogs are green, and she had no green paint.

She looked at her paint cups. She had red paint. She had blue paint. She had yellow paint. No green anywhere.

"What makes green?" she wondered.

She dipped her brush in the yellow paint. She made a yellow dot on paper. Then she dipped the same brush in the blue paint. She painted right on the yellow dot.

The dot turned green!

Natalie leaned close. Her nose almost touched the paper. She saw the wet green spot. It grew bigger as she painted more.

She filled her brush again. More yellow. Then more blue. She made a big green frog with wide eyes.

"Mama, come see!" she called.

Mama came in and looked. "What a green frog," said Mama.

"I made green myself," said Natalie. She held up her wet painting. "Blue and yellow did it."

Lillian woke up from her nap. She wanted her bunny. Bunny was not in the bed. "Where are you, Bunny?" she said.

Lillian looked in one place. She looked under her little chair. No bunny. She looked in two places. She looked in her toy box. No bunny. She looked in three places. She looked behind the pillow. No bunny. Bunny was lost.

Then Lillian saw something. Her shirt was on the floor. The shirt was cold from the tile. Bunny liked soft, warm things. Bunny liked to sleep on soft things! Maybe Bunny was hiding under something soft. Lillian looked at her blanket. The blanket had a big lump in it.

She pulled the blanket back. There was Bunny! Bunny had made the blanket into a little hill. "Found you!" said Lillian. She hugged Bunny tight. Mommy came in and smiled. "Bunny was sleepy," said Lillian. She tucked Bunny back into bed. "Sleep now, Bunny." Bunny's soft ear flopped over, and Lillian patted it.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Sienna jumped up and down. "One week, two weeks, no, one week!" she said. Grandma brought a big red truck full of her clothes. Sienna helped unpack. One shirt, two socks, three dresses. Then Grandma pulled out a soft wool sweater.

"I will wear it tomorrow," said Grandma.

The next morning, Grandma put on the sweater. "Oh dear," she said. "It is itchy." She scratched her arm. She scratched and scratched.

"Take it off!" said Sienna.

Grandma hung it over a chair. Sienna slid the chair next to Grandma. Grandma put the sweater on the chair. "Now my soft scarf can go on too," said Grandma. The chair stood there like a little coat rack.

"That is my chair!" laughed Grandma. "It holds my things."

Sienna ran to get her teddy bear. She put him on the chair too. "Four things, Grandma. Four!"

Grandma clapped her hands. Then she said, "Sienna, come here. Look what was in my truck." She held up a tiny sweater. "I made it for your teddy."

Sienna hugged Grandma and spun around. "Try it on! Try it on!" she said.
